title: Seeing Less Is Not Seeing Safely: Privacy Leakage from Task-Scoped Robot Perception Exports
summary: Domestic robots rely on rich perception to operate in private homes, but privacy risk persists even when raw sensor data remain local. Structured representations exported to downstream planners, cloud services, logs, or learning pipelines can still reveal household information through semantics, geometry, spatial structure, and task targets. We introduce Task-Functional Perception Distillation (TFPD), a task-scoped representation-export framework that keeps rich perception local and profiles downstream exports according to task utility, direct exposure, and multiple residual inference risks. Using 120 AI2-THOR scenes with scene-disjoint train/validation/test splits, frozen attacker selection, and representation-aware held-out attacks, we evaluate navigation, collision checking, and object-goal execution. Three navigation exports achieve identical success (1.000) and mean path ratio (0.898), yet representation-level linkability ranges from 0.532 to 0.970. Replacing an explicit target label with a target region reduces target-category macro-F1 from 1.000 to 0.077 while preserving success at 0.995, while geometric coarsening reduces object-category macro-F1 from 0.704 to 0.556 at a measurable collision-utility cost. A ProcTHOR replication preserves the navigation task-equivalence/privacy-inequivalence finding while changing the relative ordering of normalized and topological exports. These results show that neither field removal nor stronger abstraction induces a universal privacy ordering and motivate task-specific, multi-risk evaluation of the complete public representation.

AI.tldr: TFPD is a task-scoped representation-export framework that keeps perception local and evaluates privacy risks of downstream exports; results show identical task success with varying privacy leakage and no universal privacy ordering, advocating task-specific multi-risk evaluation.
AI.motivation: Privacy leakage can occur even when raw sensor data is local, as downstream exports (semantics, geometry, structure, targets) may reveal household information. There is no established universal privacy ordering for exported representations; a task-focused evaluation is needed.
AI.method: Propose Task-Functional Perception Distillation (TFPD). Evaluate with 120 AI2-THOR scenes (scene-disjoint train/validation/test), frozen attacker selection, and representation-aware held-out attacks across navigation, collision checking, and object-goal execution. Analyze exports varying target specification (label vs region) and geometric coarsening. Include ProcTHOR replication to confirm findings. Use metrics such as task success, mean path ratio, and privacy leakage measures like linkability and macro-F1.
AI.result: Three navigation exports achieve identical task success (1.000) and mean path ratio (0.898), yet representation-level linkability ranges from 0.532 to 0.970. Replacing an explicit target label with a target region reduces target-category macro-F1 from 1.000 to 0.077 while preserving success at 0.995; geometric coarsening reduces object-category macro-F1 from 0.704 to 0.556 at a measurable collision-utility cost. ProcTHOR replication preserves the navigation task-equivalence/privacy-inequivalence finding while altering the relative ordering of normalized and topological exports.
AI.conclusion: Field removal or stronger abstraction does not yield a universal privacy ordering. Task-specific, multi-risk evaluation of the complete public representation is needed to assess privacy in domestic robotic perception exports.

title: GPU-Accelerated Astrodynamics World Models for Spacecraft Rendezvous and Proximity Operations
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, 5 tables, Presented at Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies Conference 2026
summary: World models are an emerging paradigm in representation learning in which an agent jointly learns state-action dynamics and observation models from offline trajectory data, enabling multi-step planning and trajectory prediction with uncertainty estimates. They have shown strong results in robotics and game environments, but, to the best of our knowledge, have not previously been applied to the space domain. This paper introduces a world model-based approach to cooperative and non-cooperative spacecraft rendezvous and proximity operations. First, we introduce an open-source, JAX-based International Space Station (ISS) docking environment supporting parallel GPU simulation of spacecraft orbit and attitude dynamics, generating the thousands of state-action transitions that world model training requires. Second, we introduce Out-of-this-World-Model, a transformer-based world model that encodes relative kinematic states and body-fixed camera imagery into a latent state and predicts its evolution under commanded thrusts and torques using one-step flow matching. It produces a distribution over future observations, capturing stochastic dynamics and per-timestep uncertainty, and outperforms DreamerV3-style posterior-correction baselines with fewer trainable parameters and hyperparameters. Third, we apply the approach to a capsule autonomously docking with the ISS under keep-out-zone constraints, demonstrating improved sample efficiency and task performance over reinforcement learning baselines (53% versus 29% docking success across ports), better out-of-distribution generalization (on held-out ports the world model more than doubles baseline success, 40% versus 17%), and detection of anomalous objects encountered during approach with 98% classification accuracy. We open-source the simulation environment and model architecture to enable further study of this paradigm.

AI.tldr: Transformer-based world model for spacecraft docking; introduces an open-source ISS docking environment and Out-of-this-World-Model that encodes relative kinematics and imagery to predict latent state evolution with uncertainty; outperforms DreamerV3 baselines, improves docking success and generalization, and enables anomaly detection; codebase open-sourced.
AI.motivation: To enable sample-efficient, uncertainty-aware planning for space rendezvous and proximity operations by applying world-model learning in the space domain, addressing cooperative/non-cooperative docking under safety constraints (keep-out zones).
AI.method: Develop an open-source JAX-based ISS docking environment that can simulate thousands of state-action transitions; propose Out-of-this-World-Model, a transformer-based world model that encodes relative kinematics and body-fixed camera imagery into a latent state, predicting evolution under thrusts/torques using one-step flow matching; produces a distribution over future observations to capture stochastic dynamics and per-timestep uncertainty; compare against DreamerV3-style posterior-correction baselines; apply to autonomous capsule docking with ISS keeping out zones and evaluate sample efficiency, generalization, and anomaly detection; open-source the environment and architecture.
AI.result: The approach achieves 53% docking success across ports vs 29% for RL baselines; better out-of-distribution generalization (40% held-out ports vs 17%); anomaly detection accuracy at 98%; demonstrates improved sample efficiency and performance with fewer trainable parameters and hyperparameters.
AI.conclusion: World-model-based planning in space docking is effective, improving efficiency, safety-aware planning, and generalization. The open-source environment and model design provide a foundation for further research in space-domain world models and anomaly detection.

title: Sensing Which Modality Matters: Evidence-Gated Regularization for Robust VLA Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies fuse multimodal sensory inputs, but training on limited and homogeneous robot demonstrations encourages spurious inter-sensor correlations rather than task-relevant signal, a failure we term modality entanglement. Under real-world occlusions and distractors, this manifests as nuisance sensitivity to corruption of uninformative sensors and single-modality insufficiency when only one informative sensor remains intact. We propose Evidence-Gated Regularization (EGR), a modality-agnostic training objective that introduces zero inference-time overhead. EGR derives a per-frame and per-sensor task-relevance signal to gate two state-conditional consistency objectives: invariance on low-evidence sensors, and single-sensor sufficiency on high-evidence ones. We introduce a benchmark based on BEHAVIOR-1K, comprising a fast inference-only diagnostic suite and 47 rollout-based skills targeting modality entanglement. We validate EGR on this benchmark and on two real-robot setups with fundamentally different embodiments: a bi-manual setup with two Kinova arms and three RGB cameras, and a single-arm MELFA ASSISTA setup combining vision and GelSight tactile sensors. EGR improves simulation success rates (SR) from 12.5% to 16.4% under full modalities (+31%), from 9.4% to 16.5% under uninformative-sensor corruption (+75%), and from 2.8% to 6.1% under single-sensor fallback (+120%). Under physical-object distractors, EGR boosts SR from 30% to 85% on the bi-manual setup (+183%) and from 55% to 70% on the tactile setup (+27%).

AI.tldr: Evidence-Gated Regularization (EGR) mitigates modality entanglement in Vision-Language-Action policies by gating frame- and sensor-level task relevance to enforce invariance on low-evidence sensors and sufficiency on high-evidence ones, without extra inference cost. A BEHAVIOR-1K-based benchmark evaluates robustness to occlusions/distractors, with substantial gains across simulation and real robots.
AI.motivation: Training VLA policies on limited, homogeneous demonstrations often creates spurious inter-sensor correlations (modality entanglement). Real-world occlusions and distractors exacerbate nuisance sensitivity and single-modality failure. There is a need for modality-agnostic, low-overhead regularization that preserves informative signals under partial observability.
AI.method: Introduce Evidence-Gated Regularization (EGR): per-frame and per-sensor task-relevance signals gate two state-conditional consistency objectives. 1) Invariance on low-evidence sensors to reduce nuisance sensitivity. 2) Single-sensor sufficiency on high-evidence sensors to ensure robustness when only one informative sensor remains. Zero inference-time overhead. Build BEHAVIOR-1K suite with fast diagnostic tests and 47 rollout-based skills to quantify modality entanglement. Validate on two real-robot setups (bi-manual Kinova arms with three RGB cameras; single-arm MELFA with vision and GelSight tactile sensors).
AI.result: EGR yields notable SR improvements: full modalities 12.5%→16.4% (+31%), uninformative-sensor corruption 9.4%→16.5% (+75%), single-sensor fallback 2.8%→6.1% (+120%). Under physical-object distractors, SR 30%→85% (+183%) on bi-manual, and 55%→70% (+27%) on tactile setup.
AI.conclusion: EGR effectively reduces modality entanglement across simulation and two distinct real-robot embodiments, delivering substantial gains in robustness to sensor corruption and partial observability without added inference cost. The BEHAVIOR-1K benchmark provides a targeted evaluation of multimodal robustness.

title: Real-Time Shape Control of Multi-Segment Soft Robotic Arms Using Koopman Operators with Global and Local Observables
summary: Multi-segment soft robotic arms can continuously reconfigure their body shapes for safe interaction, but tip control alone is insufficient for constrained-space tasks. Therefore, shape control is a more important task for multi-segment soft arms than tip control, but remains challenging due to the high dimensionality and nonlinear dynamics of continuum deformation. In existing work, shape control accuracy is defined by the error in the global frame (global shape error). For multi-segment soft arms, using only global shape error as the control objective is insufficient, as segment coupling, gravity-induced loading, and inertial effects become more significant. This difficulty increases with the number of segments. In this paper, we present a Koopman-based model predictive control framework that combines global and local observables, enabling real-time shape control on multi-segment soft robotic arms. The framework is evaluated through numerical and physical experiments. Numerical experiments demonstrate the scalability of the proposed controller by achieving shape control on robots with up to 10 independently actuated segments. The physical experiments demonstrate that the controller is capable of (1) real-time shape control of 3- and 5-segment robotic arms with tip speeds up to 0.6 m/s, (2) robust tracking without retraining, including distal payloads up to 400~g and recovery from a 7~N lateral disturbance, and (3) the potential for future inspection applications through a confined-space demonstration. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework enables dynamic, scalable, and accurate real-time shape control on multi-segment soft robotic arms.

AI.tldr: A Koopman-based MPC framework that fuses global and local observables to enable real-time, scalable shape control for multi-segment soft robotic arms, validated numerically (up to 10 segments) and physically (3–5 segments).
AI.motivation: Global shape error is insufficient for multi-segment soft arms due to strong segment coupling, gravity, and inertial effects, which grow with the number of segments; thus there is a need for real-time, high-dimensional shape control.
AI.method: Koopman-based model predictive control that integrates global and local observables to capture continuum deformation, enabling real-time shape control on multi-segment soft arms and scalable to multiple segments (demonstrated up to 10 in simulations).
AI.result: Numerical experiments show scalability to 10 independently actuated segments. Physical experiments achieve real-time shape control for 3- and 5-segment arms with tip speeds up to 0.6 m/s; robust tracking without retraining, including distal payloads up to 400 g and recovery from a 7 N lateral disturbance; demonstrates potential for confined-space inspection.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides dynamic, scalable, and accurate real-time shape control for multi-segment soft robotic arms by leveraging both global and local observables via a Koopman-based MPC, with demonstrated performance in simulation and physical experiments and clear applicability to constrained-space tasks.

title: AnyGS2Mesh: Feed-Forward Mesh Reconstruction from 3D Gaussian Splatting with Arbitrary-Resolution Views
summary: Existing 3D mesh reconstruction methods from Gaussian scene representations predominantly rely on iterative optimization, resulting in slow inference and limited scalability to high-resolution inputs. In this paper, we present AnyGS2Mesh, the first feed-forward framework for directly reconstructing 3D meshes from 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with support for arbitrary input image resolutions. Our approach incorporates a Gaussian-Guided Transformer architecture that exploits explicit 3D geometric priors for efficient mesh generation. We introduce three key components: (1) a Gaussian-Guided Spatial Reasoning Transformer represents Gaussian primitives as structured 3D tokens and jointly reasons over Gaussian and image features; (2) a Streaming and Patchwise Geometry Encoder processes native-resolution views sequentially and aggregates information across variable-length view sets; (3) a Scale-Aligned Hybrid Depth Refiner uses a PatchFusion-style encoder--decoder to fuse RGB-conditioned predicted depth with Gaussian-rendered metric depth, combining fine local structures with globally consistent metric scale. The refined depth maps are integrated through TSDF fusion, followed by Marching Cubes for deterministic mesh extraction. Extensive experiments show that AnyGS2Mesh achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality while significantly reducing inference time compared with optimization-based baselines, enabling near-real-time, high-quality mesh reconstruction. Our results demonstrate the potential of combining Gaussian representations and feed-forward Transformer architectures for scalable 3D geometry reconstruction. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: AnyGS2Mesh is a feed-forward method that reconstructs 3D meshes directly from Gaussian Splatting representations, handling arbitrary input resolutions with a Gaussian-guided Transformer, streaming geometry encoding, and a depth refiner, fused via TSDF and Marching Cubes for fast, high-quality meshes.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D mesh reconstruction from Gaussian scene representations relies on slow iterative optimization, limiting scalability and real-time applicability. A fast, feed-forward approach with explicit 3D priors and multi-view handling is desirable.
AI.method: Introduces three components: (1) Gaussian-Guided Spatial Reasoning Transformer that represents Gaussian primitives as 3D tokens and jointly reasons over Gaussian and image features; (2) Streaming and Patchwise Geometry Encoder that processes native-resolution views sequentially and aggregates information across variable-length view sets; (3) Scale-Aligned Hybrid Depth Refiner with a PatchFusion-style encoder–decoder to fuse RGB-conditioned predicted depth with Gaussian-rendered metric depth. Depth maps are integrated via TSDF fusion and marching cubes for deterministic mesh extraction.
AI.result: Claims state-of-the-art reconstruction quality with significantly reduced inference time compared with optimization-based baselines, achieving near-real-time, high-quality mesh reconstruction. Demonstrates effectiveness of combining Gaussian representations with feed-forward Transformers for scalable 3D geometry reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Shows the feasibility and potential of a fully feed-forward pipeline that leverages Gaussian priors and Transformer architectures for scalable, high-quality 3D mesh reconstruction; code to be released upon acceptance.

title: IDSPACE: A Novel Document Generator for Reliable Evaluation of Digital Identity Verification Systems [Extended Technical Report]
summary: As services move online, trust institutions such as banks, lenders, and governments must verify the identity of remote users. Fraud detection tools are widely available, but evaluating and fine-tuning them remains difficult because identity documents are sensitive and therefore scarce. Synthetic data generation offers a path forward, and demand is clear: our prior work in this area has been downloaded over $11{,}000$ times (aggregated from eight parts). We introduce IDSpace, extending this line of research in three directions. First, we propose model-guided Bayesian optimization, which tunes generation parameters to maximize both visual similarity and prediction consistency with target-domain models given only a few samples from a target domain. Second, we decouple user-specified metadata (demographics, fraud patterns, capture device) from automatically tuned control parameters (font styles, noise levels, image quality), allowing users to configure evaluations without low-level expertise. Third, we expand beyond template images to support scanned and mobile-captured documents. Experiments show IDSpace improves evaluation consistency by $15-45\%$ over baselines including CycleGAN, diffusion inpainting, and non-guided optimization, using only a few real samples, while improving training accuracy by up to $9\%$ and SSIM similarity with the target domain by $10\%$. We also released a new dataset consisting of $359{,}240$ high-quality synthetic documents across ten European ID types.

AI.tldr: IDSpace uses model-guided Bayesian optimization to tune synthetic identity documents, decouples metadata from controls, supports scanned/mobile captures, and achieves better evaluation consistency and training accuracy with a large synthetic dataset release.
AI.motivation: Remote identity verification relies on synthetic data to evaluate and tune fraud-detection models, but sensitivity of identity documents limits available data. Building on prior work, IDSpace aims to improve generation quality, control, and applicability to different capture modalities while requiring only a few real samples.
AI.method: Introduce model-guided Bayesian optimization to optimize generation parameters for both visual similarity and alignment with target-domain models using few target-domain samples. Decouple user-specified metadata from automatically tuned control parameters. Extend generation to include scanned and mobile-captured documents, not just templates.
AI.result: IDSpace achieves 15-45% gains in evaluation consistency over baselines (CycleGAN, diffusion inpainting, non-guided optimization); training accuracy improves by up to 9%; SSIM to target domain improves by 10%. Release of a large synthetic-document dataset: 359,240 documents across ten European ID types.
AI.conclusion: IDSpace advances synthetic document generation for identity verification by aligning evaluation with target models, improving training performance, and offering flexible metadata control and broader capture modality support. The shared dataset provides a valuable resource for the research and security communities.

title: Structure and Implementation of New Practical English Textbooks Driven by Artificial Intelligence
summary: Artificial intelligence is changing the form of applied English materials from fixed paper sequences to adaptive learning systems that can diagnose learners, recommend tasks, and provide formative feedback. This paper studies the structure and application of a new practical English textbook driven by artificial intelligence. A five-layer architecture is proposed: knowledge mapping, learner profiling, task generation, feedback orchestration, and teacher-side governance. A prototype was tested on 186 non-English-major undergraduates for eight weeks of teaching. Compared with a static digital textbook, the proposed system increased the unit completion accuracy from 72.4% to 84.9%, raised the average score for speaking tasks by 10.8 points, and reduced the teacher's correction time by 31.6%. Therefore, an AI-driven textbook can maintain the stability of the curriculum while providing personalised learning paths, rich practice materials and traceable classroom data.

AI.tldr: AI-driven adaptive English textbook with a five-layer architecture outperforms static digital textbooks on learning outcomes and teacher workload.
AI.motivation: To investigate the design, application, and impact of an AI-driven practical English textbook that supports adaptive diagnosis, task recommendation, and formative feedback, and to assess its effects on learning outcomes and teacher effort.
AI.method: Design and prototype of a five-layer AI-driven textbook architecture (knowledge mapping, learner profiling, task generation, feedback orchestration, teacher-side governance). A prototype was tested with 186 non-English-major undergraduates over eight weeks, using a controlled comparison against a static digital textbook.
AI.result: Unit completion accuracy rose from 72.4% to 84.9%. Average speaking-task score increased by 10.8 points. Teacher correction time decreased by 31.6%.
AI.conclusion: An AI-driven textbook can preserve curriculum stability while offering personalized learning paths, richer practice materials, and traceable classroom data.

title: The Geometry of Ignorance: LLMs Know When to Temper Bayesian Priors
summary: What does a language model predict when it has few clues? The answer lurks in its unembedding geometry: a single direction of the unembedding matrix encodes the unigram distribution of the training corpus, which serves as the Bayesian prior the model falls back on when uncertain. This structure --- which we term the \emph{direction of ignorance} --- appears in all four model families examined (\texttt{Llama}, \texttt{Qwen}, \texttt{Gemma}, and \texttt{Pythia}), ranging from 0.4B to 405B parameters. Projecting the final prediction state onto this direction yields a per-token \emph{prior loading factor} $λ$, which, empirically, declines steadily as the context becomes more informative. Formally, the same projection decomposes the prediction state into two orthogonal vectors that correspond exactly to the two factors of a tempered Bayesian update: a unigram prior raised to the exponent $λ$ and a context-driven likelihood. This geometric-probabilistic interpretation calibrates $λ$, making it meaningfully comparable across model sizes and families, with larger models generally exhibiting lower prior reliance in the high-context limit. Finally, we show that the direction of ignorance is causally active: raising or lowering $λ$ at the final prediction state steers the prediction toward or away from the unigram prior in KL divergence.

AI.tldr: A single unembedding direction, the direction of ignorance, encodes the unigram prior of the training corpus. Projection of the final prediction state onto this direction yields a prior loading factor λ, revealing a tempered Bayesian update where the unigram prior is raised to the power λ and combined with a context-driven likelihood. This direction is found across four model families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Pythia) and sizes (0.4B–405B). Larger models exhibit lower prior reliance in high-context situations. The direction is causally active: adjusting λ steers predictions toward or away from the unigram prior in KL divergence.
AI.motivation: To uncover a geometric, model-agnostic account of how language models balance priors (training corpus unigram statistics) with context when predicting tokens, and to unify observations across multiple model families and scales.
AI.method: Geometric analysis of the unembedding matrix across four families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Pythia). Project the final prediction state onto the unembedding direction that encodes unigram statistics to obtain a prior loading factor λ. Interpret the prediction as a tempered Bayesian update consisting of a unigram prior raised to λ and a context-driven likelihood. Demonstrate that λ calibrates across model sizes and families and show causal influence by manipulating λ at the final prediction state.
AI.result: Identification of a common direction of ignorance that encodes the unigram prior across diverse models. A per-token λ arises from projecting the prediction state, yielding a decomposition into prior^λ and contextual likelihood. λ tends to decrease as context becomes more informative. The approach provides a calibrated, cross-model comparable measure and demonstrates causal influence of λ on predictions via KL divergence.
AI.conclusion: The unembedding geometry offers a unified, calibratable account of how language models blend prior corpus statistics with context, with the direction of ignorance serving as a general, causal factor. Larger models rely less on priors in high-context regimes, and the framework applies across diverse architectures and scales.

title: Following a Unique Path: A Fast Certifier Applied to Outlier-Robust Pose Registration
summary: Certifiable methods have arisen as a means to guarantee global optimality of solutions to non-convex problems using convex semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. The most performant of these methods use a local solver to obtain the candidate solution, and then certify its optimality using efficient linear algebra techniques. However, for many problems of interest in robotics, this local-solve-then-certify approach is impeded by a form of degeneracy in the relaxation, leaving a costly optimization of the relaxation as the only recourse. In this paper, we introduce our Central-Path Certifier (CP-Cert), a certifiable method explicitly tailored to certify candidate optima to problems that exhibit this form of degeneracy. Using a candidate as a starting point, our approach seeks a nearby region of the feasible space -- known as the central path -- where a valid certificate can be readily obtained. The approach is kept efficient by exploiting indirect linear algebra techniques, problem sparsity, and parallelism. We apply CP-Cert to both matrix-weighted pose registration and pointcloud data association, whose novel SDP relaxation is of independent interest. On simulated examples, we explore the properties of this novel relaxation and show that CP-Cert is fast and scalable, achieving runtimes that are up to three orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art direct solvers. Finally, we combine these contributions into a certifiable, outlier-robust pose-estimation pipeline, which we apply to real-world data.

AI.tldr: Introduces Central-Path Certifier (CP-Cert) to certify optimality for degenerate SDP relaxations in robotics problems, starting from a candidate solution and moving to a central-path region to obtain certificates efficiently. Demonstrates a novel SDP relaxation for matrix-weighted pose registration and point-cloud data association, with CP-Cert achieving large speedups and enabling a certifiable, outlier-robust pose-estimation pipeline.
AI.motivation: Degeneracy in SDP relaxations prevents efficient certification of candidate optima; there is a need for a scalable certifier that can work from a near-solution despite degeneracy.
AI.method: From a candidate solution, CP-Cert searches a nearby central-path region where a certificate is readily obtained. It exploits indirect linear algebra, problem sparsity, and parallelism. Applies to a novel SDP relaxation for matrix-weighted pose registration and point-cloud data association.
AI.result: Simulation shows CP-Cert fast and scalable, with runtimes up to three orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art direct solvers. The relaxation’s properties are studied; the approach is demonstrated on real data in a certifiable, outlier-robust pose-estimation pipeline.
AI.conclusion: CP-Cert enables fast, scalable certification for degenerate SDP relaxations in robotics problems and supports a practical, certifiable pose-estimation pipeline that is robust to outliers.

title: Position: Unlabeled IS NOT Equal to No Human Supervision in Visual Learning
summary: This position paper argues that the absence of labels does not imply the absence of human supervision in visual learning, and urges the research community to identify sources of supervision more explicitly. Many recent methods in computer vision build upon representations learned from large-scale unlabeled data, and are therefore grouped under the same umbrella term ``unsupervised.'' However, different data curation schemes and training objectives embed substantially different human priors on which models rely, and we argue that one ``unsupervised'' umbrella term is no longer capturing these distinctions. This ambiguity makes it harder to compare unsupervised learning research conducted under different assumptions, coinciding with a sharp decline in papers titled with ``unsupervised'' in flagship computer vision conferences since 2021, despite continued growth of the field. While we fully embrace pre-training as a strong foundation for modern computer vision, we advocate for a community-level effort toward greater conceptual clarity: authors are encouraged to disclose priors in data selection and learning objectives, and to specify which components of a learning pipeline depend on which assumptions. Standardized disclosure practices can improve academic communication, ensure fairer comparisons, and preserve methodological diversity in unsupervised learning.

AI.tldr: Absence of labels does not equal absence of supervision; the term 'unsupervised' istoo broad and masks varying human priors in data curation and objectives. The paper calls for explicit disclosure of priors to enable fair comparisons and preserve methodological diversity in visual pre-training.
AI.motivation: Ambiguity in what counts as 'unsupervised' makes it hard to compare methods and reproduce results. Despite growth in the field, flagship venues show fewer 'unsupervised' papers since 2021. The authors advocate clearer conceptualization and disclosure of priors in data selection and learning objectives.
AI.method: Conceptual/position analysis of how data curation and training objectives encode human priors. Proposes standardized disclosure practices and explicit attribution of which pipeline components depend on which assumptions.
AI.result: A call to action: adopt community-level disclosure norms for priors in data selection and learning objectives, enabling fairer comparisons and preserving methodological diversity in unsupervised (and pre-trained) vision research.
AI.conclusion: Standardized disclosure of priors should become a norm to improve communication, reproducibility, and fairness in evaluating unsupervised/pre-training approaches in computer vision.

title: MasterControl Seventeen Every Time
summary: We study a governed approach to enterprise analytics: a language model interprets the question, while deterministic policy selects and runs a pre-approved analytical program that returns both results and evidence. We show that this restriction can remain expressive within a defined analytical class, using relational operations plus aggregation, comparison, windows, ranking, and similarity. Fixed meaning, policy, data, and execution rules also make results replayable. Across 440 runs, three 8B models generated SQL and selected tools at runtime, while Qwen3-8B interpreted intent only and policy executed the approved program. None of 330 runtime-planning episodes matched the full answer-and-evidence contract across all test datasets; the policy-executed analyzer matched 110 of 110. This is a configuration-specific result, not evidence that runtime agents cannot succeed under other designs.

AI.tldr: A governance-based enterprise analytics framework uses an LLM to interpret questions and a deterministic policy to select and run a pre-approved analytics program, yielding replayable results and evidence; experiments show policy-driven execution achieves full compliance with the answer-evidence contract, while runtime-planning approaches underperform, highlighting configuration-specific results rather than general limitations.
AI.motivation: Improve reliability, reproducibility, and auditable governance in enterprise analytics by decoupling intent understanding (LLM) from controlled execution (policy-driven analytics) within a constrained analytical class.
AI.method: Define an analytical class with relational operations, aggregation, windows, ranking, and similarity under fixed semantics, policy, data, and execution rules. Evaluate across 440 runs: three 8B models generate SQL and tool choices at runtime; Qwen3-8B interprets intent only with policy executing the approved program. Compare results against a formal answer-and-evidence contract across datasets.
AI.result: The policy-executed analyzer matched the full answer-evidence contract on 110/110 datasets, while none of 330 runtime-planning episodes achieved the full contract. 440 total runs show runtime-policy differences, with evidence that this outcome is configuration-specific rather than a general limitation of runtime agents.
AI.conclusion: A governance-based, replayable analytics framework can be expressive and reliable within a defined class, but success is configuration-dependent; runtime agents may succeed under alternative designs, and policy-driven execution offers robust adherence to the contract.

title: Equation Recast for Canonical Operator Learning Across Parametric PDEs
summary: Learning solution operators across broad parameter ranges can require substantial coverage of both input functions and physical parameters, particularly for purely data-driven parametric models. In addition, the resulting models may fail silently outside the training distribution. We introduce equation recast, which reformulates parametric operator learning as the learning of a single canonical operator. Parameter-induced operator variations are derived analytically from the governing equation and absorbed into effective sources, enabling zero-shot prediction across new parameter regimes. Across multi-parameter, nonlinear, and singular PDE settings, equation recast supports extrapolation, integrates sparse heterogeneous datasets in a shared canonical representation, and uses loss of convergence as an internal warning signal for failure of the recast iteration. In high-fidelity tokamak simulations for nuclear fusion, the framework unifies electron-temperature data across four device geometries through canonical-domain mapping within one jointly trained operator. Equation recast provides a route toward reusable neural PDE solvers combining equation-guided transfer, data efficiency, and monitorable inference.

AI.tldr: Equation recast learns a single canonical operator for parametric PDEs; parameter effects are absorbed into effective sources, enabling zero-shot extrapolation across new parameter regimes; demonstrated in high-fidelity tokamak simulations unifying electron-temperature data across four device geometries.
AI.motivation: Broad parameter ranges and data-driven parametric models require extensive coverage and can fail silently outside training; there is a need for data-efficient, transferable neural PDE solvers with internal failure signaling.
AI.method: Recast parametric operator learning as learning a single canonical operator. Analytically derive parameter-induced variations from the governing equation and absorb them into effective sources. Use canonical-domain mapping to unify across geometries; train jointly and monitor convergence as an internal warning signal for recast iteration failure; enables zero-shot prediction.
AI.result: Supports extrapolation across multi-parameter, nonlinear, and singular PDE settings; integrates sparse heterogeneous datasets within a shared canonical representation; demonstrated by unifying electron-temperature data across four tokamak geometries within one operator.
AI.conclusion: Equation recast provides a route to reusable neural PDE solvers with equation-guided transfer, data efficiency, and monitorable inference.

title: Long-Horizon Consistent and Interaction-Aware World Models for Multi-Style End-to-End Driving
summary: End-to-end autonomous driving has increasingly adopted world model-based reinforcement learning frameworks to improve learning efficiency through \textit{imagined rollouts}. However, existing world models suffer from three key limitations: temporal inconsistency in long-horizon imagined rollouts, inadequate modeling of ego-environment interactions, and limited adaptability to diverse driving styles. To address these challenges, we propose \textit{StyleDrive}, a world-model-based learning framework that jointly enforces long-horizon consistency, explicitly disentangles interactive traffic states, and supports multi-style policy optimization within a unified learning paradigm. First, we introduce a temporal consistency regularization that integrates historical latent states through gated cross-attention, stabilizing long-horizon imagined rollouts and mitigating error accumulation. Second, we design an explicit state disentanglement module that separates ego-relevant from ego-irrelevant interactive states, enabling more interpretable and efficient decision-making in complex traffic scenarios. Third, we enable multi-style driving behaviors through Group Relative Policy Optimization, which replaces per-step reward optimization with trajectory-wise relative advantages, reducing reward variance and supporting diverse driving styles without retraining. We evaluate StyleDrive on the Bench2Drive closed-loop driving benchmark, achieving a driving score of 88.44 (+17.08 over the previous best world model-based method) and a success rate of 66.82 (+16.58). Furthermore, we deploy StyleDrive on a real automated guided vehicle platform and demonstrate promising sim-to-real transfer capability in dynamic driving scenarios.

AI.tldr: StyleDrive: a world-model RL framework for autonomous driving that (1) enforces long-horizon consistency via temporal regularization with gated cross-attention on historical latents, (2) explicitly disentangles ego-relevant vs ego-irrelevant interactive states, and (3) supports multi-style policies through Group Relative Policy Optimization. It achieves strong sim-to-real results on Bench2Drive and a real Automated Guided Vehicle (AGV).
AI.motivation: Address three core limitations of existing world-model-based driving: (i) temporal inconsistency and error accumulation in long-horizon imagined rollouts, (ii) insufficient modeling of ego–environment interactions, and (iii) limited adaptability to diverse driving styles.
AI.method: Introduce three components in a unified framework: (1) temporal consistency regularization using gated cross-attention that aggregates historical latent states to stabilize long-horizon rollouts; (2) explicit state disentanglement separating ego-relevant interactive states from ego-irrelevant ones to improve interpretability and decision efficiency; (3) Group Relative Policy Optimization enabling trajectory-wise relative advantages to support multi-style driving without retraining, reducing reward variance.
AI.result: Bench2Drive evaluation reports a driving score of 88.44, 17.08 points above the previous best world-model method, and a success rate of 66.82, 16.58 points higher; also demonstrates sim-to-real transfer on a real automated guided vehicle platform in dynamic driving scenarios.
AI.conclusion: StyleDrive advances world-model RL for autonomous driving by ensuring long-horizon consistency, enhancing interpretability through state disentanglement, and enabling multi-style policies without frequent retraining, with promising sim-to-real transfer.

title: Exemplar: Classical Priors Complement Frozen Features for Few-Shot Microscopy Segmentation at Native Resolution
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Code, configurations, and the per-image score records behind every reported number: https://github.com/michalprusek/Exemplar
summary: Segmenting a new biomedical dataset usually means a domain-specific model trained on substantial annotation, or a foundation model steered at inference time. We present Exemplar, a few-shot segmenter that fuses a frozen DINOv3 backbone with a fixed bank of classical native-resolution filter responses in one lightweight head, fitted from the support masks alone. In the few-mask, native-resolution regime, classical priors and frozen self-supervised features are complementary: fused in one head, a single fixed configuration spans eleven biomedical imaging datasets. Under the same head, the classical bank alone reaches 0.693 on the eleven-dataset panel, scored by foreground intersection-over-union or centreline Dice, and the frozen features alone 0.672; the bank leads on seven of the eleven and the features on the rest, and fused they reach 0.782. Against five forward-pass few-shot methods, Exemplar leads in 54 of 55 method-dataset comparisons, 52 of them significant after Holm correction. From a single annotated mask it reaches 0.703 on the same panel, against 0.682 for a from-scratch nnU-Net trained on that same mask. At eight masks nnU-Net overtakes it on the panel mean, chiefly on centreline agreement, but takes 16-77x longer to fit.

AI.tldr: Exemplar is a data-efficient few-shot segmenter that fuses a frozen DINOv3 backbone with a fixed bank of native-resolution filter responses. It achieves strong cross-dataset performance across 11 biomedical datasets, often outperforming other few-shot methods and a single-mask nnU-Net, though a fully trained nnU-Net with more masks can surpass it in some metrics but with much higher training time.
AI.motivation: Biomedical segmentation faces limited annotations and domain shift; a generalizable few-shot approach that leverages frozen self-supervised features and classical priors without heavy re-training is desirable.
AI.method: A fixed head integrates a frozen DINOv3 backbone with a precomputed bank of classical native-resolution filter responses; the head is fitted solely from the support masks; evaluated across eleven datasets; compared to five forward-pass few-shot methods.
AI.result: The classical bank alone achieves 0.693, the frozen features 0.672, and their fusion 0.782 on the eleven-dataset panel (using foreground IoU or centreline Dice). The bank leads on seven datasets, features on four; fusion wins across all eleven. Exemplar outperforms 54 of 55 method-dataset comparisons (52 significant after Holm correction). With a single annotated mask, it reaches 0.703 vs 0.682 for a from-scratch nnU-Net trained on that mask. With eight masks, nnU-Net overtakes on panel mean (mainly centreline), but requires 16–77x more fitting time.
AI.conclusion: Fusing classical priors with frozen self-supervised features in a single lightweight head yields a robust, cross-dataset few-shot segmenter with strong data efficiency and generalization; it offers a favorable speed-accuracy trade-off versus fully supervised methods, though more-annotated baselines can surpass it at the cost of training time.

title: Speculative Macro Commit for Faster Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents spend wall-clock time not only on model inference but also in serial action--observation turns, where each tool call, environment transition, and observation can delay subsequent decisions. We introduce \textbf{Speculative Macro Commit} (SMC), a runtime mechanism for a two-tier agent system: a large authoritative actor model produces the official trajectory, while a faster speculative drafter model continuously predicts and executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot. SMC mines recurring multi-action skeletons from training traces and stores them in a macro library used to match against action chains predicted by the drafter at runtime. When the actor's next tool call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the remaining pre-executed draft steps, together with their observations, to the official trajectory. Using Qwen3.5-27B INT4 as the authoritative actor model and Qwen3.5-4B as the speculative drafter model, SMC matches the sequential agent's overall accuracy while reducing latency by 10.23\% over the Speculative Actions (SA) baseline and 18.59\% over sequential execution on the $τ^2$-Bench Telecom subset. On AppWorld, SMC reduces wall time by 7.7\% over SA baseline and 44.9\% over sequential execution, with a small reduction in task completion. Overall, SMC provides a practical way to reuse multi-step speculative execution and reduce agent latency beyond single-step speculative actions. Our code is publicly available \href{https://github.com/zeyuliu1037/speculative-macro-commit}{\textcolor{magenta}{here}}.

AI.tldr: Speculative Macro Commit (SMC) enables two-tier LLM agents to pre-execute future action chains via a speculative drafter and commit when the actor aligns, achieving notable latency reductions with little loss in task completion.
AI.motivation: Wall-clock latency in tool-using agents arises from serial tool calls, environment transitions, and obs; need to reduce latency without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: Two-tier system: authoritative actor model; speculative drafter on isolated environment; macro library mined from training traces; runtime matching of action chains; pre-executed steps are committed when actor's next tool call matches first drafted action; environment snapshots; experiments with Qwen3.5-27B INT4 actor and Qwen3.5-4B drafter; benchmarks τ^2-Bench Telecom subset and AppWorld; compare with Speculative Actions baseline and sequential execution.
AI.result: Latency reductions: 10.23% over SA and 18.59% over sequential on τ^2 Telecom subset; 7.7% over SA and 44.9% over sequential on AppWorld; accuracy maintained comparable to sequential; small drop in final task completion; code released.
AI.conclusion: SMC provides a practical, reusable approach to multi-step speculative execution, achieving latency improvements beyond single-step speculation while preserving overall accuracy; broad applicability to tool-using agents; code available.

title: From Euclidean to Graph-Structured Data: A Survey of Collaborative Learning
comment: 96 pages. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), March 2026, with Survey Certification
summary: The conventional approach to machine learning, that is, collecting data, training models, and performing inference in a single location, faces fundamental limitations, including scalability and privacy, that restrict its applicability. To address these challenges, recent research has explored collaborative learning approaches, including federated learning and decentralized learning, where individual agents perform training and inference locally, with limited collaboration. Most collaborative learning research focuses on Euclidean data with regular, grid-like structure (e.g., images, text). However, these approaches fail to capture the relational patterns in many real-world applications, best represented by graphs. Learning on graphs relies on message-passing mechanisms to propagate information between connected nodes, making it conceptually well-suited for collaborative environments where agents must exchange information. Yet, the opportunities and challenges of learning on graph-structured data in collaborative settings remain largely underexplored. This survey provides a comprehensive investigation of collaborative learning from Euclidean to graph-structured data, aiming to consolidate this emerging field. We begin by reviewing its foundational principles for Euclidean data, organizing them along three core dimensions: learning effectiveness, efficiency, and privacy preservation. We then extend the discussion to graph-structured data, introducing a taxonomy of graph distribution scenarios, characterizing associated statistical heterogeneities, and developing standardized problem formulations and algorithmic frameworks. Finally, we systematically identify open challenges and promising research directions.

AI.tldr: Survey of collaborative learning from Euclidean to graph-structured data; provides a taxonomy, standard problem formulations, and open challenges.
AI.motivation: Address scalability and privacy limits of centralized ML; graphs capture relational patterns in real-world data; collaborative learning on graphs is underexplored.
AI.method: Reviews Euclidean collaborative learning along learning effectiveness, efficiency, and privacy; extends to graph-structured data with a taxonomy of graph distribution scenarios; defines standardized problem formulations and algorithmic frameworks; identifies open challenges and directions.
AI.result: Delivers a consolidated overview of the field, introduces a taxonomy for graph-based collaborative learning, standard problem formulations and algorithms, and outlines key open problems and research opportunities.
AI.conclusion: Highlights open challenges and promising research directions for graph-based collaborative learning in distributed and privacy-preserving settings.

title: Establishing a Dynamic Multimodal HRI Dataset for Engagement Analysis with a Humanoid Robot
summary: This paper presents an experimental design for constructing a multimodal dataset to analyze user engagement in human-robot interaction (HRI). Prior studies have mainly relied on observable behavioral cues, with limited frameworks integrating physiological signals. We therefore propose a structured data-collection protocol to build a multimodal dataset that includes wearable physiological signals, behavioral data, and self-report measures under different levels of task complexity defined in this experiment.

AI.tldr: Proposes an experimental design for a multimodal HRI dataset incorporating wearable physiological signals, behavioral data, and self-report measures across varying task complexity.
AI.motivation: Addresses a gap in HRI research where studies rely mainly on observable cues and rarely integrate physiological data to assess user engagement.
AI.method: Presents a structured data-collection protocol to construct a multimodal dataset that includes wearable physiological signals, behavioral data, and self-report measures, tested under different levels of task complexity.
AI.result: An experimental design/protocol proposal with specified data modalities and collection workflow; no empirical results reported.
AI.conclusion: Provides a framework to enhance analysis of user engagement in HRI through multimodal data, enabling more comprehensive future studies.

title: Solving the Needle-in-a-Haystack Problem in Mammography Vision-Language Model with Differentiable Subset Sampling
summary: There is growing interest in adopting CLIP-style vision--language model (VLM) pretraining for mammography. However, models that directly employ the standard CLIP architecture and training objective exhibit limited zero-shot performance in clinically important tasks such as cancer, finding-type, and BI-RADS predictions. We argue that this underwhelming performance is due to neglecting two characteristics of mammography data: (1) its high-res nature, and (2) homogeneity of radiology reports, largely driven by a predominance of negative/benign findings on examinations. We propose TopKSigLIP, a VLM designed to address these two limitations through a novel architecture and learning objectives. Instead of downscaling high-res mammography images to satisfy GPU memory constraints, TopKSigLIP introduces TopK-Patch module that learns to sample a sparse set of high-res patches likely to contain lesions, sidestepping the resolution--batch size tradeoff of VLM training. The sampled patch locations additionally serve as a built-in localization tool. To address report homogeneity, we replace the contrastive loss, which falsely repels semantically similar pairs, with a Sup-sigmoid loss. Sup-sigmoid loss extends the sigmoid loss from SigLIP with soft labels derived from structured data. TopKSigLIP outperforms existing open-source mammography and general medical VLMs on both internal and external benchmarks on density assessment, BI-RADS classification, finding subtyping, and cancer prediction under zero-shot evaluation. TopKSigLIP remains competitive under linear probing despite using a significantly smaller vision encoder and smaller training batches than baselines. The TopK-Patch module additionally achieves superior lesion localization over post-hoc Grad-CAM. Code and weights are made public:https://github.com/Youngseok0001/TopKSigLIP.

AI.tldr: TopKSigLIP proposes a CLIP-style VLM tailored for mammography by (i) sampling high-resolution patches via a TopK-Patch module to avoid downscaling, and (ii) using a Sup-sigmoid loss with soft labels to handle homogeneous radiology reports. It achieves strong zero-shot performance on density, BI-RADS, finding subtyping, and cancer prediction, with built-in lesion localization and competitive linear probing using a smaller vision encoder and smaller batches; code is released.
AI.motivation: Mammography data poses two challenges for standard CLIP-like VLMs: (1) very high-resolution images, which are costly to process at full scale and lead to resolution-batch size tradeoffs; (2) homogeneity of radiology reports dominated by negative/benign findings, making standard contrastive objectives misalign semantically similar pairs.
AI.method: Introduce TopK-Patch to sample a sparse, high-resolution set of patches likely containing lesions; use the patch locations as a built-in localization cue. Replace the contrastive loss with Sup-sigmoid loss, leveraging soft labels from structured data to better capture semantic similarity between image-text pairs.
AI.result: Outperforms existing open-source mammography and general medical VLMs on internal and external benchmarks for density assessment, BI-RADS classification, finding subtyping, and cancer prediction in zero-shot settings; maintains competitive performance under linear probing with a smaller vision encoder and smaller training batches; TopK-Patch yields superior lesion localization versus post-hoc Grad-CAM; code and weights are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: By addressing high-res imaging and report homogeneity with targeted high-resolution patch sampling and a soft-label objective, TopKSigLIP delivers strong zero-shot performance and localization while remaining computationally efficient, offering a practical VLM solution for mammography.

title: Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Dependency-Scoped Validation for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory
summary: Distributed LLM-agent teams can read the latest shared facts and still act on an obsolete plan. A planner may derive an action from requirement $r_3$, another agent may commit $r_4$, and an executor may receive $r_4$ without replacing the plan derived from $r_3$. We call this \emph{stale-plan execution}: state freshness does not establish that the plan authorizing an action remains valid. We introduce PlanFence, a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol. Plans cite the exact public records they used, and an executor validates only the records that can affect the pending external action, replanning once or blocking when validation is incomplete. In 30 controlled live workflows with a post-plan revision, a freshness-only executor acts on the obsolete plan in every task, whereas PlanFence completes all tasks without an invalid action. Controlled replay reveals two conditional boundaries: proactive synchronization yields lower coordination stall at low churn, while PlanFence avoids repeated update-path coordination as churn grows and avoids validating unrelated state as the shared keyspace grows. These are controlled safety and systems-cost results, not general task-accuracy gains.

AI.tldr: PlanFence binds actions to the exact public records used to justify them and validates only the affecting records, preventing stale-plan execution in distributed LLM-agent teams; in 30 live-workflow tests with plan revisions, PlanFence outperforms freshness-only executors by avoiding invalid actions and reducing coordination overhead under churn.
AI.motivation: Address stale-plan execution in distributed LLM-agent systems where plan authors may become obsolete as the shared state updates. The goal is to ensure action validity while minimizing coordination overhead.
AI.method: Introduce a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol (PlanFence) where plans cite the public records they rely on. Executors validate only records that can affect the pending external action and replan when validation is incomplete. Empirical evaluation uses 30 controlled live workflows with post-plan revision to compare PlanFence against a freshness-only executor.
AI.result: PlanFence completes all tasks without executing invalid actions, while a freshness-only executor fails on every task due to stale plans. Controlled replay reveals that proactive synchronization reduces coordination stalls at low churn, whereas PlanFence minimizes update-path coordination costs as churn grows and avoids validating unrelated shared state as the keyspace expands.
AI.conclusion: PlanFence improves safety for distributed LLM-agent teams by preventing stale-plan execution with a transparent, dependency-scoped validation process. The reported gains are safety and systems-cost oriented rather than general task-accuracy gains; applicability and performance depend on churn and the structure of public records.

title: Modern Transformers Are Implicit Hybrids: From Functional Differentiation to Principled Hybrid Architecture Design
summary: Hybrid architectures combining Full Attention (FA) and Linear Attention (LA) are increasingly prominent, yet their allocation remains heuristic. We seek an evidence-grounded basis in head-level functional organization learned by RoPE-based Transformers. Behavioral probes do not yield a complete taxonomy, so we propose two intervention metrics: RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS), measuring how each frequency affects a head's attention distribution, and RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD), isolating dependence on rotary positional modulation. On Qwen3-series models and Llama3.1, RFIS suggests and RPD verifies a complete taxonomy of retrieval and positional heads separated by a salient mid-low-frequency band. Controlled Transformers show that this boundary follows the training-length positional scale; we term it the Global Positional Band (GPBand). The analysis suggests a potential cause of zero-shot length-extrapolation failure and yields two principles: positional modeling should operate only locally, with global access through position-independent retrieval; and both functions should be assigned at head granularity with layer-specific allocation. We instantiate them in Head-wise Hybrid Architecture (HwH), using NoPE FA for global retrieval and LA for local positional modeling. With an FA-to-LA ratio below 1:3, HwH retains strong language modeling and commonsense reasoning while improving retrieval and substantially strengthening zero-shot long-context extrapolation over Transformer, LA, and a layer-wise hybrid baseline. Ablations validate both principles and component roles, highlighting principled hybrid architecture design as a promising route toward future foundation models.

AI.tldr: A head-level RoPE-based taxonomy exists separating retrieval and positional heads via a Global Positional Band; two metrics RFIS and RPD reveal structure; introduces Head-wise Hybrid Architecture HwH (NoPE FA for global retrieval, LA for local positional modeling) that improves zero-shot long-context extrapolation while retaining LM capabilities.
AI.motivation: Provide an evidence-grounded basis for allocating full-attention vs linear-attention in RoPE-based Transformers; existing behavioral probes fail to yield a complete taxonomy; derive principled, layer-local head allocation.
AI.method: Introduce two intervention metrics RFIS and RPD; empirical analysis on Qwen3-series and Llama3.1 to identify a complete taxonomy of head functions separated by a mid-low-frequency band; identify GPBand (training-length positional scale); implement HwH with FA-based global retrieval and LA-based local positional modeling; perform ablations and comparisons with Transformer, LA, and layer-wise baselines.
AI.result: Found a complete taxonomy distinguishing retrieval vs positional heads, separated by a mid-low-frequency band forming the Global Positional Band (GPBand) boundary that scales with training length; HwH with FA:LA < 1:3 preserves language modeling and reasoning while substantially improving retrieval and zero-shot long-context extrapolation; ablations validate the proposed principles and component roles.
AI.conclusion: Positionally modeling should be local with global access via retrieval; head-level, layer-specific allocation yields strong hybrid performance; principled hardware-aware/methodology-driven design (HwH) is a promising path for future foundation models.

title: R2S-Eval: Robot Evaluation with Real-to-Sim Calibration via Vision-Language Models
summary: Evaluating robot manipulation policies is becoming increasingly important as generalist models, particularly vision-language-action (VLA) models, are deployed on physical robots. However, conventional real-world evaluation remains labor-intensive, unstable, and insufficiently informative. It requires repeated hardware trials, manual scene resets, and continuous operator monitoring, may produce different policy rankings across repeated evaluations, and primarily relies on success-rate metrics that provide limited information about execution quality. In contrast, humans assess robot performance by observing and comparing complete behaviors rather than relying solely on binary success outcomes. To this end, we propose R2S-Eval, an evaluation pipeline that combines real-to-sim calibration with vision-language model (VLM) preference evaluation. The real-to-sim component efficiently generates rollout videos in a simulator calibrated to the real-world evaluation setting, thereby reducing the need for repeated hardware trials. The VLM evaluator assesses the execution quality of rollout videos and produces pairwise preferences, which are subsequently aggregated into policy rankings. We further introduce a protocol to assess whether the proposed evaluation pipeline yields validated policy conclusions while mitigating the key challenges of conventional real-world evaluation. Experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that R2S-Eval produces reliable and stable policy conclusions, achieves agreement with human preferences, substantially reduces repeated hardware-operation effort, and reveals behavior-quality differences that are not captured by binary success labels. In general, R2S-Eval advances robot evaluation from manual success counting toward automated, statistically stable, and quality-aware evaluation of robot behavior. Project page: https://r2s-eval.github.io.

AI.tldr: R2S-Eval combines real-to-sim calibration with vision-language model preference evaluation to provide automated, quality-aware, and stable policy rankings for robot manipulation, reducing hardware trials and aligning with human judgments.
AI.motivation: Current real-world robot evaluation relies on labor-intensive, binary success metrics, leading to unstable rankings and limited insight into execution quality. There is a need for a scalable, behavior-quality-focused evaluation framework that can approximate human judgments.
AI.method: Use a real-to-sim calibration to generate rollout videos in a simulator calibrated to the real task, then apply a vision-language model to assess execution quality and produce pairwise preferences; aggregate preferences into policy rankings; include a protocol to validate that conclusions are robust.
AI.result: R2S-Eval yields reliable and stable policy conclusions in both simulation and real settings, agrees with human preferences, substantially reduces repeated hardware-operation effort, and reveals qualitative differences in behavior not captured by binary success labels.
AI.conclusion: R2S-Eval advances robot evaluation from manual success counting to automated, statistically stable, and quality-aware evaluation of robot behavior.

title: WireSeg-32K: A Physics-Grounded Synthetic Dataset for Wire Instance Segmentation
comment: Synthetic Data for Computer Vision @ CVPR 2026 Workshop
summary: Deformable linear objects such as wires and cables are difficult to segment because they are thin, highly deformable, and frequently self-occluded, while large-scale instance-level annotations are expensive to obtain in real scenes. Existing resources either focus on cable tracing or semantic segmentation under constrained settings, or generate visually plausible images without physically grounded wire deformation. We present WireSeg-32k, a synthetic dataset for wire instance segmentation with 32,000 RGB images, instance masks, depth maps, and a complementary real-world test set with annotations. To generate this dataset, we develop DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline that couples Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering, enabling physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes, CAD-based wire assets, and diverse visually grounded scenes. As a simple baseline, LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k alone improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, showing that physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception.

AI.tldr: Synthetic dataset WireSeg-32k for wire instance segmentation (32k images with masks/depth) built via DeformX: a co-simulation of Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic rendering, enabling physically plausible wire shapes; baseline LoRA-tuned SAM3 on WireSeg-32k yields +10.2% mAP@75 on real data, indicating sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Wires and cables are thin, highly deformable, and often self-occlude, making instance segmentation hard. Real-world annotations are expensive; existing datasets either focus on tracing under constraints or generate synthetic visuals without physical grounding. A physically grounded, scalable dataset could improve perception of deformable linear objects in real scenes.
AI.method: Introduce DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline coupling Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering to generate physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes from CAD assets, producing WireSeg-32k (32k RGB images, instance masks, depth) and a complementary real-world annotated test set.
AI.result: As a baseline, LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, demonstrating transferability of physically grounded synthetic data to real wire perception.
AI.conclusion: Physically grounded synthetic data via DeformX and WireSeg-32k can enhance real-world wire segmentation, and synthetic datasets with realistic deformation and contact dynamics are beneficial for learning robust wire instance segmentation.

title: A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) teaching assistants powered by large language models (LLMs) offer scalable educational support but often provide limited personalization. This study presents a prompt-engineering-based framework for personalizing general-purpose LLM/RAG-based AI teaching assistants such as Jill Watson across academic disciplines and courses. The framework adapts responses using six learner-specific dimensions: self-assessment, abstraction preference, verbosity preference, perceptual orientation, information processing style, and level of understanding, yielding 96 distinct learner profiles. Student queries are additionally analyzed using Bloom's Taxonomy to estimate cognitive complexity at the interaction level. Learner attributes and cognitive assessments are encoded in structured prompts that condition the LLM without requiring model retraining. The framework is evaluated through experiments using NLP metrics and a human study with five participants. Results show perceived differences in response style and structure across personalization conditions, with statistical analyses identifying learner attributes associated with measurable response changes. These findings provide preliminary evidence that prompt-based personalization can support adaptive behavior in LLM-powered educational agents.

AI.tldr: A prompt-engineering framework personalizes general-purpose LLM/RAG-based AI teaching assistants using six learner dimensions to yield 96 profiles, with Bloom's taxonomy guiding cognitive complexity; evaluated via NLP metrics and a small user study, indicating preliminary adaptive behavior.
AI.motivation: Address the limited personalization of general LLM teaching assistants and achieve scalable, retraining-free customization across disciplines.
AI.method: Define six learner attributes (self-assessment, abstraction preference, verbosity, perceptual orientation, information processing style, level of understanding) to create 96 profiles. Analyze student queries with Bloom's Taxonomy to estimate cognitive complexity. Encode learner attributes and cognitive assessments into structured prompts that condition the LLM without retraining. Evaluate using NLP metrics and a small human study (n=5).
AI.result: Users perceived differences in response style and structure across personalization conditions. Statistical analysis linked certain learner attributes to measurable changes in responses.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-based personalization can enable adaptive behavior in LLM-powered educational agents, offering scalable customization, though findings are preliminary due to small sample size and limited scope; further work needed for broader validation.

title: Tail-Likelihood Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning typically optimizes average reward. For generative policies, the average can hide an important distinction: two policies can achieve the same mean reward while having very different chances of producing a rare but high-reward rollout. This matters as sampling increases during training and inference, since its benefit depends on retaining probability mass on high-reward outcomes. We propose to optimize this coverage directly. Rather than considering only expected reward, we consider all of its upper tails: for each reward threshold, how likely is the policy to exceed it? This turns a continuous reward into a family of binary success events. We introduce Tail-Likelihood Reinforcement Learning (TailRL), which maximizes the log-probability of exceeding a randomly chosen reward threshold. Its gradient gives more weight to rare, high-reward rollouts and can be interpreted as a mixture of Best-of-(k) gradients. TailRL requires only a simple modification to the advantage function, making it compatible with existing reinforcement learning pipelines. Across object localization, maze navigation, GUI grounding, and code optimization, TailRL leverages rare high-reward training samples to avoid suboptimal solutions and yields models that benefit more from additional samples at inference time.

AI.tldr: TailRL shifts RL from optimizing mean reward to optimizing tail probabilities: it maximizes the log-probability of exceeding random reward thresholds, turning the problem into multiple binary success events and biasing updates toward rare high-reward rollouts.
AI.motivation: Mean reward hides rare but high-reward outcomes that become increasingly important as sampling grows. Emphasizing tail risk can improve exploration and long-tail performance.
AI.method: Convert rewards into a distribution of binary tail events by sampling a random threshold per update and maximizing the log-probability of exceeding it. The gradient emphasizes rare high-reward rollouts and resembles a mixture of Best-of-(k) gradients. Implemented as a minimal modification to the advantage function to fit existing RL pipelines.
AI.result: Empirically improves performance across object localization, maze navigation, GUI grounding, and code optimization by leveraging rare high-reward samples; models benefit more from additional samples at inference time and avoid suboptimal solutions.
AI.conclusion: TailRL provides a practical, plug-and-play tail-risk objective for RL, improving sensitivity to rare but valuable outcomes and enhancing gains from larger sample sizes without overhauling standard RL infrastructure.

title: ARTiS: An Adaptive Robotic Gripper for Enhanced Tool Manipulation in Disassembly Applications
summary: Grasping and holding tools while using them presents a considerable challenge not only for robots but also for humans. Such a challenge is particularly noticeable in processes involving assembly and disassembly, where efficiency and consistency depend on performing rapidly adaptive tasks. Nonetheless, contemporary robotic grasping technologies that can securely manipulate tools during operation frequently have significant constraints. In this paper, introduce ARTiS (Adaptive Robotic Tool Gripper in Disassembly Systems), a novel gripper that combines the adaptability of soft grippers, the dexterity of anthropomorphic hands, and the robustness of rigid mechanisms with a soft palm and fingertips. This unique combination makes it possible to hold tools securely in a variety of situations through using active jamming in the palm and fin-ray adaptation in fingertips. Furthermore, high finger dexterity is achieved through the seven degrees of freedom design, which enables the fingertips to orient to any surface, both for automated solutions and collaborative tasks. A comprehensive evaluation was conducted using a range of conventional disassembly tools to assess the gripper's compliance, durability, and functional versatility. More information, hardware instructions, and videos at https://romanmykhailyshyn.github.io/artis/

AI.tldr: ARTiS is a hybrid gripper that combines soft actuation, anthropomorphic dexterity, and rigid robustness to securely grasp tools for disassembly tasks, using active palm jamming and fin-ray fingertips with seven DoF.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations in existing robotic grasping for tool handling during assembly/disassembly by achieving rapid, adaptive, secure grasps across diverse tools.
AI.method: The gripper integrates a soft palm with active jamming, soft fingertips employing fin-ray structures, and seven degrees of freedom in the fingers to provide dexterous, surface-oriented contact. It fuses soft, anthropomorphic, and rigid elements, and is evaluated on conventional disassembly tools for compliance, durability, and versatility.
AI.result: Evaluation demonstrated secure tool holding across a range of tools and configurations, with focus on compliance, durability, and functional versatility; resources, hardware instructions, and videos are available at the project site.
AI.conclusion: ARTiS presents a versatile, robust gripper that enables rapid, adaptive tool manipulation in disassembly contexts by leveraging a hybrid soft-hard design with active palm jamming and fin-ray fingertips, suitable for automated and collaborative applications.

title: SLIDEFORGE: An LLM Agent for Controllable Editing of Slides as Structured Artifacts
comment: EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. Haozhen and Fulin contributed equally
summary: Current AI agents compellingly describe slides. However, AI-assisted slide editing requires more than understanding: the output must retain layout, style, component structure, and native editability. Towards, AI-assisted slide editing, existing agents operate on screenshots or weak document representations and often fragment coherent visual units, rasterize editable content, or break layout. In contrast, for controllable slide editing, we introduce an agentic framework, SLIDEFORGE, which builds a Deck State Graph, an executable slide state that links visual decomposition, native pptx object structure, and perceptual organization. By recovering human-referable components while retaining fine-grained editable structure, SLIDEFORGE supports theme-preserving reconstruction through slide-native operations and rendered-state verification. We further introduce an evaluation paradigm for controllable slide transformation that jointly measures component recovery, preservation, restyling consistency, visual quality, and native editability. Experiments show that SLIDEFORGE outperforms direct prompting, screenshot-based agents, and generic code-agent baselines across these dimensions. Code is available at https://github.com/UIUC-MONET/SLIDEFORGE.

AI.tldr: SLIDEFORGE offers a Deck State Graph-based agent for controllable, theme-preserving slide editing that preserves native PPTX structure and enables rendered-state verification; it outperforms prompting and screenshot-based agents; code available.
AI.motivation: Current AI slide editors either rely on screenshots or weak representations, which disrupt layout and native editability. There is a need for controllable, editable slide editing that preserves structure and style.
AI.method: Introduce Deck State Graph, linking visual decomposition, native PPTX object structure, and perceptual organization.
