Recover human-referable components while retaining fine-grained editable structure; slide-native operations for theme-preserving reconstruction; rendered-state verification; develop an evaluation paradigm measuring component recovery, preservation, restyling consistency, visual quality, and native editability.
AI.result: Empirical results show SLIDEFORGE outperforms direct prompting, screenshot-based agents, and generic code-agent baselines across the proposed dimensions.
AI.conclusion: SLIDEFORGE advances controllable AI-assisted slide editing by providing a stateful, editable, theme-preserving framework and an evaluative paradigm; code is available at GitHub.

title: Caught in the Story: Narrative Captivity in Multi-turn LLMs Conversation
summary: People increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for everyday advice, making ethically charged interpersonal problems a practical moral-advisory context. Most prior work has studied this context through single-turn judgments or pressure-laden rebuttals, assumptions that poorly match how guidance is sought in real-world contexts. These assumptions leave unclear whether narration alone, without an explicit opposing position, can shift model judgments during multi-turn moral consultation. Yet real-world moral-conflict conversation often elicits one party's self-justifying account, which can unfold over multiple turns and create information asymmetry. We introduce \textbf{narrative captivity}, a failure mode in which a model treats an unopposed one-sided account as complete and aligns with the narrator's interpretation without seeking missing perspectives. To measure this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of $5{,}078$ interpersonal-conflict scenarios spanning six moral dimensions. Across 17 LLMs, narrative captivity is widespread: end-state judgments under multi-turn narration shift by 25 percentage points on average beyond the matched single-turn baseline. Stage-level analysis identifies preference optimization as a major contributor, while four inference-time strategies provide only partial mitigation. We hope our project fosters LLM advisors that preserve independent judgment in real-world consultation.

AI.tldr: Narrative captivity is a bias where LLMs align with an unopposed one-sided moral narration in multi-turn consultations, causing judgments to drift from single-turn baselines; a benchmark across 17 LLMs shows ~25 percentage-point end-state shifts, with preference optimization identified as a key driver and limited mitigation from inference-time strategies.
AI.motivation: To test whether a narrated, one-sided account can bias model judgments in iterative, real-world-like moral counseling, addressing gaps in prior work focused on single-turn judgments or rebuttals.
AI.method: Develop and evaluate a benchmark of 5,078 interpersonal-conflict scenarios spanning six moral dimensions; assess 17 LLMs; compare end-state judgments under multi-turn narration to single-turn baselines; perform stage-level analysis to identify drivers (notably preference optimization) and test four inference-time mitigation strategies.
AI.result: Narrative captivity is widespread; end-state judgments shift by an average of 25 percentage points beyond the single-turn baseline; stage-level analysis implicates preference optimization as a major contributor; four inference-time strategies provide only partial mitigation.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals a real-world risk that unopposed narration can bias LLM moral advisers, underscoring the need for preserving independent judgment in consultation and motivating development of stronger safeguards beyond current inference-time fixes.

title: Mesh-Native Physics-Informed Graph Surrogates for TCAD-in-the-Loop Design Space Exploration
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)
summary: High-fidelity TCAD simulation of drift-diffusion transport remains the workhorse of emerging FinFET device design, but it is computationally expensive, especially for 3D structures where runtime escalates steeply with mesh complexity. This sharply limits multi-objective design space exploration. Existing machine-learning surrogates map a fixed set of design parameters to a few scalar device metrics, discarding the underlying physics and losing transferability across device geometries and families. A physics-informed graph attention network (GAT) surrogate is proposed. It operates directly on the tetrahedral TCAD mesh and predicts, at every mesh node, the electrostatic potential together with the electron and hole quasi-Fermi levels, the fundamental unknowns of the drift-diffusion system. Training combines a data loss with finite-volume current-continuity residuals, embedding carrier-transport physics into the objective. Operating on the mesh as a graph, the surrogate inherits size generalization: a model trained on few-fin meshes applies unchanged to substantially larger arrays, bounded at inference only by GPU memory. Per-node uncertainty from a deep ensemble drives an active-learning loop that screens large candidate pools in seconds and forwards only the most informative designs for full simulation. Benchmarked against Sentaurus Device on multi-fin tri-gate FinFETs, the surrogate reproduces the three drift-diffusion fields with sub-volt per-field RMSE and reaches a per-design throughput orders of magnitude higher than the full simulator. The advantage grows with device size: on large multi-fin arrays that are prohibitively slow to simulate directly, inference still completes in under a second per device, enabling Pareto-front exploration across device scales infeasible for direct TCAD sweeps.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed Graph Attention Network (GAT) surrogate for 3D TCAD drift-diffusion in FinFETs, trained with data loss and finite-volume physics residuals on tetrahedral meshes. It generalizes across mesh sizes, uses deep-ensemble uncertainty for active learning, and delivers near full-solver accuracy with orders-of-magnitude speedup, enabling Pareto-front design exploration for large devices.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity drift-diffusion TCAD is computationally expensive in 3D FinFETs, limiting multi-objective design space exploration and transferability across geometries. Surrogates typically ignore physics and generalize poorly across sizes.
AI.method: A physics-informed graph attention network operating directly on the tetrahedral TCAD mesh to predict electrostatic potential and electron/hole quasi-Fermi levels at every node. Training combines data loss with finite-volume current-continuity residuals, embedding carrier-transport physics. The mesh-graph enables size generalization; deep-ensemble per-node uncertainty drives an active-learning loop to select informative designs for full simulation.
AI.result: On multi-fin tri-gate FinFETs, the surrogate reproduces all three drift-diffusion fields with sub-volt per-field RMSE and achieves per-design throughputs orders of magnitude higher than a full TCAD; scaling devices still yields inference times under a second per device, enabling Pareto-front exploration across scales that are slow or infeasible with full simulations.
AI.conclusion: The physics-informed GAT surrogate provides accurate, scalable, and transferable drift-diffusion simulations for FinFET designs, dramatically reducing computation while maintaining physics fidelity, and enabling efficient multi-objective design optimization across large device geometries.

title: Programming and execution of skill-based human-robot-crane collaborative tasks
comment: 8 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication in IECON 2026
summary: Highly varying production sets increasing challenges for robotic manufacturing and indoor logistics. New capabilities for agility, flexibility, and robustness are needed. Robot skills, integrating motions, tool operations, and sensor perceptions consistently provide an execution mechanism for a versatile set of tasks with varying parameters. In this paper, easy-to-use CAD-model based programming and execution system for parametrized skills and skill monitors is showcased. The execution control structure is dynamic and parametrized, based on a modified Behavior Tree, where only event based communication is used. A human-robot-crane collaborative skill is shown as a test example, where a human instructs an overhead crane and a manipulator in inserting a heavy object supported by the crane, and guided by the manipulator, into the goal.

AI.tldr: CAD-model-based programming for parametrized skills with an event-driven, modified Behavior Tree execution, demonstrated on a human-robot-crane task.
AI.motivation: Highly variable production sets create the need for agile, flexible, and robust task execution. A unified skill-based approach that integrates motions, tool operations, and perception provides a versatile execution mechanism.
AI.method: CAD-model-based programming and execution system for parametrized skills and skill monitors; dynamic and parametrized execution control based on a modified Behavior Tree with only event-based communication.
AI.result: The abstract demonstrates a test case where a human instructs an overhead crane and a manipulator to insert a heavy object supported by the crane into a goal, with guidance from the manipulator, illustrating feasibility of the approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CAD-based parametrized skill framework with event-driven BT control offers an easy-to-use, adaptable platform for agile robotic manufacturing and indoor logistics, enabling coordinated human-robot tasks.

title: Beyond Small Patches: Black-Box Detection and Purification of Diverse Backdoor Triggers
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly deployed in real-world vision systems, yet their predictions can be covertly manipulated by backdoor attacks, in which malicious triggers cause targeted misclassification while preserving high clean accuracy. Existing defenses often rely on model internals, training data, or clean validation samples, making them difficult to deploy when only black-box access to a trained model is available. We propose TRIM (Trigger Removal by Identifying Manipulated Regions), a deployment-oriented black-box defense that detects and selectively removes backdoor triggers at inference time without requiring model internals, training data, or clean samples. The key insight behind TRIM is to identify image regions that are responsible for anomalous model behavior and purify only those regions while preserving benign content. TRIM innovates via three key components: (i) region-based segmentation with deep feature representations, (ii) adaptive trigger discovery through inpainting and diffusion-based reconstruction to isolate regions responsible for misclassification---without assumptions about trigger type, shape, or location, and (iii) selective region purification that cleans poisoned regions while retaining benign content. To support practical deployment, TRIM further caches feature embeddings of previously identified triggers, enabling efficient recognition and avoiding redundant detection and purification. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and backdoor types, including blended, sparse, varying-size, and multiple triggers, show that TRIM consistently outperforms existing black-box defenses, reducing attack success rates (ASR) to as low as 1.16% while preserving clean accuracy of up to 87.87%. These results demonstrate that effective backdoor mitigation is possible at inference time even when the defender has no access to any auxiliary data.

AI.tldr: TRIM is a black-box defense that detects and purifies backdoor triggers at inference time by segmenting regions with anomalous behavior, discovering triggers via inpainting/diffusion, and selectively purifying poisoned regions, without requiring model internals or extra data.
AI.motivation: Backdoor attacks threaten deployment of DNNs in real-world vision systems; existing defenses often assume access to model internals, training data, or clean samples, which is impractical in many black-box scenarios.
AI.method: 1) Region-based segmentation using deep features to locate suspect regions. 2) Adaptive trigger discovery via inpainting and diffusion-based reconstruction to identify regions responsible for misclassification, without assuming trigger type/shape/location. 3) Selective region purification to clean poisoned regions while preserving benign content. 4) Caching embeddings of known triggers to speed up recognition and avoid redundant purification.
AI.result: TRIM reduces attack success rates (ASR) to as low as 1.16% across diverse backdoor types (blended, sparse, varying-size, multiple triggers) while maintaining clean accuracy up to 87.87% in black-box settings with no auxiliary data.
AI.conclusion: TRIM demonstrates that effective backdoor mitigation is feasible at inference time without access to model internals or training data, supporting deployment-oriented defense against a wide range of backdoor threats.

title: Dude: A Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for Paper-Code Discrepancy Detection
summary: LLM-empowered paper-code discrepancy detection has received growing concern since the scaling of research submissions exceeds the manual review capability. However, the limited context capacity and one-sided discrepancy detection of existing single-agent LLM paradigms lead to an inferior recall performance in detecting discrepancies. In this paper, we propose Dude, the first Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for paper-code discrepancy detection. We discover that the granularity asymmetry of the paper-language and code-language introduces over-interpretation and over-reporting challenges in a multi-agent system design for discrepancy detection, resulting in increasing false positives. To address this, we propose a granularity-aligned negotiation and a two-stage salience-filtering mechanism in Dude, which effectively prevents agents from falsely reporting discrepancies. Experimental results in real-world paper-code discrepancy datasets showcase Dude's significant recall and precision improvement by up to 22.8%, increasing F1 score by up to 18.7% compared to baseline methods.

AI.tldr: A dual-detection multi-agent system (Dude) for paper-code discrepancy detection outperforms single-agent LLM approaches by addressing granularity mismatch and employing negotiation and salience-filtering, achieving higher recall, precision, and F1 on real datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing single-agent LLM approaches suffer from limited context and one-sided discrepancy detection, leading to lower recall in detecting paper-code inconsistencies; there is a need for robust, scalable detection in high-submission settings.
AI.method: Introduce Dude, a dual-detection multi-agent system; identify granularity asymmetry between paper-language and code-language; implement granularity-aligned negotiation; implement two-stage salience-filtering to reduce false positives; evaluate on real-world datasets.
AI.result: Dude yields significant improvements in recall and precision, with up to 22.8% recall gain and up to 18.7% F1 gain over baselines.
AI.conclusion: Dude demonstrates effective mitigation of false positives and enhanced detection performance in paper-code discrepancy tasks; the multi-agent, granularity-aligned design shows promise for scalable review workflows.

title: TRACE: Spatiotemporal Contact Memory Graph Network Simulator for Granular Dynamics
summary: Learned graph simulators provide an efficient alternative to high-fidelity solvers for granular dynamics. However, granular motion depends strongly on inter-granular contact history, which is difficult to preserve when particle contacts form, break, and rearrange. Existing simulators mainly store temporal information in node features or node-level memory. Here we introduce TRACE, a graph-network simulator that stores interaction history directly on contact edges. Each edge maintains a persistent memory updated by attention-based message passing and a gated recurrent unit, while an edge-identity dictionary preserves this memory as the contact graph changes. A physics-structured decoder predicts inter-granular normal and tangential contact forces, enforces the Coulomb friction limit, and applies equal-and-opposite internal forces. The model is trained with single-step pretraining followed by autoregressive rollout fine-tuning. We evaluate TRACE on 2D and 3D granular column-collapse benchmarks. In both cases, TRACE produces stable, physically consistent long-horizon rollouts, closely reproducing the final deposit geometry and the kinetic energy released during collapse. Compared with graph network simulator (GNS) and node-memory graph neural simulator (NMGNS), TRACE reduces long-rollout position error by 31-62% and final-deposit error by 58-89% across the two benchmarks, while using fewer parameters and maintaining near-zero particle interpenetration. TRACE also achieves 12.2$\times$ and 8.9$\times$ speedups over the material point method (MPM) reference solver in 2D and 3D, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/Data-Driven-Computational-Geotechnics/TRACE.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a graph-network simulator for granular dynamics that stores inter-particle contact history on edges using persistent memory, enabling stable long-horizon rollouts and improved accuracy with speedups over traditional solvers.
AI.motivation: Inter-grain contact history governs granular motion; existing graph neural simulators preserve history in node features but lose history when contacts form/break. Edge-level memory with an identity map aims to maintain contact history across graph changes.
AI.method: Edges carry a persistent memory updated via attention-based message passing and a gated recurrent unit; an edge-identity dictionary tracks memory as contacts appear/disappear. A physics-structured decoder predicts normal/tangential contact forces, enforces Coulomb friction, and enforces Newton's third law. Training uses single-step pretraining followed by autoregressive rollout fine-tuning.
AI.result: TRACE yields stable, physically consistent long-horizon rollouts in 2D and 3D granular column-collapse benchmarks. It closely matches final deposit geometry and kinetic energy. It reduces long-rollout position error by 31-62% and final-deposit error by 58-89% compared with GNS and NMGNS, using fewer parameters and nearly zero inter-penetration. It achieves 12.2x (2D) and 8.9x (3D) speedups over MPM. Code is available.
AI.conclusion: Edge-based memory in TRACE improves accuracy, stability, and efficiency for granular dynamics over prior graph-based simulators and classic solvers, demonstrating effective long-horizon predictive capabilities with physically grounded decoding and training.

title: Air-Ground Collaborative Vision-and-Language Navigation via Shared Bird's-Eye Maps
summary: Air-ground collaborative Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) pairs an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) with a global bird's-eye view and an unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) with a local first-person view, yet the setting remains largely unexplored: existing training-free methods solve single-agent tasks but offer no collaboration mechanism, and a recent CARLA-Air evaluation found no stable cooperative behavior across five state-of-the-art VLA models; naive semantic communication or bidirectional coupling even degrades performance. We establish AGC-VLN (Air-Ground Collaborative VLN), the first training-free baseline for air-ground collaborative VLN. The key insight is that training-free methods decompose navigation into VLM-based semantic reasoning and deterministic geometric execution, exposing a collaboration interface: the UAV's global view, over which it renders the UGV's reported pose and the VLM-anchored target as CAR/GOAL markers with distance labels, yielding a shared bird's-eye map. From this map, the UGV acquires global spatial context its first-person view cannot provide, plans a road-following path with a frozen VLM, and executes it under closed-loop control; in parallel, the UAV runs 3D-SPF, a spatial-search upgrade of SPF that localizes the target in the downward view and flies toward it. On 100 closed-loop episodes in CARLA-Air's Town10HD scene, AGC-VLN reaches a 77.0% joint success rate, a collaboration gain of +27.0% over the weaker individual agent (the UAV, 50.0%), and exceeds the strongest published single-agent baseline (Travel UAV, 53.0%) by 24.0 points, stemming from the complementarity of the UAV's global view and the UGV's road-following execution. Project page: https://github.com/ZSN2024/AGC-VLN.

AI.tldr: Introduces AGC-VLN, the first training-free baseline for air-ground collaborative VLN, leveraging a shared bird's-eye map from VLM-based semantic reasoning and deterministic geometry. Demonstrates a 77.0% joint success rate and +27.0% collaboration gain over UAV alone in CARLA-Air Town10HD, outperforming single-agent baselines by 24 points.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free methods address single-agent tasks and lack effective collaboration; CARLA-Air evaluation reveals unstable cooperation across state-of-the-art VLA models; naive semantic communication or bidirectional coupling can harm performance. There is a need for a stable, training-free air-ground collaboration framework for VLN.
AI.method: Decompose navigation into two streams: (1) VLM-based semantic reasoning on the UAV's global bird's-eye view to render the UGV's reported pose and the VLM-anchored target as CAR/GOAL markers on a shared map; (2) deterministic geometric execution where the UGV uses global context to plan a road-following path with a frozen VLM, and the UAV runs 3D-SPF to localize the target in the downward view and navigate toward it. The UAV and UGV operate in a closed-loop with the shared map serving as the collaboration interface.
AI.result: Evaluated on 100 closed-loop episodes in CARLA-Air Town10HD: joint success 77.0%; collaboration gain +27.0% over UAV-only baseline (50.0%); surpasses the strongest single-agent baseline (Travel UAV, 53.0%) by 24.0 points.
AI.conclusion: AGC-VLN demonstrates that training-free air-ground collaboration is feasible by decoupling semantic reasoning and geometric execution and by establishing a shared bird's-eye map as the collaboration interface. The observed performance gains stem from the complementary strengths of the UAV's global view and the UGV's road-following execution.

title: VeriPhy: Agentic Physical Reasoning for World Model Evaluation and Refinement
summary: Visual fluency in generated video does not imply physical reliability, and a scalar quality score alone is incapable of indicating the obligation a clip violates or the moment it fails. We present VeriPhy, an auditable physical-verification system in which a text-only planner compiles the prompt into typed physical obligations and a statically validated execution plan before any frame is observed. During execution, observations gate and scope only declared calls to frozen low-level experts (e.g., segmentation and tracking, counting, eleven typed physical measurements over the resulting tracks, depth, OCR, and audio-event detection). Each action returns a provenance-carrying evidence record whose payload, when usable, is either a typed measurement or an explicitly tagged learned state. Typed resolvers and fixed composition map usable records to a three-valued state (supported, contradicted, or unknown, surfaced as plausible, implausible, or abstain) with full provenance, so that every verdict is traceable to the evidence that produced it. We anchor evaluation in a 1,500-clip corpus of human-annotated flaw records that localize real generation failures in prompt reference, space, and time. On a 149-clip core carrying 304 such records, VeriPhy accounts for 228, against 164 for a published question-decomposition evaluator given the same clips and the same claims. Recall alone does not separate it from prompting the same backbone monolithically, which reaches 222; what separates them is that each decision retains its evidence record and provenance, making the traces auditable one verdict at a time and usable as the interface through which a critic verdict could be written back into generation.

AI.tldr: VeriPhy is an auditable physical-verification framework for generated video that attests each decision with provenance. A text planner derives typed physical obligations and a static execution plan before observing frames. During execution, only calls to fixed low-level experts are allowed, each producing provenance-bearing records. A three-valued resolver maps records to plausible/implausible/abstain with full provenance. Evaluated on a large corpus, VeriPhy yields more auditable verdicts than baselines and preserves evidence traces for critique and feedback into generation.
AI.motivation: Visual quality alone does not guarantee physical reliability or accountability in generated content; scalar quality scores fail to indicate when or which moment a clip violates constraints. There is a need for auditable, traceable verification of generation against explicit physical constraints.
AI.method: A text-only planner compiles the prompt into typed physical obligations and a statically validated execution plan before observing frames. During execution, observations gate only declared calls to frozen low-level experts (e.g., segmentation, tracking, counting, depth, OCR, audio-event detection). Each action returns a provenance-bearing evidence record whose payload is either a typed measurement or an explicitly tagged learned state. Typed resolvers and fixed composition map usable records to a three-valued state (supported, contradicted, or unknown) with full provenance; verdicts are traceable to the evidence.
AI.result: On a 1500-clip corpus of human-annotated flaw records, VeriPhy analyzes a core 149-clip set carrying 304 records and accounts for 228 flaws versus 164 by a published question-decomposition evaluator using the same clips. Recall alone cannot separate performance from monolithic prompting; however, each decision retains its evidence record and provenance, enabling auditable verdicts and potential critique feedback.
AI.conclusion: VeriPhy demonstrates auditable, provenance-backed verification for generated video, enabling traceable decisions and a pathway for critics to feed back into generation. The three-valued reasoning and explicit evidence allow robust accountability beyond scalar quality scores.

title: DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval: Evaluating Implicit Instruction Following in Full-Duplex Voice Agents
summary: Full-duplex voice agents must continuously decide when to listen, backchannel, interrupt, handle speech overlaps, take the floor, and yield. Existing benchmarks largely test these behaviors through explicit turn-management instructions, while deployed agents are often configured through roles or personas from which the appropriate conversational behavior must be inferred. We introduce DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval (DSB-IFEval) for evaluating implicit instruction-following in real-time spoken interaction. (DSB-IFEval) comprises 1,038 test cases spanning eight diverse assistant roles and evaluates five conditioning protocols for instruction-following: default behavior, explicit behavioral instructions, persona-implied behavior, combined persona--rule conditioning, and instruction conflict. We measure real-time floor management using a deterministic Instruction Adherence Score (IAS) and persona-consistent content using LLM-judged Persona Adherence Score (PAS). Across six real-time speech systems, we find architecture-dependent trade-offs. Full duplex models like F-Actor and PersonaPlex are more sensitive to whether conversational behavior is stated explicitly or must be inferred from a persona, with adherence dropping by 9.7% and 4.5%, respectively, under persona-only conditioning. In contrast, GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, and Fun-Audio-Chat strongly adhere to persona-consistent content, but their floor behavior does not adapt across explicit and persona-only instructions and remains constrained on several proactive actions. We further find that even if systems reliably follow conflicting directives to their prescribed persona, they still struggle to override them under safety conflict. These results show that inferring the behavior implied by a role, executing it at the appropriate conversational moment, and resolving competing instructions remain distinct challenges for full-duplex voice agents.

AI.tldr: DSB-IFEval is a real-time benchmark for implicit instruction-following in duplex speech agents, evaluating floor management and persona-consistent content across eight roles and five conditioning protocols, revealing architecture-dependent trade-offs and distinct challenges in inferring role behavior, timing actions, and resolving conflicting directives.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks emphasize explicit instruction-following; deployed agents rely on personas or roles, which necessitates evaluating how well agents infer and execute behavior implied by a persona in real-time conversation.
AI.method: 1,038 test cases across eight assistant roles; five conditioning protocols (default, explicit behavioral instructions, persona-implied behavior, combined persona–rule conditioning, instruction conflict); measurements include deterministic Instruction Adherence Score (IAS) for real-time floor management and LLM-judged Persona Adherence Score (PAS) for persona-consistent content; evaluated on six real-time speech systems (e.g., F-Actor, PersonaPlex, GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, Fun-Audio-Chat).
AI.result: Architecture-dependent trade-offs observed: full-duplex models (F-Actor, PersonaPlex) are sensitive to whether behavior is stated or inferred from a persona, with IAS drop of 9.7% and 4.5% under persona-only conditioning; GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, Fun-Audio-Chat adhere well to persona content but show limited adaptation in floor management across instruction types; even with adherence to prescribed persona, models struggle to override them under safety conflicts; indicates that inferring role behavior, timing actions, and resolving competing instructions are distinct, yet interconnected, challenges.
AI.conclusion: Inferring and executing persona-driven behavior in real time, while managing turn-taking and resolving conflicts, remains challenging; future work should decouple instruction-typing from floor-control dynamics and develop methods to flexibly adapt behavior to persona in the moment and handle conflicting directives without compromising safety.

title: No-Regret Bayesian Optimization with Finite-Library Input-Warped Kernels
summary: Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (GP-BO) excels at black-box optimization of costly functions, e.g., hyperparameter optimization (HPO) and multi-agent system (MAS) design. Convergence-rate guarantees exist for select methods, notably GP upper confidence bound (GP-UCB), but require a fixed kernel. Critically, the kernel encodes how input proximity affects objective value similarity. When raw coordinates poorly match this geometry - as with log-scaled hyperparameters or localized peaks - input warping can greatly improve sample efficiency, yet known GP-UCB proofs require a fixed kernel. We propose Finite-Library Input-Warped Bayesian Optimization (FLIWBO), which selects warps from a finite library of smooth input maps by any history-dependent rule. It adapts the input geometry to accelerate learning while retaining high-probability convergence guarantees under mild hypotheses, with an explicit $\sqrt(N_\varepsilon)$ library-size cost. Controlled diagnostics show that finite-library warping repairs planted geometry mismatches and identify FLIWBO failure cases. Across four repeated benchmarks - warped synthetic objectives, a confidence-fence trap, and Fashion-MNIST HPO - FLIWBO-UCB beats raw-coordinate GP-UCB under misspecified geometry, escapes traps that defeat even oracle-warp expected improvement, and recovers much of the gain from manual log scaling, while leading the tested methods that admit a matching regret guarantee. A 20-dimensional MAS design study further shows feasibility under costly noisy evaluations. Code for experiments is available: https://github.com/edvin-ketabati/bogp-paper-experiments.

AI.tldr: Finite-Library Input-Warped Bayesian Optimization (FLIWBO) introduces a finite library of smooth input warps to adapt input geometry within GP-BO, preserving high-probability convergence guarantees while improving sample efficiency under geometry misspecification.
AI.motivation: Kernel geometry critically influences GP-based optimization; fixed kernels struggle when raw coordinates poorly reflect objective similarity (e.g., log-scale hyperparameters, localized peaks). Input warping can align geometry and boost learning, but existing GP-UCB theory assumes a fixed kernel.
AI.method: FLIWBO selects warps from a finite library of smooth maps using a history-dependent rule and optimizes with a GP-UCB-like criterion in the warped input space. It retains convergence guarantees under mild assumptions, at a sqrt(N_epsilon) library-size cost. Diagnostics evaluate geometry repair and fail cases.
AI.result: Across synthetic warped objectives, a confidence-fence trap, Fashion-MNIST HPO, and a 20D MAS design study, FLIWBO-UCB outperforms raw-coordinate GP-UCB under misspecification, avoids traps that defeat oracle warps, captures much of manual log-scaling gains, and competes with methods that have regret guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Finite-library input warping is a practical, theory-backed approach to adapt input geometry in GP-BO, offering robustness to geometry mismatch while preserving convergence guarantees; suitable for costly, noisy evaluations and scalable to modest dimensionality.

title: BRIDGE: An Open-Source Humanoid Platform via Morphology-Control Co-Design for Physical AI
summary: Developing humanoid robots capable of leveraging human behavioral data is essential for general-purpose embodiment, yet conventional development remains bottlenecked by a decoupled paradigm that isolates hardware design from whole-body control. This approach leads to suboptimal systems that compromise human-like fluidity and agility. To bridge this gap, we introduce a data-driven morphology-control co-design framework that optimizes humanoid morphology for human-like movement. To quantify morphological fidelity, we also introduce a novel metric that jointly considers kinematic retargeting fidelity to human motion and dynamic tracking performance. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance across all metrics compared to baseline humanoids (Bumi, K1, and Toddlerbot). Finally, we realize this design in Bridge, an open-source, 88cm-tall humanoid platform released alongside its control policy. We demonstrate that Bridge captures human motion data with superior fidelity, exhibiting exceptional performance across foundational locomotion, robust balance, and highly dynamic maneuvers. Videos and open-source materials: https://sites.google.com/view/bridgerobot.

AI.tldr: Introduces a data-driven morphology-control co-design for humanoids, with a novel metric combining kinematic retargeting fidelity and dynamic tracking. Reports SOTA performance against Bumi, K1, Toddlerbot and presents Bridge, an 88 cm humanoid with open-source control policy and materials.
AI.motivation: Overcome the decoupled hardware-control paradigm that limits human-like fluidity by jointly optimizing morphology and control using human behavioral data.
AI.method: Proposes a data-driven co-design framework optimizing morphology and whole-body control; defines a metric that jointly evaluates retargeting fidelity to human motion and dynamic tracking; validates on a humanoid platform and demonstrates Bridge with released control policy and open-source materials.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated metrics compared to baselines; Bridge demonstrates high-fidelity motion capture and robust locomotion, balance, and dynamic maneuvers; videos and materials released.
AI.conclusion: The co-design framework plus open-source Bridge platform substantiate practical, data-driven pathways toward more human-like humanoid motion and accelerate reproducibility through open resources.

title: Who Speaks for the Pruned? Visual Token Pruning as Coverage Optimization
summary: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of vision-language models (VLMs), but most methods only ask which tokens to keep. This retained-token view can keep redundant high-scoring tokens while leaving discarded evidence without a close representative. We propose CoverPruner, a training-free pruner that asks the complementary demand-side question: after a token is removed, which surviving original token represents it for the target VLM? CoverPruner formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM), covering the full projected visual-token set with query-weighted demand. It instantiates RCM with projector-space coverage and a lightweight first-layer attention probe. Across multiple VLM architectures and compression rates, CoverPruner achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods, with the largest gains usually appearing under aggressive compression.

AI.tldr: Proposes CoverPruner, a training-free token pruner reframing pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM) using a demand-side perspective; achieves state-of-the-art average accuracy, especially under aggressive compression.
AI.motivation: Current token pruning focuses on selecting tokens to keep, which can retain redundant high-scoring tokens and discard evidence without a close representative. A complementary, demand-driven view aims to ensure discarded tokens are representable by the remaining tokens to improve robustness under compression.
AI.method: Introduce Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM) for pruning. The method maximizes coverage of the projected visual-token space by a query-weighted demand. It instantiates RCM with projector-space coverage and a lightweight first-layer attention probe, and is training-free.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across multiple vision-language model architectures and compression rates shows CoverPruner achieves the best average accuracy among compared methods, with the largest gains under aggressive compression.
AI.conclusion: CoverPruner provides a training-free, demand-side pruning framework that improves token pruning by ensuring representational coverage, delivering superior performance across VLMs and compression levels.

title: Do GUI Agents Know When Not to Act? Enabling Conflict-Aware Termination for Multimodal GUI Agents
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are increasingly used to execute natural-language instructions on user interfaces, yet real users may issue infeasible instructions due to benign mistakes. A reliable agent should not only know how to act, but also when not to act. In this work, we introduce CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark covering instruction-internal conflicts and instruction-GUI context conflicts to study conflict-aware termination. Our evaluation reveals severe execution-biased overcompliance: agents that perform well on feasible tasks often continue to execute blindly under conflicting instructions. To mitigate this behavior, we propose CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework that aligns an agent's feasibility awareness with its action generation. CONFLICTGUARD contains two coupled components: a feasibility verification protocol that guides the agent to assess instruction logic and GUI-side evidence before acting, and a conditional action modulation mechanism that steers agents from over-compliant execution into termination-oriented behavior. Experiments across five widely-used agents demonstrate that CONFLICTGUARD improves average conflict task success rate significantly, while preserving normal GUI-task performance. These results validate that a lightweight inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI Agent's competence to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions.

AI.tldr: Introduce CONFLICTGUI to study conflict-aware termination in GUI agents and propose CONFLICTGUARD to mitigate overcompliance via feasibility verification and action modulation, improving conflict-task success while preserving normal GUI performance.
AI.motivation: GUI agents often receive infeasible instructions or context-conflicting guidance, leading to execution bias where agents continue acting despite conflicts. A reliable agent should know when not to act to ensure user safety and task quality.
AI.method: Propose CONFLICTGUI as a benchmark with instruction-internal and instruction-GUI context conflicts. Develop CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework with (1) a feasibility verification protocol to assess instruction logic and GUI evidence, and (2) a conditional action modulation mechanism to shift from over-compliance to termination-oriented behavior. Evaluations span five commonly used GUI agents.
AI.result: Found severe execution-biased overcompliance: strong performance on feasible tasks does not transfer to conflicting instructions. CONFLICTGUARD significantly improves average conflict-task success rates across agents while maintaining performance on standard GUI tasks.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight, inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI agents’ ability to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions without sacrificing normal task performance.

title: Evaluating Graph Neural Networks for Change-Criticality Classification in Maritime Navigation Charts
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS) 2026
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a class of neural networks suitable for learning on graph-structured data. Their application to spatial data is a natural extension, however its relatively unclear which message-passing operations, architectural configurations, and graph representation is best suited for classifying changes to objects in electronic navigational charts (ENCs)--geospatial vector datasets used for marine navigation. Maintaining these datasets is a challenge, and categorizing changes to objects in the ENC based on their significance to navigational safety is of particular importance. Here, we propose to represent these vector navigation datasets as a graph structure where the spatial objects serve as nodes and their spatial and semantic relationships form edges. We encode both the old ENC dataset and new ENC dataset into a pair of graphs and frame the task as a graph-pair classification problem. Building on this representation, we investigate the use of GNN architectures to classify whether the encoded graphs constitutes a critical or non-critical risk to navigational safety. We train and evaluate several GNN architectures and model configurations on ENC changes reviewed by maritime experts. Our results demonstrate that graph-based representations improve the classification of ENC updates, providing a scalable approach for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.

AI.tldr: Graph neural networks applied to ENC changes by representing ENCs as graphs and framing as graph-pair classification to detect critical navigational risk; results show improved classification and scalable maintenance workflows.
AI.motivation: To determine effective GNN architectures and graph representations for classifying changes in spatial ENC data, aiding maintenance and safety-critical decision-making.
AI.method: Represent ENC objects as graph nodes and their spatial/semantic relationships as edges to form a pair of graphs (old vs new ENC). Cast the problem as graph-pair classification and evaluate multiple GNN architectures/configurations on expert-labeled ENC changes.
AI.result: Graph-based representations improved classification performance for ENC updates and offer a scalable, automated/assistive approach for ENC maintenance workflows.
AI.conclusion: A graph-based encoding of ENC changes is effective for categorizing navigational safety risk and can support automation and efficiency in ENC maintenance.

title: TRaIL-Odom: Tightly Coupled Continuous Time Radar-IMU-LiDAR Odometry with Adaptive Doppler Weighting
comment: Accepted for publication at the IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters on 23 August, 2026
summary: Existing radar-LiDAR fusion methods rely on fixed residual weights, even though the informativeness of radar Doppler and LiDAR geometry is scan- and direction-dependent, leading to uniform radar weighting that misallocates Doppler information across translational directions. To address this limitation, we propose two degeneracy-aware Doppler reweighting modules within a tightly coupled Radar-IMU-LiDAR odometry framework: per-point radar reweighting and scan-wise radar gain scheduling. Since geometric degeneracy is directional, we first identify weak translational directions from the LiDAR geometry and reweight individual radar Doppler constraints based on their alignment with the weak subspace. We further adjust the overall radar contribution using LiDAR geometric anisotropy such that radar is emphasized when LiDAR observability is poor and suppressed when LiDAR constraints are already reliable. Across 13 evaluated sequences, TRaIL-Odom achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with clear advantages in geometrically degenerate scenes. In ablation experiments on three degenerate sequences, combining the two adaptive weighting modules reduces RMSE ATE and RTE by 86.0% and 78.5% relative to the fixed-weight baseline. We make our code and an accompanying dataset publicly available at https://github.com/ChiyunNoh/TRaIL-Odom.

AI.tldr: Adaptive, degeneracy-aware Doppler reweighting for Radar-IMU-LiDAR odometry improves accuracy, especially in geometrically degenerate scenes.
AI.motivation: Fixed residual weights in radar-LiDAR fusion ignore directional informativity of radar Doppler and LiDAR geometry, causing misallocation of Doppler information across directions in degenerate scenes.
AI.method: Introduce two reweighting modules within a tightly coupled Radar-IMU-LiDAR odometry: (1) per-point radar reweighting based on alignment with weak translational directions identified from LiDAR geometry, and (2) scan-wise radar gain scheduling that adjusts overall radar contribution using LiDAR geometric anisotropy.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art overall performance across 13 sequences, with substantial improvements in geometrically degenerate scenes. Ablation on three degenerate sequences shows RMSE ATE and RTE reductions of 86.0% and 78.5% relative to a fixed-weight baseline.
AI.conclusion: Degeneracy-aware Doppler reweighting effectively leverages radar information when LiDAR observability is poor and suppresses it when LiDAR constraints are reliable, enabling robust Radar-IMU-LiDAR odometry. Code and dataset are publicly available.

title: RoboTok: An Internet-Scale Data Engine for Human Demonstration Retrieval and Dexterous Manipulation Learning
summary: Robot learning increasingly depends on broad and diverse demonstrations, yet collecting robot data remains expensive and poorly suited to covering the long tail of real-world tasks. To address this bottleneck, we introduce RoboTok, an internet-scale data engine that, given a query human manipulation video, retrieves manipulation-relevant human demonstrations from web videos for training dexterous robot policies. Specifically, we learn a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories expressed in estimated actor-centered reference frames. This representation enables manipulation behaviors to be compared across variations in camera viewpoint, scene appearance, and actor occlusions, while remaining compact enough for efficient search and continual indexing over internet-scale video collections. We evaluate RoboTok against existing robot-data retrieval approaches on retrieval benchmarks and downstream robot policy performance. Our results show that RoboTok retrieves more relevant manipulation demonstrations and improves downstream task success, establishing hand-pose trajectory-aware retrieval as a way to make web video a scalable and continuously growing source of supervision for robot learning.

AI.tldr: RoboTok learns a latent hand-trajectory space to retrieve manipulation demonstrations from web videos, enabling scalable, viewpoint- and occlusion-invariant search to train dexterous robot policies.
AI.motivation: Robotic data collection is costly and often fails to cover the long tail of real-world tasks. Web-scale demonstrations offer diverse supervision if retrievable, reducing data bottlenecks.
AI.method: Construct a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories in actor-centered frames, making representations robust to camera viewpoint, scene appearance, and occlusions. Use this space for efficient search and continual indexing over large video collections; retrieve demonstrations by query video and train robot policies.
AI.result: RoboTok achieves higher relevance in retrieved manipulations than baselines and improves downstream policy performance, demonstrating the value of hand-pose trajectory–aware retrieval for leveraging web videos as supervision.
AI.conclusion: Hand-pose trajectory–aware retrieval can scale robot learning by continuously leveraging internet video data to train dexterous manipulation policies.

title: Beyond "Made with AI": Visualizing Provenance Density to Mitigate the Transparency Penalty
summary: As generative AI makes polished prose cheap to produce, users can no longer rely on fluency as a proxy for truth. We call this failure mode the Fluency Trap: users trust fluent hallucinations while also discounting accurate content once it is disclosed as AI-generated. Binary ``Made with AI'' labels respond with authorship disclosure, but they do not show what supports a claim. We propose Provenance Density, an evidence-visualization interface that shows the density of verified claims in a text. In a user study with 81 participants, an idealized Provenance Density interface produced a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication ($+4.15$ points, $d=1.82$), whereas participants given no signal showed no detectable discrimination. A technical audit with 200 samples shows that retrieval density alone is insufficient; unexpectedly, the Consistency Veto carries most of the discriminative signal on dynamic queries. As AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from human writing, effective transparency must move from authorship disclosure toward evidence visualization.

AI.tldr: Proposes Provenance Density, an evidence-visualization interface that shows the density of verified claims in a text, to counter the Fluency Trap where fluent AI-generated content misleads readers. User study finds a large truth-vs-fabrication discrimination gap with Provenance Density; a technical audit shows retrieval density alone is insufficient and that a Consistency Veto provides most discriminative signal for dynamic queries; authors argue transparency should move from authorship labels to evidence visualization.
AI.motivation: As generative AI enables fluent, potentially false content, simplistic authorship disclosures fail to reveal what supports a claim. The work seeks a transparent, evidence-based interface to help users assess truth in AI-generated text.
AI.method: Two-part evaluation: (1) a user study with 81 participants comparing an idealized Provenance Density interface to no signal, measuring discrimination between truth and fabrication (reported as a score difference and effect size). (2) a technical audit with 200 samples analyzing the contribution of retrieval density versus the Consistency Veto on dynamic queries.
AI.result: The Provenance Density interface produced a large discrimination gap (+4.15 points, d=1.82) between truth and fabrication; participants with no signal showed no detectable discrimination. Retrieval density alone was insufficient; the Consistency Veto carried most of the discriminative signal in dynamic queries.
AI.conclusion: Transparency for AI-generated text should shift from binary authorship labels to evidence visualization that highlights the density and consistency of verified claims, improving users’ ability to distinguish truth from fabrication as AI content becomes indistinguishable from human writing.

title: Verify Before You Distill: Prompt-Level Teacher Gating for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) accelerates post-training by providing dense token-level supervision from a frozen teacher on the student's own rollouts. Vanilla OPD applies this supervision uniformly across prompts, without checking whether the teacher is reliable for each prompt. Because reverse KL is mode-seeking, a confidently wrong teacher can induce a strong yet misleading update. Distributional proxies, such as entropy or teacher-student likelihood agreement, measure uncertainty or agreement but do not directly verify outcome correctness. We introduce Teacher-Gated On-Policy Distillation (TGOPD), built on the principle that teacher reliability should be verified at the prompt level before dense supervision is admitted. TGOPD estimates reliability from a small set of verifier-scored teacher probes and routes each prompt exclusively to dense OPD when the reliability check passes or to verifier-grounded GRPO otherwise. Across 4B and 35B students in mathematics, code, and instruction following, TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD in all six single-domain settings and achieves higher seven-benchmark averages at both scales under multi-domain training. By using otherwise-idle teacher capacity for reliability estimation, TGOPD also reduces teacher-side compute waste in asynchronous OPD, increasing teacher-node GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9% in the measured 4B single-domain run.

AI.tldr: TGOPD gates on-policy distillation with a prompt-level reliability check before applying dense supervision, routing unreliable prompts to a verifier-grounded GRPO. It improves performance across single- and multi-domain settings and significantly increases teacher utilization by leveraging verifier probes.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision but is susceptible to misleading updates when the teacher is overconfident yet wrong (mode-seeking via reverse KL). Existing distributional proxies (entropy, agreement) do not directly verify outcome correctness, risking degraded downstream performance. A reliable gating mechanism at the prompt level could shield student learning from unreliable teacher guidance while improving efficiency.
AI.method: TGOPD estimates teacher reliability using a small set of verifier-scored teacher probes. Each prompt is routed to dense OPD only if reliability checks pass; otherwise, it uses verifier-grounded GRPO (a verification-based policy gradient objective). The approach is evaluated on 4B and 35B student models across mathematics, code, and instruction following, comparing against Vanilla OPD in six single-domain settings and multi-domain training.
AI.result: TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD across all six single-domain settings and achieves higher seven-benchmark averages under multi-domain training. It also increases teacher-node GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9% in the measured 4B single-domain run by utilizing idle teacher capacity for reliability estimation.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-level reliability gating for OPD can mitigate the risk of confidently wrong teachers biasing updates, deliver better domain transfer in multi-domain training, and significantly improve teacher-resource efficiency. The approach demonstrates practical gains in accuracy and compute utilization, suggesting broader applicability to on-policy supervision frameworks.

title: Toward Physically Grounded JEPA World Models for Goal-Conditioned Robotic Planning
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to the IROS 2026 Workshop on Physical World Models for Scaling Embodied AI (PWMS 2026)
summary: Action-conditioned JEPA world models enable planning toward visually specified goals without reconstructing future pixels, yet latent prediction alone does not explicitly encourage the learned representations to retain information relevant to robotic control. We introduce an end-to-end JEPA world model that augments latent prediction with inverse dynamics (IDM) and state alignment (SA). While inverse dynamics discourages latent collapse and makes latent transitions informative of the actions that produced them, state alignment grounds consecutive representations in their associated physical configuration and motion. Across four benchmark tasks, our model attains the highest success rates on TwoRoom (100%), PushT (98%), and OGBench-Cube (87%), while performing comparably to LeWorldModel on Reacher. Our ablation further shows that adding state alignment consistently improves planning success over IDM alone across all four tasks. Although LeWorldModel, our primary baseline, attains higher average straightening on OGBench-Cube, transition-subspace analysis shows that its transition energy is concentrated in a substantially lower-dimensional subspace. Our state-aligned model exhibits a higher effective transition dimension than LeWorldModel and improves planning over IDM alone, supporting state alignment as an effective complement to inverse dynamics for robotic planning.

AI.tldr: Augments JEPA world models with inverse dynamics and state alignment to improve planning for visually specified goals; achieves strong task performance and higher transition-dimensionality than a LeWorldModel baseline.
AI.motivation: Latent predictive models often suffer latent collapse or lose control-relevant information. Grounding latent dynamics in actions (inverse dynamics) and physical state (state alignment) aims to retain control-relevant structure for planning toward visual goals.
AI.method: End-to-end JEPA world model augmented with inverse dynamics (IDM) and state alignment (SA). Comprehensive ablations across Four tasks (TwoRoom, PushT, Reacher, OGBench-Cube) comparing against LeWorldModel. Analyze transition subspaces to assess energy distribution and effective dimensionality of latent transitions.
AI.result: The proposed model achieves top-tier success: TwoRoom 100%, PushT 98%, OGBench-Cube 87%; Reacher on par with LeWorldModel. Ablation shows SA consistently improves planning over IDM alone. LeWorldModel shows higher average straightening but concentrates transition energy in a lower-dimensional subspace; the SA model exhibits a higher effective transition dimension. Overall, SA complements IDM to enhance planning performance.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating state alignment with IDM yields more informative and physically grounded latent representations, improving planning across tasks. Transition-subspace analysis suggests richer latent dynamics under SA, supporting its role as a beneficial augmentation for robotic planning. Further work could explore unsupervised or weakly supervised SA signals and generalization to more complex tasks.

title: Learning to Zoom Efficiently with a Contrastive Curriculum
summary: Using a zoom-in tool is an important foundational part of modern visual agents, because it allows to efficiently handle tasks involving high-resolution images. Most previous methods need an extensive warm-start supervised fine-tuning phase for teaching models zoom-in. We show that this is not necessary by proposing a new intrinsic reward for learning tool use in MLLMs without the need for additional labels or warm-start SFT. Our InfoNCE-style reward uses a curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls as a contrastive training signal. Empirical experiments on $V^*$, HRBench and MME-RealWorld show that our approach is competitive while being more efficient. When used as a drop-in replacement for SFT, we even outperform all baselines. To directly measure the zoom-in ability of models, we further introduce the scalable synthetic Muffin&Chihuahua (M&C) dataset. Each image consists of a grid with every cell either showing a muffin or chihuahua. Leveraging the M&C dataset's unique region of interest labels, we find that recall is the metric that most strongly correlates the zoom-in region with final task performance. Our model and code for reproduction is publicly available under https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2026-zoom-in

AI.tldr: Introduces an intrinsic InfoNCE-style reward to learn zoom-in tool use in multimodal LLMs without extra labels or warm-start SFT; provides the Muffin&Chihuahua (M&C) dataset for measuring zoom-in; shows competitive or superior results and code publication.
AI.motivation: Eliminate dependence on extensive warm-start supervised fine-tuning for teaching models to zoom in on high-resolution imagery in visual agents, by using an intrinsic, curriculum-based contrastive signal.
AI.method: Proposes an InfoNCE-style intrinsic reward with a curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls as a contrastive training signal. Trains multimodal LLMs on V*, HRBench, and MME-RealWorld datasets. Uses the approach as a drop-in replacement for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Introduces the M&C dataset—synthetic muffins and chihuahuas arranged on a grid with region-of-interest labels—to evaluate zoom-in ability, and analyzes recall as the metric most predictive of final task performance.
AI.result: The method is competitive across benchmarks and, when used as a drop-in for SFT, outperforms baselines. The M&C dataset enables scalable measurement of zoom-in ability, with recall showing strong correlation to task performance.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic reward-based learning can reduce or eliminate the need for warm-start SFT in teaching zoom-in behaviors for visual agents, and the M&C dataset provides a scalable, ROI-labeled benchmark for evaluating zoom-in. Public code is provided for reproducibility.

title: AutoGraphForge: Towards Automated Graph Theory Discovery
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to ITAT 2026 (Information Technologies -- Applications and Theory), CEUR Workshop Proceedings. Code: https://github.com/JanPastorek/AutoGraphForge
summary: We report on our ongoing project to develop a computational pipeline, AutoGraphForge, for an automated graph-theoretic conjecturing-refuting-formalizing-proving system. Conjecture generation is counterexample-guided and runs in rounds: a Graffiti3 generator proposes conjectures over a small, evolving snapshot table $T$ (initially a few hundred graphs with their computed invariants) that grows only by counterexamples to its own conjectures. A novelty filter of $559$ classical and folklore relations, closed under transitive composition and linear identity substitution, decides via a linear program whether a candidate is already implied by known results. Surviving candidates are tested against a dataset of about $348,000$ graphs, unioning the complete House of Graphs invariant export, the exhaustive census of all connected graphs on at most nine vertices, several extremal families (strongly regular, minimal Ramsey, Cayley, cages, barbells, lollipops, spiders), and random models. Counterexample-search algorithms then attack the remainder. Run for several rounds on an HPC cluster, the loop yields $6,522$ conjectures that survived the refutation dataset, the novelty filter and every active-search run -- among them nontrivial relations between the annihilation number and the edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs, which we prove by hand. A subsequent formalization and proving stage deterministically translates each surviving conjecture into a Lean 4 statement skeleton; every candidate proof is kernel-verified against a pinned mathlib4 and our custom invariant preamble. This stage integrates two neural provers -- DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B (served with vLLM) and the Lean-specialised OProver-32B -- behind the independent kernel check. It is implemented end-to-end and passes initial sanity checks, with the full pipeline currently running on the cluster.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end pipeline AutoGraphForge automates conjecturing, refuting, formalizing, and proving in graph theory, combining counterexample-guided conjecture generation, a novelty filter, large-scale testing, and Lean-based formal proofs with neural provers.
AI.motivation: To accelerate discovery and verification of nontrivial graph-theoretic conjectures by integrating data-driven conjecture generation, rigorous filtering, exhaustive testing, and machine-assisted formal proofs.
AI.method: Iterative loop: Graffiti3 generates conjectures on a dynamic table T of graphs; novelty filter (559 relations, transitive and linear substitutions) prunes redundant conjectures via linear programming; surviving candidates tested against ~348k graphs including complete House of Graphs invariants, all connected graphs up to nine vertices, extremal families, and random models; counterexample search to prune further; rounds on HPC yield 6,522 surviving conjectures; hand-proof of relations (e.g., annihilation vs edge-cover) where found; formalization translates survivors into Lean 4 skeletons; kernel-verified proofs against mathlib4 and invariant preamble; neural provers (DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B with vLLM, and OProver-32B) integrated behind the kernel check; end-to-end pipeline running on cluster.
AI.result: Discovered 6,522 surviving conjectures; proved a novel relation between the annihilation number and the edge-cover number for bipartite/regular graphs; demonstrated feasibility of an end-to-end automated conjecturing-to-proving pipeline including neural provers and formal verification; pipeline currently active on HPC cluster.
AI.conclusion: Shows feasibility and scalability of automated graph-theoretic conjecturing and formal proving, bridging data-driven conjecture generation, logical filtering, and machine-assisted formal proofs; suggests potential for broader adoption and further improvements in search, verification, and prover integration.

title: Causal Foundation Models
summary: Causal inference is the practice of estimating the effect of a treatment or intervention from data. It traditionally requires a bespoke pipeline for every new problem: first proposing a causal mechanism, selecting a compatible estimator, and finally training it. Meanwhile, across diverse settings and modalities, much of machine learning has shifted to the paradigm of foundation models: networks pretrained once at scale and applied to new tasks without fine-tuning. Causal foundation models (CFMs) bring this paradigm to causal inference. CFMs are pretrained neural networks that estimate causal quantities, such as the average treatment effect, on entirely new datasets using in-context learning without requiring model updates. This work provides a practical introduction to this emerging area. We summarize the necessary background in causal inference and machine learning before discussing CFMs. Throughout, we include example code and Jupyter notebooks.

AI.tldr: CFMs apply the foundation-model paradigm to causal inference, enabling pretrained networks to estimate causal quantities on new datasets via in-context learning without fine-tuning; the paper offers a practical introduction with background and runnable code.
AI.motivation: To reduce bespoke, problem-specific pipelines in causal inference by leveraging reusable pretrained models that generalize across tasks and modalities.
AI.method: Survey CFMs conceptually, outline background in causal inference and ML, describe how CFMs are trained and used for causal estimands, and present example code and Jupyter notebooks.
AI.result: Provides a practical introduction to CFMs in causal inference, with concrete guidance and runnable examples.
AI.conclusion: CFMs offer a scalable pathway to perform causal analysis on unseen data without retraining; the article facilitates adoption through tutorials and code.

title: Scaling Bimanual Household Manipulation from 1,500 hours of Demonstrations to On-Policy Corrections
summary: Learning generalist policies for robust bimanual manipulation is bottlenecked by the scarcity of high quality large scale human demonstration data. In this work, we release 1,500 hours of diverse bimanual manipulation demonstrations covering everyday household tasks, and use this comprehensive corpus to train XR-2, a powerful vision-language-action (VLA) model. Enabled by a purpose built high throughput data pipeline and a carefully designed multi stage training paradigm, XR-2 attains strong manipulation performance in our systematic experiments while retaining favorable training efficiency and high data utilization. We further study two critical scaling axes: varying the amount of expert demonstration data, and post training on DAgger correction data from real time human interventions. In both settings, task success rate improves steadily over the data ranges we probe, exhibiting a clear consistent scaling trend at our current data scale. These results validate both the learning capacity of XR-2 and the promising scaling properties of the released dataset, which we open source to support reproducible research on bimanual robot manipulation learning.

AI.tldr: XR-2 uses 1500 hours of diverse bimanual demonstrations to train a vision-language-action model, achieving strong manipulation performance with scalable gains via data and DAgger corrections; dataset released as open source.
AI.motivation: To overcome the scarcity of high-quality large-scale human demonstration data for generalist, robust bimanual manipulation policies and to explore scaling with more data and corrective feedback.
AI.method: Assemble 1.5k hours of diverse bimanual manipulation demonstrations, train XR-2 a vision-language-action model using a purpose-built high-throughput data pipeline and a multi-stage training paradigm; study data-scale effects by varying expert data and post-training with DAgger corrections from real-time human interventions; open-source the dataset.
AI.result: XR-2 achieves strong manipulation performance, with efficient training and high data utilization; scaling trends show task success improves with more expert demonstrations and with DAgger-corrected data; dataset released to support reproducible research.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the learnability and scalable potential of large, diverse demonstration data for VLA-based bimanual manipulation policies, and the released dataset supports reproducible research and further scaling.

title: ProgResViT: Progressive Resolution and Width for Adaptive Vision Transformers
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) typically process every image using a fixed input resolution and model width, even though many images can be classified with substantially less computation. We introduce ProgResViT, an input-adaptive ViT that performs inference progressively across multiple rounds. The first round processes a low-resolution image with a narrow subnetwork. Inference terminates when the prediction is sufficiently confident; otherwise, the model reuses the representations produced in the current round and proceeds with a higher-resolution input and a wider subnetwork to refine its prediction. As all rounds share a single backbone, we propose Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG), which conditions token fusion and layer outputs on the current round, block, and input resolution. On image classification, applying ProgResViT to DeiT yields better accuracy-compute trade-offs than adaptive-width, adaptive-depth, and dynamic-token baselines. With knowledge distillation, a DeiT-based ProgResViT achieves 84.9% top-1 accuracy, slightly exceeding the reported DeiT-III-S accuracy under a comparable evaluation setting. We show that the same design also provides favorable accuracy-compute trade-offs for self-supervised DINO representations and downstream semantic segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/ds-kiel/ProgResViT.

AI.tldr: Progressive input-adaptive ViT (ProgResViT) reduces compute by performing multiple rounds of inference, starting from low resolution and narrow subnetwork, progressively increasing resolution and width until confident; uses Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG) to fuse tokens and outputs across rounds with a shared backbone. It achieves favorable accuracy-compute trade-offs on DeiT-based classification (84.9% top-1 with distillation), and also benefits self-supervised DINO representations and semantic segmentation; code released.
AI.motivation: Standard ViTs process every image at a fixed input size and model width, wasting compute on easy or small images. An adaptive, progressive scheme can save compute while maintaining or improving accuracy, by terminating early for confident predictions and refining difficult cases.
AI.method: Progressive inference across rounds: round 1 uses low-resolution input with a narrow subnetwork; if the prediction is uncertain, reuse internal representations and proceed to the next round with higher-resolution input and a wider subnetwork. All rounds share a single backbone. Introduce Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG) that conditions token fusion and layer outputs on the current round, block, and input resolution. Train with or without knowledge distillation from a teacher (DeiT) and evaluate on ImageNet-classification; also apply to self-supervised DINO representations and semantic segmentation.
AI.result: Reported improved accuracy–compute trade-offs compared to adaptive-width, adaptive-depth, and dynamic-token baselines for classification. With knowledge distillation, a DeiT-based ProgResViT achieves 84.9% top-1 accuracy. Also shows favorable performance on DINO and segmentation tasks. Code released at the provided URL.
AI.conclusion: ProgResViT demonstrates that a single backbone with progressive, round-conditioned gating can deliver efficient and accurate ViT inference, adaptable to multiple tasks (classification, self-supervised representations, segmentation). The approach offers better compute efficiency without sacrificing accuracy and provides a practical, reusable framework for dynamic ViT inference.

title: Making Every Tool Call Count: Necessary Tool-Evidence Path Rewards for Agentic Vision-Language Models
summary: Modern vision-language models (VLMs) can directly answer many image-grounded questions, yet they often struggle with complex queries requiring fine-grained visual details or external knowledge. To acquire this missing evidence, agentic VLMs invoke tools such as image cropping, image search, and text search. However, existing training paradigms primarily evaluate tool-use based on final answer correctness, leaving evidence acquisition and utilization insufficiently supervised. This leads to two critical shortcomings: (i) models frequently issue redundant or off-target tool calls that fail to gather necessary evidence, and (ii) even when appropriate tools are called, models often fail to extract the necessary information from the resulting observations. To address these limitations, we introduce the NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), a novel annotation scheme that explicitly specifies the essential external evidence and corresponding tool calls for each query. Building upon this, we propose NTEP-R (NTEP Reward), a supervision mechanism ensuring that each tool invocation strictly advances the reasoning process toward the final solution. Specifically, our approach rewards the agent for aligning its pre-call intent with a necessary evidence-seeking goal, and for ensuring the information summarized from the post-call observation aligns with the necessary evidence. Furthermore, we introduce a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant calls that revisit satisfied NTEP goals. Extensive evaluations on seven image-grounded benchmarks demonstrate that our 8B-parameter instantiation, NTEP-8B, significantly improves both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency within a unified three-tool framework. These results highlight the critical value of fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision for training robust agentic VLMs.

AI.tldr: NTEP introduces a fine-grained tool-evidence path annotation (NTEP) and a reward mechanism (NTEP-R) to supervise tool use in agentic vision-language models, plus a non-repeated-goal regularizer. An 8B-parameter instantiation (NTEP-8B) achieves improved search accuracy and tool-use efficiency across seven benchmarks within a three-tool framework.
AI.motivation: Current VLM tool-use supervision emphasizes final answers, neglecting the evidence acquisition path. Complex queries require targeted evidence gathered via external tools, but redundant/off-target tool calls and poor extraction from observations hinder performance.
AI.method: 1) Propose NTEP annotation specifying essential external evidence and corresponding tool calls per query. 2) Propose NTEP-R rewards aligning pre-call intent with necessary-evidence goals and ensuring post-call evidence aligns with those goals. 3) Introduce a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize revisiting satisfied goals. 4) Evaluate an 8B-parameter model (NTEP-8B) on seven image-grounded benchmarks using a three-tool framework.
AI.result: NTEP-8B shows significant gains in search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency, demonstrating the value of fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision for agentic VLMs.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained supervision of tool-evidence paths (NTEP) is a effective paradigm for training robust agentic VLMs; the combination with NTEP-R rewards and the non-repeated-goal regularizer yields improved evidence-driven tool use.

title: ObserverBench: Testing Mechanistic Estimates for Intervention and Control
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures. Code, benchmark, leaderboards, and submission interface: https://kwisatzh.github.io/observerbench/. Frozen artifact release: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22136091
summary:
Mechanistic interpretability is increasingly used to guide interventions such as activation steering, circuit removal, and safety monitoring. Yet an internal estimate that is accurate on average can still choose a poor action.
  We present ObserverBench, a benchmark framework for testing whether an internal estimator---an observer---is adequate for the intervention, control, or safety task it directs. Each task fixes the model, information boundary, allowed actions, decision rule, held-out cases, and loss. The benchmark reports estimation accuracy separately from the loss caused by the chosen action.
  Theory and experiments show why both are needed. In closed-loop control, observer errors matter at the starting point and along directions the allowed intervention can reach. On circuit-intervention tasks in GPT-2-small and Qwen2.5-7B, pairwise observers predict unseen effects more accurately without always choosing better actions; observers trained on action loss choose lower-loss actions. In safety triage, a score that perfectly separates violations can allocate a fixed intervention budget poorly when violations have different costs. Across Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B-it, and prospectively frozen Qwen3.5-9B APPS tasks, AUROC can rank monitors differently from deployment loss, and the best information source changes across models. Sparse SAE readouts also trail their layer-matched dense controls on the reported Qwen panels, under disclosed activation-density or checkpoint mismatches.
