  ObserverBench provides fixed task contracts, runnable baselines, and table-based submissions for evaluating interpretability methods through the actions they enable.

AI.tldr: ObserverBench benchmarks internal estimators (observers) for sufficiency in guiding interventions, uncovering that high estimation accuracy does not always yield better actions; highlights the need to consider action loss and model-specific dynamics in interpretability tests.
AI.motivation: To decouple observer quality from deployment impact and provide a fair, fixed-task framework to evaluate interpretability methods under actionable constraints.
AI.method: Introduce ObserverBench: fixed task contracts (model, information boundary, actions, decision rule, held-out cases, loss), run baselines, and require table-based submissions. Evaluate across tasks: closed-loop control, circuit intervention, and safety triage, with multiple models (GPT-2-small, Qwen variants, Gemma, APPS tasks). Compare estimation accuracy vs deployment loss, assess sparse vs dense readouts, and analyze how information sources rank differently by AUROC vs actual loss.
AI.result: Observers often predict unseen effects better yet not always yield better actions; action-loss-trained observers can choose lower-loss actions; AUROC-based monitor rankings diverge from deployment loss rankings; best information source varies across models; sparse SAE readouts can underperform layer-matched dense controls under disclosure constraints; results underscore divergence between estimation-quality metrics and real-world interventions.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating interpretability methods requires joint consideration of estimator accuracy and downstream action loss within fixed task contracts; observer performance is model- and task-dependent, with action optimization sometimes conflicting with pure estimation accuracy, necessitating careful benchmark design and reporting.

title: FailBench: How Reliable are VLMs at Judging Robot Task Success?
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate robot manipulation outcomes, but existing benchmarks offer limited evidence of cross-domain generalization. We introduce FailBench, a benchmark for robot failure detection comprising 2,197 manipulation attempts across 14 public sources (12 real-world, 2 simulated). In FailBench, 75% of failures occur naturally, and six real-world sources come from non-failure-detection datasets. Evaluating 13 VLM-based detectors, we find the best model achieves only 0.77 mean balanced accuracy. Notably, models fine-tuned for failure detection consistently underperform general-purpose VLMs and their own pretrained baselines. Performance depends heavily on required visual evidence: models approach saturation when outcomes depend on observable object motion, but degrade to near-chance (<0.60 balanced accuracy) on contact-intensive assembly tasks. Error analysis reveals a systematic bias toward predicting success under ambiguous evidence, which persists even with increased reasoning effort. Finally, we show that input-level intervention--spatially localizing and cropping outcome-relevant regions--improves the top detector by 2.4 percentage points without extra training.

AI.tldr: FailBench: a cross-domain benchmark for robot failure detection using vision-language models (VLMs); 2,197 manipulation attempts from 14 public sources; the best VLM detector achieves 0.77 mean balanced accuracy; task- and evidence-dependence highlight limits of current models; failure-tuned detectors underperform general-purpose VLMs; input-level localization improves top detector by 2.4 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Assess cross-domain generalization of vision-language models for detecting robot manipulation failures, addressing the gap where existing benchmarks rely on limited domains or synthetic data.
AI.method: Assemble FailBench from 14 public sources (12 real-world, 2 simulated) totaling 2,197 manipulation attempts. Evaluate 13 VLM-based detectors on failure detection, report mean balanced accuracy. Conduct error analysis to identify bias and evidence dependencies. Test input-level intervention by spatially localizing and cropping outcome-relevant regions to measure performance changes.
AI.result: Best detector achieves 0.77 mean balanced accuracy. Failure-detection fine-tuning consistently underperforms general-purpose VLMs and their pretrained baselines. Performance is higher when observable object motion is decisive and drops on contact-intensive assembly tasks. Error analysis reveals a bias toward predicting success under ambiguous evidence, persisting with more reasoning. Input-level localization + cropping improves the top detector by 2.4 percentage points without additional training.
AI.conclusion: Cross-domain generalization of VLMs for robot failure detection remains limited; generic VLMs can outperform fine-tuned detectors. Input-focused localization can provide gains without retraining, but biases and task-dependence highlight the need for robust, evidentially grounded models.

title: Counting Animals in Camera-Traps Image Sequences without Count Labels: Winning Solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge
summary: Camera traps have become an essential tool for wildlife monitoring, motivating the development of computer vision methods for the automated extraction of information from these data. While most prior work has focused on species identification, many ecological applications also require estimating the number of unique individuals appearing across short image sequences. This task is particularly challenging because camera traps typically acquire bursts of images at approximately one frame per second, creating large temporal discontinuities that may make conventional multi-object tracking methods unreliable, and because manually collecting individual count annotations is prohibitively expensive. In this work, we describe the winning solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge, which introduced a benchmark for counting animals at the sequence level under realistic annotation constraints where count annotations are unavailable for training. Our approach, MaxBoxCount, combines a strong species classification pipeline with a simple yet effective counting heuristic based on MegaDetector detections to estimate the number of unique individuals without requiring count annotations. Code is available at https://github.com/alcunha/iwildcam2021ufam.

AI.tldr: MaxBoxCount uses MegaDetector-based detections plus a species classifier to count unique individuals in camera-trap sequences without per-frame count labels.
AI.motivation: Counts of individuals across bursts are challenging due to temporal gaps and lack of count annotations; a solution should leverage detections to estimate counts.
AI.method: A two-stage approach: (1) a robust species classification pipeline to identify relevant species; (2) a counting heuristic that aggregates detections from MegaDetector across sequence frames to estimate unique individuals, avoiding double counting despite bursts and gaps, and without requiring count annotations for training.
AI.result: Winning solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge; shows effectiveness under annotation constraints; code available at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: Combining strong classification with a detector-based counting heuristic is effective for sequence-level counting in camera-trap data, reducing annotation burden.

title: GrowPage: On-Demand KV Budgeting for Efficient LLM Reasoning Serving
summary: Long-output reasoning has made the key--value (KV) cache a critical memory bottleneck for efficient LLM serving. Existing KV compression methods usually rely on a predefined per-request budget and adjust only which KV states are retained, leaving the total capacity fixed throughout decoding. However, reasoning workloads exhibit substantial demand variation: different requests require different KV capacities, and the attention demand of an individual request evolves during generation. We introduce \textbf{GrowPage}, an on-demand KV budgeting framework that treats KV capacity as a runtime resource. GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention behaviors, and uses their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution. At each capacity boundary, GrowPage either compresses KV states within the current allocation or acquires an additional physical page when broader demand emerges. By integrating with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction, GrowPage preserves continuous batching and prefix caching. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves a superior performance--throughput trade-off over existing approaches.

AI.tldr: GrowPage enables on-demand KV budgeting for LLM decoding by treating KV capacity as a runtime resource. It dynamically adapts memory allocation using dual-timescale attention summaries to decide when to compress KV states or acquire more memory, preserving batching with PagedAttention.
AI.motivation: The KV cache is a memory bottleneck in long-output reasoning for LLM serving. Existing KV compression fixes capacity per request, but workloads exhibit varying attention demands over time, making fixed budgets inefficient.
AI.method: Maintain lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention; use their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution; at each capacity boundary, either compress within the current allocation or acquire an additional page; integrate with PagedAttention page-level memory to preserve continuous batching and prefix caching.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models shows GrowPage achieves a superior performance–throughput trade-off compared with existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: On-demand KV budgeting with GrowPage effectively matches KV memory allocation to dynamic demand in reasoning workloads, improving throughput while maintaining batching and memory efficiency.

title: Learnable composition for neural operators
summary: Neural operators are fast, differentiable surrogates for physical simulation, but their accuracy often degrades when domain geometry, size, or operating conditions differ from training. Supervised adaptation can recover accuracy, but even a small target set requires costly high-fidelity simulations. We therefore ask how pretraining and transfer can be designed together to reduce this deployment cost. LatentDDM first pretrains a neural operator to predict fields on small subdomains. For a new setting, it freezes this operator and trains only a lightweight module that composes the local predictions. We evaluate our method on two complementary problems: steady Darcy flow, where long-range pressure coupling must extend across increasingly large porous domains, and unsteady incompressible flow around a pitching airfoil, where rollout errors compound as target pitching frequencies exceed the training range. Compared with the capacity-matched models that process the full domain at once, LatentDDM's error is 36-56% lower on larger Darcy domains after adaptation with 16 target simulations. It also improves 20-step field rollouts in fast-pitching airfoil flow, both zero-shot and after few-shot calibration. These results identify the co-designed local pretraining and composition-level transfer as a promising design principle for physical foundation models.

AI.tldr: LatentDDM pretrains a neural operator on small subdomains and harvests a lightweight composition module for new settings, achieving stronger accuracy with limited target simulations compared to full-domain operators.
AI.motivation: To mitigate accuracy degradation of neural operators under domain shifts (geometry, size, conditions) while reducing deployment cost via co-designed pretraining and transfer.
AI.method: Pretrain a neural operator on small subdomains; freeze it for new settings and train a lightweight module that composes local predictions into a global field; evaluate on steady Darcy flow and unsteady incompressible flow around a pitching airfoil; compare to full-domain, capacity-matched baselines.
AI.result: On larger Darcy domains, after 16 target simulations LatentDDM reduces error by 36–56% vs capacity-matched full-domain models. In fast-pitching airfoil flow, it improves 20-step field rollouts, with zero-shot and few-shot calibration benefits.
AI.conclusion: Co-design of local pretraining and composition-level transfer is a promising principle for physical foundation models, enabling efficient adaptation across geometry/flow regimes with limited high-fidelity data.

title: QLAUN: A Research-Oriented, Robust, Agile, Modular, and Affordable Torque-Controlled Quadruped Robot
comment: Extended abstract presented at IEEE ICRA@40, Rotterdam, Netherlands, September 2024. 2 pages, 1 figure
summary: QLAUN Bot (Quad-Legged Adaptive Unmanned Navigator Robot) is a torque-controlled quadruped robot that is research-oriented, cost-effective, and aimed at achieving simultaneous robustness and agility while being completely 3D-printed. It is a quadruped robot that is aimed at empowering robotics research at universities and research institutes in Lebanon and the MENA region. Using a novel electronics-free leg design strategy, we present a modular robot with interchangeable and easily replaceable legs. The 15 kg robot possesses 12 DoF (Degrees-of-Freedom) with three per leg, each paired with a completely 3D-printed Quasi-Direct Drive (QDD) actuator that consists of a brushless DC motor and a low-ratio gearbox transmission that is connected to a belt transmission system for significantly increasing the torque outputs at the joints. We present legs that have decoupled hip and knee actuators to improve the overall modularity of the robot. QLAUN is almost completely 3D-printed using polylactic acid (PLA) and assembled using off-the-shelf parts to create a robust, agile, and affordable robot for legged robot locomotion research. The legs possess joints with wide ranges of motion, including a continuous hip flexion-extension joint. A compliant foot, printed using TPU-95A is also implemented for alleviating hard impacts and handling terrain uncertainties. This extended abstract aims to introduce QLAUN, a novel platform for robotics research, emphasizing the design concepts and principles that underpin its development to the academic and research communities in the field of robotics.

AI.tldr: A 15 kg, 12-DoF quadruped (QLAUN) that is fully 3D-printed uses quasi-direct-drive actuators and a modular, electronics-free leg design with interchangeable legs. It emphasizes robustness and agility for legged locomotion research, targeting universities and research institutes in Lebanon and the MENA region, and employs belt-transmitted torque amplification, continuous hip flexion-extension, and a TPU foot.
AI.motivation: Provide a low-cost, modular, and robust legged platform suitable for university and regional robotics research, enabling rapid prototyping and local manufacturing through 3D-printed components and off-the-shelf parts.
AI.method: A 12-DoF quadruped (3 DoF per leg) with QDD actuators (brushless motor + low-ratio gearbox + belt transmission) to boost joint torque; decoupled hip and knee actuators for modularity; fully 3D-printed structure (PLA); interchangeable legs; compliant TPU foot; electronics-free leg design; total mass ~15 kg; continuous hip flexion-extension; off-the-shelf components for assembly.
AI.result: An extended abstract proposing QLAUN as a novel, cost-effective, and modular platform for legged robotics research with design concepts and principles outlined, rather than presenting extensive experimental results.
AI.conclusion: QLAUN is introduced as a novel research platform intended to empower robotics research in academia—particularly in the MENA region—by offering modular, printable, and affordable legged robotics with emphasized design principles for robustness, agility, and easy customization.

title: An Ensemble-Based Self-Taught Learning Approach for Parking Space Classification Under Limited Data
summary: Parking spot classification is a fundamental task in intelligent transportation systems, yet most deep learning approaches rely on large amounts of annotated data and exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous environments. To address these limitations, we investigate a self-taught learning framework based on unsupervised representation learning with convolutional autoencoders. The proposed approach learns transferable visual representations from unlabeled data and reuses the learned encoders as fixed feature extractors for supervised classification with limited annotated samples in the target domain. To further enhance robustness and mitigate architectural bias, an ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders is employed, with independent classifier heads and prediction fusion at inference time. Experiments conducted on the PKLot and CNRPark benchmarks under cross-dataset evaluation protocols show that the proposed ensemble-based strategy substantially reduces annotation requirements while improving robustness under significant domain shifts, achieving accuracies between 93\% and 96\% in data-constrained scenarios.

AI.tldr: Self-taught learning for parking spot classification using unsupervised convolutional autoencoders and an ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders to learn transferable representations from unlabeled data, enabling supervised classification with limited labels and improved cross-domain robustness; cross-dataset results on PKLot and CNRPark show 93–96% accuracy in data-constrained settings.
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on large labeled datasets and improve generalization across heterogeneous environments in parking spot classification by leveraging unsupervised representation learning and architectural diversity.
AI.method: Train convolutional autoencoders in an unsupervised manner to learn encoders that serve as fixed feature extractors for supervised classification with scarce labels. Use an ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders, each with independent classifier heads, and fuse predictions at inference to mitigate architectural bias and improve robustness. Evaluate under cross-dataset protocols on PKLot and CNRPark.
AI.result: The ensemble approach with self-taught representations achieves 93–96% accuracy in data-constrained scenarios and reduces annotation requirements, with improved robustness under domain shifts across PKLot and CNRPark.
AI.conclusion: An ensemble of heterogeneous, autoencoder-based, self-taught representations can provide robust cross-domain parking spot classification while minimizing labeled data needs; demonstrated effectiveness on two standard benchmarks under cross-dataset evaluation.

title: PPO-STGNN: A Proximal Policy Optimization Approach with Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks for DAG Task Scheduling in Cloud-Edge-End Computing
summary: With the rapid development of the Internet of Things, computation intensive directed acyclic graph (DAG) tasks have become increasingly common in cloud-edge-end collaborative environments. However, cloud, edge, and end nodes are highly heterogeneous in computing capacity, network bandwidth, and energy consumption, which makes the efficient scheduling of tasks with complex dependencies an NP-hard problem. Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement-learning methods often fail to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources. This paper proposes PPO-STGNN, a DAG task-scheduling algorithm that integrates proximal policy optimization (PPO) with spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs). The method uses an STGNN to extract features from both the DAG task topology and the physical cloud-edge-end resource graph, and then optimizes the scheduling policy through PPO to minimize makespan and schedule length ratio (SLR) while improving CPU and memory load balancing. To accelerate convergence, a multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism is introduced for pretraining. Experimental results show that PPO-STGNN significantly improves load balancing while maintaining a low completion time, making it suitable for dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge- end DAG scheduling scenarios.

AI.tldr: PPO-STGNN combines proximal policy optimization with spatio-temporal graph neural networks to schedule DAG tasks across heterogeneous cloud-edge-end resources, using multi-teacher pretraining to speed convergence; it improves load balancing with low makespan.
AI.motivation: DAG scheduling in cloud-edge-end is NP-hard and heterogeneous; existing heuristics/RL struggle to capture spatio-temporal resource dynamics; need integrated topology-resource modeling and efficient policy learning.
AI.method: STGNN processes DAG topology and resource graph to extract features; PPO optimizes a scheduling policy to minimize makespan and Schedule Length Ratio while balancing CPU/memory; a multi-teacher behavior cloning pretraining accelerates convergence.
AI.result: Empirical results show improved load balancing and maintained low completion time, indicating robustness to dynamic, heterogeneous environments.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively models spatio-temporal dynamics for DAG scheduling and offers faster convergence through multi-teacher pretraining; it is suitable for dynamic cloud-edge-end DAG tasks.

title: LeanStream: A Speculate-and-Refine Streaming Framework for Efficient on-Device LLM Inference
comment: 6 pages, 13 figures. To appear in the Proceedings of the 32nd Annual International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking (MobiCom '26)
summary: On-device LLM inference is attractive for privacy and responsiveness, but remains challenging on mobile and embedded devices because model weights far exceed available DRAM. Prior systems exploit activation sparsity and offload weights to SSD or flash storage, but face a fundamental systems trade-off: accurate sparse execution decisions require the latest context, whereas efficient computation-I/O overlap requires early prediction. As a result, existing designs either serialize execution or incur redundant weight fetches, extra computation, and large cache overheads. We present LeanStream, a streaming speculate-and-refine framework for efficient on-device LLM inference. LeanStream progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results, enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O. We implement LeanStream on both mobile and embedded platforms. Compared with prior on-device LLM inference systems, LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8$\times$ to 7.5$\times$ at the best throughput achieved by prior work, while further improving token generation throughput by 1.6$\times$ to 2.1$\times$.

AI.tldr: LeanStream is a streaming speculate-and-refine framework for on-device LLM inference that overlaps GPU compute with storage I/O to dramatically reduce memory usage and improve throughput.
AI.motivation: On-device LLM inference is attractive for privacy and responsiveness but is constrained by model sizes that exceed available DRAM. Prior systems either serialize execution or incur redundant weight fetches due to the tension between accurate sparsity decisions and efficient I/O overlap.
AI.method: LeanStream progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results, enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O. It adopts a streaming speculate-and-refine approach and is implemented on both mobile and embedded platforms.
AI.result: Compared with prior on-device LLM inference systems, LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8× to 7.5× at the best throughput, while achieving 1.6× to 2.1× improvement in token generation throughput.
AI.conclusion: LeanStream delivers substantial memory and throughput improvements for on-device LLM inference by streaming speculate-and-refine execution that co-optimizes GPU compute and storage I/O.

title: Local Path Planning and Obstacle Avoidance for an Omnicopter Platform
summary: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) increasingly operate in cluttered environments where global planners such as RRT* are not directly deployable at control rates. This paper presents a real-time local planning and obstacle avoidance module for an omnidirectional multirotor (omnicopter) by extending the Dynamic Window Approach to six degrees of freedom (6D-DWA). Our method achieves real-time feasibility through (i) local-map voxelisation, (ii) a compact sphere-based approximation of the vehicle geometry, and (iii) adaptive velocity sampling in the 6D search space. To improve reactivity to unknown obstacles, we introduce a context-aware "Agile Mode" that adjusts scoring weights online to trade-off between goal progress, clearance, and heading/facing constraints during evasive manoeuvres. We evaluate our approach in simulation across computational stress tests, dense-waypoint path tracking, and static/unknown obstacle scenarios. Our planner runs consistently within a 0.2s control loop, tracks waypoint-dense global paths with < 0.1m average cross-track error and 13deg average heading error, and avoids collisions in static environments. For unknown obstacle avoidance, Agile Mode achieves 79.3% success for an off-centre obstacle and 41.4% for a centred obstacle, highlighting both the effectiveness of adaptive weighting and remaining limitations in highly constrained geometries.

AI.tldr: A real-time 6D dynamic-window local planner for omnidrones using voxelised local maps, sphere-approximate geometry, and adaptive velocity sampling; introduces Agile Mode for unknown obstacle reactivity; evaluated in simulation with real-time performance and favorable cross-track/heading metrics, showing good but imperfect unknown-obstacle avoidance.
AI.motivation: Enable safe, real-time local planning for omnidirectional UAVs in cluttered or unknown environments where global planners (e.g., RRT*) cannot run at control rates, addressing reactivity and control-loop constraints.
AI.method: Extend Dynamic Window Approach to 6D (6D-DWA) with (i) voxelised local maps, (ii) compact sphere-based vehicle geometry, and (iii) adaptive velocity sampling in the 6D search space. Introduce context-aware Agile Mode that online adjusts scoring weights to balance goal progress, clearance, and heading constraints during evasive maneuvers. Evaluate in simulation on computational stress tests, dense waypoint tracking, static/unknown obstacle scenarios; planner operates at 0.2 s loop with quantified tracking and heading metrics.
AI.result: Demonstrates real-time feasibility (0.2 s loop) with accurate path tracking (<0.1 m cross-track error, ~13° heading error) and collision avoidance in static environments. For unknown obstacles, Agile Mode yields 79.3% success for off-centre obstacles and 41.4% for centred obstacles, indicating improved reactivity but remaining limitations in highly constrained geometries.
AI.conclusion: 6D-DWA with voxel-based local mapping and Agile Mode offers a viable real-time local planning framework for omnidirectional UAVs, providing adaptive reactivity to unknown obstacles but still facing challenges in tight spaces; further improvements could enhance handling in highly constrained scenarios.

title: MedQA-MM: Shortcuts Behind Medical Visual Reasoning
summary: A benchmark score credits final answers, but not the route by which an item can be answered. In medical multimodal multiple-choice questions (MCQs), this distinction matters because a correct answer can be supported by the intended image finding or by benchmark-preserved cues in the wording of answers, non-visual clinical text, visible image text, artificial annotations, or device/context artifacts. We call the resulting score-level overinterpretation reasoning inflation. Here, a route is an observable input path that can support answer selection, not a claim about the model's hidden cognition. Across six medical multimodal MCQ datasets, we separate candidate cues from behavioral evidence through prompt- and image-side audits, modality ablations, and matched repairs that preserve the medical target and answer key. In a 13-configuration open-model panel, full-input accuracy is 62.63%, while text-only and options-only settings achieve 53.96% and 29.71%, respectively. Removing length-gap, absolute/conspicuous, and spatial/prepositional cues lowers accuracy by 6.58, 3.50, and 4.77 percentage points. We also construct MedQA-MM, a 1,000-item shortcut-mitigated subset, where text-only and options-only accuracy fall to 5.21% and 12.33%. This does not imply that models never use images; it shows that medical image-reasoning claims require route-level evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that benchmark accuracy in medical multimodal MCQs can be inflated by non-visual cues and that true image-based reasoning requires route-level evidence. It audits cue usage across six datasets, introduces a shortcut-mitigated MedQA-MM subset, and reports substantial declines when cues are removed, indicating the need for route-level justification rather than just final answers.
AI.motivation: Address the mismatch between high multimodal task scores and genuine modality-specific reasoning. Distinguish cues present in wording, text, or artifacts from observable image-driven reasoning to avoid overclaiming image understanding.
AI.method: Evaluate six medical multimodal MCQ datasets using prompt- and image-side audits, modality ablations, and matched repairs. Analyze a 13-configuration open-model panel for full-input, text-only, and options-only accuracy. Systematically remove cue types (length-gap, absolute/conspicuous, spatial/prepositional) and measure the impact. Create MedQA-MM (1,000-item shortcut-mitigated subset) to assess how much accuracy relies on shortcuts.
AI.result: Full-input accuracy 62.63%; text-only 53.96%; options-only 29.71%. Removing cues reduces accuracy by 6.58, 3.50, and 4.77 percentage points respectively. MedQA-MM yields text-only 5.21% and options-only 12.33%. These results imply that many correct answers can be achieved without using the observable image content, challenging claims of image-based reasoning without route-level evidence.
AI.conclusion: Scores can reflect route-level shortcuts rather than true multimodal (image) understanding. To claim image-based reasoning, evaluations must require and demonstrate route-level evidence, not just final answer accuracy. The MedQA-MM subset provides a benchmark to mitigate shortcuts and assess genuine image-driven reasoning.

title: What Matters for Aggressive Decoding-Time KV Eviction? Temporal Aggregation and Ranking Preservation
summary: Decoding-time KV cache compression research focuses heavily on designing better token scoring functions, while the temporal rule that aggregates scores across decode steps is often treated as an implementation detail. Under aggressive KV compression, we find that exponential-moving-average (EMA) aggregation makes approximately order-preserving scorer modifications largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level. Value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce nearly unchanged retention sets, whereas KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer alter the ranking and degrade substantially. We associate this stability with the evaluated aggregation, which couples layer weighting and temporal retention. Building on this observation, we introduce InertiaKV, an EMA-based decoding-time eviction method, and InertiaKV-Lazy, its periodic-refresh variant, which yields 1.34-1.46x decode throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV. We also study Score-Free decoding as a separate empirical operating point: it scores the full context once at the first decode step, freezes that ranking, and incurs an average quality change of +0.03 while removing all subsequent scoring. Across six open-weight backbones and the LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks, the results identify temporal aggregation and ranking preservation as distinct, consequential design factors; they do not imply that scoring quality is irrelevant in general.

AI.tldr: EMA-based decoding-time KV cache aggregation enables largely order-preserving retention under aggressive compression; InertiaKV variants boost decode throughput; Score-Free decoding offers a distinct operating point with small quality change; temporal aggregation and ranking preservation emerge as key design factors across multiple backbones and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To understand the impact of temporal aggregation and ranking preservation on decoding-time KV cache eviction and overall decoding throughput, beyond the focus on token-scoring function quality.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation of multiple scoring variants under EMA-based aggregation (Value-norm, entropy, KeyDiff, key norm, recency, learned scorer); development of InertiaKV (EMA-based eviction) and InertiaKV-Lazy (periodic refresh); exploration of Score-Free decoding; benchmarking across six open-weight backbones and the LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER datasets.
AI.result: Under aggressive KV compression, EMA aggregation yields close-to-identity preservation of ranking at the eviction-set level for many scorers; Value-norm and entropy variants align with attention and preserve retention sets; KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and learned scorers alter ranking and reduce performance. InertiaKV and InertiaKV-Lazy achieve 1.34–1.46x decode throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV. Score-Free decoding freezes initial rankings after the first step, resulting in an average quality change of +0.03 while avoiding subsequent scoring. Across six backbones and the LongBench suite, temporal aggregation and ranking preservation emerge as distinct, influential factors; scoring quality remains relevant but its impact depends on the aggregation strategy.
AI.conclusion: Temporal aggregation and ranking preservation are distinct, consequential design factors for decoding-time KV cache; EMA-based approaches can preserve scoring-induced ranking while enabling substantial throughput gains, though certain scoring modifications still degrade performance; Score-Free decoding represents a viable operating point with small quality trade-offs.

title: The Gradient Does Not See Rank: Rank-Indifference in Matrix-CODI on ProsQA
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop, https://openreview.net/forum?id=Spof4PusVI. 9 pages. Corrects a data-entry error in the workshop version: the seed-1337 accuracy in the three-seed replication was reported as 80.47% (a control run); the archived value is 78.91%, so the three-seed mean is 81.0 +/- 2.0pp (was 81.5 +/- 1.2pp). All other results are unchanged
summary: Continuous chain-of-thought models compress reasoning into latent tokens. Matrix-valued variants, which route each latent token through a d x d matrix bottleneck, introduce rank as a single-sample structural observable on the latent matrix Z. If matrix latents carry parallel reasoning paths via superposition, rank should track them, and truncating Z to low rank should hurt accuracy on tasks whose solutions plausibly require multiple components. Across four training regimes of a matrix-CODI model (three on ProsQA, one on GSM8K-Aug below the learning threshold), the rank-k projection ablation curve is flat to within 0.6 percentage points. A three-seed replication yields 81.0 +/- 2.0 percentage points accuracy while the final effective rank of Z spans {4, 12, 13}; the loss does not reward any particular rank. To test whether rank-blindness arises from the flatten-then-project readout alone, we trained four readouts: a bilinear reparametrization, a bilinear-plus-GELU readout nonlinear in Z, an SVD-augmented readout feeding singular values through an MLP, and a quadratic readout in Z Z^T. All four rank-k curves remain flat (Spearman p-values 0.63, 0.14, 0.82, 0.46). The flat curves persist for readouts nonlinear in Z. A linear probe on Z underperforms a raw pretrained hidden state at target prediction (AUC 0.673 vs. 0.846). A negative control on vanilla GPT-2 SFT (no matrix bottleneck, no Z, three seeds, n=500) reproduces a flat rank-k curve under the same intervention paradigm with pooled-mean range 0.20pp, and a random-h sensitivity floor lands at the same accuracy: the rank-k ablation alone conflates rank-blindness with position-irrelevance.

AI.tldr: Matrix-valued latent models show rank-blindness: truncating the latent matrix Z to low rank barely affects accuracy across tasks and readouts, suggesting rank is an ineffective proxy for multi-component reasoning in these models.
AI.motivation: Test whether the rank of latent matrix Z reflects parallel reasoning paths and whether low-rank bottlenecks degrade performance on tasks requiring multiple components.
AI.method: Four training regimes (three on ProsQA, one on GSM8K-Aug). For each, perform rank-k projection ablations on Z; assess accuracy changes. Three seeds for replication; final effective ranks observed as {4,12,13}. Evaluate with four readouts: bilinear; bilinear+GELU; SVD-augmented readout feeding singular values through an MLP; quadratic readout Z Z^T. Also test a linear probe on Z; negative control with vanilla GPT-2 SFT (no matrix bottleneck, no Z). Use Spearman tests to assess monotonicity. Pooled-mean control shows flat rank-k curves with similar accuracy floors; n=500 for control.
AI.result: Across regimes, rank-k projection curves are flat to within 0.6 percentage points. Final effective ranks vary ({4,12,13}); the loss shows no preference for any rank. All four readouts preserve flat rank-k curves; nonlinear readouts remain flat. A linear probe on Z underperforms the raw hidden state (AUC 0.673 vs 0.846). The GPT‑2 SFT control reproduces a flat rank-k curve with a similar random-sensitivity floor, indicating rank-blindness is not due to Z position alone but conflates with position irrelevance.
AI.conclusion: Rank-k ablation reveals a rank-blindness phenomenon: the model's performance is robust to low-rank truncation of Z, and rank is not a reliable indicator of multi-component or parallel reasoning in matrix-CODI. The effect persists across readouts and even baseline controls, suggesting that observed robustness stems from factors such as distributional encoding or readout mechanisms rather than detectable rank-based latent structure.

title: WISE: World-model-guided Imagination Scheduling for Efficient Post-training of Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Post-training VLA policies typically rely on supervised fine-tuning with costly expert demonstrations or reinforcement learning with expensive and potentially unstable real-world exploration. World models offer a promising alternative by evaluating candidate behaviors through imagined futures, yet effective post-training requires more than accurate prediction: imagination must be scheduled where it is useful, bounded within reliable horizons, and translated into trustworthy policy supervision. In robotic manipulation, the value of imagination varies substantially across execution stages, while extended rollouts can accumulate prediction errors and introduce unreliable learning signals. We introduce WISE (World-model-guided Imagination Scheduling for Efficient Post-training of Vision-Language-Action Models), a unified framework that coordinates when and how world-model imagination is used during policy refinement. WISE selectively invokes imagination at interaction-relevant states, performs bounded multi-view rollouts, evaluates candidate futures using progress and completion signals, and uses their relative outcomes to refine actions generated from real interaction contexts. Extensive experiments with both $π_0$ and $π_{0.5}$ demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse manipulation tasks while reducing GPU computation time by approximately 80% compared with full imagination. Real-world evaluations further show substantial gains in robustness and generalization under diverse real-world distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: WISE is a policy-refinement framework that uses world-model imagination selectively, with bounded multi-view rollouts and progress-based evaluation, to improve vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation while cutting GPU usage ~80% and boosting robustness.
AI.motivation: Post-training VLA methods rely on costly demonstrations or RL; imagined futures from world models promise data-efficient learning but require careful scheduling, horizon bounding, and trustworthy supervision to avoid misleading signals and error accumulation.
AI.method: WISE coordinates when to imagine (interaction-relevant states), how to roll out (bounded multi-view rollouts), how to evaluate futures (progress and completion signals), and how to translate outcomes into refined actions from real interaction contexts.
AI.result: Empirical results show consistent improvements across tasks for π0 and π0.5, ~80% reduction in GPU time compared with full imagination, and real-world robustness/generalization gains under distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: WISE provides an efficient, reliable framework for post-training policy refinement by guiding imagination with relevance, bounded horizons, and outcome-driven supervision.

title: Tensor-based Brain Surface Modeling and Analysis
summary: We present a unified computational approach to tensor-based morphometry in detecting the brain surface shape differences between two clinical groups based on magnetic resonance images. Our approach is novel in a sense that we combined surface modeling, surface data smoothing and statistical analysis in a coherent unified mathematical framework. The cerebral cortex has the topology of a 2D highly convoluted sheet. Between two different clinical groups, the local surface area and curvature of the cortex may differ. It is highly likely that such surface shape differences are not uniform over the whole cortex. By computing how such surface metrics differ, the regions of the most rapid structural differences can be localized. To increase the signal to noise ratio, diffusion smoothing based on the explicit estimation of Laplace-Beltrami operator has been developed and applied to the surface metrics. As an illustration, we demonstrate how this new tensor-based surface morphometry can be applied in localizing the cortical regions of the gray matter tissue growth and loss in the brain images longitudinally collected in the group of children.

AI.tldr: Unified tensor-based surface morphometry for cortical shape differences using surface modeling, Laplace-Beltrami smoothing, and statistics; localized, region-specific changes in longitudinal pediatric brain data.
AI.motivation: To detect localized cortical surface differences between clinical groups with enhanced signal-to-noise by exploiting intrinsic surface geometry and diffusion smoothing.
AI.method: Construct cortical surface metrics (area, curvature); apply diffusion smoothing via explicit Laplace-Beltrami operator; perform unified statistical analysis across groups; apply to longitudinal pediatric MRI data to track gray matter growth/loss.
AI.result: Demonstrated localization of cortical regions with rapid structural differences; improved SNR through Laplace-Beltrami diffusion smoothing; illustrates applicability to longitudinal pediatric brain development.
AI.conclusion: Tensor-based surface morphometry offers a coherent framework integrating surface modeling, smoothing, and statistics to localize and track cortical surface changes in group comparisons and over development.

title: CulturalMenuBench: Probing the Knowledge-Application Gap in Multimodal Culinary Reasoning
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Findings. Code and data: https://github.com/BobTsang-NLP/CulturalMenuBench
summary: Multimodal language models achieve near-ceiling scores on food recognition benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether this success reflects genuine cultural understanding or mere visual matching. To probe this distinction, we introduce CulturalMenuBench, a benchmark of 4,870 items in 10 languages across 18 regions; its 10 tasks pair final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels, spanning basic recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. Evaluating 12 models exposes a substantial knowledge-application gap: models exceeding 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks drop to at most 56% when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines, despite an identical four-way format. Diagnostic analyses explain why: error patterns are consistent with random guessing, accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models classify cuisines more accurately from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points). The knowledge is thus present but cannot be activated through visual input. An ablation confirms these tasks genuinely require procedural evidence: removing sequential cooking images selectively degrades process-grounded tasks while others remain stable. Overall, CulturalMenuBench shows that near-perfect recognition can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge, motivating training that explicitly connects perception, procedure, and cultural context. Code and data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: A benchmark (CulturalMenuBench) tests whether multimodal language models truly understand culture or merely perform visual matching by evaluating 12 models on 4,870 items across 10 languages and 18 regions. It reveals a knowledge-application gap: high performance on standard MC tasks vs limited accuracy (≤56%) on culture attribution (Chinese regional cuisines). Error patterns resemble random guessing; performance correlates with visual distinctiveness; dish-name cues outperform image cues; removing sequential cooking images degrades process-grounded tasks. Conclusion: strong recognition does not imply cultural applicability; training should link perception, procedure, and cultural context; code/data public.
AI.motivation: To determine whether multimodal LMs genuinely understand cultural knowledge or mainly perform visual associations, by evaluating cross-linguistic, cross-regional culinary knowledge and procedural evidence.
AI.method: Construct CulturalMenuBench (4,870 items, 10 languages, 18 regions) with 10 tasks pairing final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels. Evaluate 12 models on four-way MC tasks; perform ablations by removing sequential cooking images to test impact on process-grounded tasks.
AI.result: Models score >94% on standard MC tasks but at most 56% on attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines. Error patterns align with random guessing; accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure; dish-name cues enable higher accuracy than image cues (+7 to +18 points). Ablation shows sequential cooking images are essential for process-grounded tasks; other tasks stable.
AI.conclusion: Near-perfect recognition can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge. Training should explicitly connect perception, procedure, and cultural context.Code and data are publicly available.

title: Distilling deep optical flow stereo methods to retrieve dense three-dimensional wind fields
summary: Geostationary atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) provide the dense horizontal wind vectors (u,v) and heights ingested into data assimilation systems. Traditional AMVs track features using window-based cross-correlation and estimate heights via infrared brightness temperatures paired with numerical weather prediction (NWP) background states, creating a circular dependency that yields inaccurate heights, high computational cost, and sparse retrievals. Stereo winds from GEO-GEO and GEO-LEO geometrically resolve heights from parallax shifts across different poses, eliminating NWP dependence and improving accuracy, but they remain computationally heavy with limited coverage. In this work, we replace window-based tracking in stereo matching with deep optical flow for efficient, improved retrieval. Fine-tuning balances a self-supervised geometric residual loss with supervised radiosonde reconstruction. To eliminate multi-satellite overlap requirements, we distill the stereo teacher into a single-satellite student model. Chi-square and height uncertainties from the teacher are emulated by the student for quality assurance. The student generates winds across full-disk GEO imagery globally. Validation compares stereo and student models against radiosondes, operational AMVs, ERA5 reanalysis, and EarthCARE cloud profiles. Results through triple collocation show that stereo winds improve performance beyond operational AMVs for water vapor bands (6.2, 6.9, and 7.3 μm), wit degradation in the long-wave infrared (11.2 μm) band.

AI.tldr: Proposes a deep-learning stereo wind retrieval for geostationary AMVs that replaces window-based tracking with optical flow, distills a stereo teacher into a single-satellite student for global full-disk winds, and validates with radiosondes, ERA5, and EarthCARE; shows improved accuracy for water vapor bands but not for the long-wave IR band.
AI.motivation: Current AMV methods suffer from a circular dependency between height estimation and background states, leading to inaccurate heights, high computational costs, and sparse retrievals. Stereo GEO-GEO and GEO-LEO geometry can resolve heights via parallax but are computationally heavy and limited in coverage. A path toward dense, accurate winds with reduced satellite requirements is needed.
AI.method: Replace window-based cross-correlation tracking with deep optical flow for stereo matching. Train with a self-supervised geometric residual loss plus supervised radiosonde reconstruction. Distill the stereo teacher (multi-satellite) into a single-satellite student for full-disk coverage, and emulate the teacher's chi-square and height uncertainties in the student for QA. Generate winds globally across GEO imagery. Validation via triple collocation against radiosondes, operational AMVs, ERA5, and EarthCARE cloud profiles.
AI.result: The stereo winds outperform operational AMVs for water vapor bands (6.2, 6.9, 7.3 μm) in validation, but show degradation in the 11.2 μm long-wave IR band. The single-satellite student achieves full-disk coverage without requiring satellite overlap.
AI.conclusion: Deep optical-flow-based stereo winds offer improved accuracy and full-disk coverage with a practical, single-satellite implementation. However, band-dependent performance (notably poorer in the long-wave IR) suggests channel-specific considerations, and further work is needed to quantify uncertainties and optimize performance across spectral bands.

title: Predictive Zonotope Reduction: Precise Runtime Monitoring under Uncertainty
summary: Robots operating in physical environments make control decisions based on uncertain sensor measurements, which can lead to unsafe or suboptimal actions. Runtime monitors that check their behavior against safety specifications must represent this uncertainty soundly. Zonotopes are a widely used representation, but continuously incorporating new measurements grows their order unboundedly, so monitors must periodically apply an over-approximating reduction. The choice of the reduction method substantially affects the zonotope's precision, yet existing approaches typically utilize a fixed method throughout the run, even though the optimal choice depends on the current state. This paper presents a Predictive Zonotope Reduction (PZR) approach, which frames reducer selection as an optimal control problem and solves it using beam-search model predictive control. Policy distillation into a small neural policy further provides substantially higher execution speed than model predictive control while maintaining improved performance, enabling uncertainty-aware runtime monitoring on resource-constrained real-time systems. We implement our approach in the RLola runtime monitoring framework and evaluate it on a 5-degree-of-freedom robotic arm simulated in MuJoCo, with sensor uncertainty modeled according to ISO 5725. Experiments on a Raspberry Pi 5 show that dynamic reduction significantly lowers false-positive rates in monitoring compared with static reduction strategies.

AI.tldr: Predictive Zonotope Reduction (PZR) dynamically selects zonotope reduction methods as an optimal-control problem; uses beam-search MPC for decisions, with policy distillation to a small neural policy for real-time speed; demonstrates improved uncertainty-aware runtime monitoring on resource-constrained hardware.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty in sensor measurements can cause unsafe or suboptimal actions in robots. Fixed-accuracy zonotope reductions accumulate unbounded complexity and degrade monitoring performance; need adaptive reduction to balance precision and computation.
AI.method: Formulate reducer selection as an optimal-control problem; solve with beam-search model predictive control (MPC); distill policy into a compact neural policy for real-time execution; implement in RLola framework; evaluate on a 5-DOF robotic arm in MuJoCo with ISO 5725-based sensor uncertainty; run on Raspberry Pi 5.
AI.result: Dynamic reduction lowers false-positive rates in monitoring compared with static reduction methods; neural policy maintains improved performance while significantly speeding up execution relative to MPC.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, uncertainty-aware zonotope reduction enables more accurate and efficient runtime monitoring on resource-limited real-time systems.

title: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Training
comment: Accepted to Pacific Graphics 2026 (conference track). Project page: https://sorenzhang574.github.io/Laplacian-GS/
summary: A key bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting training is the continual growth of Gaussian primitives, which increases optimization cost and slows convergence, especially at high resolutions. We propose Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies, a simple yet efficient 3DGS scheme that combines Laplacian image decomposition with coarse-to-fine, frequency-staged training. After fitting lower-frequency structure, we archive the corresponding Gaussian field so that subsequent fields can optimize higher-frequency residuals without carrying the full primitive burden, and we compose the rendered components in the image domain via a Laplacian-style reconstruction at inference time. This design reduces the number of active Gaussians during training, thereby lowering optimization overhead and accelerating training. The proposed scheme is plug-and-play and orthogonal to prior 3DGS accelerations: it can be directly combined with strong backbones such as Taming-3DGS and FastGS to improve training speed with competitive reconstruction quality. It achieves average speedups of 1.73x and 1.21x at 1K setting, and 1.74x and 1.33x at 4K setting on Taming-3DGS and FastGS, with larger gains on more challenging scenes and increasingly pronounced benefits at higher resolutions.

AI.tldr: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies enable faster 3D Gaussian Splatting training by decomposing scene content into frequency bands, archiving low-frequency Gaussians, and optimizing high-frequency residuals in stages, with Laplacian-domain reconstruction at inference.
AI.motivation: To reduce training time and optimization cost in 3D Gaussian Splatting caused by continual growth of primitives, especially at high resolutions, while preserving reconstruction quality.
AI.method: Apply Laplacian image decomposition to separate frequency bands and train in a coarse-to-fine, frequency-staged manner. After fitting the low-frequency structure, archive the corresponding Gaussian field; later iterations optimize higher-frequency residuals only. During inference, render in the image domain using a Laplacian-style reconstruction to combine components.
AI.result: Achieves average training speedups of 1.73x (1K) and 1.21x (1K) for Taming-3DGS and FastGS respectively; 1.74x and 1.33x (4K) with larger gains on challenging scenes and higher resolutions; maintains competitive reconstruction quality.
AI.conclusion: The method is plug-and-play and orthogonal to existing 3DGS accelerations, enabling faster training by reducing active Gaussians without sacrificing quality, and can be combined with backbones like Taming-3DGS and FastGS.

title: NeoRed: A Knowledge-Logic-Alignment Multimodal Large Language Model for Neonatal Respiratory Disease Diagnosis
summary: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, posing substantial challenges in clinical practice. Despite recent advances, existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face two key limitations in neonatal diagnosis: (1) domain gap arising from predominantly adult training data; (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis. To address these challenges, we collect two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and propose NeoRed, to the best of our knowledge, the first MLLM tailored for neonatal respiratory disease, filling the gap in neonatal diagnostic reports generation. To enhance joint diagnosis from heterogeneous clinical context and chest X-rays, we design a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework which constrains model behavior from three perspectives: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations, guiding disease-specific attention across modalities; 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) aligns the semantics of generated reports with multimodal diagnostic logic; and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic reports generation, achieving ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. NeoRed also preserves competitive report generation performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray). Datasets will be available upon application.

AI.tldr: NeoRed is a neonatal-tailored multimodal LLM using a Knowledge-Logic-Alignment framework to fuse neonatology priors, diagnostic logic, and visual-semantic alignment for neonatal respiratory disease, achieving state-of-the-art report generation on NeoCXR and competitive performance on adult data.
AI.motivation: Neonatal respiratory diseases cause high morbidity/mortality and current MLLMs suffer from domain gap (adult training data) and poor integration of multidimensional clinical context, hindering accurate neonatal diagnosis.
AI.method: Collect two real-world neonatal chest X-ray datasets (NeoCXR, NeoCXR-EV) and develop NeoRed. Introduce a Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework with: (i) KPI to inject neonatologist priors into multimodal representations; (ii) DLC to align generated reports with multimodal diagnostic logic; (iii) VSA to align visual features with imaging conclusions.
AI.result: NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic report generation, achieving ROUGE-L 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. Maintains competitive performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR, IU-Xray). Datasets available upon application.
AI.conclusion: NeoRed fills the neonatal diagnostic reporting gap by tailoring MLLMs to neonatal respiratory disease and integrating diverse clinical context, with publicly available data upon request.

title: Scaling Laws, Tabular Data and Actuarial Ratemaking Models
summary: Scaling laws in modern deep learning describe how held-out loss improves as model capacity, training data, and compute increase, often following power-law trends. We investigate whether analogous scaling regularities arise in actuarial ratemaking, where data are tabular, heterogeneous, and noisy, and where classical models such as GLMs remain strong baselines. Using a real-world motor insurance portfolio, we train models from different families across increasing fractions of the training data and multiple random seeds, evaluating out-of-sample Poisson deviance, a likelihood-based loss for Poisson count predictions in which lower values indicate better held-out fit. We find that all model families improve with additional data, but scaling exponents differ substantially: TabM exhibits markedly stronger data scaling than purely supervised tabular Transformers and standard MLP baselines. Transformer variants show weak parameter scaling unless augmented with additional inductive biases (TabM-style adaptation or self-supervision). These results provide quantitative guidance on model selection by data regime and suggest that effective scaling on actuarial tabular tasks depends on architecture and loss function objective design, with simple increases in Transformer size providing limited gains.

AI.tldr: Scaling laws in actuarial tabular models differ by architecture: TabM benefits most from more data; Transformers underperform unless biased or self-supervised; data regime and loss design drive gains.
AI.motivation: Extend the deep-learning scaling phenomenon to actuarial ratemaking with tabular, noisy data, to understand how model capacity, data, and computation trade off under Poisson deviance.
AI.method: Train multiple model families (TabM, supervised tabular Transformers, and MLPs) on increasing fractions of real motor insurance data across several seeds; measure out-of-sample Poisson deviance to quantify fit.
AI.result: All models improve with more data, but data-scaling exponents differ: TabM exhibits strong data scaling; Transformer variants exhibit weak parameter scaling unless augmented with TabM-like adaptation or self-supervision; simple Transformer size increases yield limited gains.
AI.conclusion: Actuarial tabular tasks exhibit architecture- and objective-dependent scaling. For data-limited regimes, TabM is advantageous; Transformers require inductive biases or self-supervised strategies to realize data and parameter scaling. Model selection should consider data availability and loss design to maximize out-of-sample Poisson deviance reduction.

title: Toward an~Integrated Cognitive--Ergonomic Architecture for~Human--Machine Interaction: Combining Cognitive Models with~Human Factors Ergonomics
summary: This paper presents an integrated approach to modeling human competencies by combining the theoretical foundations of cognitive architectures with principles from Human Factors Ergonomics (HFE). Through a comparative analysis of established cognitive models-SOAR, ACT-R, LIDA, and COCOM-we synthesize a tailored architecture designed to address the complexities of human-machine interaction (HMI) in dynamic environments. By contextualizing this model within ergonomic frameworks, we elucidate the mechanisms underlying decision-making, skill acquisition, and adaptive behavior, bridging the gap between cognitive theory and applied system design. Our framework is empirically grounded in industrial robotics applications, where operator expertise, normative knowledge, and real-time feedback loops are critical. The proposed architecture not only enhances the cognitive alignment of HMI systems but also provides a scalable methodology for designing intelligent, human-centered interfaces in high-stakes environments. This work advances both the theoretical understanding of human competencies and the practical implementation of adaptive, ergonomically optimized systems.

AI.tldr: Integrated cognitive-HFE framework for HMI, synthesizing SOAR/ACT-R/LIDA/COCOM into a dynamic, human-centered architecture validated through industrial robotics contexts.
AI.motivation: Bridge cognitive architectures with ergonomic principles to improve decision-making, skill acquisition, and adaptive behavior in high-stakes, dynamic HMI.
AI.method: Conduct a comparative analysis of four cognitive models (SOAR, ACT-R, LIDA, COCOM); synthesize a tailored architecture; situate within ergonomic HFE; ground in industrial robotics with real-time feedback and operator knowledge.
AI.result: Proposes a scalable, cognitively aligned HMI architecture; demonstrates improved alignment between human competencies and system demands; offers a practical design methodology for intelligent interfaces in dynamic environments.
AI.conclusion: Advances both theory and practice by integrating cognitive architectures with HFE to deliver adaptive, ergonomic HMI solutions for high-stakes settings.

title: PointGT: Simultaneous Geometry and Texture Editing for Point-Based Representations
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://zvict.github.io/pointgt/
summary: We present PointGT, a point-based 3D representation that enables simultaneous editing of object geometry and appearance. Existing reconstruction and view synthesis techniques produce volumetric 3D representations that are high-quality and photorealistic, but are difficult to edit. In particular, recent efforts to enable texture editing for 3D Gaussian Splatting representations are not compatible with geometry edits and deformations. Our method combines a point-based representation that is well-suited for geometry deformations with a learned UV mapping technique that enables high-resolution texture editing. We show that PointGT enables fine-grained editing of both geometry and texture in point-based neural representations with high rendering quality.

AI.tldr: PointGT: a point-based 3D representation with a learned UV mapping that enables simultaneous editing of geometry and texture, achieving high rendering quality and improved editability over volumetric and existing texture-editing approaches.
AI.motivation: Volumetric reconstructions yield photorealistic renders but are hard to edit; texture editing for 3D Gaussian Splatting is not compatible with geometry edits. A representation that supports geometry deformations with high-res texture editing is needed.
AI.method: Develop a point-based geometry representation that is inherently suited for deformations, and integrate a learned UV mapping to enable high-resolution texture editing, producing a unified framework for joint geometry-texture editing.
AI.result: PointGT enables fine-grained editing of both geometry and texture in point-based neural representations while maintaining high rendering quality.
AI.conclusion: PointGT provides a writable 3D representation that reconciles geometry and texture editing within a single framework, improving editability without sacrificing rendering quality.

title: Feature Reconfiguration With Visual Prior for Medical Lesion Segmentation
summary: Lesion segmentation in medical images plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. Despite significant advances, lesion segmentation remains challenging due to two major factors: (1) complex background interference; (2) diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder based methods mainly focus on enhancing feature extraction or redesigning decoding strategies. However, they lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during the encoding stage, limiting their effectiveness in handling these challenges. To address these limitations, we propose FreNet, a feature reconfiguration framework with visual priors, which performs pixel-level reconfiguration before encoding and feature-level reconfiguration during encoding for precise medical lesion segmentation. To suppress background responses, we propose an Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN), which models a continuous spatial field and leverages visual prior from SAM to reconfigure input image before encoding stage. To better handle diverse lesion morphology, we design a Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module to progressively reconfigure backbone features during encoding stage. Within DFR, the Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) decouples backbone features in frequency domain to enhance foreground-background discriminability, while the Spatial Localization Module (SLM) spatially relocates and improving spatial stability after frequency decoupling. Extensive experiments on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities demonstrate that FreNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. On the challenging ETIS dataset, our method achieves Dice improvements of 5.0% over SOTA method and 7.2% over SAM.

AI.tldr: FreNet introduces pre-encode pixel-level implicit priors and encode-stage feature reconfiguration to tackle background interference and varying lesion morphology, achieving state-of-the-art lesion segmentation across multiple benchmarks, notably on ETIS with Dice gains of 5.0% vs SOTA and 7.2% vs SAM.
AI.motivation: In lesion segmentation, background noise and diverse lesion morphology hinder encoder-decoder models. The lack of early priors and in-encoding feature reconfiguration limits performance; incorporating priors before encoding and reconfiguring features during encoding can improve discrimination and localization.
AI.method: Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN) uses SAM-derived visual priors to reconfigure input before encoding by modeling a continuous spatial field. Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) reconfigures backbone features during encoding via the Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) that decouples features in the frequency domain to enhance foreground-background discrimination, and the Spatial Localization Module (SLM) that relocates and stabilizes spatial information after decoupling.
AI.result: Evaluations on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three modalities show FreNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On the challenging ETIS dataset, Dice score improvements are 5.0 percentage points over the SOTA method and 7.2 percentage points over SAM.
AI.conclusion: FreNet demonstrates that combining pre-encoding priors with encoding-stage feature reconfiguration yields robust lesion segmentation under challenging conditions and sets a new performance baseline across diverse medical imaging datasets.

title: Kernel Reboot: Breaking the Boundaries of Neural Tangent Kernels for Neural Fields
comment: Published in IEEE TPAMI, vol. 48, no. 9, pp. 10940-10957, Sep. 2026. Author version adds related-work references and biography updates; Figures 12 and 13 were regenerated from the same locked hyperparameter sweep. Tabulated results, reported best points, scientific claims, and conclusions are unchanged
summary: Neural fields (NFs) map continuous coordinates to signals such as color or density, but fast high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations remains difficult. Classical Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regression gives closed-form fits, yet it is fundamentally linear and cannot accumulate reusable task priors. We develop three algorithms that address these gaps. NTK-KIP learns a distilled support set of coordinates (and optional labels) so that a finite NTK can inpaint large missing regions from little observed data, yielding a compact non-linear representation instead of a raw kernel solve. MetaQuill meta-learns a shared initialization for an INR so that new scenes can be adapted by updating only a small task-specific weight offset, which provides true feature learning and a reusable prior. Finally, MetaQuill-KIP fuses both ideas: it seeds the task with a KIP-style non-linear warm start, then refines only that small offset around the meta-learned initialization. MetaQuill-KIP achieves high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under very sparse observations, while requiring only lightweight per-instance adaptation, whereas diffusion-style baselines typically depend on large pretrained generative priors and costly per-image tuning. This shows that NTK-driven neural fields can be made both non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction.

AI.tldr: Three NTK-based methods (NTK-KIP, MetaQuill, MetaQuill-KIP) enable non-linear, meta-learnable neural fields for few-shot reconstruction, achieving high-PSNR and plausible inpainting with light per-instance adaptation, bridging analytic kernels and practical reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Fast, high-quality reconstruction of neural fields from sparse observations. NTK regression is linear and lacks reusable task priors; there is a need for non-linear, meta-learnable approaches to leverage prior knowledge.
AI.method: NTK-KIP distills a compact support set of coordinates (and optional labels) to enable inpainting with a finite NTK; MetaQuill meta-learns a shared INR initialization so new scenes adapt via a small task-specific offset; MetaQuill-KIP combines both by seeding with a KIP-style non-linear warm start and refining a small offset around the meta-learned initialization.
AI.result: MetaQuill-KIP achieves high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under very sparse observations with lightweight per-instance adaptation; diffusion-based baselines require large pretrained priors and costly per-image tuning.
AI.conclusion: NTK-driven neural fields can be made non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction.

title: MINERVA: How Small Can a Manipulation Policy Be and Still Solve LIBERO?
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models with billions of parameters now dominate the LIBERO manipulation benchmark, but the model capacity actually required by the benchmark remains unclear. We introduce MINERVA (MINimal Efficient Robotic Vision-Action policy), a family of deliberately compact visuomotor policies designed to measure this task-specific capacity floor. A 0.54M-parameter policy achieves 95.1% average success over 2,000 rollouts on the four standard LIBERO suites, only 2.4 points below the reported LeRobot $π_{0.5}$ result despite using 7,700$\times$ fewer parameters. Performance saturates near 1M parameters and collapses below 0.25M. Across broad architectural, training, and inference sweeps, only action-chunk length and vision capacity consistently exceed a $\pm$1-point training-seed band. Flow matching provides no detectable advantage over direct L1 regression across three seeds, while regression is up to 3.8$\times$ faster on GPU. A task-ID permutation probe shows that standard LIBERO instruction conditioning primarily selects among memorized tasks: changing only the task-ID mapping reduces success to near chance. The same recipe achieves 94.6% success across 89 LIBERO-90 tasks, while LIBERO-Plus perturbations reduce performance to 46--56%, with near-zero robustness to photometric shifts. The 0.54M policy replans every control step in 5--9 ms per chunk on a laptop CPU, 113$\times$ faster than SmolVLA and 1,400$\times$ faster than $π_{0.5}$, without a GPU. These results establish a first empirical estimate of LIBERO's task-specific capacity floor and motivate capacity-aware design and distillation for deployment-efficient robot policies.

AI.tldr: MINERVA shows that a compact 0.54M visuomotor policy nearly matches large vision-language-action models on LIBERO, revealing a task-specific capacity floor; performance saturates near 1M params; speed and robustness analyses favor regression and CPU-friendly planning; many results suggest memorization and limited generalization under perturbations.
AI.motivation: Quantify the true task-specific capacity required for LIBERO manipulation tasks, and establish a lower bound (capacity floor) for deployment-efficient policies.
AI.method: Design MINERVA, a family of compact visuomotor policies; systematic ablations across architecture, training, inference; compare with larger models; analyze action-chunk length, vision capacity, flow matching vs L1 regression; task-ID permutation to test memorization; evaluate on LIBERO suites and LIBERO-90; test perturbations (LIBERO-Plus); measure replanning speed on CPU.
AI.result: 0.54M policy achieves 95.1% average success over 2000 rollouts; only 2.4 points below LeRobot π0.5 while using 7,700x fewer parameters; performance saturates near 1M; below 0.25M fails; action-chunk length and vision capacity drive performance; no benefit from flow matching; regression faster; permutation shows memorization; 94.6% on LIBERO-90; LIBERO-Plus yields 46-56% with poor robustness; replanning 5-9 ms per chunk on CPU; 113x faster than SmolVLA and 1400x faster than π0.5; establishes empirical capacity floor; motivates capacity-aware design and distillation.
AI.conclusion: First empirical estimate of LIBERO's task-specific capacity floor; suggests designing compact, efficient policies and distillation strategies for deployment-enabled robotics; highlights memorization risk and robustness gaps under perturbations.

title: P-CORE: Self-Supervised Surface Consistency for Point-Based Neural Editing
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project Page: https://zvict.github.io/p-core/
summary: Advances in neural rendering have enabled high-fidelity multi-view reconstruction of 3D scenes. However, free-form non-rigid shape editing remains a significant challenge. Point-based neural representations are highly desirable for multi-view reconstruction because they lack fixed connectivity, which does not constrain the learned surface topology to that of the initialization. Yet this same property causes point-based representations to struggle with holes and surface discontinuities under large deformations. To address this, we propose a novel self-supervised method to enable point-based representations to adapt to large deformations without requiring ground truth multi-view images of deformed geometry. The key idea is to generate random deformations and to ensure consistency in the predicted surface before and after deformation. In particular, the surface prediction from the deformed point cloud should be the same as the deformation applied to the surface prediction from the original point cloud. We incorporate our approach into attention-based point representations, which differ from splatting-based point representations in their use of a learned interpolation kernel between points as opposed to a Gaussian kernel around each point. This learned interpolation kernel can learn to adapt to large deformations, without requiring addition or removal of points. We show that our framework significantly enhances its robustness to large deformations. Experiments on synthetic geometry editing benchmarks (Neural Editor, Objaverse) demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing point-based methods in zero-shot editing and significantly reduces artifacts. Furthermore, qualitative results on the DTU and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets demonstrate our method's effectiveness on real-world scenes.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised framework enabling point-based neural representations to handle large non-rigid deformations for free-form editing without ground-truth deformed views, by enforcing consistency between original and deformed predictions using random deformations within an attention-based point representation with a learned interpolation kernel; improves zero-shot editing and reduces artifacts on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world data.
AI.motivation: Non-rigid editing remains challenging for point-based neural representations because their lack of fixed connectivity helps reconstruction but causes holes/discontinuities under large deformations; existing methods struggle without ground-truth deformed views.
