AI.method: Generate random deformations; enforce surface consistency such that the surface from the deformed point cloud equals the deformation of the surface from the original point cloud. Integrate into attention-based point representations with a learned interpolation kernel (instead of splatting Gaussian). No need to add/remove points. Self-supervised objective.
AI.result: Outperforms existing point-based methods in zero-shot editing on synthetic benchmarks (Neural Editor, Objaverse); reduces artifacts. Qualitative results on DTU and Mip-NeRF 360 show effectiveness on real scenes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed self-supervised approach and learned interpolation kernel significantly improve robustness of point-based neural rendering to large deformations, enabling more accurate free-form editing without ground-truth deformed views.

title: Dalek: A Constructive Agent Machine
summary:
We present Dalek, a closed machine designed for agents that realizes self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization on any substrate satisfying a general host contract. The machine is built from three primitives---actors, messages, and channels. Four obligations---a host boundary, a construction language, admissible transitions, and rule heredity---give its boundary, identity, and closure a structural basis.
  Von Neumann's 1948 self-reproducing automaton supplies a hereditary constructional core: a self-description together with a constructor, a copier, and a controller. Dalek combines this core with the four obligations and rederives its medium for a text-and-message agent substrate, adding explicit structures for boundary, identity, history, and growth. A large language model and a compiler occupy the payload position and form a general capability producer. New capabilities are authored, compiled, installed into the description, and inherited by descendants. The same path produces the machine's own organs and even its runtime, closing heredity and evolution within the machine.

AI.tldr: Dalek is a closed, self-maintaining, self-evolving, self-reproducing, and self-organizing machine for agent substrates, built from actors, messages, and channels; it embeds Von Neumann's hereditary core and four obligations, enabling inheritance of capabilities and runtime to descendants, using a large language model as the payload and compiler.
AI.motivation: To create autonomous, self-sustaining agents whose identity and closure are structurally grounded, while enabling growth, capability authorship, and heredity on any substrate meeting a host contract.
AI.method: Define three primitives (actors, messages, channels) and four obligations (host boundary, construction language, admissible transitions, rule heredity); integrate Von Neumann's self-description, constructor, copier, controller as a core; instantiate a text-and-message substrate with explicit boundary, identity, history, and growth; place a large language model and a compiler as the payload to produce, install, and inherit new capabilities; ensure heredity closes the machine's runtime and evolution.
AI.result: A formal design and implementation approach for Dalek enabling closed-loop heredity and evolution, with capabilities authored and propagated to descendants; machine can produce its own organs and runtime, embedding capability production within its description.
AI.conclusion: Dalek demonstrates a viable path to self-maintaining, evolving, reproducing agents on generic substrates by fusing classical self-reproduction concepts with modern capability production, yielding an integrated boundary-driven, hereditary machine architecture.

title: Routing Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Intra-Adapter Subspace Contention in MoE+LoRA Fine-Tuning
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 16 tables. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Multi-domain fine-tuning often combines MoE routing with LoRA, assuming that token-level routing separates domain-specific updates. We test this assumption in MoE+LoRA using Python code paired with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning. Although these domains show near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, indicating that routing separation alone may not prevent negative transfer. To localize the failure, we introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity, which measure expert sharing and update compatibility, respectively. These diagnostics indicate that interference arises mostly from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. We address this issue with SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. We evaluate SpawnLoRA on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings and find that it effectively reduces negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA. These results demonstrate that structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone.

AI.tldr: MoE+LoRA shows that domain-specific routing does not guarantee non-interference; introducing SpawnLoRA with gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts reduces negative transfer, outperforming standard and rank-adaptive LoRA.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether token-level MoE routing suffices to separate domain-specific updates in multi-domain fine-tuning, diagnose interference sources, and propose a dynamic structural solution.
AI.method: Empirical study combining Python experiments on biomedical text and mathematical reasoning within MoE+LoRA; introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity as diagnostics; propose SpawnLoRA with dynamic gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts; evaluate on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings.
AI.result: Despite near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data increases code perplexity, indicating that routing separation alone fails to prevent negative transfer. Diagnostics reveal interference arises from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. SpawnLoRA mitigates this by adding gated sub-adapters inside experts when adapter contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed, reducing negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA.
AI.conclusion: Structural separation inside MoE experts (via gated sub-adapters) provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion, offering a practical mechanism to localize and alleviate interference in multi-domain MoE+LoRA fine-tuning.

title: RoughSense: Lightweight Terrain-Induced Rover Vibration Prediction Using Point Clouds and IMU Feedback
summary: Autonomous navigation in space requires reliable terrain assessment for safe operations, especially in underground environments with limited communication, computing resources, and power budget. This paper presents a lightweight method for real-time vibration-aware traversability mapping using a Light Detecting And Ranging (LiDAR) point cloud and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) measurements. An initial vibration proxy is estimated from terrain geometry by applying Random sample consensus (RANSAC) to local point-cloud patches produced by a Simultaneous Localisation And Mapping (SLAM) algorithm. In parallel, the IMU provides local observations of the vibration experienced by the rover during traversal. The point-cloud-based prediction is then corrected online using Recursive Least Squares, allowing the system to adapt the geometric estimate to the measured rover response. The approach is evaluated in a lunar analogue environment, an outdoor field, and an underground mine.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, real-time, vibration-aware traversability mapping method for planetary rovers using LiDAR and IMU data, fusing a RANSAC-derived terrain proxy with online Recursive Least Squares to adapt to rover vibration, evaluated in lunar analogue, outdoor field, and underground mine.
AI.motivation: Autonomous navigation in space requires reliable terrain assessment under resource constraints and limited communication, especially in underground environments where vibration affects traversability and safety. Existing methods may be too heavy for rovers with tight power and compute budgets; a lightweight, real-time solution is needed.
AI.method: From SLAM-generated local LiDAR point-cloud patches, apply RANSAC to estimate a terrain-geometry-based vibration proxy. In parallel, use IMU measurements to capture rover vibration during traversal. Fuse the geometric proxy with the rover’s observed vibration online via Recursive Least Squares, allowing the geometry-based prediction to adapt to actual rover response in real time.
AI.result: The approach is evaluated in a lunar analogue environment, an outdoor field, and an underground mine, demonstrating real-time operation and applicability across diverse, challenging terrains without providing quantitative metrics in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework delivers a lightweight, real-time, vibration-aware traversability map by integrating LiDAR-derived terrain geometry with IMU-based rover vibration, online-adapted through RLS, suitable for safe underground navigation with limited resources.

title: When Depth Hurts: Reliability-Aware Geometry Distillation for Depth-Free RGB-D Salient Object Detection
summary: Depth can resolve appearance ambiguity in RGB-D salient object detection (SOD), yet sensor depth is not uniformly reliable. Missing regions, blurred boundaries, and structural artifacts can propagate through multimodal fusion and make an RGB-D detector less accurate than its RGB-only counterpart. Existing quality-aware approaches regulate observed depth but remain dependent on the same potentially defective modality. We propose \method, a reliability-aware geometry distillation framework developed for RGB-D SOD benchmarks without using dataset-provided depth during training or inference. A frozen Depth Anything V2 model serves only as a training-time teacher, transferring dense relative geometry, hierarchical spatial attention, and boundary structure to a compact edge-aware geometry branch. Pooled bidirectional interaction aligns geometry with appearance, and a pixel-wise reliability estimator selectively injects geometry that is compatible with the current RGB representation. The teacher is removed after training, leaving an RGB-only inference network. Trained on 2,985 RGB-mask pairs, \method{} achieves the best or tied-best result in 26 of 36 metric-dataset comparisons against ten recent RGB-D SOD methods, including a 13.4\% relative MAE reduction on ReDWeb-S. When retrained on DUTS-TR, it also improves the strongest prior $F$-measure by 4.2\% on PASCAL-S, showing that the distilled geometry transfers beyond a particular sensor or dataset domain. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: A reliability-aware geometry distillation approach enabling RGB-only SOD by distilling depth-based geometry from a training-time teacher; achieves strong, dataset-generalizable results without using depth at inference.
AI.motivation: Depth can help RGB-D SOD but depth data are often unreliable; existing quality-aware methods depend on depth; aim to achieve robust RGB-only SOD via distilled geometry.
AI.method: Train-time: use frozen Depth Anything V2 as teacher to transfer dense relative geometry, hierarchical spatial attention, and boundary structure to a compact edge-aware geometry branch. Pooled bidirectional interaction to align geometry with appearance. Pixel-wise reliability estimator selects geometry compatible with RGB. Inference: RGB-only. Teacher unused after training. Training data: 2,985 RGB-mask pairs.
AI.result: Achieves best or tied-best in 26 of 36 metric-dataset comparisons across 10 RGB-D SOD methods; includes 13.4% relative MAE reduction on ReDWeb-S. When retrained on DUTS-TR, improves strongest prior F-measure by 4.2% on PASCAL-S.
AI.conclusion: Distilled geometry transfers beyond a single sensor/dataset; demonstrates viability of reliability-aware geometry distillation for RGB-D SOD with RGB-only deployment.

title: GPS-Bench: A Governance Policy Benchmark for Automating Policy Analysis
summary: Policy analysis requires more than predicting whether a proposal will pass: it requires identifying who will be affected, how those actors respond, and what follows. LLM-based policy simulations model these processes at scale, but their validity is hard to establish when plausible behaviour is never compared with observed outcomes. We introduce GPS-Bench, an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that links policies to relevant actors, actor actions and downstream impacts using legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, economic data and other public evidence. Actors are reconstructed from the dated record rather than prompted as archetypes, so a persona is an evidence object with provenance; a human-annotated pool forms the Gold evaluation set, while cases labelled by a separate LLM from retrieved evidence are treated as Silver supervision and never as test labels. Because every inference mode reads the same grounded state and emits the same schema, GPS-Bench turns "does multi-agent simulation help?" into a controlled comparison: we contrast joint reasoning, independent and communicating actor agents, graph-based methods and weight-level fine-tuning over one policy state. Fine-tuning on the grounded record gives the strongest actor-level impact prediction, and decomposition does not beat it; what decomposition adds is mechanism. Agents hold private, non-identical evidence, each seeing its own exposure clause, and address named partners with concrete joint proposals, what they offer, what they need in return, and why acting together beats acting alone, so the coalitions that form can be checked against the commitments the record holds. GPS-Bench therefore gives a common empirical setting for studying when evidence, actor modelling and multi-agent interaction improve the prediction and interpretation of policy outcomes.

AI.tldr: GPS-Bench provides an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that links policies to actors, actions, and outcomes using public records, enabling controlled comparisons of inference modes and showing targeted fine-tuning on grounded data yields the strongest actor-level predictions.
AI.motivation: To establish a valid, reproducible benchmark for evaluating LLM-based governance simulations by anchoring predictions to observed evidence and peer-reviewed data, thus improving interpretability and predictive validity.
AI.method: Construct a benchmark that maps policies to relevant actors, actions, and downstream impacts using dated legislative records, lobbying, regulatory, corporate filings, and economic data. Actors are reconstructed from records as provenance-rich evidence objects rather than archetypes. Gold labels come from human annotation; Silver labels come from a separate LLM with retrieved evidence. Compare inference modes (joint reasoning, independent, communicating agents), graph-based methods, and weight-tuning on a single policy state, under a unified schema. Fine-tune on the grounded record; assess actor-level impact prediction and decomposition vs. tuning performance. Examine coalition formation via exposure clauses and partner proposals against the record.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on the grounded record yields the strongest actor-level impact predictions; decomposition alone does not beat fine-tuning, though it provides insight into mechanism. Multi-agent, evidence-grounded configurations reveal when and how coalitions form and improve outcomes, and provide a common empirical setting to study predictive and interpretive benefits of evidence, agent modeling, and interaction.
AI.conclusion: GPS-Bench offers a common, empirically grounded platform for evaluating how evidence, actor modeling, and multi-agent interaction influence policy outcome prediction and interpretation, enabling controlled comparisons across inference modes and datasets.

title: Frontier LLMs are effective batch optimizers: Assessing reasoning models in continuous and discrete settings
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have become attractive priors for optimization due to their large-scale pretraining that enables them to navigate a variety of optimization settings. However, the effectiveness of modern reasoning LLMs in batch optimization settings remains underexplored. Here we investigate the performance of the current generation of frontier LLMs as batch optimizers in both continuous and discrete settings. We find that while LLMs are competitive zero-shot batch optimizers for numerical test functions, their performance is brittle compared to classical non-LLM optimization approaches. However, LLM priors are significantly better in semantically rich settings, indicating that their batch optimization behavior is highly effective when navigating and reasoning over the discrete spaces most similar in structure to their pretraining data.

AI.tldr: Frontier LLMs can act as batch optimizers, competitive in zero-shot numeric tasks but brittle versus classical methods; they show clear strength in semantically rich, discrete-like spaces that align with their pretraining data.
AI.motivation: Assess whether large, reasoning-capable LLMs can serve as priors for batch optimization, and identify the problem regimes where they are advantageous.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of current frontier LLMs as batch optimizers in both continuous and discrete settings, comparing zero-shot performance to classical optimization approaches, across numerical test functions and semantically rich discrete domains.
AI.result: LLMs are competitive zero-shot batch optimizers for numerical test functions but exhibit brittleness compared to classical optimizers; their priors perform significantly better in semantically rich, discrete settings that resemble their pretraining data.
AI.conclusion: LLM priors can be effective batch optimizers in structured discrete domains, suggesting potential for hybrid optimization pipelines that leverage LLM reasoning where semantic structure dominates, while acknowledging limitations in general numerical optimization.

title: A Multi-Vine Soft Robot Enabling Accessible Working Channel and Steering
summary: Soft eversion robots, also known as vine robots, have attracted growing interest for navigation and inspection tasks, including minimally invasive medical applications [1]. A vine robot consists of a thin, flexible, inextensible tube folded inward that everts and grows forward when pressurized. This tip-growth enables navigation with minimal friction, making vine robots well suited for complex environments such as the human colon [2]. While their inherent softness allows passive conforma- tion to curved pathways in confined spaces, navigation performance strongly depends on environmental inter- actions, including contact angle and the length of un- constrained deployed material [3], [4]. Sharp directional changes, such as those in the sigmoid colon, often limit passive growth and necessitate active steering. Existing solutions include distributed artificial muscles [5] or dedicated tip-based steering mechanisms [6]. In addition, many applications require payload delivery, such as sensors and tools [7], [8]. Within the ERC Synergy project EndoTheranostics, this motivates the development of vine robots capable of delivering micro- surgical tools during growth. Prior work has integrated working channels within the vine body [8], [9], but these approaches constrain tool size, introduce friction, and limit access to the environment to the robot tip. In this work, we propose a multi-vine architecture in which two vine robots are coupled to an externally integrated working channel via soft mounting tips [10]. Independent vine actuation enables active tip steering while advancing the working channel without embed- ding it within the vine bodies Figure 1. Experiments demonstrate sharp steering of nearly 90 degrees during growth, highlighting the potential of this architecture for versatile medical and non-medical applications.

AI.tldr: Dual vine robot with soft-mounted external working channel enables independent tip steering and channel deployment, allowing sharp 90° turns during growth for tool delivery in confined environments.
AI.motivation: Enable active steering and tool-delivery in vine robots for minimally invasive navigation in complex, soft environments such as the colon; overcome limitations of embedded channels and passive growth.
AI.method: Two vine robots actuated independently; externally integrated working channel coupled via soft mounting tips; channel advances while vines steer; experiments demonstrate ~90° steering during growth.
AI.result: Validated ability to steer sharply while deploying a channel; shows feasibility of external channel approach without embedding within vine bodies, enabling tool delivery during growth.
AI.conclusion: The architecture expands vine robot capabilities for payload delivery and navigation; suggests strong potential for medical and non-medical applications; further work needed on control, payload limits, channel friction, integration with sensing tools, and reliability in complex environments.

title: FoRIS: Progressive Foreground Refinement for Training-Free In-Context Segmentation
summary: In-Context Segmentation (ICS) aims to precisely segment arbitrary semantic concepts, such as objects or parts, given one or a few annotated visual exemplars. In this paper, we revisit ICS from a more classical segmentation perspective, viewing it as a coarse-to-fine progressive refinement process. Rather than directly predicting the final mask through reference-query matching, we progressively refine the segmentation from coarse and ambiguous foreground responses to precise and complete foreground structures. Building upon this perspective, we propose a training-free in-context segmentation framework, termed FoRIS. Specifically, FoRIS consists of three key stages: Foreground Purification, Foreground Localization, and Foreground Consolidation, which progressively suppress background distractions, localize discriminative target regions, and recover complete foreground structures through semantic aggregation. Experimental results demonstrate that FoRIS achieves SOTA performance across semantic and part segmentation tasks, with average improvements of 4.5 and 4.8 mIoU points over existing approaches in the 1-shot and 5-shot settings, respectively. Code: https://github.com/Xi-Mu-Yu/FoRIS.

AI.tldr: A training-free in-context segmentation method (FoRIS) reframes ICS as a coarse-to-fine refinement, using Foreground Purification, Localization, and Consolidation to achieve state-of-the-art results in 1-shot and 5-shot semantic and part segmentation; substantial improvements (~4.5–4.8 mIoU) over prior work.
AI.motivation: Reinterpret In-Context Segmentation as a coarse-to-fine refinement problem and address the need for training-free methods that can adapt to arbitrary concepts with few exemplars, reducing reliance on end-to-end reference-query matching.
AI.method: FoRIS pipeline with three stages: Foreground Purification (suppress background distractions), Foreground Localization (localize discriminative target regions), Foreground Consolidation (recover complete foreground structures via semantic aggregation); designed as a training-free framework for ICS.
AI.result: FoRIS achieves state-of-the-art performance on semantic and part segmentation in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, with average mIoU gains of about 4.5 and 4.8 points over previous methods; code made available at the provided repo.
AI.conclusion: A training-free, coarse-to-fine ICS framework that significantly boosts few-shot segmentation performance, validating the efficacy of progressive foreground refinement for general concept segmentation and offering a practical, reusable solution.

title: HalluPeer: A Taxonomy-driven Benchmark for Detecting Hallucinations in Scientific Peer Reviews
summary: The growing scale of academic peer review has motivated the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as review assistants, yet LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review, where verification requires grounding claims in long, technical papers. We introduce HalluPeer, a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, providing aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews, annotated for detection, classification, and localization. Our pipeline induces a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identifies review contexts, and injects hallucinations with automated filtering. Experiments on 12K papers and 38K reviews show that existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique, while evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the critical need for source-aware verification. Our project page can be found in https://github.com/Lin-TzuLing/HalluPeer.git

AI.tldr: HalluPeer is a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, aligning paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews; defines a taxonomy, contexts, and automated injection; evaluated on large-scale data; shows current detectors struggle and real reviews exhibit the patterns, underscoring need for source-aware verification; code at GitHub.
AI.motivation: LLMs as review assistants can generate fluent but unsupported claims, threatening review reliability; existing hallucination benchmarks are not tailored to peer review, where verification requires grounding in long, technical papers.
AI.method: A pipeline to (1) induce a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, (2) identify review contexts, and (3) inject hallucinations with automated filtering, producing aligned triples of paper content, human reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews annotated for detection, classification, and localization.
AI.result: Experiments on 12K papers and 38K reviews show existing detectors struggle to distinguish hallucinations from legitimate critique; evaluation on authentic reviews indicates HalluPeer-pattern hallucinations occur in real reviews; highlights need for source-aware verification.
AI.conclusion: HalluPeer fills a gap in evaluation resources for hallucination detection in peer review, enabling development of safer, source-grounded review assistants; codebase available at the project page (GitHub).

title: Portable Causal Fairness Across Synthetic Data Generator Families
summary: When a statistical agency or regulator releases synthetic data in place of sensitive records, it chooses the generator that produces the table, and can shape that generator so unfair pathways are absent. DECAF made this concrete on one non-private GAN: three fairness definitions become three sets of edge cuts on the generator's causal graph. Whether the mechanism belongs to DECAF, or to causal factorisation itself, was untested. We port all three definitions to nine generators from three unrelated families (marginals-based, GAN, and diffusion, each with differentially private variants), across three levels of formal privacy guarantee, over 2,520 matched-pair runs on Adult and COMPAS datasets. The mechanism transfers everywhere, and our new causal diffusion backbone yields the fairest release of any family we tested, at fidelity close to the marginals tier. Applying the cut barely moves fidelity, only costs a downstream classifier about $0.07$ to $0.15$ AUC on average, and adding privacy guarantees don't make the data less fair.

AI.tldr: DECAF-style fairness via causal edge cuts transfers across nine generator families (marginals, GAN, diffusion) with DP variants; the causal-diffusion backbone yields the fairest data releases with fidelity near the marginals, and cuts cause minimal utility loss; privacy does not reduce fairness.
AI.motivation: To determine whether fairness achieved by DECAF or by causal factorization persists across diverse synthetic-data generators and privacy regimes, and whether the mechanism is tied to a specific generator family.
AI.method: Port three fairness definitions as edge cuts on generator causal graphs and evaluate across nine generator families (marginals-based, GAN, diffusion) with DP variants, under three privacy levels, using 2,520 matched-pair runs on the Adult and COMPAS datasets.
AI.result: The fairness mechanism transfers across all generator families. The new causal diffusion backbone yields the fairest releases among the tested families, with fidelity close to the marginals tier. Applying the cut has negligible impact on fidelity, incurring a downstream AUC drop of about 0.07–0.15 on average. Adding privacy guarantees does not make the data less fair.
AI.conclusion: Causal-factorization-based fairness generalizes across generator families and privacy regimes; diffusion-based generators offer the strongest fairness with minimal utility loss, implying that fairness properties are not tied to a single DECAF implementation but to the causal structure used to constrain generation.

title: Virtual Testing of Automated Driving Systems through Credible Simulations
summary: Simulation is increasingly used to support safety-related decision-making in road transport, particularly for the assessment and approval of automated driving systems (ADS). The complexity of ADS behavior and size of their operational design domains make exclusive reliance on physical testing impractical, leading to extensive use of virtual testing (VT) during the approval phase. This shift raises critical questions regarding the credibility of modelling and simulation (M&S) results used to support road safety decisions. Current VT accreditation approaches in the ADS domain typically rely on validation-only practices, which have been shown to scale poorly when applied to complex, multi-tool simulation environments. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a risk-based framework for assessing the credibility of simulation toolchains used in ADS safety evaluation, drawing inspiration from established practices in other safety-critical domains, notably NASA's STD-7009 for models and simulations. The framework extends traditional verification and validation (V&V) by explicitly linking credibility requirements to the intended use of simulation outputs and to the safety criticality of the decisions they support within the approval process. It provides a lifecycle-oriented assessment scheme integrating toolchain management, modelling assumptions and limitations, verification, validation, and sensitivity analysis. Credibility acceptance thresholds are defined proportionally, allowing differentiated requirements depending on whether simulation is used for exploratory safety analysis, partial decision support, or as a substitute for physical testing. While demonstrated for ADS, the proposed approach is directly applicable to road safety and simulation studies where VT plays a central role in safety assessment and regulatory decision-making.

AI.tldr: A risk-based credibility framework for simulation toolchains in ADS safety evaluation, extending V&V with lifecycle management and use-case–dependent thresholds to support safety decisions and regulatory approval.
AI.motivation: Physical testing is impractical for ADS due to complexity and design-domain size; current validation-centric VT accreditation scales poorly for multi-tool simulation environments.
AI.method: Develops a risk-based credibility framework inspired by NASA STD-7009, linking credibility to the intended use and safety criticality; integrates toolchain management, modelling assumptions/limitations, verification, validation, and sensitivity analysis; defines use-case–dependent credibility thresholds within a lifecycle assessment.
AI.result: Conceptual framework demonstrated for ADS; applicable to road safety and regulatory contexts; provides a scalable approach to credibility assessment for VT in safety evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Enables credible VT-based safety decisions in ADS approval and road safety studies, with differentiated requirements aligned to regulatory decision-making.

title: Exploring the Potential of Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training for Multi-Source Remote Sensing Data
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to AAAI 2027
summary: Contrastive language-image learning (CLIP) has become a key paradigm for remote sensing vision-language understanding. However, existing remote sensing contrastive learning methods are mostly built on RGB-oriented CLIP architectures, making it difficult to exploit heterogeneous sensors such as SAR, multi-spectral imaging (MSI), and hyperspectral imaging (HSI). To address this limitation, we propose OmniRSCLIP, an end-to-end contrastive learning framework that supports multi-source sensor inputs for remote sensing vision-language modeling. The key idea is to extend CLIP beyond its fixed RGB input interface without breaking the pretrained visual knowledge. To this end, OmniRSCLIP introduces Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition (SSBD), which formulates arbitrary-channel adaptation as a basis recomposition problem: pretrained CLIP patch embeddings provide transferable spatial bases, while wavelength-conditioned coefficients span sensor-specific embedding kernels within a constrained visual prior space. This design avoids forcing heterogeneous sensors into a fixed-channel input space, while aligning them in a unified image-text semantic space. We further introduce a spectral-context-aware mask-based contrastive learning scheme to suppress modality-specific redundant features and enhance fine-grained image-text alignment. Finally, to support multi-modal training, we construct OmniRS5M, the first large-scale remote sensing image-text corpus covering RGB, SAR, MSI, and HSI. Experiments on retrieval, zero-shot classification, and semantic localization show that OmniRSCLIP preserves strong RGB-domain performance while effectively extending CLIP to heterogeneous remote sensing modalities.

AI.tldr: OmniRSCLIP extends CLIP to multi-source remote sensing (RGB, SAR, MSI, HSI) via Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition and spectral-context-aware masking, trained on OmniRS5M, preserving RGB performance while enabling heterogeneous modality alignment for retrieval, zero-shot classification, and semantic localization.
AI.motivation: RGB-oriented CLIP struggles to leverage heterogeneous sensing modalities in remote sensing. There is a need to preserve pretrained visual knowledge while supporting arbitrary-channel inputs and aligning multi-sensor imagery with text in a unified semantic space.
AI.method: Introduce Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition (SSBD): pretrained CLIP patch embeddings provide transferable spatial bases; wavelength-conditioned coefficients form sensor-specific embedding kernels within a constrained visual prior space. Add spectral-context-aware mask-based contrastive learning to suppress modality-specific redundancy. Build OmniRS5M, a large-scale image-text corpus covering RGB, SAR, MSI, and HSI for multi-modal training.
AI.result: Experiments on retrieval, zero-shot classification, and semantic localization show that OmniRSCLIP maintains strong RGB-domain performance and effectively extends CLIP to heterogeneous remote sensing modalities.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates viable end-to-end multi-source sensor vision-language modeling for remote sensing, preserving existing RGB-capabilities while enabling cross-modal alignment across SAR, MSI, and HSI; the OmniRS5M dataset supports scalable training.

title: The Attention Triangle in Audio-Video Models
summary: Audio-video diffusion models rely on cross-modal attention to coordinate text, sound, and visual content, yet this same mechanism can introduce subtle and systematic semantic leakage. We study these models by probing and analyzing the ``attention triangle,'' comprising the three cross-attention edges connecting the text, audio, and video streams, and examine how semantic information is routed across modalities during generation. Our analysis reveals that routing along the audio-video edge is bidirectional: audio can influence video generation, while video can influence audio generation. This edge is shaped by biases encoded in the model's parameters and emerges as a major contributor to leakage: when prompts are in tension with learned priors, cross-modal interactions may override the intended conditioning and reroute semantics toward visually canonical but incorrect outcomes. These effects suggest that semantic artifacts arise not merely from attention spreading beyond its intended target, but from structured, bias-driven interactions along specific pathways. Building on this perspective, we extract attention-derived signals that expose how semantics are distributed and grounded across modalities, and use them as a diagnostic tool to both analyze and deliberately incur leakage under controlled conditions. This enables us to probe the internal dynamics of cross-modal routing and isolate the role of individual interactions. We further leverage these signals to guide inference-time interventions that encourage more consistent cross-modal alignment. Extensive experiments support our analysis and demonstrate improved semantic grounding while preserving generation quality.

AI.tldr: Analyzes semantic leakage in audio-video diffusion models via cross-modal attention. The text-audio-video attention triangle reveals bidirectional audio-video influence, biased routing causes leakage, and attention-derived signals diagnose and provoke leakage for study; inference-time interventions improve cross-modal alignment without harming quality.
AI.motivation: Understand how cross-modal attention in audio-video diffusion models can cause semantic leakage and structured bias-driven interactions, and develop diagnostics and interventions to improve grounding.
AI.method: Probe and analyze the cross-attention triangle among text, audio, and video streams; extract attention-derived signals to map semantics across modalities; conduct controlled leakage experiments; test inference-time interventions to improve alignment while maintaining quality; extensive experiments.
AI.result: The audio–video edge is bidirectional: audio can influence video generation and vice versa; leakage is shaped by model biases and can override conditioning to yield visually canonical but incorrect outputs; attention-derived signals reveal semantic distribution across modalities; interventions can promote more consistent cross-modal alignment and improve grounding without sacrificing generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Semantic artifacts arise from bias-driven, structured cross-modal interactions rather than mere broad attention. The proposed diagnostic signals enable analysis and deliberate leakage under control, and inference-time interventions can enhance cross-modal grounding while preserving quality.

title: Language-encoded network topology enables large language models to reason about complex networks
summary: Networks describe systems in biology and beyond, from protein interactions and social relationships to power grids and citation records. Reasoning about such systems requires understanding their structure: which elements are central, which connections bridge separate communities, and how it changes when elements are removed. Although large language models (LLMs) excel at natural language, they struggle with such questions when networks are given as edge lists, sentences or measurement tables, because their structural meaning must be inferred. Here we introduce BioGlyph, which compiles network topology into an interpretable and transferable language of structural roles. BioGlyph combines graph partitioning and structural measurements to identify roles such as hubs, community cores and cross-community connectors, and fixed rules to translate them into a universal vocabulary. The representation describes each element through its structural role, supporting evidence and semantic consequences, leaving both the network and the LLM unchanged. Across twenty networks spanning five domains, BioGlyph substantially improves open LLMs' ability to answer structural reasoning questions, outperforming edge-based, numerical and learned representations by up to 26 percentage points in system accuracy. Ablations show that the gain comes from explicitly encoding structural roles in semantically interpretable terms. The gain is more prominent in dense, community-structured networks and diminishes in sparse networks whose topology is more readily inferred from text. In a budding-yeast protein-interaction network, BioGlyph exposes biological organization: cross-community connectors are enriched for essential genes, whereas peripheral proteins are depleted. BioGlyph thus provides an interpretable representation for both language models and scientists to reason about network structure.

AI.tldr: BioGlyph converts network topology into an interpretable structural-role language to boost LLM-based structural reasoning, achieving gains across many networks.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle to reason about networks when input comes as edge lists or tables; a transferable, semantically interpretable representation of structural roles is needed to support reasoning without changing the data or the model.
AI.method: Integrates graph partitioning and structural measurements to assign roles (e.g., hubs, cores, cross-community connectors) and translates these roles into a fixed, universal vocabulary. The representation includes the element's structural role, supporting evidence, and semantic consequences, while leaving the network data and LLM unchanged.
AI.result: Evaluated on 20 networks across five domains; open LLMs' structural reasoning accuracy improved by up to 26 percentage points over edge-based, numerical, and learned representations. Ablations show gains stem from explicit encoding of structural roles in interpretable terms. Gains larger in dense, community-structured networks and smaller in sparse networks. In a budding-yeast PPI network, cross-community connectors are enriched for essential genes; peripheral proteins are depleted.
AI.conclusion: BioGlyph provides an interpretable, transferable representation for both LLMs and scientists to reason about network structure across domains.

title: Robot Aware Computational Design of Object Specific Passive Grippers for Additive Manufacturing
summary: This paper presents an end-to-end computational pipeline that converts a selected object mesh, a measured object state, and a selected six-axis robot into an object-specific, unactuated, additively manufacturable gripper. The method couples exact-mesh RGB-D/ICP pose registration, deterministic surface-contact sampling, uncertainty-aware wrench screening, selection among six passive capture mechanisms, object-conformal surface synthesis, full-orientation robot inverse kinematics, a swept-volume-aware manufacturing domain, directional fused-deposition finite-element screening, and constrained three-dimensional SIMP topology optimization. Unlike workflows that treat grasp selection, tool geometry, motion, and structural design as separate problems, every exported design is bound to the source mesh, object pose, robot flange, contact set, and insertion hypothesis by a traceable design identifier. We derive the implemented registration, contact, fit-tolerance, finite-element, and density-optimization equations and prove three properties of the numerical construction: nodal load preservation, monotonic compliance sensitivity under SIMP interpolation, and voxel-domain containment after topology post-processing. Four archived object-specific attempts - a rabbit, camera flange, 3DBenchy, and faceted bust - meet the nominal fit, uncertain-wrench, runtime-sweep, and baseline/post-topology FEA gates. A deliberately enlarged +/-3 mm, +/-5 degree pose stress check differentiates the designs, retaining 29-134 of 160 simulated trials. Their reconstructed topologies retain 92.0-97.6% of the FE domain because functional regions are protected. Archived robot photographs show the corresponding printed assemblies qualitatively, while nominal material properties and absent coupon-calibrated, instrumented tests keep all four at digital-screening status rather than operational release.

AI.tldr: End-to-end pipeline for object-specific, additively manufacturable grippers tightly coupled to mesh, pose, and robot, integrating registration, contact sampling, FE screening, topology optimization, and traceable design IDs; digital screening shows strong FE-domain retention but no physical validation.
AI.motivation: To overcome fragmented grasp-design processes by unifying geometry, pose, contact, and manufacturing constraints into a traceable, end-to-end workflow for object-specific grippers.
AI.method: 1) exact-mesh RGB-D/ICP pose registration; 2) deterministic surface-contact sampling; 3) uncertainty-aware wrench screening; 4) selection among six passive capture mechanisms; 5) object-conformal surface synthesis; 6) full-orientation robot inverse kinematics; 7) swept-volume-aware manufacturing domain; 8) directional fused-deposition finite-element screening; 9) constrained 3D SIMP topology optimization; 10) traceable design identifier binding to source mesh, pose, robot flange, contact set, and insertion hypothesis; 11) derivation and proof of nodal load preservation, monotonic compliance sensitivity under SIMP, voxel-domain containment; 12) four object cases subjected to nominal-fit, uncertain-wrench, runtime-sweep, and baseline/topology gates.
AI.result: Four archived objects (rabbit, camera flange, 3DBenchy, faceted bust) meet the nominal-fit and screening gates; 29–134 of 160 simulated trials survive under an enlarged pose stress check (+/-3 mm, +/-5°); topologies retain 92.0–97.6% of the FE domain; printed assemblies shown qualitatively; all work remains in digital-screening status due to absence of coupon-calibrated, instrumented physical tests.
AI.conclusion: The study delivers a tightly integrated, end-to-end, traceable design pipeline for object-specific grippers with strong numerical properties and FE/topology safeguards, but it remains digitally validated; physical validation and broader generalization remain for future work.

title: Neural-Collapse-guided Task-Free Continual Anomaly Detection
summary: Recent years have witnessed growing interest in continual anomaly detection for industrial visual inspection. However, real-world manufacturing environments exhibit unpredictable shifts in data distributions, rendering task-dependent continual learning assumptions impractical. To address this limitation, we formulate industrial anomaly detection as a task-free continual learning problem and propose NC-TFAD, a neural-collapse-inspired, geometry-driven framework for learning from non-stationary data streams without task boundaries. NC-TFAD freezes a pretrained backbone and aligns streaming features to a simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) prototype space to stabilize representation geometry under non-stationary streams. To satisfy the NC-inspired geometric construction in the absence of real anomalies, we generate synthetic anomaly samples as auxiliary anchors during training. Building on this geometry, we further introduce inter- and intra-class regularization together with a Focal Neural Collapse Contrastive (FNCC) loss to suppress representation drift and improve normal-anomaly separability. Finally, a normal-patch-prototype-guided localization branch constructs calibrated patch-wise deviation maps from normal training samples and fuses them with a weak self-attention prior, producing anomaly heatmaps without pixel-level annotations. Extensive experiments on MVTec AD and VisA show that NC-TFAD consistently outperforms representative task-free continual learning methods adapted from general vision, as well as unified anomaly detection baselines, in both image-level detection and pixel-level localization under the task-free continual learning protocol. These results highlight that geometry-driven modeling offers an effective and robust solution for task-free continual anomaly detection in real-world industrial applications.

AI.tldr: Task-free continual anomaly detection for industrial inspection using NC-TFAD: a geometry-driven approach that aligns streaming features to a simplex ETF prototype space, with synthetic anomaly anchors and a focal neural collapse contrastive loss, enabling pixel-level localization without annotations and outperforming baselines on MVTec AD and VisA.
AI.motivation: Industrial settings exhibit non-stationary data streams with unpredictable distribution shifts and lack of clear task boundaries; conventional task-based continual learning is impractical for real-time anomaly detection.
AI.method: Freeze a pretrained backbone and map streaming features to a simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) prototype space. Generate synthetic anomaly anchors to satisfy NC geometry in absence of real anomalies. Apply inter- and intra-class regularization and a Focal Neural Collapse Contrastive (FNCC) loss to reduce drift and enhance normal–anomaly separation. Introduce a normal-patch-prototype-guided localization branch to produce calibrated patchwise deviation heatmaps from normal data, fused with a weak self-attention prior for pixel-level anomaly localization without pixel annotations.
AI.result: NC-TFAD consistently outperforms representative task-free continual learning methods adapted from general vision and unified anomaly detection baselines in both image-level detection and pixel-level localization on MVTec AD and VisA under a task-free continual learning protocol.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-driven modeling provides an effective, robust solution for task-free continual anomaly detection in real-world industrial applications.

title: KC-Bench: A Dynamic Interactive Benchmark for Evaluating Knowledge Conflicts in LLM Agents
summary: As LLMs increasingly act through tools, they must reconcile user instructions, parametric knowledge, and dynamic environmental observations before taking actions. We introduce KC-Bench, a controlled multi-turn benchmark for measuring this capability across world-knowledge conflicts, input inconsistencies, and multi-source temporal conflicts. Its 238 tasks are manually screened from more than 1,000 generated candidates and combine a user simulator, stateful tools, deterministic environment assertions, an open-source natural-language evaluator, and human trajectory verification. Evaluation of nine models, including DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3, shows substantial cross-domain variation: no model handles factual correction, identity consistency checking, and temporal conflict resolution reliably across all settings. In the simulated environments, missed conflicts can propagate to tool calls or synthetic protected-data flows. KC-Bench isolates this model-level behavior rather than ranking complete agent frameworks, and provides a reproducible diagnostic for developing conflict-aware reasoning and execution safeguards.

AI.tldr: KC-Bench is a controlled, multi-turn benchmark to evaluate how LLMs reconcile user instructions, fixed knowledge, and dynamic environment observations when using tools. It features 238 tasks mined from 1,000+ candidates, a full evaluation pipeline, and nine models, revealing widespread cross-domain weaknesses in factual correction, identity consistency, and temporal conflict resolution.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly operate via tools, there is a need to quantify model-level conflict handling across world-knowledge conflicts, input inconsistencies, and multi-source temporal conflicts, rather than only evaluating end-agent pipelines.
AI.method: 238 tasks, manually screened from more than 1,000 generated candidates. The benchmark combines a user simulator, stateful tools, deterministic environment assertions, an open-source natural-language evaluator, and human trajectory verification. Nine models (e.g., DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, MiniMax-M3) were evaluated across cross-domain scenarios.
AI.result: There is substantial cross-domain variation; no model reliably handles factual correction, identity consistency checking, and temporal conflict resolution across all settings. In simulated environments, missed conflicts can propagate to tool calls or synthetic protected-data flows. KC-Bench isolates model-level behavior and provides a reproducible diagnostic for conflict-aware reasoning and execution safeguards.
AI.conclusion: KC-Bench offers a reproducible diagnostic platform focused on model-level conflict resolution, enabling development of conflict-aware reasoning and safeguards, rather than ranking whole agent frameworks.

title: The 2026 PNPL Competition: Word Classification and Efficient Cross-Subject Generalisation in LibriBrain100
summary:
The ambition of the 2025 PNPL competition (Landau et al., 2025) was to launch a multi-year curriculum for non-invasive speech decoding. Designed to progress from foundational tasks toward the linguistic complexity required for a practical brain-computer interface (BCI), it set the stage with speech detection and phoneme classification tasks. Winning submissions reached F1-macro scores of 95.6% and 73.6% on the respective tasks (Elvers et al., 2026), highly significant advances. This success was built on the LibriBrain dataset (Özdogan et al., 2025), the largest within-subject MEG dataset recorded at the time with ${\sim}50$ hours of data for one subject. However, while within-subject scale drives strong decoding performance, a practical BCI must generalise to new users from minutes of data, not hours.
  The 2026 PNPL competition responds to this challenge with LibriBrain100 (Mantegna et al., 2026), an extended LibriBrain dataset with 32 additional subjects (${\sim}40$ minutes each) plus even more within-subject data (${\sim}80$ hours). Advancing the curriculum of tasks to focus on word classification, two complementary tracks are presented in this competition: the Deep track targets within-subject word classification at scale, aiming at the best possible performance; the Broad track targets cross-subject generalisation, progressively reducing the amount of subject-specific fine-tuning data from ${\sim}40$ to ${\sim}20$ to ${\sim}10$ minutes, a duration that falls within a clinically feasible range and brings us a step closer to a non-invasive BCI capable of restoring communication to people living with profound paralysis.

AI.tldr: Progression from within-subject MEG-based speech decoding to cross-subject generalization for non-invasive BCI via PNPL competitions and LibriBrain datasets; demonstrates high within-subject performance and moves toward clinically feasible data needs, via two competition tracks.
AI.motivation: Address generalization and data-efficiency challenges in non-invasive speech decoding for BCI, by building scalable curricula and datasets that progress from detection to word classification and by contrasting within-subject and cross-subject performance.
AI.method: Two competitions: PNPL 2025 with tasks of speech detection and phoneme classification; LibriBrain dataset (~50 hours/subject). PNPL 2026 LibriBrain100 adds 32 subjects (~40 min each) and more within-subject data; two tracks: Deep (within-subject word classification) and Broad (cross-subject generalization with reduced fine-tuning data from ~40 to ~20 to ~10 minutes).
AI.result: Winning submissions achieved F1-macro scores of 95.6% and 73.6% on respective tasks; LibriBrain100 expands dataset for wider validation; progress indicates strong within-subject performance and potential for cross-subject generalization as data efficiency improves.
AI.conclusion: The curriculum and dataset evolution show a clear trajectory toward practical non-invasive BCI speech decoding, with significant gains in within-subject decoding and a structured path to reducing subject-specific data needs to clinically feasible levels. Cross-subject generalization remains a key challenge to address.

title: A comparative study on the accuracy & repeatability of mobile robotic platforms for the delivery of precision NDE measurement
summary:
Mobile robotic platforms offer a flexible alternative to fixed manipulators for non-destructive evaluation (NDE) of large aerospace structures, but their base-positioning accuracy and how that accuracy should inform deployment have not been assessed under a common, externally referenced protocol. This work presents a laser tracker-based evaluation workflow (ground truth approximately 6 micrometers) that measures the static and segmented trajectory positioning accuracy of five commercial mobile platforms (KUKA KMP-1500, KUKA KMR, MiR250, Boston Dynamics Spot, Clearpath Husky) under a common protocol. A coupled multi-corner calibration recovers the laser-to-robot transformation and reflector offsets; ordinary least squares over all poses is used, with robust estimation retained only as a blunder check.
  Static positioning accuracy ranged from a median of 8.2 mm (KMP-1500) to 63.5 mm (Spot), with the wheel-odometry-only Husky uncalibratable. Dynamic path following was characterised by cross-track error; the component was insensitive to temporal alignment, which ranged from 6.9 mm (KMP-1500) to 112.1 mm (Spot). Both accuracy and calibratability tracked localisation capability, from the newest LiDAR SLAM platform to map-free visual odometry. No configuration meets the 0.2 to 1.0 mm aerospace NDE tolerance from the base alone; the results are framed as a design input that sizes the supplementary sensing each platform requires: roughly one order of magnitude for the best platform and nearly two for the worst, providing a reproducible basis for platform selection rather than a feasibility claim.

AI.tldr: Laser-tracker based evaluation of five mobile robots for NDE base-positioning accuracy under a common protocol; none meet aerospace tolerance; findings guide need for supplementary sensing.
AI.motivation: Assess base-positioning accuracy of mobile robotic platforms for non-destructive evaluation of large aerospace structures under an externally referenced protocol, and to inform deployment decisions and platform selection.
AI.method: Laser tracker-based evaluation workflow with ground truth ~6 μm; five platforms (KUKA KMP-1500, KUKA KMR, MiR250, Boston Dynamics Spot, Clearpath Husky); coupled multi-corner calibration to recover laser-to-robot transform and reflector offsets; ordinary least squares over all poses; robust estimation retained only as blunder check.
AI.result: Static positioning accuracy medians: 8.2 mm to 63.5 mm; dynamic cross-track error: 6.9 mm to 112.1 mm; Husky uncalibratable; no platform meets 0.2–1.0 mm aerospace NDE tolerance; results indicate design inputs for supplementary sensing needs, roughly one order of magnitude for best, nearly two for worst.
AI.conclusion: Base-positioning alone cannot meet tight aerospace NDE tolerances; use supplementary sensing; provides a reproducible basis for platform selection and design of external sensing requirements under a common evaluation protocol.

title: Mudragen: Geometrically Supervised Generation of Interacting Two-Hand Mudras for Preserving Indian Classical Dance Heritage
comment: Accepted for publication in ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage (JOCCH) Special Issue on Visual Heritage
summary: Automatic generation of hand gestures is essential for the transmission of Indian classical dance and critical for its preservation. Indian classical dance gesture datasets are inherently low-resource, and the canonical Sanskrit definitions of many mudras lack precise textual descriptions, limiting the effectiveness of conventional text-conditioned image generation models. We present \textbf{MudraGen}, a conditional diffusion framework that synthesizes realistic RGB images of \textit{Samyukta Hasta Mudras} -- interactive two-hand gestures from Bharatanatyam (an Indian classical dance form). Unlike prior work on simple hand signs or single-hand gestures, MudraGen introduces geometry-aware supervision to capture the precise coordination, anatomical validity, and cultural nuance of interacting hands. We formulate three geometry-aware objectives: Keypoint Loss for 3D joint alignment, Joint Offset Loss for inter-hand spatial coherence, and Shape Consistency, which serves as an anatomical regularizer by encouraging consistent hand morphology while allowing independent hand poses. Together, these objectives guide the diffusion model toward anatomically plausible and well-coordinated hand configurations, enabling the synthesis of photorealistic and pose-accurate gesture images. Experimental results show that MudraGen surpasses existing state-of-the-art generative approaches in visual realism, anatomical correctness, and preservation of fine hand-pose structure, enabling faithful reproduction of complex Samyukta Hasta mudras. Beyond quantitative gains, its ability to generate culturally grounded and structurally consistent gestures highlights practical applications in cultural preservation and dance education.

AI.tldr: MudraGen uses a geometry-aware conditional diffusion model to synthesize photorealistic two-hand Samyukta Hasta mudras with joint-level supervision for anatomical plausibility and inter-hand coordination.
AI.motivation: Indian classical dance gestures (mudras) are low-resource and lack precise textual descriptions. Conventional text-conditioned image models struggle to capture complex two-hand coordination and cultural nuance, hindering digital preservation and education.
AI.method: A diffusion-based framework conditioned on pose, trained with three geometry-aware losses: Keypoint Loss (3D joint alignment), Joint Offset Loss (inter-hand spatial coherence), and Shape Consistency (anatomical regularizer for consistent hand morphology while allowing independent poses).
AI.result: MudraGen achieves superior visual realism, anatomical correctness, and preservation of fine hand-pose structure compared to prior generative methods, enabling faithful reproduction of Samyukta Hasta mudras and offering practical value for cultural preservation and dance education.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware supervision enhances plausibility and cultural fidelity in two-hand gesture synthesis, with potential to generalize to other cultural gestures and interactive-hologram-like educational tools.

title: A computable representation of the physical laboratory enables verifiable workflows
summary: Making science computable requires representations of both scientific knowledge and the physical world in which scientific claims are tested. A computable representation of the physical laboratory is established through typed research objects, capability-bound operations and a compositional workflow algebra. It provides the physical-world counterpart to machine-readable knowledge, expressing workflows as programs over evolving laboratory states with explicit dependencies, decisions, iteration and concurrency. The representation was implemented in a modular agentic robotic laboratory by binding formal operations to executable Function Skills. For diverse scientific intents, capability-relative workflows were generated, while stateful simulation propagated object transformations and verified operation preconditions and laboratory constraints before dispatch. The proposed representation and its engineering framework jointly establish a general computational interface between agent reasoning and capability-bound physical transformations, providing a foundation for end-to-end autonomous scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: A typed, capability-bound, compositional workflow formalism for computable lab operations, implemented in a modular robotic lab to enable stateful simulation, precondition verification, and autonomous scientific discovery.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between machine-readable knowledge and physical laboratory execution; support end-to-end autonomous experimentation by handling dependencies, decisions, iteration, and concurrency in laboratory workflows.
AI.method: Introduce typed research objects, capability-bound operations, and a compositional workflow algebra. Implement in a modular agentic robotic laboratory by binding formal operations to executable Function Skills. Use stateful simulation to propagate object transformations and verify operation preconditions and lab constraints before dispatch. Generate capability-relative workflows for diverse scientific intents.
AI.result: Proposes a general computational interface between agent reasoning and capability-bound physical transformations. Demonstrates end-to-end autonomous scientific discovery within a modular robotic lab, with stateful simulation validating preconditions and constraints prior to operation dispatch and enabling diverse workflow generation.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a scalable, general computational framework that links reasoning to physical lab actions, providing the foundation for autonomous scientific discovery and adaptable, capability-aware laboratory workflows.

title: B2B Customer Conversion Prediction: A Document Representation, Graph Theory, and CatBoost Driven Methodology
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Presented at the 2nd Workshop on End-End Customer Journey Optimization at KDD 2023
summary: In the one-time selling B2B context, the buying cycle may last months or even years. During the long process, targeting customers that have a high potential to make purchases and recommending personalized campaigns accordingly are important for effective marketing. For this goal, we study the following problems, B2B customer data aggregation, customer feature generation, and prediction of whether a B2B customer would show interest in making a purchase (i.e., prediction of conversion into sales funnel). We propose an algorithm to aggregate individual contacts to the B2B customer level based on multiple keys. For non-standardized keys such as company names, we propose a novel architecture to cluster them in a domain encompassing irregularities such as spelling mistakes and spelling variants. We then define and generate a set of features and apply the CatBoost model for customer conversion prediction. Our framework achieves 91\% prediction accuracy. Based on the prediction results and analysis of the model, we then discuss personalized campaign recommendations to foster conversion.

AI.tldr: A framework for B2B conversion prediction using aggregated account-level features from multiple contacts, including a novel clustering architecture for non-standardized company names, features, and CatBoost modeling that achieves 91% accuracy, enabling personalized campaign recommendations.
AI.motivation: To improve targeting in long B2B sales cycles by identifying high-potential customers from fragmented contact data and delivering personalized campaigns.
AI.method: Aggregate contacts to the B2B customer level using multi-key mappings; cluster non-standardized company names to handle spelling variants; generate a feature set; train a CatBoost model to predict conversion into the sales funnel; analyze results to guide campaign recommendations.
AI.result: The model achieves 91% prediction accuracy in predicting B2B customer conversion to the sales funnel and provides insights that support personalized campaign recommendations.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that integrated data aggregation, robust entity resolution for irregular company identifiers, and CatBoost-based prediction can effectively identify high-potential B2B customers and inform targeted marketing campaigns.

title: FWBC-VLA: Force-Aware Whole-Body Compensation for Contact-Rich Loco-Manipulation
summary: Contact-rich loco-manipulation requires a bridge between semantic action generation and physical interaction control. Existing Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate task-level actions from visual and linguistic observations, but cannot interpret the physical interactions induced by those actions. While the whole-body control (WBC) policy can stabilize the robot, it cannot distinguish task-relevant interaction forces from forces induced by external disturbances during manipulation. Although force/torque sensors provide direct measurements of physical interactions, retrofitting them entails additional hardware costs and substantial integration effort, particularly for platforms not designed with sensor integration in mind. To address this problem, we propose FWBC-VLA, a force-aware framework that bridges task-level VLA action generation and low-level whole-body compensation control for wheeled-legged robots. First, we introduce HSR-Force, a sensorless residual-torque estimator for inferring contact strength and its temporal variation. These contact estimates are then encoded as tokens and injected into the VLA action expert during action decoding, enabling the policy to perceive contact onset, sustained loading, and release. For loco-manipulation tasks, all parameters of the pretrained VLA backbone are fine-tuned on our WL\&Arm Dataset, which comprises more than 5,000 episodes. Moreover, the robot's proprioceptive state, the Jacobian-derived body-frame force estimate, and the estimated contact state are jointly fed into a compensation generator to produce corrective actions. The manipulation-centric actions are subsequently combined with the corrective actions and passed to the WBC policy for execution. Real-world experiments on whiteboard wiping and door opening with a door closer demonstrate the effectiveness of our FWBC-VLA in contact-rich loco-manipulation.

AI.tldr: A force-aware framework (FWBC-VLA) links vision-language action generation with force-aware low-level control for wheeled-legged robots; introduces sensorless contact estimation and token-based communication to improve contact-rich loco-manipulation.
AI.motivation: Current VLA models are unable to interpret the physical interactions induced by actions; WBC cannot distinguish task-relevant interaction forces from external disturbances; attaching force/torque sensors is costly and integration-heavy; a sensorless, integrated solution is desirable.
AI.method: Develop HSR-Force sensorless residual-torque estimator to infer contact strength and its variation; encode contact estimates as tokens injected into the VLA action decoder; fine-tune all pretrained VLA backbone parameters on WL&Arm dataset (>5,000 episodes); feed proprioceptive state, Jacobian-derived body-frame force estimate, and estimated contact state into a compensation generator to produce corrective actions; combine manipulation-centric actions with corrective actions and pass to WBC for execution; validate on whiteboard wiping and door opening with a door closer.
AI.result: Real-world experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FWBC-VLA in contact-rich loco-manipulation.
AI.conclusion: FWBC-VLA successfully bridges semantic action generation and physical interaction control for wheeled-legged robots, reducing reliance on explicit force sensing and enabling robust manipulation in contact-rich scenarios; shows promise for broader loco-manipulation tasks.

title: When Do Frozen VLMs Respond to Image-Free Object-Token Edits? An Answer-Key-Free Protocol and What It Reveals
summary: Answering what-if queries about a scene with a VLM usually means injecting the assumption as text or repainting the scene with a generative model. We instead move the edit to the representation level, before the model input. The image is abstracted into a set of object-level tokens, and the original image never enters the VLM. This design rests on an open question: when do frozen VLMs actually respond to such token edits? We introduce an answer-key-free protocol: no post-edit answer is annotated. It scores edits whose answers are logically determined, and audits itself by reversing each scoreable choice. The protocol reveals three structures. The response is not free: explicit edit teaching, not ordinary VQA training, produces it in dense scenes and multiplies it in sparse ones, on all three operations. Once on, it is governed by token cleanliness and density, with deployable detector+segmenter tokens competitive with the oracle and outperforming it on VRSBench. And reading is a separable axis: the image-free token route preserves 92-96% of a matched patch-token baseline's free-text VQA, and the answers measurably depend on the tokens. The response, cleanliness, and reading structures are sign-preserved across two remote-sensing datasets (iSAID, VRSBench) and three frozen LM backbones. We release the probe generator, records, judge logs, and code.

AI.tldr: Proposes object-level token edits in VLMs with an answer-key-free protocol to study when frozen VLMs respond to input edits, revealing three persistent structures and showing token cleanliness/density and a reading axis govern performance; validates across datasets and backbones; releases tools.
AI.motivation: Understand when frozen vision-language models respond to representation-level edits and develop a protocol that does not rely on post-edit answers.
AI.method: Represent the image as object-level tokens without feeding the original image into the VLM; edit tokens instead of pixels; use an answer-key-free scoring protocol with self-auditing by reversing scoreable choices; analyze three editing operations, token cleanliness/density, and deployable detector+segmenter tokens; evaluate on two remote-sensing datasets (iSAID, VRSBench) across three frozen LM backbones; compare to oracle baselines and assess reading as an image-free token route.
AI.result: Identify three preserved structures: (1) response depends on explicit edit teaching, especially in dense scenes; (2) token cleanliness and density govern performance; (3) a separable 'reading' axis exists for image-free token routes; detector+segmenter tokens can rival or outperform the oracle; the approach preserves 92-96% of a matched patch-token baseline’s free-text VQA; results hold across datasets and backbones; code and data release.
AI.conclusion: Editing at the representation level reveals durable response-structures in frozen VLMs, enabling accurate evaluation and tooling for token-level manipulations; the protocol and artifacts enable reproducible study of VLM sensitivity to token edits.

title: Analysis of Prompt Engineering for Drug Toxicity Prediction
summary: Clinical trials in the UK can cost up to £1.3 million, with approximately 90% drug failure rate. Toxicity is a major contributing factor in drug failure. Testing is time and cost intensive. In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence has been increasingly explored to aid in the prediction of drug toxicity, with extensive use of large language models (LLMs). However, LLMs can show considerable variation when minor changes are made to prompts, which raises concerns about their sensitivity to prompt engineering. Prompt engineering is used to optimise a prompt given to an LLM to generate the desired output. This paper proposes a method to analyse prompt engineering for drug toxicity prediction. The aim of the paper is to investigate the importance of prompt phrasing for drug toxicity prediction. LLMs were prompted to identify chemical properties of significance when predicting drug toxicity. Prompts were constructed to investigate; job role, prompt structuring, and rule interpretation. LLMs were then used to generate datasets, using the identified features from initial prompting, which were then passed to machine learning algorithms. The experiments show that the natural variance which occurs in LLMs outweighs any fine-tuning of prompts. There were, however, substantial improvements in model performance when using chemoinformatic code to extract features instead of using LLM-generated values. The proposed analysis methodology is applicable to a wide range of prompt types across different areas of bioinformatics.

AI.tldr: Assesses prompt engineering for LLM-based drug toxicity prediction; finds intrinsic LLM variability dominates over prompt tweaks, while chemoinformatic feature extraction substantially improves performance; the method is generalizable to bioinformatics prompts.
AI.motivation: High cost and failure rate of UK clinical trials due to toxicity; need reliable toxicity prediction. LLMs offer promise but are sensitive to prompt design, prompting the need to analyze prompt engineering's impact.
AI.method: Prompt LLMs to identify toxicity-relevant chemical properties with prompts varied by job role, prompt structure, and rule interpretation. Use LLM outputs to create feature datasets, then train conventional ML models. Compare with models using features derived from chemoinformatics instead of LLM-generated data.
AI.result: Natural variance in LLM outputs outweighs any benefits from prompt fine-tuning. Substantial performance gains occur when using chemoinformatic features instead of LLM-derived values. The analysis framework is applicable to a broad range of prompts in bioinformatics.
AI.conclusion: Prompt formulation has limited impact relative to intrinsic LLM variability; leveraging robust chemoinformatic features yields better predictive performance. The proposed methodology for analyzing prompt effects is broadly applicable to bioinformatics prompts.

title: FlowBalance: Verifier-Grounded Self-Improvement from On-Policy Reasoning Experience
comment: 28 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Code and blog available
summary: A reasoning model can improve from its own on-policy experience, but this inner loop is fragile: terminal verifiers provide reliable yet sparse supervision, while dense same-model guidance can reinforce false confidence or overconcentrate learning on a narrow solution mode. We introduce FlowBalance, a verifier-grounded self-improvement method that learns a normalized distribution over complete responses. For each on-policy trajectory, a frozen training-time view of the same policy uses privileged context to produce token-level log-probability gains, which are aggregated into a trajectory-level self-guidance score. FlowBalance calibrates this score with the verifier-derived group advantage: guidance is retained on positive-advantage trajectories, reversed on negative-advantage trajectories, and disabled when the rollout group provides no outcome preference. The resulting energy exponentially reweights a reference policy, and profiled trajectory balance fits the normalized target with one log-partition estimate per rollout group. This realizes outcome-calibrated self-guidance via trajectory balance, without a separate token-level imitation loss. Our analysis establishes within-group contrast preservation, a minimum-change reverse-KL characterization, monotonic verifier control of target reward, and an exact correction against false-positive self-guidance on rejected responses.
