On mathematical reasoning, FlowBalance improves average performance over FlowRL on both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, while also improving training speed and stability, avoiding direct OPSD's response-length collapse, and exhibiting higher correct-strategy diversity in a controlled AIME24 diagnostic.

AI.tldr: FlowBalance is a verifier-grounded self-improvement method that learns a normalized distribution over full responses, calibrating trajectory-level self-guidance with verifier group advantage to improve on-policy reasoning without token-level imitation losses.
AI.motivation: To address the fragility of inner-loop self-improvement: sparse, reliable terminal verifications versus dense but potentially misleading self-guidance; provide a principled, verifier-calibrated, energy-based reweighting mechanism to guide on-policy learning.
AI.method: For each on-policy trajectory, freeze a training-time view of the policy to use privileged context and compute token-level log-probability gains; aggregate to a trajectory-level self-guidance score; calibrate with the verifier-derived group advantage: retain guidance on positive-advantage trajectories, reverse on negative-advantage trajectories, disable when no outcome preference; reweight a reference policy via an energy formulation with one log-partition estimate per rollout group; optimize via trajectory balance without a separate token-level imitation loss.
AI.result: FlowBalance improves average performance on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B compared to FlowRL, with faster training, better stability, avoidance of OPSD-like response-length collapse, and higher correct-strategy diversity on a controlled AIME24 diagnostic.
AI.conclusion: The method yields outcome-calibrated self-guidance via trajectory balance, with verifier-controlled target rewards and exact correction against false-positive self-guidance; it provides stronger reasoning performance and stability without token-level imitation loss, and is supported by theoretical analyses (within-group contrast preservation, minimum-change reverse-KL, monotonic verifier control, and correction against rejected responses).

title: A hybrid pipeline for dynamic ontology-based semantic mapping
summary: Semantic mapping plays a crucial role in the ability of a robot to interact with objects, operate and navigate a complex environment. The most common pipeline for semantic mapping consists of geometric mapping and localization (SLAM), perception, semantic fusion and semantic representation. However, more recent works also integrate a form of prior knowledge in their application, most notably knowledge graphs or semantic scene graphs, to improve contextual understanding of the environment. In this paper, we present a hybrid pipeline for semantic mapping. Our system incorporates an external calibrated camera using homography projection for geometric mapping and localization, combined with object detection, persistent object tracking and ontology driven semantic updates to build a dynamic semantic world model. Linear regression models are also used for correction of the estimated values of real world coordinates. The system continuously updates object instances, spatial properties and semantic relations based on real time sensory data. Ontologies are selected as form of knowledge representation due to their hierarchical structure, semantic expressiveness and support for dynamic world modelling.

AI.tldr: Hybrid semantic mapping pipeline combining geometric SLAM with object detection/tracking and ontology-driven updates to maintain a dynamic semantic world model, using homography-based localization, linear regression for coordinate refinement, and ontologies for structured knowledge representation.
AI.motivation: Enhance robot contextual understanding by fusing geometric mapping with prior knowledge representations (knowledge graphs/semantic scene graphs) to enable dynamic and expressive scene reasoning.
AI.method: Use an external calibrated camera with homography projection for mapping and localization; integrate object detection and persistent tracking; perform ontology-driven semantic updates to update object instances, spatial properties, and relations; apply linear regression to correct estimated real-world coordinates; continuously update a dynamic semantic world model; select ontologies for their hierarchical structure and expressive semantics.
AI.result: The system maintains a continuously updated dynamic semantic world model with evolving object instances, spatial properties, and semantic relations, leveraging ontologies to structure knowledge and support reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Ontologies are well-suited for semantic mapping in dynamic environments due to their hierarchical organization, expressive semantics, and support for dynamic world modelling, enabling enhanced contextual understanding through knowledge-based representations.

title: OCR-EDR: Rendering-Aware Diagnosis and Repair for Closed-Loop OCR Improvement
summary: Although document OCR systems perform increasingly well on routine documents, complex formulas, structured text, and long-tail formats remain error-prone. OCR predictions may omit fine-grained content or hallucinate unsupported outputs, while equivalent encodings of the same visible content must be accommodated. Existing OCR evaluation methods mostly report aggregate metrics, offering limited support for analyzing case-level errors and improving OCR performance. We propose OCR-EDR (OCR Error Diagnosis and Repair), a rendering-aware framework that advances from fine-grained diagnosis to iterative repair. Given a source image, an editable OCR prediction, and its rendered image, OCR-EDR first jointly assesses whether the prediction and its rendering are consistent with the source, preserving valid predictions, including rendering-equivalent ones, while diagnosing and localizing genuine errors. It then applies executable edits and may request an updated rendering for iterative reassessment. We construct OCRErrBench from diverse real OCR predictions, covering text and formulas, exact and rendering-equivalent positives, and genuine errors, and develop the DocEDR model to execute the diagnosis--repair loop. On OCRErrBench, DocEDR achieves 94.78% diagnostic accuracy. It repairs 86.23% of erroneous inputs to visual consistency, raises formula Case-F1 by 30.99 percentage points over DOCR-Inspector-7B on DOCRcaseBench, and improves formula CDM by up to 4.62 percentage points on the identified Bad subsets of four OCR systems on UniMER-Test. These results show that OCR-EDR turns fine-grained OCR analysis into verified corrections and performance gains.

AI.tldr: OCR-EDR is a rendering-aware OCR error diagnosis and repair framework that analyzes OCR outputs against rendered content, diagnoses errors, and iteratively repairs predictions, validated on OCRErrBench/DocEDR.
AI.motivation: Current OCR evaluation focuses on aggregate metrics and ignores case-level errors and rendering-equivalence; there is a need to diagnose, localize, and repair errors by considering rendering.
AI.method: Jointly assess source image, an editable OCR prediction, and its rendered image to determine consistency; preserve valid and rendering-equivalent predictions; diagnose genuine errors; apply executable edits; may request updated renderings for iterative reassessment; construct a benchmark (OCRErrBench) and train a DocEDR model for the diagnosis–repair loop.
AI.result: On OCRErrBench, DocEDR achieves 94.78% diagnostic accuracy; repairs 86.23% of erroneous inputs to visual consistency; improves formula Case-F1 by 30.99 percentage points over DOCR-Inspector-7B on DOCRcaseBench; improves formula CDM by up to 4.62 percentage points on Bad subsets of four OCR systems on UniMER-Test.
AI.conclusion: OCR-EDR demonstrates that turning fine-grained OCR analysis into verified corrections yields substantial performance gains and makes OCR outputs more reliable, especially for complex content like formulas.

title: Synthetic Semantic Supervision for Contrastive Code Representation Learning in Small Transformers: An Empirical Study
summary: General-purpose code embeddings power tools for code search, classification, and retrieval. Compact transformer encoders for code typically rely on either human-written docstrings (labor-intensive and inconsistent) or mined structural signals such as execution traces (setting-specific and costly to collect). We empirically study an alternative: contrastive pretraining of small encoders with synthetically generated natural-language descriptions emphasizing code functionality and intent, paired with code in a dual-encoder framework at training and discarded at inference. We benchmark this approach against pretraining-based baselines, generalist LLMs, and embedding-specific models on eight retrieval, classification, and generation tasks across C, C++, and Java. Synthetic semantic supervision yields statistically significant gains over pretraining baselines of the same inference-time size on five of eight tasks, with parity on two more; once fine-tuned, it matches or exceeds zero-shot models two orders of magnitude larger on classification, and it stays on par with execution-aware supervision at matched pretraining data, suggesting a scalable, effective alternative to existing code-representation paradigms.

AI.tldr: Contrastive pretraining of small code encoders using synthetic natural-language descriptions of code functionality within a dual-encoder setup, trained but discarded at inference, yielding competitive performance across eight tasks (C/C++/Java) and multiple tasks, offering a scalable alternative to docstrings or execution traces.
AI.motivation: Develop compact, effective code representations without relying on labor-intensive docstrings or costly execution traces. Explore synthetic natural-language supervision to guide semantic understanding of code.
AI.method: Pretrain small encoders with contrastive learning using synthetically generated NL descriptions that emphasize code functionality/intent. Use a dual-encoder architecture during training (code and NL description encodings) but discard NL encoders at inference. Evaluate on eight tasks (retrieval, classification, generation) across C, C++, Java, comparing to pretraining baselines, generalist LLMs, and embedding-specific models.
AI.result: Synthetic semantic supervision yields statistically significant gains over pretraining baselines of the same inference-time size on five of eight tasks, with parity on two more. After fine-tuning, it matches or exceeds zero-shot models two orders of magnitude larger in classification, and is competitive with execution-aware supervision given the same pretraining data.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic NL-based supervision is a scalable, effective alternative for code representation learning, offering strong performance with compact models, approaching or matching larger, more resource-intensive baselines and execution-aware methods.

title: Selective Hypergraph Refinement for Frozen Graph Clustering
summary: Existing graph-clustering methods typically improve clustering performance by optimizing model parameters and node representations. Effective means of further improving the clustering results of an already trained and frozen model, however, remain limited. We study post-processing for frozen graph clustering. After checkpoint fixation, the procedure uses no labels and updates neither model parameters, node representations, nor the original graph structure. Instead, it exploits an attribute hypergraph to supplement higher-order relations that ordinary graphs cannot readily express, thereby refining existing cluster assignments. Because global hypergraph refinement can yield both performance gains and erroneous updates, we propose Selective Hypergraph Refinement (SHR). The method generates candidate residual directions from the hypergraph and evaluates their reliability using graph structure, node attributes, and matched-null evidence. It updates only nodes with sufficient support and otherwise retains their original assignments. Further analysis shows that whether a node changes cluster is jointly governed by its native assignment gap and the directional strength of the refinement. In a controlled common-suite evaluation, 13 of 15 backbone-dataset cells had a positive mean macro gain, one produced exact no-action, and one was negative. The cell-equal macro gain was 0.066 pp (95% bootstrap CI, [0.030, 0.107] pp), while only 0.209% of hard assignments changed on average. A broader 15-combination native-interface evaluation yielded a macro gain of 0.137 pp at a mean change ratio of 0.375%. These results indicate that frozen clustering outputs retain a limited but measurable refinement space after training. The effect is heterogeneous across backbone-dataset pairs, and broader coverage also increases exposure to negative transfer.

AI.tldr: Post-processing for frozen graph clustering using an attribute hypergraph to refine cluster assignments via Selective Hypergraph Refinement (SHR). Small average macro gains with very few assignment changes; gains are heterogeneous and risk negative transfer with broader coverage.
AI.motivation: Address the limited options for improving clustering after a model is trained and frozen, by leveraging higher-order relations without updating models or graphs.
AI.method: After checkpoint fixation, build an attribute hypergraph to capture higher-order relations. Generate candidate residual directions, evaluate their reliability using graph structure, node attributes, and matched-null evidence, and update only nodes with sufficient support. Changes depend on the native assignment gap and directional strength; no labels or parameter updates are performed.
AI.result: Common-suite: 13/15 backbone-dataset cells show positive mean macro gain; 1 exact no-action; 1 negative. Macro gain = 0.066 pp (CI [0.030, 0.107]); 0.209% of hard assignments changed on average. 15-combination native-interface: macro gain = 0.137 pp at mean change ratio = 0.375%. Refinement space exists but is heterogeneous; broader coverage increases exposure to negative transfer.
AI.conclusion: Frozen clustering retains a limited but measurable refinement space; SHR provides non-invasive, small but positive gains with low change rates, yet effectiveness varies across backbone-dataset pairs and can incur negative transfers if coverage broadens.

title: Revisiting Topological Graphs for Macro Action based Closed-loop Reinforcement Learning of Vision Language Navigation in Continuous Environment
summary: Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires an agent to follow natural language instructions through unseen environments. Existing imitation learning (IL) pipelines struggle in this closed-loop setting: behavior cloning suffers from distribution shift, and DAgger's expert actions become ambiguous upon trajectory deviation. While Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers a natural paradigm to address this, directly applying RL to micro action spaces is sample-inefficient due to reward sparsity. To overcome this bottleneck, we reformulate VLN-CE as a Hierarchical Markov Decision Process (MDP), explicitly decoupling high-level planning from low-level control. By abstracting the environment into a topological graph, our high-level policy operates on a macro action space of frontier nodes, with a training-free low-level controller acting as its state transition, which significantly compresses the decision horizon and makes closed-loop RL tractable. To support RL optimization on the macro MDP, we propose an action-aware value head to effectively evaluate state values under the dynamic frontier action space, powering a graph-based PPO. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our architecture. Finally, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical VLN-CE with macro-action planning on a topological graph, using a training-free low-level controller and an action-aware value head to enable tractable closed-loop RL, achieving SOTA on R2R-CE and RxR-CE.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning faces distribution shift and ambiguity in closed-loop IL (BC and DAgger) and RL struggles with sparse rewards in micro-action spaces; a scalable, tractable RL framework for VLN-CE is needed.
AI.method: Formulate VLN-CE as a hierarchical MDP by abstracting the environment into a topological graph. The high-level policy operates on macro actions (frontier nodes) while a training-free low-level controller handles state transitions. Introduce an action-aware value head to evaluate state values under dynamic frontier actions and train with graph-based PPO.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the approach is effective and yields state-of-the-art performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling planning and control via macro-action space and a training-free low-level controller enables tractable RL for VLN-CE and achieves SOTA, validating the hierarchical ML approach.

title: Preserving Knowledge across Space and Time for Continual Video Deepfake Detection
comment: Accepted by ECCV 2025. Code will be available at github.com/rama0126/MSFD
summary: The continuous emergence of high-quality video deepfakes requires detectors that continually adapt to new forgery patterns, yet existing approaches, which are designed for deepfake images, fail to capture video-specific cues. Unlike deepfake images that contain only spatial artifacts, deepfake videos leave distinct evidence along both spatial and temporal axes, necessitating the separate preservation of each modality during sequential model updates. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a continual deepfake video detection framework, Modality-Specific Frequency Distillation (MSFD), that explicitly decomposes video features into spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal modalities in the frequency domain. This decomposition enables independent preservation of each modality, as different deepfake video types exhibit varying reliance on spatial and temporal cues across tasks. Furthermore, MSFD adopts a cross-modality decorrelation loss that encourages spatiotemporal representations to remain orthogonal to single-modality cues. Extensive experiments show that our framework achieves stronger adaptation and preserves performance more effectively than state-of-the-art methods across diverse continual deepfake video scenarios.

AI.tldr: Introduces MSFD, a continual deepfake video detector that decomposes features into spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal frequency modalities and uses cross-modality decorrelation to preserve modality-specific cues during continual updates, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Deepfake videos exhibit both spatial and temporal artifacts; existing image-focused detectors do not capture video-specific cues and struggle to preserve modality-specific information during sequential learning across tasks.
AI.method: Decompose video features into spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal modalities in the frequency domain and preserve each modality independently during continual updates. Introduce a cross-modality decorrelation loss to enforce orthogonality between spatiotemporal and single-modality cues, enabling better separation of cues across tasks.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show stronger adaptation and better preservation of performance across diverse continual deepfake video scenarios compared with state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: MSFD provides a principled frequency-domain, modality-specific approach to continual deepfake video detection, improving adaptability and retention of detection performance across tasks; the cross-modality decorrelation loss helps maintain orthogonal representations between modalities.

title: Counterfactual Routing Using Integer Programming with Constraint Generation
summary: We present our submission to the IJCAI 2025 'Counterfactual Routing Competition' (CRC 25). The goal of the competition is to find counterfactual explanations for the shortest path problem. This requires deciding what the minimal changes to a road network would make a route chosen by the user the optimal route. This enables explanations such as "Your suggested route would indeed have been optimal, if road X were not a bicycle path." Our solution models the problem as an integer program, iteratively incorporating constraints until an exact solution is found. In the final evaluation on held-out test instances, our method ranked fourth in solution quality and obtained its solution fastest on every instance, with an average runtime of 9.0 seconds compared to 118.8 seconds for the next-fastest submission.

AI.tldr: IP-based counterfactual explanations for the shortest-path problem; achieves fast runtimes and competitive solution quality in CRC 25.
AI.motivation: Provide explainability for routing by identifying minimal changes to the road network that would make the user's route optimal.
AI.method: Model the task as an integer program and iteratively incorporate constraints until an exact counterfactual solution is found; searches for minimal network modifications that shift the optimality.
AI.result: In held-out test instances, the method ranked fourth in solution quality and was the fastest on every instance (average runtime 9.0 seconds) versus 118.8 seconds for the next-fastest submission.
AI.conclusion: An exact, efficient IP-based approach yields practical counterfactual explanations for shortest-path routing, delivering strong speed advantages with competitive solution quality.

title: Latent Energy Action Planning with World Models
summary: Latent world models support efficient model predictive control from high-dimensional observations, yet optimizing a single learned latent objective can favor action sequences whose decoder-predicted terminal descriptor does not match the goal descriptor. We introduce Latent Energy Action Planning (LEAP), which treats the complete action horizon as a differentiable variable and optimizes it through a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). LEAP couples terminal latent goal matching with a terminal-window state energy. Low energy requires the predicted terminal latent to agree with the goal latent and the decoder-predicted terminal descriptor to agree with the goal descriptor. A frozen goal-conditioned proposal initializes the search, a quasi-Newton solver refines actions through the autoregressive rollout, and post-optimization projection enforces the admissible action range. Across four control domains using the officially released LeWM checkpoints, the complete LEAP planning system raises mean success from 77.5% for LeWM planned with the cross-entropy method (LeWM+CEM) to 94.8% under a matched protocol, a 17.3-percentage-point improvement, while retaining the frozen LeWM representation and predictor.

AI.tldr: LEAP optimizes the entire action horizon in latent space to align terminal latent states and decoder-predicted descriptors with the goal, using a frozen LeWorldModel and a differentiable objective for MPC.
AI.motivation: To address the mismatch between a single latent objective and the goal descriptor in latent world models, improving planning performance with high-dimensional observations.
AI.method: Treat the action horizon as a differentiable variable; minimize a combined terminal latent-goal energy and terminal descriptor energy using a frozen LeWM. Initialize with a frozen goal-conditioned proposal, refine actions via a quasi-Newton method with autoregressive rollouts, and apply a post-optimization projection to keep actions in bounds.
AI.result: On four control domains with LeWM checkpoints, LEAP raises mean success from 77.5% (LeWM+CEM) to 94.8% (matched protocol), a 17.3-point improvement, while keeping the frozen LeWM representation and predictor.
AI.conclusion: LEAP effectively couples terminal latent goal matching with terminal descriptor alignment, enabling efficient planning with frozen latent models and yielding substantial performance gains.

title: Toward Unified Robot Learning: Bridging Representation, Vision-Language-Action, and World Models
summary: For robots to operate reliably in real-world environments, they need to perceive their surroundings, act, and reason about the consequences of those actions. Rapid progress in the domains of representation learning, VLA models, and world models has significantly enhanced the capabilities of robot learning systems, enabling robots to work in increasingly complex environments. However, these paradigms are typically developed in isolation, resulting in fragmented systems that struggle with generalization, long-horizon temporal reasoning and planning, and deployment in unstructured environments. In this survey, we present a unified perspective on robot learning by organizing the existing methods along three complementary axes: understanding through representation learning, acting through VLA models, and reasoning through world models. We introduce a structured taxonomy that captures key design choices in environment representation, policy learning, and predictive modeling, and summarize the recent progress in these domains. Beyond classifying the existing works, we analyze how these components interact, discuss common limitations, and highlight emerging trends towards more integrated systems. Through this lens, we identify the challenges in the domain of robot learning, including uncertainty quantification, out-of-distribution generalization, cross-embodiment transfer, long-context understanding, and long-horizon planning. We argue that these challenges arise not only from limitations within individual components but also from the lack of integration across perception, action, and reasoning. Building on this analysis, we outline future directions towards unified, physically grounded, and probabilistic robot learning to develop robust robotic systems that maintain consistent internal representations and support decision making over extended interactions in real-world environments.

AI.tldr: A survey that unifies perception, action, and reasoning in robot learning, proposing a taxonomy and arguing for integrated, probabilistic, physically grounded systems to improve generalization and long-horizon planning.
AI.motivation: Current robot learning approaches are fragmented across representation learning (perception), VLA models (action), and world models (reasoning), hindering generalization and deployment in unstructured, real-world settings. There is a need to integrate these components to handle uncertainty and long-horizon reasoning.
AI.method: Proposes a structured taxonomy across environment representation, policy learning, and predictive modeling; analyzes interactions among components; reviews recent progress; discusses limitations and trends; outlines future directions toward unified robot learning.
AI.result: Provides a unified taxonomy, synthesis of recent work, and identification of key challenges such as uncertainty quantification, out-of-distribution generalization, cross-embodiment transfer, long-context understanding, long-horizon planning; proposes directions for unified, probabilistic, physically grounded robot learning.
AI.conclusion: Advocates for unified, physically grounded, probabilistic robot learning to build robust systems with consistent internal representations enabling extended decision making in real-world environments.

title: STARS-GS: Structure-Aware Regularized Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale Aerial Surface Reconstruction
summary: Large-scale 3D surface reconstruction from aerial imagery is fundamental to geospatial mapping and urban modeling. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated considerable potential for this task. However, existing methods still face three major challenges in large and complex scenes: scene partitioning may split continuous scene elements across independently optimized sub-regions; geometric constraints mainly focus on the attributes of individual Gaussians while overlooking their local organization; and uniform regularization struggles to accommodate heterogeneous geometric structures. To address these issues, we propose STARS-GS, a structure-aware 3DGS framework for large-scale surface reconstruction. First, we introduce a structure-aware scene partitioning strategy that better preserves continuous scene structures during partitioning and reduces cross-region geometric inconsistencies and stitching artifacts through boundary refinement. Second, we develop neighborhood-aware Gaussian organization that extends geometric constraints from individual primitives to their neighborhood organization, encouraging Gaussians to better conform to local surface geometry. Third, we introduce adaptive surface regularization that adjusts the regularization strength according to local geometric characteristics, promoting geometric consistency in structured regions while preserving plausible variations in unstructured regions. Extensive experiments on large-scale aerial photogrammetry benchmarks demonstrate that STARS-GS consistently outperforms the evaluated Gaussian-based methods in surface reconstruction. It increases the average F1-score from 0.640 for the second-best method to 0.698, corresponding to a relative improvement of approximately 9.1\%, demonstrating effective improvements in geometric accuracy and surface completeness.

AI.tldr: Structure-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (STARS-GS) for large-scale aerial reconstruction; introduces structure-aware partitioning, neighborhood-aware Gaussian organization, and adaptive regularization, achieving ~9.1% relative improvement in F1-score (0.640→0.698) on aerial benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To address three core issues in large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting: (1) partitioning-induced cross-region artifacts that break continuous structures, (2) focus on individual Gaussians rather than local neighborhood organization, and (3) uniform regularization failing to capture heterogeneous geometric structures across large-scale scenes.
AI.method: 1) Structure-aware scene partitioning with boundary refinement to preserve continuity and reduce cross-region inconsistencies; 2) Neighborhood-aware Gaussian organization that enforces local geometric constraints across Gaussian neighborhoods; 3) Adaptive surface regularization that modulates strength by local geometry to balance structure preservation and plausible variation.
AI.result: On large-scale aerial photogrammetry benchmarks, STARS-GS outperforms Gaussian-based methods, increasing average F1-score from 0.640 to 0.698 (≈9.1% relative improvement), indicating better geometric accuracy and surface completeness.
AI.conclusion: STARS-GS delivers consistent improvements for large-scale surface reconstruction by jointly optimizing partitioning, local Gaussian organization, and adaptive regularization, demonstrating robust performance in complex aerial scenes.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Energy Optimization in Data Centers
summary: Data centers are increasingly optimized by artificial intelligence and, at the same time, increasingly loaded by it. The literature treats these as two unrelated problems: control studies model workload as an exogenous arrival process, while sustainability studies model infrastructure as a fixed multiplier. We screen roughly 194 papers retrieved through a documented protocol, code 63 of them, and report what the coding shows. Of 28 primary control-oriented studies, 18 are validated in simulation alone and 5 reach physical hardware or a production facility; none account for water withdrawal, and none account for embodied carbon. Reported savings intervals across four technique families overlap almost completely, which means the field cannot presently rank its own methods. Ten recurring gaps are scored for consequence and tractability, and we set out CLEAR-DC, a framework coupling a control-policy branch to a workload-demand branch through an explicit elasticity term, reads out net rather than direct benefit, and emits a schema-conformant record covering energy, carbon, water, embodied share and validation venue. The framework is an architectural and methodological proposal, not a trained system; the contribution we defend empirically is the corpus analysis and the reporting schema derived from it. Coding sheet, derived statistics and all result artifacts: https://github.com/Kimalice/AI-for-Energy-Optimization-in-Data-Centers-Closing-the-Optimizer-Load-Loop

AI.tldr: A systematic literature analysis reveals fragmentation between AI-driven data-center control and sustainability-focused studies. Most control work is validated in simulation, with little attention to water withdrawal or embodied carbon. A novel CLEAR-DC framework is proposed to couple a control-policy branch with a workload-demand branch and to report net, multi-maceted benefits; core empirical contribution is corpus analysis and a reporting schema.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between control-theory-based workload management and sustainability accounting in AI-enabled data centers, addressing missing holistic metrics (water, embodied carbon) and inadequate validation venues.
AI.method: Systematic literature screening of ~194 papers using a documented protocol; coding 63 studies; classification into control-oriented vs other; evaluation of validation venues; scoring of ten gaps for consequence and tractability; proposal of an architectural/methodological framework (CLEAR-DC).
AI.result: Among 28 primary control-oriented studies, 18 rely on simulation alone and 5 reach hardware/production facilities; none account for water withdrawal or embodied carbon; reported savings intervals across four technique families overlap, hindering ranking; ten gaps identified and scored; CLEAR-DC couples a control-policy branch to a workload-demand branch via an explicit elasticity term, outputs net rather than direct benefit, and emits a schema-conformant record covering energy, carbon, water, embodied share, and validation venue; framework is not a trained system.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes a corpus analysis and a reporting schema, with an explicit framework (CLEAR-DC) to integrate control with demand dynamics and broaden validated metrics; all data, code, and artifacts are available in the linked GitHub repository.

title: Geometry-Aware Graph Construction via Adaptive Spectral Bandwidth Control
comment: Accepted at IEEE MLSP 2026. 6 pages, 4 figures
summary: Kernelized graph methods - spectral clustering, diffusion maps, and sparse kernel -regression graphs - that use Gaussian kernels depend on the choice of Gaussian bandwidth sigma, which governs the spectral character of the local kernel operator. When sigma is too small, the kernel overestimates local complexity and treats each sample as an independent direction; when sigma is too large, the kernel collapses multiple directions together, the condition number diverges, and all geometric discrimination is lost. We propose a choice of scale to make the spectral complexity of the kernel consistent with the intrinsic complexity of the underlying manifold. We propose a per-node bandwidth criterion that operationalizes this principle by jointly matching the kernel's effective rank to the local intrinsic dimension estimated via minimum spanning tree, anchoring the search in the manifold-consistent log-log scaling regime. We evaluate SSL embeddings from six encoders on CIFAR-100, showing that adaptive bandwidth consistently improves leave-one-out (LOO) classification and label propagation (LP) accuracy over fixed-bandwidth methods and competing adaptive methods.

AI.tldr: Adaptive per-node Gaussian bandwidth selection aligns kernel complexity with local intrinsic manifold structure, improving SSL performance on CIFAR-100 compared to fixed/adaptive baselines.
AI.motivation: Kernelized graph methods rely on Gaussian kernels; the choice of bandwidth sigma critically shapes spectral properties. Fixed or poorly chosen bandwidths can over-smooth or under-smooth, distorting manifold geometry and harming downstream SSL tasks.
AI.method: Introduce a per-node bandwidth criterion that matches the kernel's effective rank to the local intrinsic dimension estimated via minimum spanning tree, exploiting a manifold-consistent log-log scaling. Evaluate SSL embeddings from six encoders on CIFAR-100, comparing leave-one-out and label propagation accuracy against fixed-bandwidth and other adaptive methods.
AI.result: Adaptive bandwidth consistently improves LOO classification and LP accuracy over fixed-bandwidth methods and competing adaptive methods across six encoders on CIFAR-100.
AI.conclusion: A data-driven, manifold-consistent bandwidth choice enhances the spectral discrimination of kernelized graphs and yields stronger SSL performance, highlighting the importance of local intrinsic geometry in bandwidth selection.

title: Automated Weld Seam Recognition and 3D Mapping for Robotic Post Processing Using Photogrammetry and Semantic Segmentation
comment: Extended abstract not yet published to a conference or journal
summary: Accurate identification of weld seam geometries is essential for automated robotic post processing operations such as grinding, finishing, and inspection. For large workpieces, complete surface scanning using high precision laser scanners or structured light sensors can be time consuming and often generates substantial amount of data that are not relevant. This paper presents an experimental vision based pipeline for the approximate localization of weld seams. This serves as a preliminary stage before high precision measurement. The proposed approach aims to reduce the overall scanning effort and data acquisition efficiency. The proposed method includes capturing images of the workpiece from multiple viewpoints, identifying weld seams from the images using semantic segmentation, reconstructing the workpiece using photogrammetry, and projection of identified weld seams into the reconstructed model.

AI.tldr: Vision-based pipeline for approximate weld seam localization to reduce scanning effort; multi-view imaging, semantic segmentation, photogrammetry reconstruction, and seam projection onto the model before high-precision measurements.
AI.motivation: Accurate weld seam geometry is critical for automated post-processing, but full-surface high-precision scanning on large workpieces is time-consuming and data-intensive; a preliminary localization reduces scan duration and data load.
AI.method: Capture images from multiple viewpoints; identify weld seams via semantic segmentation; reconstruct the workpiece using photogrammetry; project identified seam locations into the reconstructed model.
AI.result: The abstract proposes a pipeline for coarse localization; no quantitative results are reported; intended to reduce scanning effort and improve efficiency prior to high-precision measurement.
AI.conclusion: Provides a preliminary stage that enables faster data acquisition and directs high-precision measurement resources to seam regions; effectiveness to be validated with quantitative evaluation in future work.

title: Preprocessing Failure and Adversarial Detection in Depthwise-Separable Edge Vision Systems
summary: Preprocessing-based defenses are the standard first-line response to adversarial attacks on edge vision systems, requiring no retraining, no architectural changes, and widely recommended as model-agnostic mitigations. Yet the foundational evaluations of these defenses were conducted on residual or Inception-class architectures, not on the depthwise-separable CNNs that dominate edge deployments. This untested assumption leaves a gap in the security evaluation literature. This paper closes that gap by evaluating six preprocessing defenses against adversarial perturbations across both architecture families. Across all perturbation levels and defenses tested, the two depthwise-separable architectures show consistently poor recovery while the residual architecture shows partial recovery; ablation results are consistent with an architectural rather than parametric explanation, though only three architectures and one attack family are evaluated. Crucially, this failure is not merely a negative result. The same output divergence that disqualifies preprocessing as a recovery mechanism reveals a detection opportunity: preprocessing consistently disrupts clean predictions while leaving adversarial predictions largely unchanged, an asymmetry that is directly measurable without retraining or architectural modification. We further show that standard image quality metrics are unreliable proxies for defense effectiveness, a methodological gap in current evaluation practice. A practitioner decision framework is provided for adversarially resilient edge vision deployment.

AI.tldr: Preprocessing defenses fail to robustly recover predictions for depthwise-separable edge CNNs; residual nets recover partially; defenses may enable detection via output divergence; standard image quality metrics are unreliable; a practitioner framework for edge deployment is proposed.
AI.motivation: Address architecture-aware evaluation gap: prior defenses were tested on residual/Inception-like nets, not on depthwise-separable CNNs common in edge devices. Determine whether preprocessing defenses remain effective and explore potential detection opportunities.
AI.method: Evaluate six preprocessing defenses against adversarial perturbations across two architecture families (depthwise-separable CNNs and residual networks), across multiple perturbation levels and one attack family; include ablation analyses; analyze output divergence and potential detection signal; assess reliance on image quality metrics; provide a practitioner decision framework.
AI.result: Depthwise-separable architectures show consistently poor recovery to adversarial perturbations; residual architecture shows partial recovery. Ablations support an architectural rather than parametric explanation. Preprocessing disrupts clean predictions while preserving adversarial ones, enabling a measurable detection signal without retraining. Standard image quality metrics are unreliable proxies for defense effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Preprocessing defenses are not universally effective across edge architectures; they present detection opportunities rather than robust recovery. Highlights the need for architecture-aware evaluation and methodological rigor; offers a practitioner decision framework for deploying adversarially resilient edge vision systems.

title: Proactive Service Agents: A Unified Decision Framework, Methods, and Evaluation
summary: Large language model agents can plan, invoke tools, and modify external states, yet most systems still take an explicit user instruction as a fixed starting point. Proactive service moves the decision upstream: an agent must infer service opportunities from incomplete environmental and user signals, choose among remaining silent, asking, assisting, and acting, and account for interruption, misunderstanding, overreach, and privacy costs. This survey gives an operational definition centered on initiative and formulates the problem as a partially observable sequential decision process constrained by authorization and risk. The formulation represents timing, content, and delivery within one structured action, while making explicit the option value of waiting, the decision value of questions, and feedback-induced state changes. On this basis, we organize existing methods along one decision pipeline (state and need estimation, intervention gating, action construction, and feedback adaptation) and describe prescribed, predictive, model based, and return optimizing mechanisms as nonexclusive policy-construction components. We further normalize decision units and three-axis evidence descriptors across streaming dialogue, screen, video, software-engineering, and human-agent collaboration resources, and formalize metrics for triggering, timing, calibration, user burden, safety, and policy value. The synthesis shows why offline classification performance alone does not predict deployment benefit and why long-term memory is not a defining condition of proactivity. Reliable proactive service instead requires calibrated incremental intervention value, verifiable authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence.

AI.tldr: Proactive service in LLM agents treats initiative as a structured, uncertain decision process: infer opportunities from signals, choose among waiting, asking, assisting, or acting, with risk, privacy, and authorization constraints, organized into a decision pipeline and evaluated by calibrated, counterfactual metrics; deployment hinges on incremental value and recoverable execution rather than offline accuracy alone.
AI.motivation: To address the gap where current LLM agents rely on explicit user instructions, this work formalizes proactive, upstream decision-making under uncertainty and constraint, aiming to improve user experience while managing risk, privacy, and interruption costs.
AI.method: Define an operational notion of initiative; formulate proactive service as a partially observable sequential decision process with constraints on authorization and risk; unify timing-content-delivery into one action; assess the value of waiting vs asking vs acting; propose a decision pipeline (state/need estimation, intervention gating, action construction, feedback adaptation); categorize methods as prescribed, predictive, model-based, and return-optimizing as components of policy construction; normalize decision units and evidence descriptors across modalities; formalize metrics for triggering, timing, calibration, user burden, safety, and policy value.
AI.result: Synthesis clarifies why offline classification alone cannot predict deployment benefits and why long-term memory is not essential for proactivity; it identifies requirements for reliable proactive service: calibrated incremental intervention value, verifiable authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence.
AI.conclusion: Reliable proactive service emerges from calibrated, defensible intervention value and robust governance (authorization, recoverable actions, counterfactual signals). The work provides a unified framework, a decision-pipeline taxonomy, and metrics to guide design, evaluation, and deployment of proactive LLM agents.

title: Risk and Anomaly Identification for Distribution Network Optimal Operation Based on Reinforcement Learning and Uncertainty Quantification
summary: Reliable operation of modern distribution networks requires timely identification of operational risks and anomalous events under pervasive uncertainty. In practice, operators must identify risks that are inherent in stochastic yet in-distribution conditions, and anomalies that correspond to out-of-distribution behaviors such as unusual load patterns, extreme weather or cyber-physical attacks. This paper addresses this joint risk and anomaly identification problem for optimal distribution network operation and proposes a deep reinforcement learning framework that is explicitly uncertainty aware. We integrate distributional and Bayesian deep reinforcement learning to realize a second- order uncertainty quantification scheme that decomposes total uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components, which are respectively used to characterize inherent risk and out-of- distribution anomalies. The resulting epistemic estimates drive both exploration during training and out-of-distribution detec- tion with fallback control during deployment, whereas aleatoric estimates are used to characterize intrinsic operational risk. Simulation results demonstrate the performance of our DRL agent and the effectiveness of the uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: A deep reinforcement learning framework for distribution networks that jointly identifies operational risk and out-of-distribution anomalies by fusing distributional and Bayesian DRL to quantify second-order uncertainty (aleatoric and epistemic). Epistemic uncertainty guides exploration and OOD fallback control; aleatoric uncertainty characterizes inherent risk; validated via simulations.
AI.motivation: Operational reliability of power distribution networks under pervasive uncertainty requires distinguishing intrinsic stochastic risk from anomalous, out-of-distribution events (e.g., extreme weather, cyber-physical attacks). A method that explicitly quantifies both types of uncertainty can improve decision-making, exploration, and safety.
AI.method: Integrates distributional DRL (capturing a distribution over returns) with Bayesian DRL to achieve second-order uncertainty quantification. Decomposes total uncertainty into aleatoric (inherent risk) and epistemic (model/estimation uncertainty). Uses epistemic estimates to drive exploration during training and to perform out-of-distribution detection with fallback control during deployment; uses aleatoric estimates to characterize operational risk. Demonstrates performance gains through simulation experiments.
AI.result: Simulation results show that the proposed uncertainty-aware DRL agent effectively identifies and manages joint risks and anomalies, and that the uncertainty quantification components assist exploration, OOD detection, and risk characterization.
AI.conclusion: A practical DRL framework with explicit uncertainty quantification for joint risk and anomaly identification in distribution networks. The combination of distributional and Bayesian DRL enables second-order uncertainty control, improving exploration, OOD handling, and intrinsic risk assessment; validated by simulations.

title: MulDP: Multimodal Diffusion Policy for Autonomous Quadruped Parkour Navigation across Complex Terrains
summary: Quadruped robots have demonstrated impressive agility in parkour locomotion across complex terrains. However, most systems still rely on human intervention for high-level planning, and autonomous parkour navigation remains underexplored. The key challenges include fine-grained velocity regulation, long-horizon anticipatory behaviors, and tight coupling between perception and embodied execution. To address these challenges, we propose a Multimodal Diffusion Policy (MulDP) that integrates visual perception with robot proprioception and goal information to generate temporally coherent and anticipatory navigation velocity commands, tightly coupling perception with embodied control to enable robust autonomous navigation. To support the training of MulDP, we construct the first Quadruped Parkour Navigation Dataset (QPND), a multimodal dataset that encompasses diverse navigation behaviors and complex terrains. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that MulDP enables robust long-horizon autonomous navigation and effective traversal across complex terrains.

AI.tldr: MulDP: a multimodal diffusion policy for quadruped parkour navigation, introducing QPND and showing robust long-horizon autonomous traversal on complex terrains.
AI.motivation: Address gaps in autonomous parkour navigation for quadrupeds: fine-grained velocity control, long-horizon anticipatory behavior, and tight perception-action coupling.
AI.method: A multimodal diffusion policy that fuses visual perception, proprioception, and goal information to generate temporally coherent velocity commands; creates QPND for training; validated in simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.result: Demonstrates robust long-horizon autonomous navigation and effective traversal across complex terrains with improved anticipation and perception-execution coupling.
AI.conclusion: MulDP and QPND advance autonomous quadruped parkour by tightly integrating perception with embodied control; promising for real-world deployment, though requires further evaluation of generalization, runtime efficiency, and safety across diverse platforms.

title: BMCTrack-d: Pig re-identification and tracking via back marks in challenging camera settings
summary: Automated pig monitoring is essential for assessing their health, behaviour, and welfare. To date, most pig monitoring solutions operate on the group-level, because individual-level monitoring requires reliable long-term identification and tracking of each animal. For domesticated pigs this remains challenging because pigs of the same breed often have highly uniform appearances. Moreover, research on pig monitoring is almost exclusively reported in top-down view camera settings, which considerably ease tracking, but are not always an option in practice. In this work, BMCTrack-d is presented, a novel tracking-by-detection approach that leverages unique back marks to enable robust pig re-identification and tracking in a challenging side-view camera setting, afflicted by rapidly moving pigs, severe occlusions and low resolution. The method first predicts the detected pigs' identities using a neural network-based back mark classifier. To improve re-identification reliability over time, two dedicated post-processing stages are introduced: a temporal prediction consistency check, which validates the identity assignments against the recent prediction history, and deduplication, which resolves conflicting identity assignments in each time step. By explicitly prioritising accurate, appearance-based re-identification over continuous tracking, the proposed approach addresses a key limitation of existing trackers for individual-level monitoring scenarios. On a demanding test set BMCTrack-d outperforms two strong baselines, BoT-SORT-ReID and TrackTrack-ReID, by 9.11% and 1.03%, respectively, in higher-order tracking accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of back mark-based re-identification and tracking for robust individual-level pig monitoring in challenging settings.

AI.tldr: BMCTrack-d introduces back-mark-based re-identification for pig tracking in side-view videos with post-processing (temporal consistency and deduplication) to achieve superior individual-level monitoring; it outperforms BoT-SORT-ReID and TrackTrack-ReID on a challenging test set.
AI.motivation: Need for reliable long-term individual pig monitoring despite uniform appearance and non-ideal top-view setups; existing trackers struggle with re-id under occlusions and low-res side views.
AI.method: Back mark classifier predicts pig identities from back marks; temporal prediction consistency check over recent history; deduplication per frame to resolve identity conflicts; prioritizes appearance-based re-id over continuous tracking.
AI.result: On a demanding test set, outperforms two strong baselines by 9.11% and 1.03% in higher-order tracking accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Back mark-based re-identification with the two post-processing steps yields robust individual-level pig monitoring in challenging settings; addresses limitations of existing trackers for such scenarios.

title: SimSkill: A Lifelong Learning AI Agent for Autonomous Mastery of Traffic Simulation
summary: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly capable, the long-term value of AI systems depends not only on solving individual requests, but also on transforming experience and accumulated knowledge into durable, reusable competence. We introduce SimSkill, a self-evolving agent built around the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) traffic simulator. SimSkill identifies capability gaps, generates and solves environment-grounded tasks, verifies solutions through an action--critic loop, and consolidates experience into episodic, procedural, and semantic memory without updating the backbone model. Through autonomous exploration, it builds a reusable library spanning the traffic-simulation workflow. We evaluate SimSkill on two held-out benchmarks with three backbone LLMs and independent artifact-based verification. SimSkill improves verified completion by up to 25 percentage points, while ablations show complementary contributions from procedural and semantic memory. Its benefits remain backbone- and budget-dependent: memory does not improve every model or uniformly reduce inference cost. More broadly, SimSkill illustrates a design paradigm in which natural language preserves and composes computational capabilities, while executable tools and code provide precise and reproducible execution. All code and experimental data are publicly available at https://github.com/qiliuchn/SimSkill-V1.

AI.tldr: SimSkill introduces a self-evolving agent that uses the SUMO traffic simulator to autonomously identify capability gaps, generate and solve environment-grounded tasks, and consolidate experience into episodic, procedural, and semantic memory without updating the backbone LLM, creating a reusable library for traffic-simulation workflows. It improves verified completion by up to 25 percentage points; memory benefits depend on backbone and budget.
AI.motivation: To achieve durable, reusable AI competence by preserving and recombining capabilities learned by LLMs. Current models struggle to meaningfully consolidate experience into lasting skills; the work proposes persistent, cross-task memory (episodic/procedural/semantic) and executable tools to realize durable competence.
AI.method: Build SimSkill around SUMO; identify capability gaps, generate environment-grounded tasks, apply an action–critic loop to solve them, and consolidate results into multiple memory forms without updating the backbone model. Conduct autonomous exploration to assemble a reusable library across the traffic-simulation workflow. Validate on two held-out benchmarks with three backbone LLMs and artifact-based verification.
AI.result: Up to 25 percentage-point gains in verified completion. Ablations indicate procedural and semantic memory contribute complementarily. Benefits are backbone- and budget-dependent; memory does not uniformly improve all models or lower inference costs.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a design paradigm where natural language preserves and composes computational capabilities, while executable tools ensure precise, reproducible execution; highlights the value of durable, reusable knowledge for AI systems and provides public code/data.

title: DE-Venus: A Data-Efficient RLVR Framework for Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves large language model reasoning, but its practical scaling is constrained by expensive on-policy rollouts and the cost of obtaining reliable targets at scale. Existing methods address sample selection, incomplete supervision, or noisy labels separately, often entangling supervision logic with distributed training and hindering controlled comparison and reuse. We present DE-Venus, a unified framework for data-efficient RLVR that treats supervision as evolving state across data preparation and policy optimization. It organizes this lifecycle into three modules: Active Data Selection allocates training and annotation budgets; Weak Supervision Construction derives learning signals from unlabeled examples; and Training-Time Supervision Refinement filters or corrects unreliable supervision. DE-Venus supports seven representative methods and a data-selection pipeline by expressing method-specific decisions as offline dataset transitions or online transformations of targets, rewards, batches, and advantages while preserving verl's distributed execution contracts. Across public benchmarks and three business scenarios, separate configurations preserve or improve model quality with only 10% of labels or as little as 13% of relevant data; selected business configurations also reduce observed convergence steps by 63%--75%. DE-Venus thus reduces annotation and training costs without sacrificing scalable RL execution.

AI.tldr: DE-Venus offers a unified, data-efficient RLVR framework that decouples supervision from training via three modules, achieving comparable model quality with far less labeling/data and faster convergence.
AI.motivation: RLVR scaling is hindered by expensive on-policy rollouts and costly reliable targets; existing methods address isolated aspects (sampling, incomplete supervision, noisy labels) and hinder comparability and reuse. A unified, data-centric approach can enable efficient scaling and fair evaluation.
AI.method: Organizes supervision lifecycle into three modules: (1) Active Data Selection to allocate training and annotation budgets, (2) Weak Supervision Construction to derive learning signals from unlabeled data, and (3) Training-Time Supervision Refinement to filter or correct unreliable supervision. Treats method-specific decisions as offline dataset transitions or online transformations of targets, rewards, batches, and advantages, while preserving distributed RL execution contracts. Supports seven representative methods and a data-selection pipeline within this unified framework.
AI.result: Across public benchmarks and three business scenarios, configurations preserve or improve model quality with only 10% of labels or as little as 13% of relevant data; selected configurations also reduce observed convergence steps by 63%–75%.
AI.conclusion: DE-Venus reduces annotation and training costs without sacrificing scalable RL execution, enabling data-efficient RLVR at scale.

title: Adaptive Vision-Language Grasping via Composable Foundation Priors and Generalizable Grasp Synthesis
summary: This paper proposes AdaRoboVLG, a task-adaptive Vision-Language-Grasp (VLG) framework that supports generalizable grasp synthesis across different robotic hands. Unlike existing VLG methods that tightly couple foundation models with end-to-end grasp policies, AdaRoboVLG learns an efficient generalizable base policy that generates and evaluates physically feasible grasp candidates through explicit kinematic mapping and force-closure-based stability estimation, while offloading task-dependent understanding to specialized foundation-model modules. These modules provide composable priors that are integrated into the grasp synthesis process, enabling contextually adaptive grasp synthesis without retraining the underlying grasp policy. Through extensive simulation and real-world experiments, we demonstrate that (i) the base policy exhibits efficient learning and strong cross-hand generalization, (ii) the framework effectively incorporates spatial, cognitive, and temporal priors to address three representative grasping challenges without compromising grasp synthesis performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, and (iii) these priors can operate jointly to enable functional grasping in cluttered and dynamic environments. These results indicate that decoupling physical grasp synthesis from task-dependent understanding provides a scalable paradigm for robotic grasping, allowing future advances in foundation models to be directly translated into improved grasp capabilities without redesigning or retraining the underlying grasp policy. Supplementary videos are available at https://adarobovlg.github.io/

AI.tldr: AdaRoboVLG decouples base grasp synthesis from task-dependent understanding using a generalizable base policy and foundation-model modules that provide composable priors, enabling cross-hand generalization and context-aware grasping without retraining.
AI.motivation: To achieve scalable, generalizable robotic grasping across diverse hands and tasks by separating physical grasp synthesis from task understanding, avoiding retraining of the grasp policy as new priors are incorporated.
AI.method: A task-adaptive Vision-Language-Grasp framework with a learnable base policy that generates/evaluates grasps via explicit kinematic mapping and force-closure-based stability, while task-specific priors from foundation-model modules are integrated into the synthesis process (spatial, cognitive, temporal priors). Priors are composable and do not require retraining the base policy.
AI.result: In simulation and real-world tests, the base policy shows efficient learning and strong cross-hand generalization; the framework leverages spatial/cognitive/temporal priors to tackle three grasping challenges without sacrificing grasp-synthesis performance vs. state-of-the-art; priors can jointly enable functional grasping in cluttered/dynamic environments.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling physical grasp synthesis from task-dependent understanding yields a scalable paradigm for robotic grasping, enabling foundation-model advances to improve grasp capabilities without retraining the core policy.

title: SafeRestore: Detector-Relative Risk Certificates for Selective Industrial Image Restoration
comment: 27 pages, 10 figures, 6 main-text tables, and 17 supplementary tables. Shares the Carinthia-S image identities with arXiv:2607.17401 by the same authors; the overlap and the distinct estimand are stated in Section 2.4 and Table 1
summary: Industrial inspection pipelines often restore a measured image before a detector acts on it, yet restoration can suppress detector-supported defect structure or create clean-region activations. We formulate restoration as a selective action problem over the measured display, five restored candidates, and review. SafeRestore ranks candidates with action-specific fitted scores, chooses a gate on threshold-tuning data, and evaluates the fixed gate on a disjoint certification sample with two one-sided exact binomial bounds: one for the positive-conditional evidence-loss incident rate and one for the all-accepted excess-activation incident rate. The guarantee is marginal for one policy fixed before its certification outcomes are observed, under an image-level i.i.d. working model. In a retrospective split-sample study of 4,591 public Carinthia-S images, the protocol yields auditable risk-coverage behavior. The primary all-action policy passes in one of five training repetitions (12.0% +/- 26.9% pass-gated test coverage when failures count as zero), whereas fixed bicubic and reduced-complexity variants pass more often. On reserved morphologies, evidence-loss incidence rises to 81.1-90.3%, and KolektorSDD lacks both detector competence and enough positive certification images for the stated target. The contribution is therefore an auditable, detector-relative framework for deciding when a transformed image may be returned automatically and when review remains necessary -- not a claim that adaptive routing outperforms simpler policies on the present evidence.

AI.tldr: Proposes SafeRestore: an auditable, detector-relative framework for automatically returning transformed images in industrial inspection by selecting among restoration candidates with a gating threshold, backed by disjoint certification and exact binomial risk bounds.
AI.motivation: Ensure auditable risk-coverage when deciding whether to restore and display images in detector-supported pipelines, avoiding loss of defect signals or unnecessary human review.
AI.method: Formulate restoration as a selective action problem over measured images and five restored candidates; rank candidates with action-specific fitted scores; tune a gating threshold on data; evaluate the fixed gate on a disjoint certification sample using two one-sided exact binomial bounds (positive-evidence-loss conditional rate and all-accepted excess-activation rate); assess under an image-level i.i.d. model; retrospective split-sample study on 4,591 Carinthia-S images.
AI.result: The primary all-action policy passes in one of five training repetitions (12.0% ± 26.9% pass-gated coverage when failures count as zero); fixed bicubic and reduced-complexity variants pass more often. On reserved morphologies, evidence-loss incidence rises to 81.1–90.3%; KolektorSDD lacks detector competence and enough positive certification images for target. The work yields an auditable, detector-relative framework for automatic vs. review-needed decisions, rather than claiming adaptive routing superiority on current evidence.
AI.conclusion: An auditable framework that ties automated restoration decisions to verifiable risk coverage in detector-influenced inspection pipelines. It emphasizes the need for robust certification data and candid acknowledgement of limitations in generalization and guarantee strength.

title: Rethinking World Models for Safety-Critical Embodied Systems
summary: World models have progressed from compact latent dynamics to generative, controllable, and interactive simulators of embodied environments. However, high predictive likelihood and visual fidelity do not necessarily ensure that a model preserves the evidence required for safe decision-making. This perspective identifies three structural mismatches in current world modeling: likelihood versus risk, prediction versus intervention, and finite-horizon prediction versus accumulated consequences. We propose the Risk-Informed World Model (RIWM) as a decision-centric research direction for safety-critical embodied systems. RIWM organizes world modeling around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability, and integrates four interdependent capabilities: decision-relevant representation, counterfactual reasoning, safety-critical episodic memory, and runtime safety assurance. It distinguishes physical, social, and operational consequences while using epistemic uncertainty to qualify the evidence supporting action. We further discuss open challenges in identifying consequential futures, validating counterfactual reasoning, maintaining revisable safety memories, translating learned consequences into executable constraints, and determining when evidence is sufficient to act. This perspective argues that future world models should move beyond predicting likely futures toward identifying which futures matter, revising judgments through experience, and recognizing when to act, revise, sense, defer, or abstain.

AI.tldr: A perspective proposing RIWM: a risk-informed, decision-centric world model framework that prioritizes consequences, counterfactuals, and safety memories to support safe action in embodied agents, addressing three structural mismatches in current world models.
AI.motivation: To ensure safe decision-making in safety-critical embodied systems by aligning world modeling with risk and consequences rather than solely maximizing predictive likelihood.
AI.method: Introduce the Risk-Informed World Model (RIWM) as a decision-centric framework organized around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability; integrate four interdependent capabilities—decision-relevant representation, counterfactual reasoning, safety-critical episodic memory, and runtime safety assurance.
AI.result: A theoretical framework and design blueprint for safe world modeling; no empirical results, but a clear identification of capabilities and open challenges for future work.
AI.conclusion: Future world models should identify consequential futures, revise judgments through experience, and decide when to act, sense, defer, or abstain, while leveraging evidence sufficiency and safety constraints.

title: A Large Open Multi-Energy Corpus of Soil Compaction Tests, with Machine-Learning Baselines
summary: Every engineered fill is specified by a maximum dry density and an optimum moisture content. Each determination needs a full Proctor test. Published correlations rest on one to four hundred specimens, usually from one laboratory at one compactive energy, and are seldom released. This paper releases a corpus without those limits. It holds 2,854 laboratory compaction tests from six public sources, across 162 provenance groups and four Proctor energy levels, with fines from 1.5 to 100%. Every record is audited to the Proctor method its source names, and no energy is inferred. Screening on the zero-air-voids condition removed 11.8% of harmonised records, and 5.7% of those with a measured specific gravity. A material share of published compaction data is physically impossible. The optimum degree of saturation over the corpus is 0.815 at a coefficient of variation of 11%. That is a baseline, not a constant. Both parameters are then estimated from one classification suite and the compaction standard. A tabular foundation model reaches R2 0.824 for density and 0.784 for water content under random folds. It reaches 0.727 and 0.696 with folds drawn around provenance, and 0.520 and 0.614 with a whole source held out. Compactive energy is negligible marginally yet decisive conditionally. Density on the 66 modified-Proctor records is predicted at R2 0.740 with it and -0.651 without. Symbolic regression yields closed forms coupled through a phase relation. No predicted pair can then exceed the zero-air-voids line. The predictions are for screening, not acceptance.

AI.tldr: A large, audited corpus of 2,854 Proctor compaction tests from six sources analyzes dry density and optimum moisture content; shows data quality issues in published data; demonstrates a tabular foundation model achieving strong predictive performance on random validation, weaker when generalizing to provenance or sources; compactive energy has conditional effect; symbolic regression yields physically consistent closed forms; predictions are intended for screening.
AI.motivation: Address scarcity and unreliability of single-lab, single-energy correlations by assembling a broad, audited dataset across energies and provenance to improve prediction of compaction outcomes and to establish baseline generalization performance.
AI.method: Harmonise six public data sources into 2,854 records across 162 provenance groups and four Proctor energies; audit Proctor method; reject energy inference; screening by zero-air-voids; quantify saturation; build a tabular foundation model; evaluate with random folds, provenance-fold cross-validation, and leave-one-source-out; analyze 66 modified-Proctor tests; apply symbolic regression to derive closed-form relations constrained by zero-air-voids; interpret and discuss usage for screening.
AI.result: Key results: (1) Verified dataset yields optimum degree of saturation ~0.815 (CV ~11%) as baseline; (2) Tabular foundation model achieves R^2 ≈ 0.824 for density and 0.784 for water content under random folds; performance degrades to ≈0.727/0.696 with provenance folds and ≈0.520/0.614 when a whole source is held out; (3) Compactive energy has a negligible average effect but conditional significance; (4) For the 66 modified-Proctor records, density is predicted at R^2 ≈0.74 with energy and ≈0.65 without; (5) Symbolic regression yields closed-form expressions linked by a phase relationship; no predicted pair exceeds the zero-air-voids line; (6) Predictions are intended for screening, not acceptance.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the value of a large, harmonized compaction data corpus for data-driven screening of density–moisture targets; predictive performance contracts when generalizing to unseen provenance or source; confirms the physical constraint of zero-air-voids and highlights conditional importance of compactive energy; data quality concerns in existing literature remain, but the approach offers a reproducible baseline for future work.

title: Corner Cases: Headland Coverage Path Planning for Autonomous Driving in Arable Farming
summary: This paper presents a new method for headland coverage path planning for arable fields. Several earlier approaches suggest covering the headland with nested polygons and smooth turns, however, covering the field corners entirely requires manoeuvres with reversing. In the new method, the polygon corners are modified to allow a reversing turn. A comparison to two other methods considering gap, overlap, and crossing the field boundary shows an improvement in the coverage result especially in field corners of around 90 degrees, and 240 degrees and above. Applicability of the new method is shown with several examples of real polygonal field maps.

AI.tldr: New method modifies polygon corners to allow reversing turns in headland coverage path planning, improving corner coverage (notably at ~90° and ≥240°) compared to two prior methods; validated on real polygonal field maps.
AI.motivation: Overcome inefficiencies in headland coverage where previous polygon-based methods require reversing maneuvers at corners to maintain coverage, causing gaps/overlaps especially at sharp corners.
AI.method: Modify polygon corners to permit reversing turns within the headland coverage framework; compare against two existing methods by evaluating gap, overlap, and field-boundary crossing; tested on real polygonal field maps.
AI.result: Improved coverage quality, particularly at challenging corners (≈90° and ≥240°), with applicability demonstrated across multiple real-field examples.
AI.conclusion: Corner-modified headland coverage method provides a practical enhancement for arable-field coverage, enabling reversing turns to reduce gaps and overlaps; validated on real field maps.

title: Tree species mapping in Denmark: A comparison of spectral-temporal features with geospatial foundation model embeddings
comment: Submitted to Remote Sensing of Environment. This preprint presents a national-scale tree species mapping framework for Denmark using Sentinel-1/2 time series, National Forest Inventory data, and EO foundation model embeddings. The resulted national map can be found here: https://zenodo.org/uploads/22108850
summary: We map tree species across Denmark using National Forest Inventory plots and EO data, while evaluating the potential of foundation models for large-scale forest characterization. We compare two alternative input representations for tree species classification: (i) manually engineered spectral-temporal features (STF) derived from multi-temporal Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 observations, and (ii) embeddings generated by the EO FMs TESSERA and AlphaEarth. Both representations are complemented with canopy height information. Random forest, XGBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) classifiers are evaluated for all input representations, with separate assessments for pure and mixed forest stands. The STF-based MLP achieves the highest classification performance, yielding macro F1 scores of 0.843 and 0.653 for pure and mixed stands, respectively. The MLP trained on TESSERA embeddings delivers competitive performance for pure stands, achieving results within 1.1 percentage points of the best-performing model. TESSERA consistently outperforms STF-based models when fewer than approximately 25% of training plots are available, demonstrating a substantial advantage under limited training data. Multi-year observations systematically improve classification accuracy relative to single-year inputs, while ablation experiments reveal the complementary contributions of Sentinel-1 backscatter, spectral indices, and canopy height data. The best-performing model is subsequently applied at the national scale to generate a 10 m tree species map of Denmark. Area-adjusted validation indicates an overall map accuracy of 79.9%. The resulting map, released as an open-access product, is the first high-resolution national tree species map of Denmark and provides a valuable resource for forest monitoring, ecological research, and land management applications.

AI.tldr: A study comparing STF-based features and EO foundation model embeddings for Danish tree species mapping, finding STF-MLP best overall, with TESSERA embeddings excelling under limited training data, resulting in an open-access 10 m national tree species map with 79.9% area-adjusted accuracy.
