AI.motivation: To achieve high-resolution, national-scale tree species maps using both traditional engineered features and foundation model embeddings, evaluate input representations across pure and mixed stands, and assess data availability effects and multi-year improvements.
AI.method: Compare two input representations for tree species classification: (i) manually engineered spectral-temporal features (STF) from multi-temporal Sentinel-1/2, and (ii) embeddings from EO foundation models TESSERA and AlphaEarth, both with canopy height. Train and evaluate Random Forest, XGBoost, and MLP classifiers for pure and mixed stands. Analyze single-year versus multi-year inputs, perform ablation to assess contributions of backscatter, spectral indices, and height. Identify best model and apply at national scale to generate a 10 m Danish tree species map, validate with area-adjusted accuracy.
AI.result: STF-based MLP achieves macro F1 of 0.843 (pure) and 0.653 (mixed). MLP with TESSERA embeddings is competitive for pure stands, within 1.1 percentage points of the best model. TESSERA outperforms STF-based models when training plots <~25%. Multi-year inputs improve accuracy over single-year inputs. Ablations show complementary contributions of Sentinel-1 backscatter, spectral indices, and canopy height. The best model applied nationally yields a 10 m Denmark tree species map with area-adjusted accuracy of 79.9%, open-access.
AI.conclusion: Foundational model embeddings (notably TESSERA) can rival engineered features for pure-stand classification and offer strong advantages in low-data regimes, while multi-year, multi-sensor data and height information provide complementary gains. The study delivers the first high-resolution national tree species map for Denmark as a useful resource for monitoring and management.

title: DNative-Twin: Decision Graphs and Digital Twins for Reconstructable Agentic Decisions
summary: AI agents increasingly gather evidence, invoke tools, apply constraints, and produce decisions that people or software may commit to action. A final output alone cannot show which evidence, tool state, rule, authorization, or action path produced it. We present DNative-Twin, a graph-native digital twin that records a committed agentic decision as a typed trajectory and re-executes its decision mechanism under declared conditions. The graph links the state observed by the agent, the path it followed, and the authority behind the resulting action. The twin synchronizes this information, replays the mechanism in isolation, and compares it under controlled changes. We instantiate the framework in enterprise decision processes using three public process logs and controlled replay suites. The experiments identify a specific failure: graph structure localizes represented changes but cannot determine the consequence of an unobserved tool state. In a three-condition controlled experiment with 300 injected instances, unresolved-divergence recall increased from 0 to 0.667 when replay-contract state was added and to 1.0 when verification results were also available; the held-out set contained no critical-class instance. Across 500--5,000 BPI 2020 cases, median end-to-end time increased from 0.794 to 8.889 seconds on the reported platform. These results separate the roles of graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence in reviewing a decision mechanism.

AI.tldr: Introduces DNative-Twin, a graph-native digital twin that records committed AI decisions as typed trajectories and replays the decision mechanism under declared conditions to audit evidence, tool states, and paths behind the final output.
AI.motivation: Provide auditable, verifiable insight into autonomous decision-making by AI agents, addressing the gap where final outputs do not reveal the underlying evidence, tool states, or decision paths.
AI.method: Propose a graph-native digital twin (DNative-Twin) that links observed state, decision path, and governing authority; synchronizes the twin with the agent's state, replays the mechanism in isolation under controlled changes, and compares outcomes. Instantiated in enterprise decision processes using three public process logs and controlled replay suites. Conducted a three-condition controlled experiment with 300 injected instances and evaluated 500–5,000 BPI 2020 cases.
AI.result: Identified a failure: graph structure localizes changes but cannot determine consequences of unobserved tool state. In a 3-condition experiment, unresolved-divergence recall rose from 0 to 0.667 with replay-contract state and to 1.0 when verification results were available; held-out set had no critical-class instances. End-to-end time median increased from 0.794s to 8.889s on the platform.
AI.conclusion: Differentiate the contributions of graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence for auditing and reviewing decision mechanisms; highlights trade-offs between traceability, verification, and performance.

title: Gradients Know What Outcomes Don't: Unlocking Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning with Gradient-Aligned Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) drives chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models, yet its binary outcome reward cannot distinguish among correct trajectories. Existing dense reward alternatives, from surface heuristics to process reward models, either ignore the expert solutions already present in training corpora or require expensive offline annotation. We propose Gradient-Aligned Reward (GAR), which operates in the policy's own gradient space: truncated backpropagation through the output projection layer extracts a compact gradient vector for each rollout, and cosine similarity with an expert-anchor gradient yields a dense, reasoning-aware reward with less than 9% wall-clock overhead. We prove that this cosine admits a multiplicative decomposition into prediction-error and activation-pattern factors, providing a concrete characterization of what the alignment signal measures. On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, GAR consistently improves over GRPO and other baselines on competition-level math benchmarks and transfers to GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro without domain-specific data. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LQgdwind/GAR.

AI.tldr: GAR introduces a gradient-aligned reward in policy gradient space by truncating backprop to extract a compact gradient vector per rollout and using cosine similarity to an expert-trigger gradient, yielding dense, reasoning-aware rewards with low overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing RL rewards are binary or heuristic and fail to leverage expert solutions in training corpora; a dense, reasoning-aware signal is needed to guide chain-of-thought reasoning without costly offline annotation.
AI.method: For each rollout, perform truncated backpropagation through the output projection layer to obtain a compact gradient vector. Compute cosine similarity with an expert-anchor gradient to produce a dense reward. Prove a multiplicative decomposition of this cosine into prediction-error and activation-pattern factors. Evaluate on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B against GRPO and baselines on math benchmarks, then transfer to GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro. Provide code and data at GitHub.
AI.result: GAR yields consistent improvements over baselines on competition-level math benchmarks and transfers to GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro with less than 9% wall-clock overhead.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-space alignment via GAR provides a scalable, reasoning-aware dense reward by leveraging existing expert contributions, improving performance and transferability without domain-specific annotations.

title: GIFT: Guided Intermediate Feature Training via Action-Oriented Structural Supervision for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language pre-training and predictive world modeling provide robot policies with rich semantic and dynamic visual features, but their native action and visual-prediction objectives may omit critical physical and task structure while retaining control-irrelevant visual redundancy. We call this mismatch between visual richness and control utility the action-sufficiency gap. We investigate whether this gap can be bridged by guiding intermediate features to preserve three control-relevant structure in robotic manipulation: geometry governing motion feasibility, affordance encoding instruction-relevant entities, and goals grounding instructions in task-relevant regions. To this end, we present GIFT (Guided Intermediate Feature Training), an architecture-flexible framework for learning intermediate features that translates these structures into training-time constraints through geometry alignment, affordance prediction, and goal-region reconstruction. We instantiate GIFT in a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy, a direct-action World-Action Model (WAM), and an inverse-dynamics WAM while retaining each model's action formulation. Under zero-shot transfer to LIBERO-Plus, GIFT-VLA, GIFT-WAM-Fast, and GIFT-WAM-IDM outperform StarVLA-OFT, Fast-WAM, and Fast-WAM-IDM by 4.6, 12.6, and 5.2 points, reaching 79.6%, 72.6%, and 87.8%, respectively. On RoboCasa, the three GIFT variants reach 61.4%, 83.6%, and 82.3%, outperforming their counterparts by 12.6, 9.0, and 8.4 points, respectively. Together, these results establish learning functionally structured intermediate features as a reusable principle across model-specific action formulations, with especially large gains on articulated-object tasks and high-precision real-world manipulation under unseen visual and spatial perturbations. Project page: https://openphoenix-team.github.io/GIFT-pages.

AI.tldr: GIFT bridges the action-sufficiency gap by guiding intermediate features to preserve geometry, affordances, and goal-region information, improving zero-shot transfer across VLA and WAM models on LIBERO-Plus and RoboCasa, with notable gains on articulated-object tasks.
AI.motivation: Vision-language pre-training and predictive world models provide rich visuals but may miss control-relevant structure, leading to inefficiencies; there is a mismatch between visual richness and control utility that reduces manipulation performance.
AI.method: Introduce GIFT (Guided Intermediate Feature Training), an architecture-flexible framework that imposes training-time constraints on intermediate features via three structures: geometry alignment (motion feasibility), affordance prediction (instruction-relevant entities), and goal-region reconstruction (task grounding). Instantiate GIFT in three model families—VLA policy, and two World-Action Models (WAMs: Fast and IDM)—while preserving each model's native action formulation.
AI.result: GIFT variants achieve strong zero-shot transfer: LIBERO-Plus—GIFT-VLA 79.6%, GIFT-WAM-Fast 72.6%, GIFT-WAM-IDM 87.8% (outperforming baselines by 4.6, 12.6, and 5.2 points). RoboCasa—61.4%, 83.6%, 82.3% (outperforming baselines by 12.6, 9.0, and 8.4 points). Gains are especially large on articulated-object tasks and under unseen visual/spatial perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Learning functionally structured intermediate features is a reusable principle across model-specific action formulations, enabling robust, high-precision real-world manipulation in zero-shot transfer settings.

title: Residual Optimal Transport-Based Experts Collaboration Towards Modality-Aware Infrared-Visible Object Detection
summary: Infrared-visible object detection (IVOD) integrates complementary evidence from visible and infrared sensors for reliable perception in challenging scenes. In practice, sensors may fail or drop frames, leaving one modality unavailable or intermittent. Existing methods for IVOD assume both modalities are always present, and fixed fusion collapses when one stream is missing. Furthermore, it remains a critical challenge to reliably estimate semantic correlation across heterogeneous modalities, especially under spectral distribution discrepancy. We present FlexibleFusion, a unified and adaptive method that flexibly allocates integration pathways and fusion strength, operating seamlessly across complete and missing-modality regimes. At its core, the Modality-Aware Experts Collaboration (MAEC) mechanism selectively activates and aggregates cross-modal or intra-modal expert pathways. It allows cross-modal fusion when full modalities are available and falls back to self-fusion under missing conditions. Additionally, we design Residual Self-Paced Entropic Optimal Transport (RSPEOT) to align heterogeneous feature distributions from a transport perspective. Instead of relying on the fixed sparsity coefficient in standard entropic optimal transport (EOT), RSPEOT introduces a residual-driven self-paced update that prioritizes reliable matches and progressively refines harder ones. This design alleviates the additional optimization burden of standard EOT while preserving reliable semantic alignment. Comprehensive experiments under complete and missing-modality protocols show consistent performance across arbitrary modality configurations. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: FlexibleFusion introduces a unified, adaptive framework for infrared-visible object detection that remains robust when modalities are missing. It combines MAEC for modality-aware expert collaboration with RSPEOT for robust cross-modal alignment, achieving consistent performance across complete and missing-modality configurations.
AI.motivation: IVOD systems suffer from modality dropout; fixed fusion fails when a modality is unavailable, and cross-modal semantic alignment is challenged by spectral distribution discrepancies between infrared and visible data.
AI.method: MAEC selectively activates and aggregates cross-modal or intra-modal expert pathways, enabling cross-modal fusion when all modalities are present and self-fusion when a modality is missing. RSPEOT aligns heterogeneous feature distributions using a residual-driven, self-paced update of entropic optimal transport, prioritizing reliable matches and progressively refining harder ones.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments demonstrate stable performance across complete and missing-modality protocols across arbitrary modality configurations. Qualitative and quantitative results support improved robustness and semantic alignment, with code slated for release upon publication.
AI.conclusion: FlexibleFusion provides a robust, unified solution for IVOD in both complete and missing-modality settings, achieving reliable fusion and alignment without incurring the optimization burden typical of standard entropic OT approaches.

title: Transfiver: Human-AI Co-Inference through a Shared Editable State
summary:
Long-term human-AI interaction is difficult because the information that guides inference is updated implicitly by the model and is not directly inspectable or controllable by the user. We introduce the TRANSparent Framework for Interactive, Verifiable, Editable Representation (Transfiver), an architecture for human-AI co-inference through a shared editable state. Its central idea is that interaction-specific information is maintained in a single persistent state $(S_t)$ that both the model and the human update.
  Transfiver distinguishes two modes of state evolution. In an implicit stream update, the model interprets ongoing interaction and decides whether new information revises an existing state item or creates a new one. In an explicit directed edit, a human inspects and modifies an addressed item. Both act on the same underlying state, so a human correction changes the state that subsequent computation reads, rather than adding another instruction or separate record.
  The architecture separates shared parameters $(θ)$, learned before ordinary use, from the persistent state $(S_t)$, which evolves during deployment without parameter retraining. Extending Transfiver to rich natural-language, relational, and large-scale shared states remains open.

AI.tldr: A framework (Transfiver) for human-AI co-inference using a single persistent, editable shared state S_t updated by both model and user, enabling interaction traceability and non-retraining adaptation.
AI.motivation: Long-term human-AI interaction is hard because guiding information is implicitly updated in the model and not directly inspectable/controllable; a persistent shared state could make interaction effects verifiable and editable.
AI.method: Architectural split between shared parameters θ and a mutable persistent state S_t. Two state-evolution modes: (i) implicit stream updates where the model revises or adds to S_t based on ongoing interaction; (ii) explicit directed edits where humans inspect/modify items in S_t. Both operate on the same state, ensuring user corrections affect subsequent computation without retraining. Deployment without parameter updates; discussion of extending to richer, multimodal shared states.
AI.result: Conceptual framework and architecture for interactive co-inference. Defines how a single persistent state is updated by both model and user to influence future computation, enabling verifiable/editable interaction memory. Highlights deployment without retraining and notes open challenges for rich linguistic/relational/large-scale states.
AI.conclusion: Transfiver offers a path toward verifiable, editable, and persistent interaction memory in human-AI systems; practical realization and extension to richer shared states remain open research directions.

title: From Zero to Hero: An Open LLM Ecosystem for Armenian
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, 13 tables. Data and model: https://huggingface.co/collections/COPA-AI/armenian-llm-ecosystem. Code: https://github.com/COPATeam/armenian_llm_ecosystem
summary: Pretraining data for Armenian, a morphologically rich and low-resource language, is scarce, and no open Armenian LLM has been released with the data and recipe needed to reproduce it. To address this gap, we curate and release two datasets. ArmWeb is an extensively validated corpus of 4.37M Armenian news documents. ArmSTEM is a parallel English-Armenian collection of 373K math and science problems with step-by-step solutions, translated into Armenian and verified through both answer-preserving LLM judgment and human evaluation. Continued pretraining of Gemma-4-E4B on these datasets yields arm-gemma-e4b, which outperforms every existing open Armenian model as well as its unadapted base, and is the first open Armenian LLM with complete training data and recipe. Our ablations show that news-only continued pretraining improves fluency while eroding knowledge, a pattern we also observe in existing Armenian models, and that a small share of verified translated STEM data reverses the loss. We further find that the largest public Armenian corpora overlap web-derived evaluation panels heavily, including a train/test self-overlap inside FineWeb-2. We openly release all data, models, and code.

AI.tldr: Proposes ArmWeb and ArmSTEM datasets for Armenian LLM pretraining; continues pretraining Gemma-4-E4B to arm-gemma-e4b; reports state-of-the-art among open Armenian models; ablations show news-only training boosts fluency but harms knowledge, stem data mitigates; data leakage concerns; releases all data, models, code.
AI.motivation: Armenian is morphologically rich and low-resource; lack of open LLMs with trainable data and recipe; need reproducible baselines.
AI.method: Curates ArmWeb (4.37M news docs) and ArmSTEM (373K translated STEM problems with step-by-step solutions). Performs continued pretraining of Gemma-4-E4B on these datasets to create arm-gemma-e4b. Evaluates via ablations and comparisons; verifies translations with LLM judges and human evaluation; tests overlap with FineWeb-2; releases data, models, code.
AI.result: arm-gemma-e4b outperforms all existing open Armenian models and the unadapted base. Ablations show news-only training increases fluency but reduces knowledge; adding STEM translations partially reverses loss. Highlights data leakage risk due to web corpora overlap with evaluation panels. All data/models/code released.
AI.conclusion: Provides an open Armenian LLM with complete training data and recipe; demonstrates the value of curated parallel STEM data and cautious pretraining mix; emphasizes reproducibility and transparency.

title: Neural Video Compression Based on Deformable Temporal Alignment and Difference-aware Fusion
summary: In conditional coding-based neural video compression, the quality of temporal context directly affects compression per- formance. Existing methods mostly construct context from prop- agated reference features, but they are vulnerable to motion esti- mation and local alignment errors in regions with complex mo- tion, occlusion, and high-frequency textures, resulting in inaccu- rate temporal information. To address this issue, this paper pro- poses a method combining deformable temporal alignment and difference-aware spatial selective fusion. A Context-aware Tem- poral Alignment Module is used to generate complementary tem- poral context, while a Difference-aware Spatial Selective Fusion module adaptively selects reliable temporal information and sup- presses misalignment. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves certain rate-distortion performance improve- ment over DCVC-DC.

AI.tldr: A deformable temporal alignment plus difference-aware spatial selective fusion approach improves temporal context for conditional coding-based neural video compression, achieving RD improvements over DCVC-DC.
AI.motivation: Temporal context quality strongly affects compression; current methods relying on propagated references suffer from motion/alignment errors in complex motion regions, occlusion, and high-frequency textures.
AI.method: Introduce Context-aware Temporal Alignment Module to generate complementary temporal context via deformable temporal alignment; Difference-aware Spatial Selective Fusion to adaptively select reliable temporal information and suppress misalignment.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows rate-distortion improvements over DCVC-DC on tested benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed modules effectively enhance temporal context usage in neural video compression, yielding better RD performance.

title: Govern the Model, Not Only the Data: Storage, Circulation, and Learning in Creative AI
summary: Federated learning is increasingly presented as a privacy-preserving advance: personal data remain on the device, and only model updates are shared. It borrows the vocabulary of the federated social web, yet inverts its logic, distributing computation while the resulting model stays with whoever convened the training. We argue that federation is not in itself a remedy for extractive AI, because outcomes depend on who governs the data and the model and who has agency over the practices that shape them. We describe three layers at which a creative community can hold its work: storage, circulation, and learning. Examining artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures, we show that creator governance is established at storage and circulation but stops at learning: contributors can consent to training, yet have little say over the resulting model or its federation. We map the research space this opens, pairing technical open problems with the human questions from which they unfold. We propose four design principles for a creative data commons that governs models and their federation, not only datasets: govern the model, not only the corpus; make the terms legible at the moment of contribution; design for refusal as a first-class state; and decide stewardship in the open and account for it.

AI.tldr: Federated learning is not a governance fix for extractive AI. The paper shows three governance layers—storage, circulation, and learning—where control is established up to storage/circulation but not over the resulting model or its federation. It analyzes artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures, maps the research space connecting technical and human questions, and proposes four design principles for a creative data commons to govern models and federation: govern the model, make terms legible at contribution, design for refusal as a first-class state, and decide stewardship openly and accountably.
AI.motivation: To critique the assumption that federated learning automatically preserves privacy and to explore governance, agency, and consent in creative data practices, highlighting who governs data and models and how practices shape outcomes.
AI.method: Conceptual/philosophical analysis across three layers of governance (storage, circulation, learning); examination of artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures; mapping of the design space coupling technical questions with human considerations; proposition of design principles.
AI.result: Articulates that governance for data works at storage and circulation but not at learning; identifies a gap in contributor control over trained models and federations; offers four design principles to create a creative data commons that governs models and federation, not only datasets.
AI.conclusion: To address extractive AI in practice, governance must extend to the model and its federation. The four principles—govern the model, legibility of terms at contribution, design for refusal, and open stewardship—provide a framework for responsible, participatory AI in creative contexts.

title: Time Without Timesteps: Simulating Coupled Dynamical Systems via Self-Consistency
summary: Numerical simulation of dynamical systems is usually organized as a causal march through time: each state is computed from the previous one. We explore a different formulation for coupled systems. For each subsystem type we train a neural surrogate mapping a full driving trajectory and initial condition directly to a full output trajectory; following classical waveform relaxation, coupled systems are assembled by enforcing self-consistency among these trajectories: simulation becomes a fixed-point problem over complete trajectories rather than a stepwise rollout. On coupled van der Pol oscillators and Hodgkin-Huxley neuron networks, sequential depth becomes the number of solver iterations: 4-10 Newton iterations where the reference integrator takes 1500 steps. The gradient likewise loses its time recursion: it becomes a linear system solved by GMRES at memory independent of solver depth. A single scalar measured from the learned operator, the spectral radius of its Jacobian, predicts in advance where the coupled solve will converge; past that boundary, unrolled backpropagation diverges and a Neumann adjoint fails, while the implicit gradient remains correct to 0.04%. We report where the approach succeeds and where surrogate error degrades it.

AI.tldr: Neural surrogate operators per subsystem enable fixed-point, trajectory-level coupling (waveform relaxation) for dynamical systems; gradients computed via implicit differentiation; spectral radius predicts solvability; demonstrated on coupled van der Pol and Hodgkin–Huxley networks; performance shows 4–10 Newton iterations versus 1500-step references; implicit gradient robust to solver depth with about 0.04% error; surrogate quality bounds applicability.
AI.motivation: address inefficiency and rigidity of stepwise time integration for coupled dynamical systems; enable trajectory-level self-consistent solves and differentiable training; provide a diagnostic predictor to anticipate convergence and guide design.
AI.method: Train a neural operator per subsystem that maps a full driving trajectory and initial condition to a full output trajectory. Assemble coupled system by enforcing self-consistency across subsystem trajectories, forming a fixed-point problem over complete trajectories (waveform-relaxation style). Solve with Newton iterations (4–10 in reported cases) rather than stepping through time. For gradients, use implicit differentiation; GF-based linear solves via GMRES with memory independent of solver depth; monitor a scalar: the spectral radius of the Jacobian of the learned operator to predict convergence.
AI.result: Sequential depth equals solver iterations (4–10 Newton steps) vs ~1500 steps for a reference integrator. Gradient computation uses GMRES; memory scales independently of solver depth. The spectral radius of the learned operator’s Jacobian serves as a forward predictor of convergence; beyond the predicted boundary, unrolled backpropagation diverges and Neumann adjoint fails; the implicit gradient remains correct to about 0.04%. Empirical findings include where the approach succeeds and where surrogate error degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: The trajectory-level neural surrogate with waveform-relaxation is a viable, differentiable framework for simulating and optimizing coupled dynamical systems, with clear convergence diagnostics via the Jacobian spectral radius. Its success hinges on surrogate accuracy and proximity to the convergence boundary; demonstrated on coupled van der Pol oscillators and Hodgkin–Huxley neuron networks.

title: SV-WAM: An Efficient Surround-View World-Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: World models (WMs) have demonstrated strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by learning predictive representations of future scene dynamics. However, generating future videos during inference introduces substantial computational overhead, leading many recent driving WMs to adopt a single front camera as input for efficient deployment. This design restricts spatial coverage in safety-critical maneuvers such as lane changes, merges, and turns. To address this limitation, we propose SV-WAM, a surround-view world-action model (WAM) that preserves full six-camera observations while maintaining efficient inference. SV-WAM leverages future-video prediction as dense training supervision for action learning within a shared generative model, rather than as an inference-time output. At the core of this design is an action-centered causal mask that prevents action tokens from attending to future-video tokens during joint action-video denoising. Consequently, the video branch can be discarded at deployment, enabling efficient action-only planning. Furthermore, we introduce a differentiable drivable-area compliance regularizer that penalizes vehicle-footprint corners approaching or crossing drivable boundaries, improving planning safety and boundary awareness. Extensive experiments on the closed-loop NAVSIMv2 benchmark and the open-loop nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that SV-WAM achieves state-of-the-art planning performance with low inference latency and competitive zero-shot transfer capability.

AI.tldr: SV-WAM introduces a surround-view world-action model that uses an action-centered causal mask and training-time future-video supervision to achieve efficient, six-camera planning without inference-time video generation, with state-of-the-art planning and low latency on NAVSIMv2 and nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Preserve full six-camera surround-view for safety-critical driving maneuvers while avoiding the computational overhead of generating future videos at inference time.
AI.method: A shared generative world-model where future-video prediction provides dense training supervision for action learning. An action-centered causal mask prevents action tokens from attending to future-video tokens during joint action-video denoising, enabling the video branch to be discarded at deployment for action-only planning. A differentiable drivable-area compliance regularizer penalizes vehicle-footprint proximity to drivable boundaries.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art planning performance with low inference latency on NAVSIMv2 (closed-loop) and nuScenes (open-loop), with competitive zero-shot transfer.
AI.conclusion: SV-WAM successfully decouples training-time future-video supervision from inference-time outputs, enabling efficient, safe surround-view planning with full camera coverage and practical deployment benefits.

title: TruncGradGS: Improved 3D Gaussian Splatting via Truncated Gradient Updates
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has become a de facto scene representation for novel view synthesis, yet robustly learning 3D Gaussian primitives from visual input remains challenging. Standard optimization relies on gradient-based updates, but a common issue is the gradient vanishing phenomenon: a pixel far from a Gaussian primitive often has diminishing gradient magnitudes to influence primitive attributes, resulting in suboptimal scene reconstruction. In this paper, we propose a method to address gradient vanishing with a piecewise truncated gradient formulation that improves the optimization stability and robustness to initializations. We show that our method consistently improves 3D Gaussian Splatting with random and COLMAP initializations while being generalizable across static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting. As a by-product, we also examine the limitations of current benchmarks for dynamic scenes, and introduce a novel dataset for benchmarking dynamic Gaussian Splatting using synthetic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in both static and dynamic settings for the public benchmarks and our proposed dataset.

AI.tldr: Introduces a piecewise truncated gradient to combat gradient vanishing in learning 3D Gaussian primitives for Gaussian Splatting, boosting optimization stability and robustness across initializations and scene dynamics; also provides a new synthetic dataset for dynamic Gaussian Splatting.
AI.motivation: Gradient vanishing: pixels far from a Gaussian primitive contribute diminishing gradients, hindering accurate reconstruction and robust training across random/COLMAP initializations; need a stable optimization approach and fair benchmarks for dynamic scenes.
AI.method: A piecewise truncated gradient formulation that bounds and redistributes gradient magnitudes to improve signal for primitive updates, compatible with standard initialization settings (random, COLMAP), and applicable to both static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting.
AI.result: Consistent improvements on static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting across public benchmarks; robustness to initialization; introduction of a synthetic dataset for benchmarking dynamic Gaussian Splatting; demonstration of effectiveness in both static and dynamic settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed gradient formulation stabilizes optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting, enhances robustness and generalization across initializations and dynamic/static cases, and highlights gaps in current benchmarks with a new synthetic dataset to benchmark dynamic scenes.

title: SVG-Score: Human-Aligned Evaluation of Text-to-SVG Generation
summary: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation is attracting increasing attention as generative models improve in expressiveness and controllability. Progress, however, is held back by the lack of domain-specific evaluation protocols: current practice relies on metrics designed for natural images, most notably CLIPScore, which was never trained on vector graphics and aligns only partially with human judgment. We introduce \textbf{\ours}, a human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation. Through controlled caption and image perturbations, we first show that CLIP-based scores barely react to the errors SVG generators actually make, such as wrong colors, counts, and spatial relations, and that off-the-shelf Vision-Language Model (VLM) judges, while more sensitive, respond unevenly across error types and SVG styles. We then introduce a human-annotated dataset for \textit{Semantic Alignment}, measuring how faithfully a generated SVG reflects its caption. Building on it, we develop two complementary evaluators: CLIP scorers adapted to vector graphics and then aligned to human preferences, for fast large-scale evaluation, and a VLM judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning, for more expressive and interpretable assessment. Using both, we benchmark major open-source, commercial, and optimization-based SVG generators on an independent caption set.

AI.tldr: A human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation, combining perturbation-based diagnostics, a semantic-alignment dataset, and two evaluators (vector-adapted CLIP scores and a supervised+RL VLM judge) to enable scalable, human-consistent assessment and benchmarking of SVG generators.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation relies on natural-image metrics (e.g., CLIP-based scores) that do not reflect common SVG errors (color, count, spatial relations). There is a need for vector-graphics–specific, human-aligned evaluation protocols.
AI.method: 1) Controlled caption and image perturbations to reveal metric sensitivity to SVG errors; 2) a human-annotated Semantic Alignment dataset measuring faithfulness of SVGs to captions; 3) develop two evaluators: (a) CLIP-based scores adapted to vector graphics aligned to human preferences for fast scaling, (b) a Vision-Language Model judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning for expressive, interpretable evaluation; 4) benchmark major SVG generators on an independent caption set using both evaluators.
AI.result: CLIP-based scores largely fail to detect SVG errors such as incorrect colors, counts, or spatial relations; off-the-shelf VLM judges are more sensitive but exhibit uneven performance across error types and styles. The proposed vector-adapted evaluators align better with human judgments and enable fast, scalable (CLIP) and more expressive (VLM) evaluation. A human-annotated Semantic Alignment dataset supports interpretable benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a human-aligned, scalable, and interpretable evaluation suite for text-to-SVG generation, enabling robust benchmarking across models and guiding future improvements in SVG generation and evaluation.

title: SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. https://openreview.net/forum?id=wPfw7GkMns
summary: Proteins are fundamental to biological processes, with their function determined by the complex interplay between the amino acid sequence and the three-dimensional structure. Developing generative models capable of understanding this intrinsically multi-modal relationship is crucial for fields like drug discovery and protein engineering. Existing models often rely on a multi-stage training process where autoencoders that tokenize data into latent representations are trained in a first stage. Secondly, a generative model is trained on the latent representation of the autoencoder(s), i.e., generative modeling in a latent space. We hypothesize that this multi-stage training is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models and thus present SimpleDesign, an effective multi-modal protein design model trained directly in the data space. SimpleDesign leverages a single-stage end-to-end objective that combines discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures. In order to effectively model the difference in sequence and structure modalities, we develop a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that allows modality-specific processing while keeping global self-attention over both modalities. We train SimpleDesign on over 2M sequence-structure pairs achieving strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Single-stage end-to-end multimodal protein design (SimpleDesign) that jointly models sequence and structure using a Mixture-of-Transformers and is trained directly in data space on ~2M sequence-structure pairs.
AI.motivation: Address the inefficiencies of multi-stage latent-space training (autoencoders + latent generative models) for protein design; aim for simpler, potentially more effective co-design.
AI.method: Mixture-of-Transformer architecture enabling modality-specific processing with global cross-modal self-attention; end-to-end objective combining discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures; trained directly on 2M sequence-structure pairs.
AI.result: Strong performance on co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks, demonstrating effective multimodal learning without latent-space pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Multi-stage latent-space training may be unnecessary for high-performance multimodal protein design; direct data-space training with modality-aware architecture is effective.

title: Understanding Autonomous Driving Datasets by Describing Differences between Image Subsets in Natural Language
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, submitted to the IEEE Open Journal of Intelligent Transportation Systems (OJ-ITS), our implementation and benchmark dataset are available at https://github.com/KIT-MRT/AD-Diff
summary: Understanding the composition of large-scale autonomous driving datasets is essential for safety, robustness, and reliable operation across domains. For example, domain shift between locations could lead to the operating environment being misaligned with the training data, resulting in potentially dangerous performance degradation. Yet, existing data analysis pipelines largely rely on metadata, predefined labels, or manual inspection, which provide limited semantic insight or do not scale. This paper studies set difference captioning: given two subsets of images, the goal is to produce a natural-language hypothesis describing differences between the target and reference set. Building on a two-stage formulation, we adapt the method to autonomous driving by focusing on object-centric patches derived from object detection, which simplifies aggregation and enables attribution of differences to specific object instances or categories. To evaluate this setting in-domain, we introduce a new benchmark, AD-Diff Bench. Low-concentration experiments assess the suitability of set-difference-captioning approaches to sparse, real-world differences. We restrict our experiments to open-weight models to support reproducibility and ease of deployment. The proposed benchmark and analysis provide a step towards practical, human-interpretable dataset introspection for autonomous driving datasets. Our implementation and benchmark dataset are available at https://github.com/KIT-MRT/AD-Diff

AI.tldr: Introduces set-difference captioning for autonomous-driving datasets to describe differences between two image subsets, using object-centric patches; presents AD-Diff Bench benchmark and a low-concentration regime; aims for interpretable dataset introspection with open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Domain shifts and distribution differences in autonomous driving datasets can degrade safety and robustness. Existing analytics rely on metadata or manual inspection and lack semantic, scalable insights. A natural-language description of differences would enable interpretable, scalable dataset introspection.
AI.method: A two-stage set-difference captioning framework adapted to autonomous driving: 1) extract object-centric patches via object detection, 2) generate natural-language hypotheses describing differences between target and reference sets, enabling attribution to specific object instances or categories. Evaluates in-domain using a new benchmark (AD-Diff Bench) and tests low-concentration, sparse differences; uses open-weight models for reproducibility.
AI.result: Proposes AD-Diff Bench as a benchmark for set-difference captioning in autonomous driving and demonstrates the method's feasibility in capturing meaningful differences between image subsets. Demonstrates that object-centric patches facilitate attribution to specific objects or categories, and shows viability of open-weight models in this setting.
AI.conclusion: Set-difference captioning with object-centric patches is a promising direction for practical, human-interpretable dataset introspection in autonomous driving, enabling targeted understanding of domain shifts and dataset biases; the AD-Diff Bench provides a standardized evaluation platform and baseline results.

title: SafeRI: Recognition and Intervention for Token-Level Safety Intervention in Large Vision Language Models
comment: Preprint. 13 pages, 4 figures. Main paper with appendix
summary: Existing safety alignment methods for vision-language models usually modify the model behavior globally: once the safety parameters are trained or loaded, they participate in both unsafe and already-safe generations. This always-on intervention can unnecessarily perturb the model's original reasoning path and degrade general multimodal capabilities. We argue that safety alignment should be an on-demand intervention rather than a permanent modification to every decoding trajectory. To this end, we propose a streaming recognition and gated LoRA framework for intrinsic VLM safety. During autoregressive generation, a lightweight recognizer estimates whether the current pre-token generation state is safe or unsafe. Its output updates the LoRA gate for the following decoding step; otherwise, generation follows the frozen-backbone policy. The LoRA module is trained from unsafe prefixes, transition statements, and safe continuations, so that it learns to redirect unsafe generations back to safe responses after activation. Experiments across multiple safety and general-purpose benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in post-alignment settings.

AI.tldr: An on-demand safety-alignment framework for vision-language models using streaming recognition and gated LoRA, which only activates safety interventions when unsafe states are detected, preserving core capabilities.
AI.motivation: Current safety methods are always-on, perturbing both unsafe and safe outputs and degrading general multimodal performance. There is a need for selective, minimal-interference safety control.
AI.method: Propose streaming recognition and gated LoRA. During autoregressive generation, a lightweight recognizer assesses whether the current pre-token state is safe. Its output gates the LoRA update for the next token; if unsafe, the generation follows the frozen backbone policy while the LoRA can redirect unsafe outputs. The LoRA is trained on unsafe prefixes, transition statements, and safe continuations to learn how to steer unsafe generations back to safe responses.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across multiple safety and general-purpose benchmarks demonstrates the method’s effectiveness in post-alignment settings, preserving safety while maintaining performance.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment for vision-language models should be an on-demand intervention. The streaming recognizer + gated LoRA approach provides targeted, reversible safety control that minimizes interference with normal capabilities and supports post-alignment scenarios.

title: CauseCollab: Causal Unified and Modality-Agnostic Network for Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception
summary: Collaborative perception enhances environment understanding through multi-agent information sharing, but its performance in real-world scenarios is constrained by heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architectures. Recent protocol-based two-stage methods alleviate this problem by mapping heterogeneous features into a shared protocol space; however, independently trained modality-specific converters often generate modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions, leading to semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, which is particularly pronounced in scenarios with large modality discrepancies. To address this issue, we propose CauseCollab, a causal unified and modality-agnostic network. CauseCollab formulates representation learning in the protocol space from a causal perspective, explicitly disentangling semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders via causal metric learning. Meanwhile, CauseCollab adopts context-guided Unified Converter for heterogeneous modalities to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. In addition, integrating new modalities only requires training adapters with minimal parameters. Extensive experiments on the OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets demonstrate that CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.

AI.tldr: CauseCollab introduces a causal, modality-agnostic network for collaborative perception that disentangles semantic factors from modality confounders in a shared protocol space and uses a context-guided Unified Converter; adapters enable low-parameter modality expansion, achieving state-of-the-art results especially with large modality gaps.
AI.motivation: Two-stage, protocol-based methods map heterogeneous features to a shared space but suffer from modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions due to independently trained converters, causing semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, especially with large modality discrepancies.
AI.method: Learn representations in protocol space via causal metric learning to explicitly disentangle semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders. Employ a context-guided Unified Converter to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. Introduce adapters for new modalities requiring only small additional parameters.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets shows state-of-the-art performance, with more pronounced gains in scenarios with large modality gaps.
AI.conclusion: CauseCollab provides a causal, unified framework for cross-modality collaborative perception that maintains semantic consistency, offers modular adapters for scalable modality inclusion, and exhibits robust performance under heterogeneous sensor configurations.

title: RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory
summary: Repeating a small block of middle layers increases a language model's effective inference depth without adding parameters or generating extra tokens, and recent work shows that this latent recurrence improves reasoning. However, two design choices limit these gains. Each iteration sees only the previous output and cannot directly access earlier computations. Moreover, a fixed loop count wastes depth on easy inputs while leaving hard ones with too little computation. We introduce RecurTrace, which addresses both limitations using the loop's own trajectory. Specifically, Loop Memory Attention lets each looped layer attend to its own states from previous iterations along the loop-time axis, so the model can revisit earlier computations instead of relying on the latest state alone. A halting head then reads the loop state and predicts whether to continue, with supervision from an oracle that identifies when additional depth still reduces loss. In a controlled MathQA comparison on the same looped backbone, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, exceeding the best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute. By comparison, ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop, and CALM reaches only 54.1% with 5.6 loops, while the stronger LoopUS-Conf and TaH-Mismatch baselines reach 55.3% at 3.2 loops and 55.7% at 2.1 loops. Finally, RecurTrace improves generation accuracy over same-budget fine-tuned baselines at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, with the gain growing with model size from 0.6 to 3.4 points.

AI.tldr: A looped recurrence with loop-state attention and a halting controller enables adaptive, deeper inference without extra parameters or tokens; achieves higher MathQA accuracy and improved generation under the same compute, outperforming prior latent recurrences and fixed-depth baselines.
AI.motivation: To overcome two design limitations of prior latent recurrence: (1) each iteration only uses the latest output and cannot access earlier computations, and (2) fixed loop depth wastes depth on easy inputs while undercomputing hard ones.
AI.method: Propose Loop Memory Attention to let each looped layer attend to its own past states along the loop-time axis; introduce a halting head supervised by an oracle indicating when additional depth reduces loss; evaluate on a controlled MathQA setup using the same looped backbone; compare against ACT, PonderNet, CALM, LoopUS-Conf, TaH-Mismatch; assess generation accuracy across model scales (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B).
AI.result: On MathQA, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, beating the best fixed-depth model by 2.2 points at matched compute. ACT and PonderNet collapse to 1 loop; CALM reaches 54.1% with 5.6 loops; LoopUS-Conf 55.3% at 3.2 loops; TaH-Mismatch 55.7% at 2.1 loops. For generation, RecurTrace improves accuracy over same-budget fine-tuned baselines at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, with gains growing from 0.6 to 3.4 points as model size increases.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive loop-depth computation via Loop Memory Attention and a halting mechanism yields stronger reasoning and generation performance than prior latent recurrence and fixed-depth approaches, with benefits increasing at larger model scales.

title: DropClick: Semi-Automated One-Click Segmentation for Agricultural Robotic Data
summary: Labelling vision datasets, especially for segmentation tasks, is a laborious and costly process that stymies novel developments in agricultural robotics. In this paper, we present DropClick, a click-guided segmentation tool that simplifies the annotation process. Our system utilises single-click inputs on objects to generate pseudo-labels, which can replace manual annotations. DropClick stands out as it is a semi-automated approach and does not require a click for every object in the scene. It can therefore further reduce the required amount of user input drastically. We evaluate our method on two challenging agricultural robotic datasets, SB20 and BUP20 for plant and fruit segmentation, respectively. DropClick is first trained on a small subset of just 5 images from the original training data. This DropClick model can then be deployed as a one-click segmentation system and achieves comparable or higher performance than other one-click methods achieving an mIoU of 70.0 and 72.6 points, for SB20 and BUP20 respectively. DropClick then excels at maintaining high performance when clicks are not given (e.g. dropped); when 50% of the clicks are missing it still maintains an mIoU of 68.9 and 71.3 points, for SB20 and BUP20 respectively. We validate DropClick as a pseudo-labelling approach by taking its outputs to train a Mask2Former instance-based segmentation model in a semi-supervised manner. In this process, partially removing user input from DropClick yields similar high performance when compared to providing all clicks, at 70.1 vs 70.7 points AP50 for SB20 and no difference for BUP20 at 77.0 for both models; at the same time saving 46.3% of total input for SB20 and 31.9% for BUP20.

AI.tldr: Semi-automatic click-guided segmentation (DropClick) reduces annotation effort in agricultural datasets SB20 and BUP20 by using single-click inputs to generate pseudo-labels; trained on 5 images, achieving competitive mIoU (~70) and strong robustness to missing clicks; can be used for pseudo-labeling to train Mask2Former in semi-supervised fashion with substantial input savings.
AI.motivation: Annotation bottleneck for segmentation in agricultural robotics; need a low-effort, scalable labeling tool that can produce high-quality pseudo-labels and support semi-supervised training.
AI.method: DropClick accepts single-clicks on objects to generate pseudo-labels; trained on a small subset (5 images). Functions as a one-click segmentation system; tolerates missing clicks (up to 50%). Outputs are used as pseudo-labels to train a Mask2Former instance-based segmentation model in a semi-supervised pipeline; evaluated on SB20 (plants) and BUP20 (fruits).
AI.result: One-click mIoU: 70.0 (SB20) and 72.6 (BUP20). With 50% of clicks missing: 68.9 (SB20) and 71.3 (BUP20). For pseudo-labeling to train Mask2Former: AP50 ~70.1 (SB20) vs 70.7 with full clicks; no difference for BUP20 at 77.0. Input savings: 46.3% (SB20) and 31.9% (BUP20).
AI.conclusion: DropClick offers a practical, semi-automated labeling solution that reduces manual annotation effort and remains robust when inputs are incomplete. Its pseudo-label outputs can effectively train standard segmentation models in a semi-supervised setting, enabling scalable annotation in agricultural robotics.

title: WIDE: Wildcard Inference with Dynamic Expansion for Cross-Modal Generative Retrieval
comment: Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026). 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: Generative retrieval has demonstrated significant success by unifying representation learning and search into a single sequence-to-sequence generation task. However, extending this paradigm to cross-modal retrieval reveals a critical challenge arising from the inherent information asymmetry across different modalities, such as the gap between concise text queries and dense visual candidates. This structural mismatch causes the autoregressive decoder to suffer from forced hallucination when generating identifiers via standard trie-constrained beam search, where the model is severely penalized for failing to guess fine-grained details absent from the query, allowing irrelevant candidates to hijack top rankings. To address this issue, we propose Wildcard Inference with Dynamic Expansion (WIDE). WIDE employs Adaptive Entropy Thresholding (AET) to calibrate layer-specific uncertainty boundaries offline. During the decoding generation phase, Asymmetry-aware Wildcard Decoding (AWD) detects semantic blind spots and emits wildcards instead of forced deterministic identifiers, dynamically expanding the search space without incurring log-probability penalties. Finally, Blind-Spot Re-ranking (BSR) evaluates the expanded candidate pool using a hybrid scoring mechanism that combines discrete generation confidence with continuous semantic similarity. Extensive experiments on the M-BEIR benchmark demonstrate that WIDE outperforms state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods, effectively suppressing forced hallucination while maintaining compact index structures.

AI.tldr: WIDE is a cross-modal generative retrieval framework that reduces hallucination and maintains compact indices by combining adaptive entropy thresholding, asymmetry-aware wildcard decoding, and blind-spot re-ranking, validated on M-BEIR.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal retrieval faces information asymmetry between concise text queries and dense visual candidates. This mismatch causes autoregressive decoders to hallucinate and forces the model to guess fine-grained identifiers, degrading ranking quality.
AI.method: Adaptive Entropy Thresholding (AET) calibrates layer-specific uncertainty offline. Asymmetry-aware Wildcard Decoding (AWD) emits wildcards at semantic blind spots to expand the search space without log-probability penalties. Blind-Spot Re-ranking (BSR) combines discrete generation confidence with continuous semantic similarity to re-rank an expanded candidate pool.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the M-BEIR benchmark show WIDE outperforms state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods, effectively suppressing forced hallucination while preserving compact index structures.
AI.conclusion: WIDE addresses information asymmetry in cross-modal generative retrieval and demonstrates robust performance gains with a dynamic, wildcard-based decoding strategy and hybrid re-ranking.

title: Semantic Bayesian World Models
summary: Knowledge graphs describe reality in crisp assertions, while the systems now consuming them, foundation models and autonomous agents, reason natively in probabilities. We argue that this mismatch is why the integration of language models and knowledge graphs remains a data-feeding pipeline rather than a unified reasoning architecture. We envision Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs): a Web that describes the world not as a database of facts but as a shared, evolving fabric of beliefs over knowledge graphs, where ontological axioms constrain priors, observations update beliefs by Bayesian conditioning, and actions intervene upon the world. We work through what an agent gains from such a model: a home-security agent deciding whether the figure at the gate is a courier or a burglar, an actuarial estimate aggregated by entailment rather than by string frequency, a planning task that language models reliably fail, and the estimation of quantities that no document has ever stated. We then set out what the community must build to make them possible: belief annotation over RDF~1.2, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and protocols by which agents that have never met can exchange, and disagree over, calibrated beliefs.

AI.tldr: Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs) treat world knowledge as evolving probabilistic beliefs over RDF/knowledge graphs, updated by Bayesian conditioning, enabling probabilistic reasoning and cross-agent belief exchange.
AI.motivation: There is a mismatch between deterministic knowledge graphs and probabilistic, reasoning-oriented foundation models. A unified reasoning architecture should integrate KG priors, observations, and actions within a probabilistic framework.
AI.method: Propose a framework where beliefs live over RDF 1.2 graphs, priors are constrained by ontological axioms, beliefs are updated by Bayesian conditioning on observations, and actions intervene on the world. Includes agent demonstrations and design goals for exchange protocols.
AI.result: Conceptual framework with illustrative examples (home-security agent, actuarial entailment, planning tasks, unseen quantities) rather than empirical results; outlines the required building blocks.
AI.conclusion: Advocate developing belief annotation over RDF 1.2, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and interoperable belief-exchange protocols to realize SBWMs as unified reasoning architectures.

title: TIGPO: Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Graph-based policy optimization improves credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents by organizing rollout trajectories into state-transition graphs. However, existing methods construct graphs independently within each policy update, discarding transitions discovered by earlier policies and limiting advantage estimation to small, batch-local rollout groups. We propose \emph{Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization} (TIGPO), which extends graph-based credit assignment across policy updates. TIGPO maintains a persistent transition graph for each task, allowing valid transitions discovered by different policy versions to jointly determine credit for current rollouts. To actively reconnect current exploration with historical experience, TIGPO allocates a fixed rollout budget between Exploration slots for ordinary task sampling and Revisit slots for delayed reattempts of previously explored tasks. For each revisit, TIGPO pairs the current rollout group with its corresponding earlier Exploration group to construct a cross-temporal reference. The enlarged reference is designed to stabilize relative advantage estimation under small rollout groups, while comparison on the same task directly captures policy improvement across training stages. Historical transitions and scores serve only as structural and detached statistical references and are never replayed in the policy loss. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.

AI.tldr: TIGPO extends graph-based policy optimization by maintaining a persistent, cross-update transition graph and a dual rollout budget (exploration and revisit) to stabilize credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents.
AI.motivation: Improve credit assignment and leverage long-horizon rollout data by reusing transitions across policy updates; address small batch limitations of existing graph-based methods.
AI.method: Maintain a task-specific persistent transition graph; allocate fixed rollout budget between Exploration slots and Revisit slots; for revisits, pair current rollouts with earlier Exploration data to form cross-temporal references; use enlarged cross-temporal references to stabilize advantage estimation, while historical data serves as structural references not replayed in loss.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on ALFWorld and WebShop shows TIGPO outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.
AI.conclusion: TIGPO enables cross-update credit assignment with cross-temporal references, improving stability and performance on long-horizon tasks without reusing historical data in loss computation.

title: Building Pretraining Data for World Models: An Unreal Engine-Based Pipeline for Action-Conditioned Video Generation
summary: Action-conditioned video models require large-scale visual data paired with control signals that are temporally aligned with the resulting scene transitions. Such supervision is difficult to obtain from ordinary real-world video because the actions that caused each visual change are typically unknown. We present a large-scale synthetic data production pipeline built on Unreal Engine for generating action-conditioned, multi-view video. To accommodate the different execution requirements of real-time physics and high-quality offline rendering, the pipeline executes trajectory generation and final rendering in two stages: Stage I runs real physics in PIE and records per-frame character states, control inputs, and camera states into an intermediate trajectory representation; Stage II replays those trajectories in a new engine process and renders them offline with Movie Render Queue (MRQ). Around this core, we develop a distributed production system with cache-aware task partitioning, node-local slot scheduling, automated scene screening, aesthetic and luminance filtering, partial-output recovery, asynchronous upload, and continuous cluster health monitoring. The production cluster contains 25 servers with eight NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs per server. From 2,384 asset packs, 429 levels were retained for production together with a pool of 40 humanoid characters. The pipeline has produced 2,691 hours of 1080p video and 6,076 hours of 720p video. We describe the system architecture, the implementation decisions that emerged from production failures, and the limitations of using perceptual quality proxies for world-model data curation. The pipeline described in this report constitutes the Unreal Engine synthetic-data production component used in EchoWM.
