title: Adapting to Evolving Requirements: Agentic AI for Retail Supply Chain Operations
summary: Retail supply chain operations rely on coupled decision modules that must adapt as requirements evolve. LLMs offer a natural-language interface for this task, but existing methods primarily focus on individual optimization models. Extending them to heterogeneous decision pipelines is challenging because a requirement may admit multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects. We formulate requirement-driven adaptation as the joint selection of an intervention route and an admissible module-level change, and propose a graph-constrained agentic framework in which domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces and a central processor searches over bounded intervention paths. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs. In collaboration with a large retail partner, we evaluate 100 warehouse requirements elicited from practitioner interviews, with GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek as base LLMs. Relative to direct LLM reformulation, our framework improves correctness and end-to-end success across all three models, raising end-to-end success from 72--76% to 79--83%.

AI.tldr: A graph-constrained agentic framework for requirement-driven adaptation in retail supply chains that jointly selects intervention routes and admissible module changes; demonstrates improved end-to-end success across GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek from 72-76% to 79-83% on 100 warehouse requirements.
AI.motivation: Retail supply chains rely on interdependent decision modules that must adapt to evolving requirements; existing LLM-based approaches address isolated models and struggle with coupled, multi-path interventions; formalize adaptation as joint route and module-change selection and validate via downstream KPIs.
AI.method: Introduce a graph-constrained agentic architecture: domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces; a central processor searches bounded intervention paths; evaluate on 100 warehouse requirements elicited from practitioner interviews; compare GPT, Qwen, DeepSeek as base LLMs against direct reformulation.
AI.result: Our framework outperforms direct LLM reformulation across all three models, increasing end-to-end success from 72-76% to 79-83%; improvements in correctness and end-to-end performance.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively handles heterogeneous decision pipelines and shows practical viability in a real industrial setting; potential for broader application to other coupled decision systems and beyond retail with bounded search for intervention paths.

title: Inferred Generative-Process Diversity Predicts Correlated Failure Across Language Models
summary: Diversity is a widely observed factor in the resilient function of collective systems, yet the type of diversity that matters depends on the properties and failure modes of the system. This distinction is important for systems composed of multiple language models. Different models may be treated as independent components even when their behaviour and failures remain strongly correlated. Assessments of language-model populations using semantic similarity demonstrate limited semantic diversity, but this captures only differences in the meaning of observed outputs. We argue that a more fundamental notion of model diversity is generative-process diversity, the differences between processes capable of generating the observed outputs. Drawing from Algorithmic Information Theory, we use Normalised Compression Distance between raw model outputs, residualised against a permutation control, as a measure of inferred generative-process diversity. Across 38 language models, this measure identifies population structure missed by semantic similarity and predicts cross-task variation in chance-corrected correlated failure among model pairs across ten disjoint benchmark families, beyond semantic similarity and model-pair capability. The cross-benchmark partial rank association is $-0.216$ with a 95% interval of $[-0.309,-0.122]$, and the estimate is negative on all ten benchmarks. These results indicate that increased generative-process diversity is associated with reduced correlated failure in model pairs that is not attributable to semantic similarity or capability. Inferred generative-process diversity offers a novel and practical approach for investigating diversity of multi-model systems in safety-relevant contexts.

AI.tldr: Generative-process diversity, measured by Normalised Compression Distance (NCD) on raw model outputs residualised by permutation control, captures diversity among 38 language-models beyond semantic similarity and capability, and better predicts cross-task correlated failure across ten benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Semantic similarity underestimates the diversity of generative processes in model populations and fails to account for correlated failures in multi-model systems; a process-level diversity measure is needed to improve safety and reliability.
AI.method: Compute NCD on raw outputs across 38 language models, residualised against a permutation control to remove superficial similarities; assess population structure not captured by semantic similarity; evaluate cross-task variation in chance-corrected correlated failure across ten benchmark families; compare with semantic similarity and model-pair capability.
AI.result: NCD-based generative-process diversity reveals population structure missed by semantic similarity and predicts cross-task variation in correlated failure among model pairs across ten benchmarks (partial rank correlation = -0.216, 95% CI [-0.309, -0.122], negative across all benchmarks). This diversity is associated with reduced correlated failure beyond what semantic similarity or capability explain.
AI.conclusion: Inferred generative-process diversity offers a practical framework for studying diversity in multi-model systems in safety-relevant contexts, capturing differences in underlying generative processes that reduce correlated failures not detectable by semantic similarity alone.

title: GraFT: A Training-Free Framework for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models via 3D Scene Graphs
summary: 3D spatial reasoning underpins understanding and acting in the physical world, yet it remains unreliable in current multimodal large language models (MLLMs). These models falter at precise geometric measurement, at transforming between egocentric and allocentric viewpoints, and at grounding fine-grained appearance. The most common remedies fine-tune the model on large-scale curated spatial-reasoning datasets or attach dedicated encoders for 3D geometry, which typically couples the solution to costly supervision and a specific backbone. We instead introduce GraFT, a training-free framework that supplies the missing 3D structure through a compact, easily maintained 3D scene graph (3DSG). From this 3DSG, GraFT provides three spatial reasoning capabilities: (1) deterministic geometry through symbolic tools, (2) allocentric layout through a bird's-eye-view (BEV) rendering, and (3) visual-attribute grounding through task-relevant egocentric frames. On ScanQA, GraFT improves every metric over the same-backbone baseline, raising CIDEr by 27%. On VSI-Bench, GraFT improves frozen MLLMs by up to 65%, surpassing every proprietary and general-purpose open-source baseline, and several prominent fine-tuned spatial models.

AI.tldr: GraFT is a training-free framework that injects 3D structure via a compact 3D scene graph to enable three spatial reasoning abilities in MLLMs, yielding significant gains on ScanQA and VSI-Bench without model fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal LLMs struggle with precise 3D geometry, viewpoint transforms between egocentric and allocentric frames, and fine-grained appearance grounding. Common fixes rely on costly supervision and backbone-specific encoders, tying performance to supervised data or architectural changes. GraFT aims to decouple 3D reasoning from model training by supplying a lightweight 3D context.
AI.method: Provide a compact 3D scene graph (3DSG) as input to frozen MLLMs, enabling (1) deterministic geometry via symbolic tools, (2) allocentric layout through a bird's-eye-view (BEV) rendering, and (3) visual-attribute grounding via task-relevant egocentric frames. The approach is training-free (no fine-tuning or new encoders).
AI.result: On ScanQA, GraFT raises CIDEr by 27% over the same-backbone baseline. On VSI-Bench, it improves frozen MLLMs by up to 65%, surpassing proprietary and general-purpose open-source baselines and several prominent fine-tuned spatial models.
AI.conclusion: A compact 3D scene graph can empower 3D spatial reasoning across LLM backbones without retraining, yielding substantial gains across diverse benchmarks.

title: FlashRender: Few-Step Generative Rendering via Camera-Controlled Video MeanFlow
summary: We present FlashRender, a few-step generative rendering framework that retakes a source video along a target camera trajectory in seconds. We identify sampling-step-dependent camera control as a prominent manifestation of discretization error in existing multi-step generative rendering models and show that resolving this inconsistency substantially lowers denoising trajectory curvature, facilitating subsequent step distillation. To this end, we introduce Representation Transformation and Alignment (RETA), which aligns hidden source-video representations with target-video features from a frozen visual geometry model. This directly encodes the geometric transformation within the source-video stream, enabling sampling-step-consistent camera control. We then fine-tune the model with the MeanFlow objective on the lower-curvature denoising trajectory induced by RETA, allowing the model to more effectively address discretization error. Finally, we apply on-policy flow map distillation to correct self-rollout errors under fixed few-step sampling. Extensive experiments show that RETA, MeanFlow, and on-policy flow map distillation play complementary roles in few-step generative rendering. Together, they enable our approach to match multi-step baselines in video quality and geometric consistency at 25x lower sampling cost while achieving superior camera controllability, even under out-of-distribution target camera trajectories.

AI.tldr: A few-step generative rendering framework (FlashRender) reduces sampling cost by aligning source-video representations to target camera features via RETA, then improves denoising with MeanFlow and on-policy flow map distillation, achieving multi-step-like quality with 25x speedup and robust camera control.
AI.motivation: Discretization error in multi-step generative rendering causes sampling-step-dependent camera control and high denoising trajectory curvature, limiting speed and controllability. A fast, controllable pipeline is needed to retarget a source video to new camera trajectories with high fidelity.
AI.method: Introduce RETA to align hidden source-video representations with target-video features from a frozen geometry model, encoding geometric transformation into the source stream for sampling-step-consistent camera control. Fine-tune with the MeanFlow objective on lower-curvature trajectories. Apply on-policy flow map distillation to correct self-rollout errors under fixed few-step sampling.
AI.result: RETA, MeanFlow, and on-policy flow map distillation collectively enable few-step rendering to match multi-step baselines in video quality and geometric consistency at 25x lower sampling cost, with superior camera controllability and robustness to out-of-distribution trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively mitigates discretization error in few-step generative rendering, offering a practical approach for fast, controllable video retargeting by integrating representation alignment, flow-based denoising optimization, and on-policy distillation.

title: Bioinfoysis Technical Report
summary: Large language model agents have shown promise in bioinformatics, but most existing systems focus primarily on producing final answers, treating planning, tool use, and code execution as transient interactions. This design is poorly suited to long-horizon bioinformatics tasks, where conclusions must remain connected to the data, computations, and intermediate evidence that support them. We introduce \textbf{Bioinfoysis}, a multi-agent harness that represents each request as a persistent, artifact-grounded analysis run. Bioinfoysis combines global planning with step-wise, evidence-driven replanning: the planner maintains an executable checklist and revises pending steps using structured handoffs returned after each worker execution. These handoffs bind intermediate results to their responsible agent, checklist step, and plan generation, preventing stale evidence from being silently reused after replanning. A controlled runtime validates generated scripts, tables, and figures before they are used in downstream analysis or reporting, while role-specific context, persistent memory, and governed bioinformatics skills support reliable execution over long analysis trajectories. We evaluate Bioinfoysis on BixBench and two question-answering tracks of LAB-Bench 2. On BixBench, Bioinfoysis achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 82.4\%. Across four underlying language models, Bioinfoysis increases average accuracy from 27.81\% to 64.13\% on SeqQA2 and from 3.13\% to 31.25\% on DbQA2. These results demonstrate that reliable bioinformatics automation depends not only on model capability, but also on the harness that governs planning, execution, memory, and evidence flow. We hope that the emergence of Bioinfoysis will play a driving and leading role in the development of the bioinformatics community. Our demo website can be seen in https://report.bioinfoysis.com/.

AI.tldr: Bioinfoysis is a multi-agent, artifact-grounded analysis harness for long-horizon bioinformatics tasks that uses persistent analysis runs, executable checklists, and evidence-driven replanning to improve planning, execution, and memory management, achieving state-of-the-art results on BixBench and significant accuracy gains on SeqQA2 and DbQA2 across multiple LLMs.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of long-horizon bioinformatics tasks where conclusions must be traceable to data, computations, and intermediate evidence; conventional LLM agents treat planning and execution as transient interactions, leading to stale evidence and poor reliability.
AI.method: A multi-agent harness where each request becomes a persistent analysis run with global planning and step-wise replanning. It uses an executable checklist, structured handoffs linking results to agents, plan steps, and evidence. A runtime validates generated scripts, tables, and figures. It includes role-specific context, persistent memory, and governed bioinformatics skills to sustain reliable long trajectories.
AI.result: Bioinfoysis achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on BixBench (82.4%). Across four LLMs, it raises SeqQA2 accuracy from 27.81% to 64.13% and DbQA2 accuracy from 3.13% to 31.25%. These gains demonstrate that harness design (planning, execution, memory, evidence flow) is critical for reliable bioinformatics automation.
AI.conclusion: The work highlights the importance of governance of planning, execution, memory, and evidence flow in AI-assisted bioinformatics. It suggests Bioinfoysis can catalyze progress in the field and provides a scalable demo and toolkit for future long-horizon analysis.

title: TraveL: Transformer-based Multi-view Path Distributional Representation Learning
summary: Path representation learning (PRL) for road networks has received increasing research attention, due to various path-related applications. Existing works on PRL typically exploit the co-occurrence relationship among road segments and paths to learn a vector as the path representation, without exploring the varied traveler behaviors and the regional correlation on the path. In this work, we propose to learn distributional representations, which provide valuable information for use in path-related applications, by capturing the varied traveler behaviors as well as the various dependencies within regions of road segments. We propose a novel Transformer-based Multi-view Distributional Representation Learning (TraveL) framework to encode a path along with a travel starting time to a distributional representation, which can be used to decode possible samples of on-path traveler behavior. Moreover, by analyzing the regional correlation which reveals various road segment relationships, we propose a regional attention to encode these correlations in a path. Also, we explore the idea of Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test to compare the sampled traveler behavior against the collected ground truth to facilitate training. Experimental results show that the proposed TraveL model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets, by 14.7% in Mean K-S distance for travel time distribution estimation, 16.7% in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for path similarity prediction, and 3.97% in MAE for destination prediction.

AI.tldr: Introduces TraveL, a Transformer-based framework that learns distributional path representations from road networks by modeling travel-time behavior and regional dependencies, using KS-based training, and achieving state-of-the-art gains on multiple tasks.
AI.motivation: To capture diverse traveler behaviors and regional correlations in road networks beyond co-occurrence-based path embeddings, enabling distributional representations for downstream tasks.
AI.method: A Transformer-based multi-view architecture (TraveL) encodes a path and starting time into a distributional representation; regional attention captures regional road segment correlations; training uses Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test to compare sampled traveler behavior with ground truth.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real-world data: ~14.7% improvement in Mean K-S distance for travel time distribution estimation, ~16.7% improvement in MAE for path similarity prediction, ~3.97% improvement in MAE for destination prediction.
AI.conclusion: TraveL provides distributional path representations that reflect traveler variability and regionalstructure, improving multiple downstream tasks and demonstrating effectiveness across data regimes.

title: Catalogue Photography as a Cold Start: Toward Deployable Carbide Burr Recognition
comment: Extended abstract not yet published to a conference or journal
summary: Verifying that manufactured batches of milling tools or carbide rotary burrs conform to production order sheets remains a largely manual and error-prone quality assurance task. Automating this process with computer vision faces a critical cold-start constraint since no labelled imagery is available, leaving manufacturer catalogue photography as the sole source of supervision. We investigate how far catalogue supervision can support an industrial recognition pipeline under domain shift, explicitly measuring the gap between catalogue separability and performance on held-out field photographs. Our findings reveal three key insights. First, off-the-shelf frozen feature extractors do not reliably separate the two task attributes, head shape and tooth profile, motivating targeted representation learning. Second, metric learning produces near-perfect unsupervised cluster discovery on catalogue images (adjusted Rand index 0.94--0.97), but less than half of this gain transfers to field photographs. Third, the largest transfer gains do not come from model scale or representation complexity, but from simple changes that reduce domain sensitivity: converting images to grayscale (+0.22) and constraining retrieval using the known order sheet via Hungarian assignment (+0.11). We therefore treat catalogue photography as a useful cold start rather than a deployment-ready training domain, and provide empirical baselines and an evaluation protocol for catalogue-to-field transfer in precision tool manufacturing.

AI.tldr: Catalogue supervision can bootstrap an industrial recognition pipeline under domain shift but provides limited transfer to field data; gains stem from simple domain adaptations rather than larger models.
AI.motivation: Automate QA for manufactured tool batches with scarce labeled field data; quantify the gap between catalogue-based separability and real-world performance; establish a baseline for catalogue-to-field transfer in precision tooling.
AI.method: Assess pre-trained feature extractors; apply metric learning to catalogue images to enable unsupervised clustering; evaluate transfer to field photographs; examine domain shift mitigation via grayscale conversion and retrieval constraints using Hungarian assignment; propose evaluation protocol for catalogue-to-field transfer.
AI.result: Frozen features fail to reliably separate head shape vs tooth profile; metric learning enables near-perfect unsupervised clustering on catalogue images (adjusted Rand index ~0.94–0.97) but transfers to field data are substantially weaker (less than 50%). Largest transfer gains come from simple adjustments: grayscale conversion (+0.22) and constrained retrieval via known order sheet with Hungarian assignment (+0.11). Catalogue imagery should be treated as a useful cold start, not deployment-ready; the work provides baselines and an evaluation protocol for catalogue-to-field transfer in precision tooling.
AI.conclusion: Catalogue imagery offers valuable cold-start supervision for precision-tool QA under domain shift but requires targeted representation learning and careful evaluation to achieve deployment-ready performance; simple domain-robustness tweaks can outperform scaling in transfer efficacy.

title: Occlusion-Robust Multimodal Emotion Recognition in VR via Fusion of Facial Images and EMG
comment: Joint Proceedings of the ACM Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI) Workshops 2026
summary: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) fundamentally limit emotion recognition in virtual reality (VR): by occluding the upper face, they render conventional image-based facial expression analysis incomplete, particularly for applications requiring real-time affective assessment. We address this challenge by fusing lower-face video with facial electromyography (EMG) from the occluded upper face to classify seven emotional categories (six basic emotions plus neutral). We introduce a synchronized multimodal dataset from 20 participants, pairing lower-face video with seven-channel upper-face EMG elicited by validated emotion stimuli. Under subject-independent test, our proposed late-fusion architecture merging convolutional visual embeddings with RBF-kernel EMG representations achieves 51% macro-F1, outperforming both image-only (41%) and EMG-only (43%) baselines. These results demonstrate that upper-face EMG provides robust complementary information under HMD-induced visual occlusion and establish a foundation for multimodal emotion recognition in naturalistic VR environments. This approach facilitates affect-adaptive applications, including communication training and therapeutic interventions. The dataset will be shared upon request under an ethical-use agreement.

AI.tldr: Late-fusion multimodal emotion recognition in VR using synchronized lower-face video and upper-face EMG yields 51% macro-F1 (7 emotions) in subject-independent tests, outperforming image-only (41%) and EMG-only (43%) baselines; dataset from 20 participants, shared upon ethical-use request.
AI.motivation: HMDs occlude the upper face, hindering conventional image-based emotion recognition. Integrating EMG from the occluded region with lower-face video provides complementary cues for real-time affective assessment in VR.
AI.method: A synchronized multimodal dataset (20 participants) pairing lower-face video with seven-channel upper-face EMG. A late-fusion architecture merges CNN-based visual embeddings with RBF-kernel EMG representations. Subject-independent evaluation.
AI.result: Achieves 51% macro-F1 on seven emotion categories (six basic emotions + neutral), outperforming image-only (41%) and EMG-only (43%) baselines.
AI.conclusion: Upper-face EMG delivers robust complementary information under HMD occlusion, enabling multimodal emotion recognition in naturalistic VR; supports affect-adaptive applications and training/therapy; dataset available on request under an ethical-use agreement.

title: STAIR (STructure Aware Information Retriever): A novel dataset and LLM based retriever for document structure augmentation
summary: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a key component for generating accurate and hallucination free answers using Large Language Models (LLMs). LLMs are improving at handling long context, but still suffer from "lost in the middle" problem. Thus, precise and accurate retrieval is important. Current retrievers chunk long context into length-based manageable chunks - in the process throwing away rich and informative semantic global structure in the corpus. We introduce a novel retrieval system STAIR that empowers an LLM to exploit global structure in a corpus such as a Table of Contents (ToC) to efficiently store and retrieve information from its model parameters. Our thorough and careful ablation studies with a finetuned Differentiable Search Index (DSI) system show that ToC helps build a low hallucination (less than 0.05%) generative Information Retrieval (IR) system and can generalize to examples where very few training samples are available. To further research in this novel direction of ToC based retrieval we release SearchTome - a diverse benchmark created from 18 books across 6 diverse domains to further research in this novel direction. STAIR achieves a high Recall@1 score of 82.6% on SearchTome as compared to DSI (76.9%), where the difference is found to be statistically significant. STAIR easily beats other strong baselines such as BM25 (59.5%), DPR (68.7%) and out-of-the-box Mistral (13.8%).

AI.tldr: STAIR uses a Table-of-Contents (ToC) global-structure retrieval with a Differentiable Search Index (DSI) to store/retrieve information in LLM parameters, enabling low-hallucination generative IR and strong retrieval performance on a new SearchTome benchmark; outperforms BM25, DPR, and Mistral.
AI.motivation: Mitigate the 'lost in the middle' problem in retrieval for RAG by preserving global, semantic structure of the corpus instead of only local, chunk-based representations; reduce hallucinations and improve generalization, including few-shot scenarios.
AI.method: Propose STAIR framework that leverages ToC as a global corpus structure and finetunes a Differentiable Search Index (DSI). Conduct extensive ablations. Create SearchTome, a benchmark from 18 books across 6 domains, to study ToC-based retrieval.
AI.result: STAIR achieves Recall@1 of 82.6% on SearchTome (DSI: 76.9%; p<0.05). It achieves extremely low hallucination (<0.05%). Outperforms BM25 (59.5%), DPR (68.7%), and Mistral (13.8%) in out-of-the-box settings. The approach generalizes well with limited training data.
AI.conclusion: ToC-based retrieval is a promising direction for low-hallucination, high-precision IR in RAG systems. The STAIR pipeline, together with the SearchTome benchmark, provides a strong foundation for exploring global-structure retrieval and few-shot generalization.

title: It's the Problem, Not the Path: Budget and Difficulty Confounds in LLM Reasoning Trajectories
comment: 25 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables. Also available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22261107. Code and pre-registered protocols: https://github.com/bulutyigit/problem-not-path
summary: Reasoning traces of large language models are widely read as containing "breakthrough" moments and early-legible fates. Both readings rest on measurements missing a counterfactual control at the level of the claim; we supply both controls. First, a restart-controlled truncation probe separates when a solution fits the continuation budget from when a prefix carries value that fresh computation cannot buy, comparing per-anchor continuation solve rates against from-scratch restart curves at matched total generated-token budget. Applied to 178 problem-model cells (89 MATH problems x two small open models, an outcome-blind but difficulty-targeted cohort), exactly 1 of 178 cells survives as prefix-limited; restart dose-response separates a compute-starved model from a capability-limited one; and wherever the matched budget lies inside the restart grid, continuing the model's own prefix beats restarting (9 of 9) -- predominantly compute compression rather than expanded reachability. Second, a pre-registered, difficulty-controlled test finds no detectable outcome information in early-window internal signals beyond a problem-difficulty baseline, and two generation-free analyses of public corpora show why this control is needed: a trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches AUROC 0.873 on 192K DeepSeek-R1 generations -- inside the published probe range -- and a closely matched reconstruction of the closest published early-window positive recovers a comparable pooled result (0.849) while within problem it is statistically indistinguishable from chance at all ten anchors (0.496 at t=4); a post-hoc within-targeted probe finds only a small average residual, concentrated in three low-failure problems. High pooled probe AUROCs cannot by themselves establish within-attempt information; a question-only baseline or within-problem evaluation is required.

AI.tldr: Two counterfactual controls cast doubt on early internal reasoning signals in LLMs: continuation-contest via restart budgets and difficulty-controlled probes show that many observed signals do not reflect deployable, within-attempt information; continuing prefixes often under perceived budgets does not outperform restart, and high AUROCs can emerge from baselines rather than genuine reasoning.
AI.motivation: To test whether claimed early 'breakthrough' reasoning signals in LLMs reflect true internal capabilities or are artifacts of evaluation design; provide counterfactual controls at the level of the claim to distinguish continuation from restarting and to separate problem difficulty from signal leakage.
AI.method: 1) Restart-controlled truncation probe across 178 problem-model cells (89 MATH problems × two small open models) comparing per-anchor continuation solve rates to from-scratch restart curves at matched token budgets; 2) pre-registered, difficulty-controlled test to detect outcome information in early-window internal signals; 3) generation-free analyses of public corpora (trace-blind difficulty proxy AUROC on 192K DeepSeek-R1 generations; reconstruction of closest published early-window positive); 4) post-hoc within-targeted probe to assess residual signals.
AI.result: Only 1 of 178 cells is prefix-limited under restart control; when budgets lie within the restart grid, continuing the model's own prefix beats restarting (9/9) — indicating compute compression rather than expanded reachability. The difficulty-controlled test finds no detectable outcome information in early signals beyond a problem-difficulty baseline. Public-corpus analyses show that high AUROCs can arise from difficulty proxies (AUROC ≈ 0.87–0.85) and that sharp early-window positives collapse to chance within-problem anchors (0.496 at t=4); a post-hoc probe reveals only small residuals in a few low-failure problems.
AI.conclusion: High pooled probe AUROCs do not establish within-attempt information without proper controls; a question-only baseline or within-problem evaluation is essential. The results argue against widespread, early, deployable reasoning traces and emphasize rigorous counterfactuals to validate claims about LLM reasoning capabilities.

title: Subspace Inference Enables Efficient Active Reward Learning from Preferences
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a powerful yet sample-inefficient approach for learning reward models from human preferences, making active learning a critical component in synthesizing informative preference queries. However, effective uncertainty quantification required for active learning remains a key challenge for large neural network reward models. In this paper, we introduce PreferenceEKF, a sample-efficient approach that tracks reward model uncertainty by framing active preference learning as a sequential Bayesian filtering problem. Instead of relying on computationally prohibitive posterior inference over the full neural network parameter space, our method performs sequential inference via an extended Kalman filter within a low-dimensional parameter subspace, continuously updating the reward model posterior as new preference queries arrive. Our approach enables scalable sampling of neural network parameters to efficiently compute acquisition functions for active reward learning. Experiments on the D4RL and V-D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves better sample efficiency, runtime, scalability, and calibration compared to other Bayesian deep learning approaches, and the learned reward models lead to competitive offline reinforcement learning policy performance. This highlights the potential of scalable Bayesian methods for preference-based reward modeling in RLHF. Our code is available at https://github.com/yutaizhou/bnn_pref.

AI.tldr: PreferenceEKF uses an extended Kalman filter in a low-dimensional subspace to sequentially update a reward model's posterior from human preferences, enabling scalable, sample-efficient active learning in RLHF.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification for active learning with large neural network reward models is sample-inefficient and computationally challenging; scalable Bayesian methods are needed.
AI.method: Frame active preference learning as sequential Bayesian filtering. Apply an extended Kalman filter within a low-dimensional parameter subspace to update the reward-model posterior as each new preference arrives, enabling efficient sampling of neural-network parameters to compute acquisition functions.
AI.result: Outperforms other Bayesian DL approaches in sample efficiency, runtime, scalability, and calibration on D4RL and V-D4RL; achieves competitive offline policy performance.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of scalable Bayesian methods for preference-based reward modeling in RLHF; code released.

title: Drive-HWM: Hierarchical World Models for Dynamic-Latent Guided Autonomous Driving
summary: World models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by predicting how traffic scenes may evolve and using such predictions to support action generation. However, existing approaches either separate future prediction from action generation or jointly predict them at the same temporal scale, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve long-horizon anticipation and responsive, observation-grounded decision making. We present Drive-HWM, a hierarchical slow--fast world modeling framework that organizes future representation prediction and action generation at complementary temporal scales. The slow world model predicts multi-step future representations to capture extended scene evolution. To explicitly model the abundant motion dynamics in driving environments, we introduce Dynamic-Aware Latents learned through optical-flow prediction. Guided by these future representations, the fast model uses a lightweight multimodal backbone and an autoregressive expert to jointly predict the next frame and the immediate action from the latest observation. Next-frame prediction encourages the fast model to capture imminent scene evolution, while one-step action generation allows decisions to be continuously updated as new observations arrive. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 demonstrate the strong driving performance of Drive-HWM. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the hierarchical slow--fast design, dynamics-aware future representations, and joint next-frame and action prediction.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical slow–fast world model Drive-HWM combines long-horizon future representations with fast next-frame and action prediction, using dynamics-aware latents via optical flow; validated on NAVSIM with ablations.
AI.motivation: To resolve the trade-off between long-horizon scene anticipation and responsive, observation-grounded decision making in autonomous driving by separating temporal scales.
AI.method: A two-level architecture: a slow world model predicting multi-step future representations (including dynamics-aware latents learned from optical flow) and a fast model with a lightweight backbone and autoregressive expert that jointly predicts the next frame and the immediate action from the latest observation; one-step action updates enable continuous adaptation.
AI.result: Strong driving performance on NAVSIM v1 and v2; ablation studies confirm benefits of the hierarchical slow–fast design, dynamics-aware representations, and joint next-frame and action prediction.
AI.conclusion: Drive-HWM effectively balances long-horizon anticipation with real-time decision-making, with empirical validation; demonstrates the value of hierarchical temporal modeling and dynamics-aware latent representations for autonomous driving.

title: Xiaomi-TabLDM: A Tabular Foundation Model Technical Report
summary:
We introduce Xiaomi-TabLDM, a tabular large data foundation model for classification and regression via in-context learning, which delivers superior prediction accuracy without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Pretrained exclusively on synthetic data generated from structural causal models (SCMs), our model enables more flexible context utilization and more efficient capacity scaling.
  i) A new performance standard. Strong regression performance across benchmarks: Xiaomi-TabLDM ranks 1st on OpenML-CTR23 and 2nd on regression across TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO, demonstrating consistently strong regression performance across four complementary benchmark suites. Favorable performance--efficiency trade-off: Xiaomi-TabLDM combines strong predictive performance with substantially lower computational cost. For example, on TabArena regression, it achieves the second-highest Elo while using 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than the top-ranked TabFM.
  ii) Large-scale synthetic pretraining. Xiaomi-TabLDM expands the coverage and diversity of synthetic tabular data used for pretraining. We also adopt a three-stage training strategy together with dual-stream feature grouping, lightweight Attention Residual, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts, enabling Xiaomi-TabLDM to learn richer feature interactions and expert specialization across diverse tabular tasks.
  iii) Test-time scaling. Xiaomi-TabLDM further extends tabular prediction through test-time compute scaling, where allocating additional computation at inference time consistently improves predictive performance over the base model.

AI.tldr: Xiaomi-TabLDM is a tabular foundation model pretrained on synthetic SCM data, enabling strong in-context learning for classification and regression with test-time scaling and improved efficiency, achieving top performance on OpenML-CTR23 and competitive results across multiple tabular benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To deliver accurate tabular predictions without task-specific fine-tuning by leveraging synthetic data from structural causal models, enabling flexible context use and scalable capacity.
AI.method: Three-stage training with dual-stream feature grouping, lightweight Attention Residual, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts; pretraining exclusively on synthetic data from SCMs; in-context learning for classification/regression; test-time compute scaling to improve predictions.
AI.result: Strong regression performance: 1st on OpenML-CTR23; 2nd on regression across TALENT, TabArena, BCCO; consistent strength across four benchmark suites; favorable efficiency: on TabArena regression, second-highest Elo with 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than the top-ranked TabFM.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic SCM-based pretraining expands data coverage and, with test-time scaling, yields strong, efficient tabular prediction without task-specific fine-tuning.

title: Guide, Not Bind: Why Defeasible Priors Fail in Augmented Lagrangian Causal Discovery
summary: Differentiable causal discovery methods increasingly encode expert priors as forbidden-edge constraints enforced by an Augmented Lagrangian (ALM) penalty, on the assumption that a data-adaptive relaxation mechanism will discount and eventually override a rule the data consistently contradicts. We show this design, which we call \emph{guide, not bind}, fails for two independent, precisely characterized reasons, and that directly repairing both restores it only partially. First, sequential penalty-ramping ALM suppresses a wrongly-forbidden true edge before any counterfactual check can detect it: we give three necessary conditions any adaptive relaxation must satisfy to avoid this (Proposition~\ref{prop:conditions}), prove that DADU---the natural relaxation rule this paper introduces as the object of study---violates all three (Corollary~\ref{cor:dadu_failure}), and confirm the failure across 3{,}072 training runs spanning graphs from 4 to 32 nodes, where a single wrong prior suppresses a true edge in 87--97\% of trials under DADU. Second, and independent of any fix to the mechanism, we prove in closed form that the standard correlation-matching objective ties a true edge and its reverse to an identical cost of exactly $2r^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tie}), not because the underlying equal-variance model is unidentifiable, but because normalizing to correlation discards exactly the variance information that would make it identifiable; covariance matching instead separates the two directions by a provable margin of at least $w_0^4$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:separation}).

AI.tldr: The abstract critiques differentiable causal discovery with ALM-based enforcement of expert priors (forbidden edges) via a 'guide, not bind' approach, showing two independent failures: (1) the DADU relaxation can suppress a true edge before counterfactual checks with three necessary conditions violated; empirical validation across 3,072 runs (4–32 nodes) shows 87–97% suppression by a single wrong prior; (2) correlation-matching collapses a true edge and its reverse to identical cost 2r^2 due to loss of variance information, while covariance matching separates directions by at least w0^4. The repairs restore only partially; overall, the proposed fixes are insufficient without a covariance-aware objective.
AI.motivation: To assess the reliability and fundamental limits of using adaptive relaxation to encode expert priors in differentiable causal discovery and to identify mechanisms that prevent correct causal edge recovery.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of adaptive relaxation for forbidden-edge priors (DADU). Proves three necessary conditions for safe relaxation (Proposition). Demonstrates DADU violation (Corollary). Closed-form proofs regarding correlation-matching vs covariance-matching (Lemma on tie; Lemma on separation). Extensive empirical validation across 3,072 training runs on graphs with 4–32 nodes to measure suppression of true edges.
AI.result: DADU fails under all three necessary conditions. On average, a single wrong prior suppresses a true edge in 87–97% of trials. The standard correlation-matching objective ties a true edge and its reverse with equal cost (2r^2). Covariance matching resolves this with a provable separation margin of at least w0^4.
AI.conclusion: The 'guide, not bind' approach is fundamentally flawed for reliable causal discovery with priors. Even with repair, the issues persist partially; a covariance-aware objective or alternative priors are needed to avoid identifiability loss and to prevent wrongful suppression of true edges.

title: Continuous Actions from Discrete Minds: Latent-Aligned Planning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Bridging the gap between the discrete reasoning of Vision-Language Models and the continuous, physics-constrained nature of autonomous driving remains a significant challenge. In this work, we introduce LaPla, a unified Vision-Language-Action (VLA) framework featuring latent-aligned planning to seamlessly ground semantic understanding in precise motion execution. We first design an action tokenizer based on a residual vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE), capturing vehicle kinematics and encoding trajectory features into a structured latent space. Rather than discrete codebook lookups that inevitably introduce quantization errors, LaPla repurposes this representation as a physical prior to bridge the modality gap between high-dimensional semantics and the raw action space. Specifically, given multimodal inputs integrating multi-view images, historical actions, and textual instructions, LaPla incorporates concurrent action queries to causally attend to the multimodal context in a single forward pass, projecting hidden states directly into the pretrained VQ-VAE latent space. The frozen decoder then translates these continuous latents into actions, effectively eliminating quantization errors and ensuring physically plausible trajectories while bypassing time-consuming autoregressive generation. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that LaPla achieves competitive open-loop performance, reducing long-horizon L2 error by 15.52% compared to state-of-the-art VLA methods. Closed-loop evaluations on the NVIDIA AlpaSim simulator further confirm its superior capability in ensuring smooth driving progress, improving the success rate by 33.34 percentage points with significantly reduced inference latency.

AI.tldr: LaPla introduces a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that uses a residual vector-quantized VQ-VAE-based action tokenizer to map multimodal inputs to a continuous latent space and a frozen decoder to generate physically plausible actions, achieving improved open-loop and closed-loop driving performance with lower latency.
AI.motivation: Disparate discrete reasoning in Vision-Language models clashes with the continuous, physics-constrained nature of autonomous driving. Quantization in discrete codebooks and autoregressive generation introduce errors and latency; a continuous latent space can better ground semantics into executable motion.
AI.method: Design a residual vector-quantized VQ-VAE-based action tokenizer to encode trajectory features into a structured latent space. Use multimodal inputs (multi-view images, historical actions, text) with concurrent action queries that attend to context and project hidden states directly into the pretrained VQ-VAE latent space. A frozen decoder translates these continuous latents into actions, bypassing quantization errors and autoregressive generation. Evaluate open-loop on nuScenes and closed-loop on NVIDIA AlpaSim.
AI.result: LaPla achieves competitive open-loop performance with a 15.52% reduction in long-horizon L2 error over state-of-the-art VLA methods. In closed-loop simulations, it improves driving success rate by 33.34 percentage points and reduces inference latency, demonstrating smoother progress and efficient inference.
AI.conclusion: Latent-aligned planning with a VQ-VAE-based action tokenizer enables effective grounding of semantic signals into continuous, physically plausible actions, bridging the modality gap between vision-language representations and motion execution while delivering both accuracy and efficiency gains.

title: Text2Thermal: Physics-Aware Thermal Image Synthesis from Textual Priors
summary: Thermal infrared imaging offers reliable perception in darkness and adverse weather, but thermal datasets remain scarce, motivating extensive work on translating abundant RGB images into thermal. Such translation is fundamentally ill-posed as thermal appearance is governed by surface emissivity and object temperature, neither of which is observable in the visible spectrum, so a single RGB image is consistent with many valid thermal outputs. We argue that language offers a natural means of resolving this ambiguity, and propose Text2Thermal, a framework for physics-aware thermal image synthesis from textual priors. Rather than inferring the unobservable radiometric factors from RGB, we supply them explicitly through thermally grounded captions encoding material, weather, time-of-day, and heat-emission state, and adapt a pretrained Stable Diffusion backbone to the thermal domain. Because the radiometric content is determined entirely by the prompt, Text2Thermal synthesizes thermal imagery without requiring a registered RGB image at inference; where spatial guidance is desired, an optional control signal imparts scene geometry without disturbing the prompt-specified radiometry. Experiments on M3FD, FLIR, and FMB show that Text2Thermal achieves state-of-the-art FID among thermal image synthesis methods while offering text-level control that translation-based approaches cannot provide.

AI.tldr: Text2Thermal: language-guided, physics-aware thermal image synthesis that uses textual priors to specify material, weather, time-of-day, and heat-emission state, enabling RGB-free inference and controllable radiometry; achieves state-of-the-art FID on thermal datasets by adapting Stable Diffusion to the thermal domain.
AI.motivation: Thermal datasets are scarce and RGB-to-thermal translation is ill-posed because emissivity and temperature are not observable in RGB; language offers a natural mechanism to disambiguate radiometric content.
AI.method: Supply radiometric content through thermally grounded captions encoded in prompts and adapt a pretrained Stable Diffusion backbone to the thermal domain; radiometric factors are prompt-driven, enabling RGB-free inference; optional control signal for scene geometry to guide spatial structure without altering radiometry.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art FID among thermal image synthesis methods on M3FD, FLIR, and FMB datasets; provides text-level control unavailable to translation-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Language-conditioned, physics-aware synthesis can overcome RGB-thermal ambiguity without paired RGB-thermal data, enabling controllable and realistic thermal imagery; dataset generation and downstream tasks may benefit from such controllable synthesis.

title: Inferring Affective Consciousness in an Artificial Agent: A Case Study
summary: Creatures that display 'hedonic place preference behaviour' are thought by many scientists to experience feelings, on the assumption that their attraction to pleasure-producing substances which lack nutritional value (e.g. cocaine, morphine) cannot easily be attributed to unconscious instinctual behaviour. In this paper, we discuss how a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system engaging in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources can similarly display hedonic place preference behaviour -- through an apparently subjective form of information processing -- while simultaneously being entirely deter-ministic. We outline some implications of this artificially engineered behaviour for our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will.

AI.tldr: A deterministic artificial agent with an affective system can exhibit hedonic place preference-like behavior, suggesting subjective processing without consciousness; implications for consciousness and free will.
AI.motivation: Examine whether hedonic (pleasure-seeking) behaviors require conscious feelings and how deterministic systems could mimic such behavior, informing the debate on the physical basis of consciousness and free will.
AI.method: A theoretical/modeling argument describing a simple artificial agent endowed with an affective architecture that experiences felt uncertainty about intrinsic needs versus environmental resources; shows hedonic-place preference-like behavior arising from information processing.
AI.result: The agent demonstrates hedonic place preference behavior while remaining fully deterministic, via apparently subjective information processing, challenging the necessity of conscious experience for such behavior.
AI.conclusion: If hedonic preferences can emerge in deterministic systems with affective-like processing, this bears on the physical basis of consciousness and the nature of perceived free will, suggesting that subjective experience may be separable from ontological determinism in certain architectures.

title: Beyond Straightness: Non-Crossing Flow Matching via Quantile AlignTree Coupling
summary: The performance of Flow Matching largely depends on the quality of the coupling between the source and target distributions. However, independent coupling often leads to path crossings and local velocity ambiguity, while OT-based couplings typically incur high construction costs. To address this challenge, we propose Quantile AlignTree Flow Matching (QAT-FM), an efficient structured coupling strategy that constructs a hierarchical coupling between a Gaussian prior and the target data distribution via a quantile-aligned tree structure. QAT-FM constructs the coupling in $\mathcal{O}(Nd\log N)$ time and supports per-pair source sampling with $\mathcal{O}(d)$ complexity, enabling scalable training for large-scale high-dimensional generative tasks. Theoretically, we prove that the QAT coupling satisfies marginal consistency, induces non-crossing linear interpolation paths, and consistently improves path separation at intermediate times compared with independent coupling, thereby alleviating local velocity ambiguity. QAT-FM further extends naturally to conditional generation, enabling structured conditional coupling while preserving global Gaussian alignment. Experiments across diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that QAT-FM achieves competitive generative performance while substantially reducing coupling construction cost.

AI.tldr: Proposes Quantile AlignTree Flow Matching (QAT-FM), a hierarchical, quantile-aligned coupling between a Gaussian prior and the target distribution that enables efficient coupling construction and scalable sampling.
AI.motivation: To address path crossing and velocity ambiguity from independent couplings and high cost of OT-based couplings, enabling scalable, high-dimensional flow-based generative models.
AI.method: Constructs a hierarchical, quantile-aligned tree that couples Gaussian priors to target data in O(N d log N) time; per-pair source sampling costs O(d); proves marginal consistency, non-crossing interpolation paths, and improved path separation; extends naturally to conditional generation.
AI.result: Theoretical guarantees established and experiments show competitive generative performance with substantially reduced coupling construction cost.
AI.conclusion: QAT-FM delivers an efficient, scalable structured coupling that reduces local velocity ambiguity, supports conditional generation, and maintains competitive generation quality while lowering computational cost.

title: A Low-Cost, Open Platform for End-to-End Autonomous Driving on a Miniature Ackermann Vehicle
summary: This paper presents a low-cost, open experimental platform for research in end-to-end autonomous driving with miniature Ackermann vehicles. The platform combines a physical vehicle, a printed urban track, data collection tools, trajectory registration, and a Webots digital twin, enabling controlled experiments that connect simulation-based autonomous-driving methods to real-world execution. As a first baseline, we implement command-conditioned behavior cloning, in which a neural policy receives an on-board camera image and a high-level navigation command and outputs steering and speed. The system is evaluated both on the physical vehicle and in simulation. In real closed-loop experiments, the learned policy follows lanes and executes commanded turns, reaching a mean cross-track error of 6.1 cm with respect to the reference route, close to the 4.7 cm observed in human demonstrations. In the digital twin, camera field of view has a strong effect on performance, reducing the mean cross-track error from 35.6 to 3.3 cm when widened from 58 to 120 degrees. Using the digital twin to generate synthetic driving data and a learned sim-to-real image translator to reduce the appearance gap, we further show that a higher-capacity policy trained on this synthetic data combined with real demonstrations is the only configuration that completes all four track routes in closed loop, whereas the compact baseline and the same network trained on real data alone complete fewer. These results establish the open platform as a practical testbed for sim-to-real studies and provide an initial command-conditioned imitation-learning baseline; we release it to support reproducible research.

title: Lose the Order, Keep the Hierarchy: Deordering HTN Plans
summary: Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning is a powerful planning formalism based on task decomposition. Although most of the literature studied plan generation, comparatively less attention has been paid to post-plan optimization. In particular, plan deordering has been extensively studied in classical planning but remains under-researched in the HTN setting. Plan deordering removes unnecessary ordering constraints between actions in a plan whilst keeping the plan valid. In this paper, we adapt two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning by extending the techniques to account for hierarchical decomposition constraints. We evaluate our proposed approaches on the IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks and we compare them against Optiplan, an HTN planner that generates partially ordered plans directly. Our results show a substantial reduction in number of ordering constraints in both our implementations. Although we also observe a reduction in critical path length, the improvements are less pronounced.

AI.tldr: Adapts two classical plan deordering techniques to HTN planning, reducing ordering constraints in HTN plans; evaluated on IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks against Optiplan; substantial constraint reduction with modest critical-path improvements.
AI.motivation: HTN planning has limited post-plan optimization research, particularly for plan deordering under hierarchical constraints; extending deordering techniques to HTN could improve plan quality and efficiency.
AI.method: Extend two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning to HTN by incorporating hierarchical decomposition constraints; apply to HTN plans and compare with Optiplan; evaluation on IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks.
AI.result: Both implementations achieve substantial reductions in the number of ordering constraints; reductions in critical path length are observed but are less pronounced.
AI.conclusion: Plan deordering is effective for HTN planning, yielding simpler, less constrained partial orders; improvements on critical path length are modest, suggesting room for further enhancement and broader comparisons.

title: A Two-Stage Forecasting System for CPU Workload Prediction in Private Clouds
summary: Accurate cloud resource forecasting is essential for proactive resource provisioning, maintaining Quality of Service (QoS), and reducing operational costs in dynamic cloud environments. The existing forecasting approaches predominantly estimate future CPU workload directly from historical resource traces, which often overlook the relationship between customer service demand and subsequent resource consumption. This study proposes a two-stage integrated forecasting model that explicitly models this dependency by first forecasting customer service requests, expressed as Transactions Per Second (TPS), and subsequently estimating future CPU workload from the TPS forecast. Both the forecasting component and resource prediction component employed the XGBoost model within a cascaded learning architecture, complemented by adaptive online retraining using an expanding-window strategy to address concept drift in continuously evolving cloud workloads. The proposed work was evaluated using real-world traces collected from a private cloud environment comprising ten applications. Experimental results demonstrate robust forecasting performance by achieving Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (SMAPE) below $7\%$ for most applications, with the best-performing application achieving an MAE of $0.7372$, RMSE of $1.1866$, SMAPE of $3.57\%$, and an R2 of $0.9185$. Horizon-wise drift analysis confirmed stable recursive forecasting behavior with controlled error accumulation across a 60-step prediction horizon. Compared with the conventional direct CPU forecasting method, the proposed two-stage integrated model gives improved forecasting robustness, computational efficiency, and interpretability, making it well-suited for proactive resource management and intelligent auto-scaling in cloud computing environments.

AI.tldr: Two-stage integrated forecasting for cloud resources: predict TPS (service requests) first, then estimate CPU workload from TPS using XGBoost in a cascaded model with expanding-window online retraining; shows robustness and interpretability with SMAPE < ~7% for most apps and strong horizon performance.
AI.motivation: Cloud environments require proactive provisioning and QoS; existing methods forecast CPU directly from historical traces and ignore the link between customer demand and resource consumption. Modeling TPS demand first captures the dependency and potentially improves accuracy and responsiveness.
AI.method: Two-stage cascaded learning using XGBoost for both stages. Stage 1 forecasts Transactions Per Second (TPS); Stage 2 uses the TPS forecast to predict future CPU workload. The model employs expanding-window online retraining to handle concept drift in evolving workloads. Evaluation on real traces from ten applications in a private cloud.
AI.result: SMAPE < 7% for most apps; best app metrics: MAE 0.7372, RMSE 1.1866, SMAPE 3.57%, R2 0.9185. Horizon-wise drift analysis shows stable recursive forecasting over a 60-step horizon. Outperforms direct CPU forecasting in robustness, efficiency, and interpretability.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage integrated model effectively captures the TPS-to-CPU dependency, enhancing robustness, interpretability, and efficiency for proactive resource management and auto-scaling in cloud environments.

title: Auditing Patient Privacy in Medical Generative Models: Scalable Memorization Detection with DeepSSIM++
summary: While deep generative models offer new opportunities for medical image synthesis and data sharing, their ability to memorize and reproduce training samples raises serious concerns about patient confidentiality. Detecting such memorization at scale remains challenging: traditional pixel-based metrics are sensitive to generation artifacts, whereas generic embedding-based metrics often lack the anatomical sensitivity required for medical data. To address this challenge, we introduce DeepSSIM++, a self-supervised similarity metric for scalable memorization auditing in medical generative models. By leveraging multi-scale feature aggregation and anatomy-preserving augmentations, DeepSSIM++ learns an embedding space where cosine similarity approximates the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), eliminating the need for exact pixel-level registration. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, DeepSSIM++ achieves an average Macro F1 improvement of 33 percentage points under ideal alignment and 46 percentage points under realistic spatial and intensity perturbations. Furthermore, it accelerates large-scale similarity computation by several orders of magnitude compared with analytical SSIM. By combining anatomical sensitivity and computational efficiency, DeepSSIM++ provides an open-source tool for scalable memorization auditing in medical generative AI. Code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/brAIn-science/DeepSSIM.

AI.tldr: DeepSSIM++ is a self-supervised embedding metric that approximates SSIM for scalable memorization auditing in medical generative models, improving detection performance and computational efficiency, with open-source release.
AI.motivation: Medical image generative models risk memorizing training samples, raising patient privacy concerns. Pixel-based metrics are sensitive to artifacts, while generic embeddings lack anatomical sensitivity; a scalable, anatomy-aware evaluator is needed.
AI.method: Multi-scale feature aggregation with anatomy-preserving augmentations to learn an embedding space where cosine similarity aligns with SSIM, eliminating the need for pixel-level registration.
AI.result: DeepSSIM++ achieves an average Macro F1 improvement of 33 percentage points under ideal alignment and 46 percentage points under realistic perturbations, and computes similarities orders of magnitude faster than analytical SSIM.
AI.conclusion: Anatomically sensitive and computationally efficient memorization auditing tool for medical generative AI, released as open-source.

title: Value-Preserving Architectures for Agentic AI Systems
comment: Accepted to AgenticDev Workshop at ASE 2026
summary: The emergence of agentic AI and LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) presents unprecedented opportunities for automating complex tasks, while simultaneously raising critical concerns about the preservation of fundamental human-centered values, such as privacy, fairness, and safety. Although software engineering has traditionally focused on functional correctness, the adoption of LLMs and AI agents into complex socio-technical systems has intensified the need for responsible software engineering and robust value alignment. In MAS, architectural design decisions, such as coordination mechanisms, communication protocols, and system topologies, play a central role in shaping system behavior and the outcomes they produce. This paper argues that architectural choices influence not only the functionality and performance of MAS but can also promote value-oriented system behavior. Therefore, we investigate how different architectural designs support different human-centered values, discussing the following value-preserving architectural patterns: (i) a privacy-aware architecture with a federated topology, (ii) a distributed architecture to promote pluralism and diversity, and (iii) a guard-agent architecture to detect and mitigate unfairness. Finally, we introduce representative use cases to illustrate the proposed architectures in real-world scenarios. By linking architectural design with human-centered values, this work lays the foundation for a unified set of architectural patterns and guidelines towards the design of trustworthy MAS.

AI.tldr: Value-preserving architectural patterns for multi-agent systems: privacy, pluralism, and fairness guarded by federated, distributed, and guard-agent designs to align MAS with human-centered values.
AI.motivation: The rise of agentic AI and LLM-based MAS raises privacy, fairness, and safety concerns; architectural design strongly influences system behavior and value alignment; need patterns to preserve values.
AI.method: Propose and analyze three architectural patterns, discuss how each supports specific values, provide representative use cases, and argue for a unified pattern library for trustworthy MAS.
AI.result: Three patterns identified: privacy-aware federated topology; distributed architecture promoting pluralism; guard-agent architecture to detect/mitigate unfairness; use cases illustrate applicability; foundation for guidelines.
AI.conclusion: Architectural design is central to value alignment in MAS; the patterns offer practical directions toward trustworthy MAS and motivate future work on a consolidated pattern catalog.

title: Mind the Gap: Robustness Risks in PII Detection Systems
summary:
Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection is a foundational component of data protection infrastructure where missed entities constitute direct privacy and security risks. Although modern PII systems report strong performance on standard benchmarks, we show that these evaluations mask substantial robustness failures under realistic distribution shifts encountered in deployment. Rather than comparing state-of-the-art accuracy, we study how different PII detection paradigms fail under noisy, unstructured, and informal inputs. We construct a stress test benchmark spanning seven categories of natural distribution shift and evaluate representative systems from three widely deployed architectural families: encoder-based NER (SpaCy), rule-based hybrid detection (Presidio), and generative LLM extraction (Qwen2.5-3B).
  All three exhibit significant degradation on out-of-distribution inputs, but with distinct and complementary failure modes. Encoder models primarily fail on unseen surface forms and boundary detection, rule-based systems fail on non-standard formats, and LLMs exhibit entity-type confusion and generation instability. These results show that aggregate benchmark scores obscure deployment-critical weaknesses and that no single architecture is uniformly reliable across PII categories. Motivated by these findings, we propose a hybrid detection pipeline with a QA-driven feedback loop for iterative risk mitigation, and release our benchmark to support OOD-aware evaluation of PII systems.

AI.tldr: PII-detection robustness under distribution shifts is lacking; a hybrid QA-driven pipeline with an open benchmark is proposed to address OOD weaknesses.
AI.motivation: Standard benchmarks mask real-world robustness; deployment involves noisy, unstructured data leading to privacy risks from missed entities.
AI.method: Construct a stress-test benchmark spanning seven natural distribution-shift categories; evaluate encoder-based NER (SpaCy), rule-based hybrid detection (Presidio), and generative LLM extraction (Qwen2.5-3B); analyze failure modes across architectures; propose QA-driven feedback loop and release benchmark.
AI.result: All three architectures degrade on out-of-distribution inputs with distinct failure modes (encoders: unseen forms/boundaries; rule-based: non-standard formats; LLMs: entity-type confusion/generation instability); no single architecture is uniformly reliable across PII categories; aggregated benchmarks mask critical deployment weaknesses.
AI.conclusion: A hybrid detection pipeline with QA-driven feedback mitigates risk; releasing the benchmark enables OOD-aware evaluation and supports improvements across PII-detection paradigms.

title: EraseSAE: Surgical Concept Erasure in Text-to-Video Diffusion Models via Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Recent advances in text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable generative capabilities, yet their reliance on loosely curated training data raises pressing safety and copyright concerns. Concept erasure offers a principled remedy by removing unwanted semantics from pretrained models while preserving remaining concepts. However, existing approaches typically operate at a coarse granularity misaligned with the fine-grained, distributed nature of concept representations, leading to incomplete removal or degraded generation quality. We argue that surgical erasure fundamentally requires intervention at the level of monosemantic features, where each unit encodes a single interpretable concept. To this end, we propose EraseSAE, a novel framework that leverages sparse autoencoders to achieve surgical concept erasure in DiT-based T2V diffusion models via a principled decompose-attribute-erase pipeline. We first introduce the Partitioned Convolutional Sparse Autoencoder, which decomposes dense spatiotemporal activations into disentangled, interpretable sparse features while preserving spatiotemporal coherence. A contrastive attribution mechanism then contrasts activations from paired prompts to isolate concept-specific feature kernels. At inference, timestep-resolved spatiotemporal masks derived from the identified kernels confine erasure to regions where the target concept is active, leaving unrelated content intact. Extensive experiments across diverse diffusion models and concept erasure tasks demonstrate that EraseSAE achieves precise and robust concept removal with minimal quality degradation, substantially outperforming state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/HiDream-ai/EraseSAE.

AI.tldr: Proposes EraseSAE, a surgical concept erasure framework for DiT-based text-to-video diffusion models using sparse autoencoders to decompose activations into monosemantic features, identify concept-specific kernels via contrastive attribution, and apply inference-time, timestep-resolved masks to erase concept regions while preserving remaining content and quality.
AI.motivation: Safety and copyright concerns in T2V diffusion models due to loosely curated training data; existing coarse erasure methods fail to remove fine-grained concepts without harming generation quality. A monosemantic, surgical approach is needed to target individual concepts without collateral damage.
AI.method: Introduce Partitioned Convolutional Sparse Autoencoder to decompose dense spatiotemporal activations into disentangled sparse features while preserving spatiotemporal coherence. Use a contrastive attribution mechanism to compare activations from paired prompts and isolate concept-specific feature kernels. At inference, generate timestep-resolved spatiotemporal masks from the kernels to confine erasure to regions where the target concept is active, leaving unrelated content intact.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations across diverse diffusion models and erasure tasks show precise and robust concept removal with minimal degradation to image/video quality, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. The authors provide code at the project URL.
AI.conclusion: EraseSAE demonstrates that surgical concept erasure is feasible in diffusion-based text-to-video models by operating on monosemantic, kernel-level features, enabling targeted removal with preserved generation quality and broader safety/copyright benefits.

title: Speak for Me: Giving LLMs the Situational Awareness to Participate in a Meeting
summary: In online meeting delegation, LLM agents fail to recognize when to speak. With no structured way to track stances, coverage, and floor, they miss the moments where they should contribute. Prompt-only delegates stay silent on 51.4% of the absent participant's talking opportunities on the AMI corpus. We present CAPA (Collaborative Agent Predictive Architecture), an architecture for online meeting delegation. A Perceiver updates the meeting state from each observed turn. A Predictor forecasts how the conversation will continue. A Controller decides whether to speak and which proposition to surface. A Generator phrases the chosen contribution in the participant's style. Two judges score the forecast and the action against the next observed turn. A Recalibrator updates the meeting state from those verdicts for future decisions. To evaluate online delegation, we introduce an episode-level protocol that scores whether, when, and what a delegate contributes around the participant's actual idea units. The protocol's schema-constrained LLM judges align with human annotations at Cohen's kappa = 0.71. On 137 AMI meetings, CAPA reduces the silence rate from 51.4% to 2.5%, doubles credited recovery (26.1 --> 52.2), and keeps hallucination at 0.6%. The failure mode shifts from omission to selection, with each residual near-miss attributable to a specific module of the architecture. Mechanism ablations identify the meeting state as the lever that closes the recognition gap, where raw-context scaling alone does not.

AI.tldr: CAPA is a modular architecture that turns LLMs into effective online meeting delegates by stateful update, prediction, control, and generation, achieving strong evaluation and large reductions in silence.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in online meetings fail to recognize when to speak due to the lack of structured tracking of stances, coverage, and floor; on AMI data, prompt-only delegates are silent in 51.4% of opportunities.
AI.method: A Perceiver updates meeting state from observed turns; a Predictor forecasts how the conversation will continue; a Controller decides whether to speak and which proposition to surface; a Generator phrases the chosen contribution in the participant's style; two judges score the forecast and action against the next observed turn; a Recalibrator updates the meeting state from those verdicts; an episode-level protocol evaluates whether, when, and what is contributed; schema-constrained LLM judges align with human annotations (kappa=0.71).
AI.result: On 137 AMI meetings, CAPA reduces silence from 51.4% to 2.5%, doubles credited recovery (26.1% to 52.2%), and keeps hallucination at 0.6%; residual errors are due to module-specific issues with a shift from omission to selection; mechanism ablations show meeting state as the key lever.
AI.conclusion: The meeting state is the primary lever to close the recognition gap; raw-context scaling alone is insufficient; the CAPA architecture enables accurate online delegation with robust evaluation and manageable failure modes.

title: Spectral characteristics of autoencoder parameters as a vector representation of data
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures. This is a shortened (theorem proofs are skipped) and translated version of the paper published in a Russian-language peer-reviewed journal, the citation is in the paper footnote
summary: This paper examines the relationship between the parameters of autoencoder models and the statistical properties of the data on which they are trained. Autoencoders are defined as models with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained to reconstruct input data through a compressed latent representation. It is proposed that the model parameters can be viewed as a dense vector representation of the corresponding sample. To test this hypothesis, a theoretical and experimental study is conducted in which a vector representation is formed based on the spectral characteristics of the autoencoder parameter matrices. Theoretical analysis shows that the singular values of the model parameter matrices are related to the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the training data, ensuring the transfer of information between the data space and the parameter space. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and FashionMNIST datasets confirm that the resulting vector representations allow for a high degree of accuracy in distinguishing between models trained on different data subsets, without resorting to complex vector generation algorithms or using the original samples. These results suggest that the parameters of trained autoencoders can be viewed as sample representations.

AI.tldr: Autoencoder parameters may encode sample information; spectral characteristics of parameter matrices reveal links to data covariance, enabling parameter-based sample representations that distinguish models trained on different data subsets (validated on CIFAR-10 and FashionMNIST).
AI.motivation: To determine whether trained autoencoder parameters form a dense, informative representation of training samples and to relate parameter space to data statistics.
