AI.method: Theoretically relate singular values of parameter matrices to eigenvalues of the data covariance; construct vector representations from spectral characteristics; empirically test on CIFAR-10 and FashionMNIST by comparing models trained on different data subsets without using original samples.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows a link between parameter singular values and data covariance eigenvalues, enabling data–parameter information transfer; experimental results demonstrate that spectral-based parameter vectors can accurately distinguish models trained on different data subsets.
AI.conclusion: Autoencoder parameters can be viewed as sample representations, implying that trained networks encode meaningful statistics of training data within their parameter matrices.

title: Stabilizing Camera-Controlled Novel View Synthesis at Inference Time
summary: Training-free, camera-controlled novel view synthesis from a single image using pre-trained video diffusion models often becomes unstable under large camera motion and long generation horizons. Existing approaches commonly combine several inference-time components, making it unclear which design choices are most important for stability. We show that the main source of stability is simple. Decomposing camera motion into small autoregressive steps limits per-step geometric distortion and reduces error accumulation. A controlled camera-step study shows that performance remains stable for small motions and degrades more strongly as the per-step motion approaches $18$-$20^\circ$. We further evaluate geometry-constrained spatial attention and low-frequency appearance anchoring as supporting refinements, together with an efficient registration-free warping pipeline. Across RealEstate10K and MegaScene, CamTrol++ improves temporal and geometric consistency, downstream 3D reconstruction quality, and generation efficiency over training-free baselines. The method remains effective for 56-frame generation and under substantial controlled depth corruption. These results show that careful control of camera motion at inference time can substantially improve the stability of camera-controlled novel view synthesis without retraining or modifying the diffusion backbone.

AI.tldr: Decompose camera motion into small autoregressive steps to stabilize training-free, camera-controlled novel view synthesis using pre-trained video diffusion models; per-step motion should be kept under ~18–20 degrees; CamTrol++ adds geometry constraints and low-frequency appearance anchoring with a registration-free warping pipeline; achieves higher temporal/geometric consistency on RealEstate10K and MegaScene for up to 56-frame generation, without retraining.
AI.motivation: Training-free, camera-controlled NVS with diffusion models often destabilizes under large camera motions and long horizons. The complexity of inference-time components obscures which design choices truly matter for stability; identifying a simple, effective remedy is needed.
AI.method: CamTrol++ decomposes camera motion into small autoregressive steps to limit per-step distortion. It includes geometry-constrained spatial attention, low-frequency appearance anchoring, and an efficient registration-free warping pipeline. Evaluation uses RealEstate10K and MegaScene, focused on 56-frame generation and robustness to depth corruption.
AI.result: Improved temporal and geometric consistency, better downstream 3D reconstruction quality, and faster generation compared to training-free baselines. The approach remains effective for 56-frame generation and under depth corruption; stability degrades as per-step motion approaches 18–20 degrees, indicating a practical motion bound for stability.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time control of camera motion is a simple, effective way to stabilize camera-controlled NVS without retraining or modifying the diffusion backbone; CamTrol++ demonstrates that small-step motion is key and that additional refinements provide further gains.

title: Towards Numerical TOHTN Planning with SMT-based HTN-SAT Encoding
summary: While HTN planning has received significant attention in recent years, support for numerical reasoning remains very limited. In this paper, we investigate numerical Totally-Ordered HTN (TOHTN) planning and show how standard SAT-based encodings can be naturally extended with SMT to handle numeric fluents. In addition, we introduce a benchmark suite for numerical TOHTN planning, providing a first common basis for evaluation in this setting. Experimental results show that this simple encoding already constitutes a competitive baseline. This work opens the way to more expressive approaches to HTN planning.

AI.tldr: Extends SAT-based HTN encodings with SMT to handle numeric fluents in TOHTN, introduces a benchmark suite, and reports competitive baselines, enabling more expressive HTN planning.
AI.motivation: Overcome limited numerical reasoning in HTN planning and provide a common benchmark for numerical TOHTN to evaluate new approaches.
AI.method: Extend standard SAT-based encodings with SMT to support numeric fluents within Totally-Ordered HTN planning; formalize and implement a benchmark suite for numerical TOHTN planning.
AI.result: The proposed SMT-augmented encoding is a simple yet competitive baseline for numerical TOHTN planning.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates feasibility of integrating SMT into HTN planning for numeric reasoning and paves the way for more expressive HTN planners.

title: Restricted Eigenvalues Beyond Gaussian Width: Threshold Occupancy under Heavy Tails
summary: Restricted eigenvalue (RE) bounds govern stable recovery by norm-regularized estimators. For isotropic sub-Gaussian measurements, the benchmark sample size is $1+w(A)^2$, where $w(A)$ is the Gaussian width of the normalized descent cone. The COLT 2015 open-problem note (Banerjee et al., 2015) asked whether the same law follows for heavy-tailed designs from a uniform small-ball condition alone. We give an explicit and systematic negative answer to the general question as formulated there: the proposed law fails in its full dimension-free, arbitrary-set form, and the missing obstruction is simultaneous threshold occupancy. A constant-width polyhedral descent cone with fixed small-ball constants has zero empirical RE on every sample path up to half the ambient dimension. More generally, every finite range space admits exact threshold encoding in an arbitrarily narrow spherical cap and a lift to a full polyhedral descent-cone section. For every fixed threshold VC dimension $d$, as $β\downarrow0$, the sharp worst-case sample complexity is $Θ(β^{-1}[d\log(1/β)+\log(1/δ)])$. The separation persists under exact isotropy and all finite moments: on the same constant-width cone, Gaussian measurements succeed with $O(1+\log(1/δ))$ samples, whereas an isotropic heavy-tailed design fails pathwise for $n\lesssim\sqrt{p/\log p}$. Gaussian smoothing yields an everywhere-positive $C^\infty$ density while retaining arbitrarily poor RE. Under isotropy, a distribution-free fallback governed by affine dimension times squared enclosing radius is sharp on this family.

AI.tldr: The COLT 2015 universal RE-bound for heavy-tailed designs fails in full generality: a dimension-free, arbitrary-set law does not hold due to an obstruction called simultaneous threshold occupancy. For fixed cone and small-ball constants, the empirical RE is zero up to near half the ambient dimension; as VC-dimension d is fixed and beta→0, worst-case sample complexity scales as Θ(β^{-1}[d log(1/β)+log(1/δ)]). Gaussian measurements achieve far better, with O(1+log(1/δ)) samples, while heavy-tailed isotropic designs fail pathwise below about √(p/log p). Gaussian smoothing preserves bad RE, and a distribution-free fallback depends on affine dimension and enclosing radius.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether heavy-tailed measurement designs admit the same RE-based stable recovery guarantees as isotropic sub-Gaussian designs under the small-ball condition, addressing the COLT 2015 open problem on dimension-free laws.
AI.method: Construct explicit counterexamples and general constructions: (i) a constant-width polyhedral descent cone with fixed small-ball constants that yields zero empirical RE on all sample paths up to about p/2; (ii) encode threshold information in finite range spaces via precise spherical caps and lift to full descent-cone sections; (iii) analyze worst-case sample complexity as a function of VC dimension d and threshold parameter β; (iv) compare with Gaussian designs and apply Gaussian smoothing; (v) derive a distribution-free fallback bound dependent on affine dimension and squared enclosing radius.
AI.result: Demonstrates a fundamental obstruction to a universal RE law for heavy-tailed designs: the law fails in the general, dimension-free form; heavy-tailed designs require substantially more samples or different structural assumptions; Gaussian measurements can realize near-optimal sample complexity in the same framework, while heavy-tailed designs fail pathwise unless the sample size scales as at least Θ(√(p/log p)); smoothing does not eliminate the poor RE; a distribution-free bound based on affine dimension and radius persists.
AI.conclusion: Stable recovery guarantees for norm-regularized estimators under heavy-tailed designs cannot mirror the Gaussian-sub-Gaussian behavior in a dimension-free manner. The obstruction of simultaneous threshold occupancy shows up even with fixed small-ball constants; the results point to the necessity of additional assumptions (beyond a uniform small-ball condition) or more refined geometric/descent-cone analyses to recover RE-based performance with heavy-tailed measurements.

title: Tree-Structured Vector Quantization For Efficient And Progressive Image Compression
summary: Vector-quantization based image compression has achieved strong rate--distortion performance, yet most of them still produce a separate compressed representation for each target bitrate. Such variable-rate behavior allows one model to operate at multiple rates, but it does not necessarily provide a progressive bitstream whose prefixes are themselves decodable and can be refined by appending additional bits. We propose \textbf{Tree-VQ}, a progressive tree-structured vector quantization framework for learned image compression. Tree-VQ organizes discrete codewords as a hierarchical binary tree and represents each latent token by a routed root-to-leaf path. Crucially, every prefix of this path corresponds to a valid quantized representation, so shallow internal nodes serve as coarse reconstruction codes and deeper nodes provide successive refinements. This allows a compressed image to be decoded from an early prefix and progressively improved as more branch symbols are received, rather than being re-encoded for different target rates. To make this structure practical for compression, we introduce a prefix-compatible tree entropy model that codes progressive continuation decisions and routed branch refinements using only causally available decoded contexts. We further use rate-aware refinement scheduling to decide which spatial blocks should receive additional tree bits under a given prefix budget, and hierarchical prefix supervision to ensure that internal nodes are directly decodable at low rates. Experiments show that Tree-VQ achieves a superior performance--efficiency trade-off, delivering the best perceptual compression results with much fewer parameters and lower latency than competing methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes Tree-VQ, a progressive tree-structured VQ for learned image compression enabling decodable prefixes and progressive refinement, with a prefix-compatible entropy model and rate-aware scheduling, achieving superior perceptual RD with fewer parameters and lower latency.
AI.motivation: Need for a progressive, prefix-decodable bitstream across target bitrates in learned image compression, avoiding re-encoding for different rates.
AI.method: Hierarchical binary tree of discrete codewords; each latent token is routed along a root-to-leaf path; every prefix yields a valid quantized representation. Introduces a prefix-compatible entropy model using only causally available decoded context, rate-aware refinement scheduling to allocate bits across spatial blocks, and hierarchical prefix supervision to ensure internal nodes are decodable at low rates.
AI.result: Empirical results show Tree-VQ delivers superior performance-efficiency trade-off, achieving best perceptual compression with far fewer parameters and lower latency than competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Tree-VQ enables progressive, prefix-decodable bitstreams for learned image compression, combining a tree-structured VQ with entropy modeling, scheduling, and supervision to deliver strong perceptual rate–distortion performance with lower complexity.

title: More Criticism Does Not Make a Better Review: EquiReview-R
summary: AI reviewers can now produce many specific criticisms, but more criticism is not necessarily a better review. A review may miss a consequential weakness or retain an allegation that available evidence does not support. These failures require opposite corrections, yet generation-oriented systems and aggregate measures obscure the distinction. We therefore recast AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of a structured concern set, with omission and overcritique treated as separate risks. Building on this formulation, we introduce EquiReview-R, which resolves existing concerns against localized evidence, searches for missing issues from independent and review-conditioned perspectives, and returns stop, continue, or defer. To expose the failure mode that motivates this design, we construct an evidence-linked trajectory corpus. Its retrospective analysis shows why revision must precede further search: nearly all concerns in a high-recall review lack a definitive evidential disposition, while an earlier refinement mechanism cannot revise them. On a frozen cohort of previously unseen papers, EquiReview-R satisfies the prespecified non-inferiority criterion for major omission, reduces major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%, and attains a one-sided omission upper bound of 9.9% while stopping on 52.4% of papers. Computation-matched controls, controlled pairs, and ablations show that the gain comes from revision rather than extra inference or shorter output. We release the corpus as ReviewTrace, an evidence-linked resource for studying review revision, disagreement, and provenance.

AI.tldr: Recasts AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of a structured concern set and introduces EquiReview-R to revise and decide on next steps; demonstrates improved omission/overcritique metrics and releases ReviewTrace as a resource.
AI.motivation: Addresses the gap where more criticisms do not guarantee better reviews; separate risks of omission and overcritique are not well captured by generation-focused or aggregate metrics; seeks a revision-first, evidence-based workflow for AI-assisted reviews.
AI.method: EquiReview-R performs evidence-guided refinement, searches for missing issues from independent and review-conditioned perspectives, and returns stop/continue/defer. An evidence-linked trajectory corpus is built (ReviewTrace) to study revision, disagreement, and provenance. Evaluation uses a frozen cohort of unseen papers, non-inferiority testing for major omission, and ablations with computation-matched controls and controlled pairs.
AI.result: On unseen papers, EquiReview-R achieves non-inferiority for major omission, reduces major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%, and yields a one-sided omission upper bound of 9.9%. It stops on 52.4% of papers. Ablations suggest gains arise from revision rather than extra inference or shorter outputs. Release of ReviewTrace provides an evidence-linked resource.
AI.conclusion: Revision-before-search is essential to reliable AI-assisted reviews. The approach highlights a concrete failure mode, offers a reproducible evaluation framework, and provides a data resource to study revision, disagreement, and provenance in review workflows.

title: An Adversarial Zero-Shot Learning Approach for Anomaly Detection in Multivariate IoT Traffic Data
summary: Anomaly detection in Internet of Things (IoT) networks presents unique challenges due to the diversity of devices, lack of labeled data, and domain variability across environments. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection that leverages adversarial learning and contrastive loss within a sequence-based Variational Autoencoder (VAE) architecture. Our method enables zero-shot domain adaptation by jointly optimizing domain-invariant latent representations and semantically structured embedding spaces, without requiring labeled data or raw feature transfer. To address the heterogeneity of IoT deployments, we introduce encoder and decoder adaptor layers that align feature distributions across domains while preserving contextual semantics. Additionally, we propose a destination-based segmentation strategy to better model real-world communication structures in IoT traffic. Our framework is comprehensively evaluated on six distinct datasets spanning industrial, enterprise, general-purpose, smart home, and military automation domains across 44 transfer scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization in several cross-domain settings and competitive performance against a contrastive domain-adaptation baseline under realistic, heterogeneous, and privacy-constrained IoT conditions.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot domain-adaptive framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection in IoT using a sequence-based VAE with adversarial and contrastive losses, plus domain-adaptor layers and destination-based segmentation.
AI.motivation: IoT anomaly detection faces device heterogeneity, lack of labeled data, and cross-environment variability; there is a need for domain-invariant representations and semantic alignment under privacy constraints.
AI.method: A sequence-based Variational Autoencoder augmented with adversarial learning and contrastive loss to learn domain-invariant latent representations and semantically structured embeddings. introduces encoder/decoder adaptor layers to align feature distributions across domains while preserving context, and a destination-based segmentation strategy to model IoT traffic structure.
AI.result: Evaluated on six datasets across industrial, enterprise, general-purpose, smart home, and military automation domains, covering 44 transfer scenarios. Demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization in several cross-domain settings and competitive performance versus a contrastive domain-adaptation baseline under heterogeneous, privacy-constrained conditions.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides effective zero-shot domain adaptation for IoT anomaly detection with competitive performance. Further work should detail ablations, computational cost, and real-time deployment considerations, and expand testing to additional environments.

title: PL-SCEA: Reconfiguring Pretrained Attention for Few-Shot Industrial Anomaly Detection
summary: Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) provide transferable patch representations for few-shot industrial anomaly detection, but their attention computation is typically inherited from pretraining objectives centered on semantic aggregation. This creates a potential mismatch: token relations that support semantic recognition may not adequately expose the localized texture and structural deviations required for anomaly localization. We therefore investigate the hypothesis that the attention computation of a frozen VFM can be reconfigured as a task-relevant component of anomaly detection. We instantiate this idea with Power-Law Self-Correlation Enhanced Attention (PL-SCEA), which retains the semantic context of pretrained query-key attention while constructing token-adaptive self-correlations over contextualized value features. Positive-correlation filtering and power-law reweighting then emphasize relations that are salient relative to each token's relational background, without introducing additional trainable attention projections. The resulting features are modeled by a lightweight variational autoencoder that provides a fixed-size reconstruction-based representation of category-specific normality. The two stages serve complementary roles: attention reconfiguration shapes how local relational deviations are represented, while reconstruction-based modeling converts deviations from learned normality into anomaly scores. Across MVTec AD and VisA, the complete framework achieves competitive image-level detection and consistently strong pixel-level localization across the evaluated few-shot settings. Ablations further show that PL-SCEA improves localization with either the VAE or a memory bank under the tested setting. These results support the view that task-aligned attention reconfiguration can improve the anomaly-localization capability of frozen pretrained representations.

AI.tldr: Proposes PL-SCEA to reconfigure frozen Vision Foundation Models for anomaly localization. Uses token-adaptive self-correlations over contextualized values with positive-correlation filtering and power-law reweighting, paired with a lightweight VAE for reconstruction-based normality; achieves strong pixel-level localization and competitive image-level detection on MVTec AD and VisA in few-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Pretrained VFMs optimized for semantic aggregation may misalign with anomaly localization, which requires localized texture/structure deviations. Reconfiguring attention without retraining can align features with anomaly detection tasks while leveraging frozen representations.
AI.method: Modify frozen query-key attention to form token-adaptive self-correlations over contextualized value features (PL-SCEA). Apply positive-correlation filtering and power-law reweighting to emphasize relations salient to each token’s background. No additional trainable attention projections. Feed resulting features to a lightweight variational autoencoder (VAE) to obtain a fixed-size reconstruction-based normality representation. Two-stage design: attention reconfiguration shapes local relational deviations; reconstruction-based modeling yields anomaly scores. Ablations include using a memory bank in place of or alongside the VAE.
AI.result: On MVTec AD and VisA, achieves competitive image-level anomaly detection and consistently strong pixel-level localization in few-shot settings. Ablations show PL-SCEA improves localization with either the VAE or a memory bank.
AI.conclusion: Task-aligned attention reconfiguration can enhance the anomaly-localization capability of frozen pretrained representations; combining attention reconfiguration with reconstruction-based modeling provides complementary mechanisms for detecting and localizing anomalies.

title: FiMI Banking: A Sovereign Model for Indian Retail Banking
summary: Banks need conversational systems that can answer product questions, assist customers with account-related requests, and operate safely within strict operational and regulatory constraints. General-purpose language models do not reliably meet these requirements. They fall short when a task requires grounded information, correct tool use, or cautious handling of bank-specific sensitive situations. We introduce FiMI Banking, a controlled Indian retail-banking setting. We build it from vetted banking documents, structured ground truth, synthetic customer backgrounds, and banking tools. We evaluate two post-training approaches: preference optimization for response-level behavior, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-turn tool-use tasks. Preference optimization improves safe behavior substantially: out-of-scope refusal rises from 52% to 80%. Reinforcement learning improves edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718 and order-sensitive task performance from 0.590 to 0.679, while using 29% fewer generated tokens. These results show that preference optimization and verifiable-reward reinforcement learning address complementary requirements for reliable banking agents.

AI.tldr: FiMI Banking demonstrates improved safety and task performance for banking agents via two post-training methods (preference optimization and verifiable-reward RL) in a vetted Indian retail-banking setting.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LMs struggle with grounded information, correct tool use, and handling bank-specific sensitive situations; need reliable, compliant conversational agents in banking.
AI.method: Build FiMI Banking from vetted banking documents, structured ground truth, synthetic customer profiles, and banking tools; evaluate two post-training approaches: (1) preference optimization for response-level behavior, (2) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-turn tool-use tasks.
AI.result: Preference optimization raises out-of-scope refusals (OSR) from 52% to 80%. RL with verifiable rewards improves edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718 and order-sensitive task performance from 0.590 to 0.679, while reducing generated tokens by 29%.
AI.conclusion: Preference optimization and verifiable-reward RL address complementary requirements for reliable banking agents.

title: LongCounsel-8: A Benchmark Suite for Longitudinal Depression Tracking from Multi-Session Counseling Dialogues
summary: Tracking depression from multi-session counseling dialogues requires estimating both current symptom severity and how it changes across sessions. Yet progress on this task is constrained by the scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with standardized session-level depression labels. Existing resources typically provide either multi-session conversations without depression labels or labeled interviews in a single session. Building such a benchmark poses three challenges: maintaining longitudinal consistency and diversity, grounding symptom progression in empirical patterns, and expressing controlled depression states naturally without exposing target labels. To address these challenges, we introduce LongCounsel-8, a benchmark suite of three independently generated datasets totaling 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories, grounded in real-world client profiles, depression trajectories, symptom compositions, and counseling patterns. We combine profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization to address these challenges. Across the benchmark, simulated self-reports closely recover the controlled states, supporting label fidelity. Experiments on existing depression tracking methods reveal three key findings: (1) lower single-session score error does not guarantee accurate identification of trend, i.e., improvement or worsening; (2) existing methods are consistently less reliable on worsening trajectories; and (3) additional session history may reduce the accuracy of trend prediction. Together, these findings establish LongCounsel-8 as a foundation for advancing depression assessment from static, single-session prediction toward reliable longitudinal tracking of mental-health change.

AI.tldr: LongCounsel-8 introduces 3 independently generated datasets totaling 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories to benchmark longitudinal depression tracking, grounding simulated trajectories in real client profiles and empirical patterns. It demonstrates that current methods struggle with trend prediction and that longer histories can sometimes hurt accuracy, establishing a baseline for longitudinal assessment.
AI.motivation: To overcome the scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with session-level depression labels and to enable reliable tracking of symptom progression over sessions.
AI.method: Profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization to create longitudinal counseling trajectories with controlled depression states and grounded symptom compositions.
AI.result: Simulated self-reports recover the controlled states closely; experiments reveal three findings: (1) single-session score accuracy does not imply correct trend identification; (2) worsening trajectories are harder for existing methods; (3) additional sessions may reduce trend prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LongCounsel-8 provides a benchmark to move from static, single-session prediction to reliable longitudinal tracking of mental-health change.

title: Rethinking 3D Noise: Learning 3D-Aware Video Priors via Optimization-Free Morphological Perturbations
summary: 3D scene representations like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) suffer severe artifacts in sparse-view settings. Recent generative 3D artifact fixers attempt to address this, but rely on paired corrupted and clean renders requiring costly, per-scene reconstructions across varying view configurations. While 2D image augmentations act as instant regularizers, no explicit equivalents exist for 3D representations to preserve spatial consistency across views, an essential property for 3D-aware training. We propose 3D Morphological Perturbations as an optimization-free regularizer that preserves spatial consistency. Leveraging explicit 3DGS, we treat each Gaussian as a fundamental building block - analogous to a 2D pixel - and apply perturbations across its morphological parameter space via scale, rotation, and pruning. Our method eliminates per-scene 3DGS optimization loops from dataset curation while enabling models to learn stronger geometric priors than sparse-view baselines in diagnostic ablations conducted on a lightweight video diffusion sandbox. Scaled to a 14B-parameter video model via ControlNet, our approach maintains visual fidelity while reducing mean depth error by 12.5% over state-of-the-art image-to-image 3D artifact refiners, ultimately boosting downstream robotics policy success rates by up to 8.0% across 3 of 4 manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Optimization-free 3D morphological perturbations for 3D Gaussian Splatting improve cross-view consistency and depth accuracy in sparse-view NeRF-like models, lowering depth error and boosting robotics task success.
AI.motivation: Sparse-view artifacts in NeRF/3DGS and the lack of explicit 3D regularizers to enforce spatial consistency across views; reliance on costly per-scene optimization limits scalability.
AI.method: Introduce 3D Morphological Perturbations: treat each Gaussian primitive in explicit 3DGS as a pixellike unit and perturb its morphology (scale, rotation, pruning). This regularizer is optimization-free during data curation, removing per-scene 3DGS optimization loops. Evaluation uses a lightweight video diffusion sandbox and scales to a 14B-parameter video model via ControlNet.
AI.result: Mean depth error reduced by 12.5% compared to state-of-the-art image-to-image 3D refiners. Visual fidelity maintained. Robotics policy success rates boosted by up to 8.0% across 3 of 4 manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: 3D Morphological Perturbations provide an effective, optimization-free regularizer that improves 3D consistency and downstream performance, enabling scalable training with weaker supervision and explicit 3D priors.

title: Interface-Induced Trajectory Censoring
comment: 39 pages, 14 pages main text. Code, data, and pre-registrations: https://github.com/nebula-1999/Interface-Induced-Trajectory-Censoring
summary:
Agent evaluations report a tool-call rate read off the serving stack. That number can be zero while the model is emitting well-formed calls: the interface censors the trajectory before anything downstream sees it.
  On BFCL v4's own data, executor and scorer, holding weights, cases, decoding and seeds fixed and changing only the serving adapter, the same model scores 0.00 or 0.96 / 0.19. A 2x2 over chat template and parser locates the effect exactly: both main effects are exactly zero and all of it sits in the interaction -- no component is defective, and repairing one side of the contract buys precisely nothing. On tau-bench's 115 interactive retail tasks the same swap moves server-parsed calls from 0 to 636 and tasks reaching any tool execution from 0 to 103. Our probe reproduces the funnel across a 21x scale range of Qwen2.5-Coder: the server parses 0/100 at every size while well-formed emitted calls rise to 80/100 at 32B (~72 after calibration against an adjudicated gold standard). Under a matched envelope, across a comparable scale span, the silent fraction stays at 0-2, a prediction committed to the repository before the run. Llama-3.1-8B's 23% rate of calling the task function itself as a tool falls to 0 under one strict:true flag.
  The mismatch reaches inside the training loop, and its consequence is scale-dependent: in verl's AgentLoop at 7B, 45 of 115 generations carry a complete call; 0 are accepted, 0 execute, 0 return an observation. At 1.5B the same zero is over-determined, so we report the two scales separately. At evaluation time, repairing the adapter restores the mechanism but not a significant outcome gain: parsing 0->84, rescues 0->9, pass rate 53->62 (n.s.). We release a 98-line preflight check that catches every silent failure here. The observed tool-call rate is not a property of the model alone; it is a property of the model-interface stack that measures it.

AI.tldr: Tool-call rate in LLMs is governed by the end-to-end model-interface stack, not the model alone; experiments reveal silent/censorship effects, adapter-induced changes, and scale-dependent outcomes. A 98-line preflight check helps detect silent failures; improving parsing or adapters can restore tool-use but not necessarily improve results.
AI.motivation: Quantify how interface components (serving adapters, templates, parsers) shape observed tool-use, isolate silent failures, and assess whether model capabilities translate into usable tool calls.
AI.method: 2x2 experimental design varying chat template and parser; multiple models/datasets (BFCL v4, tau-bench, Qwen2.5-Coder, Llama-3.1-8B, verl AgentLoop); cross-scale tests; matched envelopes; strict:true flag; introduced a 98-line preflight check; metrics include tool-call rate, parsed vs emitted calls, and outcomes under different adapters; calibration against a gold standard.
AI.result: Tool-call rates range from 0 to high values depending on interface; some configurations yield zero tool calls despite well-formed emissions; server parsing can dominate tool-call counts; a 21x scale range shows large discrepancies; a strict flag can suppress calls; repairing adapters restores mechanism but may yield limited outcome gains; silent failures can be caught with preflight checks; silent fraction observed is 0-2% under matched setups.
AI.conclusion: The observed tool-call rate is an emergent property of the full stack, not the model alone. Reliable evaluation and practical tool-use require end-to-end assessment and safeguards (preflight checks) to detect silent failures; adapter-level changes can affect parsing without guaranteeing performance gains.

title: LeanGRPO: Eliminating Redundant Recomputation in Diffusion RL
summary: Diffusion reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved significant success in post-training image and video generative models. However, most diffusion RL methods, including DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO, recompute selected timesteps with gradient tracking after rollout. Under on-policy training with the same backend for rollout and update, this recomputation is mathematically redundant. Intuitively, the rollout and policy update steps can reuse the same feed-forward backbone to avoid redundant computation, but doing so can incur a large memory overhead during rollout. To address the issue, we present LeanGRPO by restructuring the data-parallel layout and introducing two recompute-free training schedules for trajectory-logprob diffusion RL: (1) LeanGRPO-Retain enables gradient tracking during rollout and directly reuses the resulting computation graphs and saved activations for backward during update, requiring no recomputation; and (2) LeanGRPO-Reweight also enables gradients during rollout, but immediately backpropagates each selected step using a provisional advantage and delays gradient synchronization, then corrects the provisional gradients with the true advantage after the trajectory is completed. These schedules target different model scales and input sizes. Across FlowGRPO/DanceGRPO with FLUX.1-dev and Wan, LeanGRPO achieves up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup while preserving the original optimization objective.

AI.tldr: LeanGRPO introduces two recompute-free training schedules (LeanGRPO-Retain and LeanGRPO-Reweight) for trajectory-logprob diffusion RL to remove gradient-recompute overhead during rollout, achieving up to 1.83x speedup while preserving the original objective.
AI.motivation: Reduce redundant gradient recomputation and memory overhead in on-policy diffusion RL methods (e.g., DanceGRPO, FlowGRPO) when sharing a common backbone for rollout and update.
AI.method: Reorganize data-parallel layout; LeanGRPO-Retain stores activations/graphs during rollout for backward pass; LeanGRPO-Reweight computes provisional gradients along the trajectory with delayed gradient synchronization and later corrects with true advantages after completion; both enable gradient tracking during rollout with no recomputation.
AI.result: Up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup on FlowGRPO/DanceGRPO with FLUX.1-dev and Wan, preserving the original optimization objective.
AI.conclusion: Recompute-free training via two schedules offers memory/compute efficiency across different model scales and input sizes; enables higher throughput without altering the optimization objective; practical implications for diffusion RL pipelines requiring on-policy rollout and update using the same backend.

title: Cross-Dataset Transfer and Reliability of Explainable Artificial Intelligence for RhythmFormer Remote Photoplethysmography
summary: Background. Remote photoplethysmography estimates the cardiovascular pulse from facial video, and its explanations have rested on inspecting heatmaps rather than on quantitative evidence about where a model reads it. We quantified the explanations and asked whether such explanations transfer between datasets and track model performance. Method. We trained eight condition-specific RhythmFormer models on NCKU-rPPG, recorded under three illumination levels, speaking, rotation, and cycling, estimated one heart rate per 5.12-second clip, and set them beside a UBFC-rPPG reproduction. Raw attention, rollout, attention flow, and Beyond Intuition were assessed by skin coverage and the Salience-guided Faithfulness Coefficient (SaCo). Results. Beyond Intuition ranked highest on both datasets, at median coverage 0.789 and SaCo 0.837 on Static level 3 against 0.826 and 0.917 on UBFC-rPPG; lower ranks differed. Within one participant of one condition, neither measure was related to a clip's heart-rate error, waveform correlation, or signal-to-noise ratio on either dataset: 186 of the 252 coefficients fell below $|ρ|=0.10$ and 28 reached $p<0.05$ against the 13 expected by chance. Across the eight scenarios only Beyond Intuition's coverage followed the three performance measures, at $ρ=-0.43$, $+0.57$, and $+0.43$, while the attention-only methods' SaCo ran opposite to each. It failed at 40 lux alone, its median coverage falling to 0.180 and its median SaCo to $-0.178$, whereas motion degraded the estimates far more without such a drop. Conclusions. Skin coverage and SaCo carry information complementary to the performance measures rather than a proxy for them: attributing to the skin does not guarantee an accurate estimate. What an attribution reveals about a condition is where the model looks rather than how faithfully its map is ordered.

AI.tldr: The work quantifies and compares explanations for remote photoplethysmography models across datasets and conditions, evaluating whether attribution metrics reflect performance; findings show attribution methods based on skin coverage (and SaCo) do not reliably proxy heart-rate estimation performance, with Beyond Intuition performing best among tested explanations but still only partially aligned with performance.
AI.motivation: To move beyond qualitative heatmap inspection by quantitatively evaluating where models attend and how that aligns (or not) with predictive accuracy, and to test transferability of explanations across datasets and conditions.
AI.method: Train eight condition-specific RhythmFormer models on NCKU-rPPG under three illumination levels plus speaking, rotation, cycling; compare to a UBFC-rPPG reproduction. Evaluate explanations using raw attention, rollout, attention flow, and Beyond Intuition via skin coverage and the Salience-guided Faithfulness Coefficient (SaCo). Assess correlations with heart-rate error, waveform correlation, and SNR within participants and across eight scenarios.
AI.result: Beyond Intuition achieved the highest skin coverage and SaCo on both datasets, but internal correlations between explainability metrics and performance were weak; only Beyond Intuition’s coverage showed modest, dataset-spanning associations with performance measures (ρ around -0.43 to +0.57). Attention-only SaCo often contradicted performance trends, and a sharp drop in performance occurred at 40 lux with low skin-coverage; motion degraded estimates more than lighting alone.
AI.conclusion: Skin coverage and SaCo provide information complementary to, rather than proxies for, model performance. An attribution highlights where a model looks but does not guarantee an order-faithful mapping to predictive accuracy; reliable explanations require more than adherence to attribution metrics.

title: Common-Witness Certificates and Sharp Feature Bounds for Counterfactual Image Auditing
summary: An image editor may satisfy every regional plausibility constraint separately even when no single latent explanation fits the complete output. We formalize this local-to-global failure using a common witness grade and witness nerve. The framework separates auditing from causal identification: shared exogeneity alone allows every coupling of the regime marginals, whereas an externally justified witness relation yields sharp partial-identification bounds for prespecified image features. Helly-type arguments provide short incompatibility certificates for quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases; a blocker-hypergraph formula gives exact repair counts. Simultaneous confidence regions for the regime marginals give finite-sample outer coverage of the complete identified interval. Controlled MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB studies demonstrate the predicted local-global separation, while synthetic experiments test sharp bounds, certificate recovery, and structured computation. The method audits a declared feature relation and does not identify unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals.

AI.tldr: A local-to-global audit framework for image editors using a joint witness structure to separate auditing from causal identification, yielding sharp partial-identification bounds and repair counts with finite-sample guarantees, validated on MNIST-like datasets.
AI.motivation: Locally plausible regions can coexist with globally incompatible outputs; need audit methods that separate verification of feature relations from latent causal explanations and provide verifiable bounds rather than unrestricted counterfactuals.
AI.method: Introduce a common witness grade and witness nerve to formalize local-to-global failure; separate auditing from causal identification; rely on an externally justified witness relation to obtain sharp partial-identification bounds for prespecified image features; apply Helly-type arguments for quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases; use blocker-hypergraph formulas to compute exact repair counts; provide simultaneous confidence regions for regime marginals to guarantee finite-sample outer coverage of the identified interval; validate with controlled MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB, plus synthetic experiments.
AI.result: Derives short incompatibility certificates for local-global inconsistencies, exact repair counts, and finite-sample outer coverage of the identified set; demonstrates local-global separation in experiments and shows effective certificate recovery and structured computation.
AI.conclusion: The method audits a declared feature relation and does not identify unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals, offering a principled auditing framework with explicit assumptions and verifiable bounds.

title: Coupled Scaling: A Representational Accessibility Framework for Neural Scaling Laws
comment: 35 pages, 2 figures. Code and reproducibility artifacts: https://github.com/quintonvina/coupled-scaling/tree/v1.0-reanalysis
summary: Existing theories derive neural scaling from data geometry or a specified data-model spectrum, but systems trained on the same data can scale differently when architecture or optimization changes the representations they can efficiently reach. We introduce Coupled Scaling, a task-conditioned framework in which finite-budget scaling depends on the relation between task structure and the geometry accessible to an architecture-optimization system. In a solvable mode-truncation model, loss separates into target energy outside architectural support and an unresolved supported tail. For an arbitrary priority order, the residual lies between the best-N supported tail and the tail beyond the largest completed high-value prefix. If the cumulative-tail and coverage log-rates are $γ_{A,T}$ and $ρ_{A,O,T}$, the residual exponent lies in $[ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T},γ_{A,T}]$. Under bounded off-prefix gain, the completed prefix is rate-determining and $α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T}$; for $a_{A,T,j}\asymp j^{-b_{A,T}}$, this gives $α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T}-1)$. A fixed-kernel specialization derives the training-time exponent from the near-zero tail of a task-weighted spectral measure defined independently of the loss fit. The framework separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and motivates two tests: static task-relevant geometry should track loss at a common budget, while multiscale geometry should track coupling-specific exponent ordering, including reversal across contrasting tasks. An audit of released emergence trajectories identifies the controls needed for a direct factorial test that measures geometry separately from the scaling fit.

AI.tldr: Coupled Scaling: a task-conditioned framework separating architectural reach from finite-budget scaling, deriving bounds on residuals and exponents, and proposing geometry-based tests.
AI.motivation: Neural scaling on the same data can differ with architecture/optimization due to representational reach. Existing theories tying scaling to data geometry or spectrum cannot capture these coupling effects across tasks, architectures, and budgets.
AI.method: Mode-truncation loss decomposes into target energy outside architectural support and an unresolved tail. For any priority order, the residual lies between the best-N supported tail and the tail beyond the largest completed high-value prefix. With cumulative-tail log-rate γ_{A,T} and coverage log-rate ρ_{A,O,T}, the residual exponent lies in [ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T}, γ_{A,T}]. If the completed prefix is rate-determining under bounded off-prefix gain, α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T}; for a_{A,T,j} ~ j^{-b_{A,T}}, this gives α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T}-1). A fixed-kernel specialization derives the training-time exponent from the near-zero tail of a task-weighted spectral measure defined independently of the loss fit. The framework separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and motivates two tests: static task-relevant geometry should track loss at a common budget, while multiscale geometry should track coupling-specific exponent ordering, including reversal across contrasting tasks. An audit of released emergence trajectories identifies the controls needed for a direct factorial test that measures geometry separately from the scaling fit.
AI.result: Key theoretical results include bounds on the residual exponent between ρ γ and γ, and explicit formulas for α under different growth assumptions (α = ρ γ or α = ρ(b−1)). The framework yields testable predictions: geometry should correlate with loss at fixed budgets, and multiscale geometry should determine the ordering of coupling exponents; an audit suggests how to design experiments to isolate geometry and scaling.
AI.conclusion: Coupled Scaling decouples architectural reach from finite-budget acquisition, providing a principled way to study how task structure and geometry interact to shape scaling; it also prescribes practical empirical tests (geometry-focused tracking and factorial experiments) to validate the framework.

title: ARCOS: Zero-shot Boundary Localization for Corneal Layer Segmentation Across Optical Coherence Tomography Devices
summary: Accurate segmentation of corneal layers in optical coherence tomography (OCT) is essential for quantitative assessment of corneal morphology, including layer thickness and structural changes associated with disease or surgery. However, automatic segmentation remains challenging because corneal interfaces are thin, affected by speckle noise, and variable across acquisition devices. In this work, we propose ARCOS, a patch-based zero-shot boundary localization framework for corneal layer segmentation in clinical anterior-segment OCT images. Rather than performing conventional region classification, the method predicts boundary heatmaps for the main corneal interfaces from overlapping native-resolution patches. Patch-level predictions are stitched across the full B-scan and converted into boundary locations to obtain continuous, anatomically ordered layer segmentations. The network combines multi-scale feature fusion with a self-conditioned refinement module that uses intermediate boundary information to improve local heatmap predictions while preserving spatial detail. The method was evaluated on clinical OCT images acquired from multiple devices and compared with representative segmentation baselines using boundary localization and derived thickness metrics. The proposed method achieved an off-by-one boundary localization accuracy of 95.1% and a mean absolute boundary error of 0.514 pixels on the matched-device test set. In zero-shot cross-device evaluation, it maintained an average off-by-one accuracy of 84.3% and a mean absolute boundary error of 0.855 pixels across unseen acquisition devices, outperforming the baseline models. Thickness estimates derived from the predicted boundaries showed low error across corneal regions, supporting the method's use for quantitative corneal OCT analysis.

AI.tldr: ARCOS: a patch-based zero-shot boundary localization approach for corneal layer segmentation in anterior-segment OCT, achieving high boundary localization accuracy and cross-device generalization.
AI.motivation: Automatic corneal boundary segmentation is challenging due to thin interfaces, speckle noise, and device variability; existing methods often require device-specific training and struggle with cross-device generalization.
AI.method: ARCOS predicts boundary heatmaps for main corneal interfaces from overlapping native-resolution patches. Patch predictions are stitched across B-scans to obtain continuous, anatomically ordered layer segmentations. It combines multi-scale feature fusion with a self-conditioned refinement module that uses intermediate boundary information to refine heatmaps while preserving spatial detail.
AI.result: On matched-device data, off-by-one boundary localization accuracy 95.1% and mean absolute boundary error 0.514 pixels. In zero-shot cross-device evaluation across unseen devices, average off-by-one accuracy 84.3% and MAE 0.855 pixels. Thickness estimates from predicted boundaries show low error across corneal regions.
AI.conclusion: ARCOS demonstrates strong boundary localization and thickness estimation performance with robust cross-device generalization, making it suitable for quantitative corneal OCT analysis.

title: The Dually Flat Geometry of Planning as Inference
summary: We present an alternative characterization of the occupancy measure of reinforcement learning, obtained by embedding the planning criterion into the dynamics through a resetting planning process. Its stationary measure, which we term visitation measure, is the object on which the information geometry of decision making is most naturally expressed. The achievable visitation measures form a dually flat statistical manifold whose two affine charts are the visitation probabilities and the log-policies, dual under the conditional entropy. This structure makes planning-as-inference generalize from linear rewards to nonlinear functionals of the visitation, each iterate solved by one natural-gradient step, and gives the temporal-difference error the interpretation of a marginal-utility estimate. We develop the geometry and its consequences for reinforcement learning and theoretical neuroscience.

AI.tldr: Introduces visitation measure as the stationary occupancy under a resetting planning dynamic, revealing a dually flat information-geometric structure that unifies planning-as-inference and RL via natural-gradient updates; interprets TD error as marginal utility.
AI.motivation: To provide a geometric, probabilistic foundation for planning in RL and to generalize planning-as-inference from linear rewards to nonlinear functionals, bridging reinforcement learning and theoretical neuroscience.
AI.method: Embed planning criterion into dynamics using a resetting planning process; define the visitation measure; show the achievable visitation measures form a dually flat statistical manifold with two affine charts (visitation probabilities and log-policies) dual under conditional entropy; develop natural-gradient iterations; interpret TD error as marginal-utility.
AI.result: Characterizes occupancy as visitation measure with a dual-flat geometry; provides a principled, geometry-driven RL framework and a neuroscience interpretation; lays groundwork for nonlinear functionals in planning and inference-based RL algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The visitation-measure geometry offers a unifying, information-geometric foundation for RL and neuroscience, enabling planning-as-inference beyond linear rewards and linking TD errors to marginal utilities.

title: WeatherNext 3: Increasing resolution and performance of global weather models with raw observations
summary: State-of-the-art AI weather models have shown impressive medium-range forecast skill and computational efficiency, but suffer two key shortcomings: their forecasts have lower spatial and temporal resolution than the best physics-based models and they are exclusively initialized with and trained on analysis data. As a result, they cannot directly make use of observations, and any biases in the analysis are inherited by the forecast. WeatherNext 3 addresses these shortcomings and establishes a new state-of-the-art for probabilistic medium-range forecasting skill. First, WeatherNext 3 generates new forecasts every hour (rather than every 6 hours like traditional global models) by ingesting low-latency geostationary satellite data. Second, WeatherNext 3's temporal and spatial resolution are on par with physics-based global models, with hourly time steps and 0.1 degree resolution for single-level variables, including solar radiation and cloud cover. Third, WeatherNext 3 moves beyond traditional analysis variables by learning to predict satellite-derived precipitation estimates, as well as tropical cyclone and station observations. Modelling sparse station data allows WeatherNext 3 to make 2m temperature and dewpoint predictions at any location and time, conditioned on local geographical features, with substantially lower error than competing global models, even when evaluated against unseen stations. Together, WeatherNext 3's capabilities move operational AI-based weather forecasting beyond emulating the traditionally distinct stages of data assimilation, forecasting and post-processing, which helps to further push the frontier of performance and granularity for global weather prediction.

AI.tldr: WeatherNext 3 delivers probabilistic medium-range forecasts at hourly cadence and 0.1° resolution by directly learning from satellite data and sparse observations, surpassing prior AI models that rely on coarse analysis data.
AI.motivation: Address key limitations of existing AI weather models: reliance on analysis inputs, lower spatial/temporal resolution, and inability to leverage direct observations without propagating analysis biases.
AI.method: A three-pronged approach: (1) hourly forecasts by ingesting low-latency geostationary satellite data; (2) alignment with physics-based models via hourly time steps and 0.1° resolution for single-level variables; (3) learning to predict satellite-derived precipitation estimates, tropical cyclone metrics, and station observations, including sparse stations to predict 2 m temperature and dewpoint using local geographic features.
AI.result: Establishes state-of-the-art probabilistic medium-range forecasting; achieves higher spatial/temporal granularity; lower forecast error for 2 m temperature/dewpoint, even at unseen stations, and directly leverages observations.
AI.conclusion: Unifies data assimilation, forecasting, and post-processing in an AI framework, pushing the frontier of global weather prediction granularity and performance by reducing dependence on analysis biases.

title: Do Video Generators Track the World Across Segments? A Benchmark and Method for World-State Reasoning in Video Continuation
summary: Video generators build long videos by composing shorter parts, either by generating segments one after another or by autoregressively extending chunks. Each new part usually depends on memories of historical observations, such as recent frames, selected key frames, memory banks, or cached features. These memories preserve visible evidence from the past, but current generators do not reliably turn such evidence into a world-state interface: what holds in the video world after previous actions and how it should change under the next prompt. A past frame remains valid history, but it may not describe the state needed by the next segment; some states must instead be inferred from occluded or implicit changes rather than copied from a directly observed frame. This creates a simple but overlooked question for video continuation: given a previous video, its prompt, and a new prompt, can a model generate a continuation that reflects the state determined by both the historical video and the new prompt? To answer this question, we introduce Statebench, a benchmark that targets this gap by testing continuations over three state categories: past-visible states, occluded-process states, and complex-transition states. We further propose Stateagent, which explicitly maintains an entity-state representation, updates it under the new prompt, grounds the predicted post-action state as a future end frame, and renders the next video. Experiments show that our method improves controlled video continuation by raising the all-case state score (SCS-All) from 45.2 to 69.3, and also benefits story generation at the one-minute scale. Code is avaliable at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/StateAgent.

AI.tldr: Introduces Statebench and Stateagent for controlled video continuation that explicitly models entity-state updates across three state types (past-visible, occluded-process, complex-transition). Demonstrates substantial improvement in all-case state scoring (SCS-All: 45.2 → 69.3) and benefits long-form storytelling; code available at GitHub.
AI.motivation: Current video generators rely on memories of past observations but lack a formal world-state interface to coherently propagate state changes through prompts. Some future states cannot be inferred directly from visible history due to occlusions or implicit dynamics. A benchmark and method that capture and manipulate an explicit state representation are needed to evaluate and improve controllable video continuation across diverse state categories.
AI.method: Statebench is a benchmark that tests continuations across three state categories: past-visible states, occluded-process states, and complex-transition states. Stateagent explicitly maintains an entity-state representation, updates it under the new prompt, grounds the predicted post-action state as a future end frame, and renders the next video.
AI.result: Experiments show a strong performance gain: all-case state score (SCS-All) increases from 45.2 to 69.3. The approach also benefits long-form story generation at the one-minute scale. Code is available at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/StateAgent.
AI.conclusion: The work identifies a core gap in video continuation—the need for an explicit world-state interface—and demonstrates that explicit state modeling with grounding to an end-frame video improves controllable continuation and story generation.

title: LLM4CKD: Large Language Models for Early Stage Chronic Kidney Disease Screening
summary: Early screening of chronic kidney disease (CKD) is critical for timely intervention, yet most machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches require labeled data and model training, limiting their use in real-world screening settings. This study evaluates the effectiveness of large language models (LLMs) for CKD screening under zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning settings and compares them with traditional ML and DL methods. We propose a framework that uses clinically selected tabular features and structured prompt templates to enable LLM-based inference without task-specific training. LLM performance is evaluated across multiple prompt styles, feature configurations, and data settings, and compared with standard ML, DL, and tabular foundation model (TFM) baselines, and existing CKD screening tools. The results show that LLMs can achieve competitive performance using only a small number of examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings. However, their performance remains model-dependent and less stable as input complexity increases. In contrast, ML, DL, and TFM models show more consistent improvement with larger training data. Overall, the findings highlight a trade-off between data efficiency and stability, suggesting that LLMs may serve as a flexible complementary approach for CKD screening when labeled data are limited.

AI.tldr: LLMs enable zero-shot/few-shot CKD screening via structured prompts and selected tabular features, achieving competitive results in data-scarce settings and offering a flexible complement to traditional ML/DL/TFM methods; stability declines with input complexity, while conventional models improve with more data.
AI.motivation: To reduce reliance on labeled data and model training for CKD screening by leveraging in-context learning of LLMs, enabling effective screening in real-world, low-data environments.
AI.method: A framework that uses clinically selected tabular features and structured prompt templates for LLM-based inference without task-specific training; evaluation across multiple prompt styles, feature configurations, and data settings; comparative analysis against standard ML, DL, tabular foundation model (TFM) baselines, and existing CKD screening tools.
AI.result: LLMs achieve competitive performance with few-shot examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings; performance is model-dependent and less stable as input complexity increases; ML, DL, and TFM models show more consistent improvement with larger training data.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can serve as a flexible complementary approach for CKD screening when labeled data are limited, balancing data efficiency and stability, rather than replacing traditional methods; they are best used to augment conventional screening pipelines in data-scarce scenarios.

title: Neural-Network Maxent: a general extension with learned nonlinearity, applied to time-series for Desert Locust distribution modelling
summary: Species Distribution Modelling (SDM) is essential for understanding how environmental conditions shape biodiversity, particularly for destructive pests such as the Desert Locust (Schistocerca gregaria), whose breeding dynamics are tightly coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions. Maxent has become the dominant method for presence-only data, but its reliance on a linear combination of hand chosen feature transforms limits its ability to capture the nonlinear, temporal relationships common in ecological monitoring, where covariates such as precipitation, soil moisture, and vegetation indices evolve meaningfully over time. Standard implementations flatten time-series covariates into independent features, discarding sequential structure that carries critical signal. We introduce RNN Maxent, an extension of the Maxent framework that replaces the fixed feature dictionary with a neural network, specifically a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), trained end to end via backpropagation. The approach preserves Maxent's presence only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, differing only in that the nonlinearity is learned from data rather than fixed in advance. We apply RNN Maxent to map suitable habitat for the Desert Locust using 50 day environmental time series derived from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, maintaining a 7 day gap between covariates and presence records to yield forecasting behavior. Compared against standard Maxent, RNN Maxent improves performance across metrics (ROC AUC 0.862 std 0.036 vs. 0.792; F1 0.671 std 0.056 vs. 0.590).

AI.tldr: RNN Maxent replaces fixed feature transforms in Maxent with a GRU-based neural network for presence-only SDM, improving Desert Locust habitat mapping by capturing nonlinear temporal dynamics.
AI.motivation: SDM with presence-only data is limited by linear feature transforms and loss of temporal structure in time-series covariates. Desert Locust outbreaks depend on rapidly changing environmental conditions; there is a need to preserve sequential information and nonlinear relationships to improve forecasting.
AI.method: An extension of Maxent where the feature dictionary is replaced by a GRU-based neural network trained end-to-end, preserving presence-only foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration. Uses 50-day time-series covariates from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3 with a 7-day lag between covariates and presence records to enable forecasting.
AI.result: RNN Maxent outperforms standard Maxent with ROC AUC 0.862 (std 0.036) versus 0.792, and F1 0.671 (std 0.056) versus 0.590 across metrics.
AI.conclusion: Integrating a GRU into Maxent yields superior prediction by learning temporal nonlinearities while maintaining the SDM framework, enabling improved forecasting of Desert Locust habitat suitability.

title: CoFiE: Coarse-to-Fine Evidence Selection for Efficient Streaming Video Understanding
summary: Streaming video understanding requires Vision Language Models (VLLMs) to process growing video streams and answer user questions under tight latency constraints. Existing methods improve efficiency through token pruning and memory-bank schemes, but mainly reduce visual tokens after visual encoding. Consequently, downstream token pruning alone cannot substantially reduce end-to-end latency because the expensive frame encoding cost has already been incurred. We propose CoFiE, a Coarse-to-Fine Evidence Selection framework that decouples evidence selection into a coarse, query-agnostic filtering stage before the vision encoder and a fine, query-specific refinement stage during LLM prefill. CoFiE introduces Novelty-Guided Frame Filtering to retain visually distinctive candidate frames and Query-Specific Evidence Refinement to select the frames most relevant to the user query. This design removes substantial redundancy before frame encoding while preserving query-specific refinement once semantic information becomes available. Experiments show that CoFiE establishes a new state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off across multiple video understanding benchmarks, reaching 78.86% accuracy on StreamingBench and 68.72% on OvO-Bench, with improvements of up to 3.15% over prior methods. Even with up to 80% evidence-frame filtering, CoFiE outperforms strong open-source multimodal models while improving end-to-end inference latency by up to 2.54 times.

AI.tldr: CoFiE introduces a coarse-to-fine evidence selection framework that filters frames before vision encoding and refines evidence during LLM prefill, achieving a superior accuracy-latency trade-off in streaming video understanding.
AI.motivation: Streaming video QA with strict latency: frame encoding dominates end-to-end cost, and post-encoding token pruning cannot sufficiently reduce latency. A pre-encoding, coarse evidence filter paired with query-specific refinement can cut encoding cost while preserving answer quality.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) novelty-guided frame filtering (coarse, query-agnostic) before the vision encoder to drop redundant frames; (2) query-specific evidence refinement during LLM prefill to select frames most relevant to the user query.
AI.result: New state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off on streaming video benchmarks: 78.86% on StreamingBench and 68.72% on OvO-Bench, with up to 3.15% absolute accuracy gains over prior methods. End-to-end inference latency improved by up to 2.54x, even with as high as 80% evidence-frame filtering.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling evidence selection into a coarse pre-encoder stage and a fine prefill stage reduces encoding redundancy and preserves query-aligned refinement, yielding substantial latency reductions without sacrificing accuracy across multiple benchmarks.

title: InSituMeasure: Probing Situated Measurement Grounding in Industrial Scenes with Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: For trained operators, gauge reading requires little specialized knowledge, low cognitive effort, and high repeatability. Yet Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) remain unreliable in continuous-valued measurement despite strong results on general multimodal benchmarks. Existing benchmarks expose this weakness but isolate measurement from realistic, knowledge-grounded settings, with limited situated context, specialized instruments, real-world noise, and matched diagnostic annotations, reducing realism and constraining root-cause analysis. We introduce InSituMeasure to evaluate situated measurement grounding. It contains 2,922 real industrial monitoring scenes across eight functional categories of professional engineering instruments, with dense gauge-attribute annotations and noise tags for failure diagnosis. We define metrics for numerical accuracy under predefined tolerances and unit consistency, rejection of fake or unanswerable tasks, and alignment between model failures and annotated error factors. Across 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs, the best model reaches only 25.7\% joint value-unit accuracy and 51.8\% confidence-diagnosis F1, revealing a substantial gap between general multimodal competence and reliable situated measurement. Further analysis identifies failures from text-induced shortcuts, overconfident responses, and authentic industrial noise, including mixed disturbances, viewpoint deviation, occlusion, and environmental interference.

AI.tldr: Introduces InSituMeasure, a realistic benchmark for situated gauge-reading with real industrial scenes; current MLLMs struggle (25.7% joint value-unit accuracy; 51.8% confidence-diagnosis F1).
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks lack realism for numerically grounded measurement tasks and fail to capture knowledge-grounded, noisy, context-rich settings; a realistic benchmark is needed to diagnose root causes and improve reliability of MLLMs in industrial measurement.
AI.method: Builds InSituMeasure dataset with 2,922 real industrial monitoring scenes across eight instrument categories, with dense gauge-attribute annotations and noise tags; defines metrics for numerical accuracy within tolerances, unit consistency, rejection of unanswerable tasks, and alignment between model failures and annotated error factors; evaluates 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs.
AI.result: Best model achieves 25.7% joint value-unit accuracy and 51.8% confidence-diagnosis F1, revealing a large gap between general multimodal capability and reliable situated measurement; analysis points to failures from text-induced shortcuts, overconfident responses, and authentic industrial noise (mixed disturbances, viewpoint deviation, occlusion, environmental interference).
AI.conclusion: The work highlights the need for robust grounded measurement in MLLMs and provides a realistic benchmark with diagnostic annotations to guide error analysis and model improvements.

title: On the Interaction Between Model Compression and Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Deep neural networks deployed in the wild must be both efficient and adaptable, requiring model compression and test-time adaptation (TTA). While both are well studied in isolation, their interaction remains poorly understood. We systematically analyze how structured compression affects a model's ability to adapt under distribution shift. Using ResNet-18 and ViT-Base on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C, we evaluate multiple compression methods combined with standard TTA techniques. We introduce a diagnostic framework that examines representational expressivity and adaptation subspace compatibility. Our results reveal a consistent gap: although compressed models retain high accuracy under supervised adaptation, their TTA performance degrades significantly with increasing compression. We show that this stems from reduced representational diversity and structural constraints that limit recoverability. These effects strongly depend on the compression method, highlighting the need to design compression strategies that preserve adaptability.

AI.tldr: Compressed models retain accuracy under supervised adaptation but show degraded test-time adaptation (TTA) performance as compression increases, due to reduced representational diversity and structural constraints; degradation is method-dependent.
AI.motivation: To understand how structured model compression interacts with test-time adaptation under distribution shift, addressing a gap in literature on combining efficiency and adaptability.
AI.method: Evaluate ResNet-18 and ViT-Base on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C with multiple structured compression methods and standard TTA techniques; develop a diagnostic framework assessing representational expressivity and adaptation subspace compatibility.
AI.result: Compression preserves supervised adaptation accuracy but degrades TTA performance increasingly with higher compression; degradation is linked to reduced representational diversity and constraints on recoverability, and effects vary by compression method.
AI.conclusion: Compression strategies should be designed to preserve adaptability; when deploying compressed models under distribution shift, TTA performance must be considered, and method choice is crucial for maintaining adaptability.

title: FLY-EVAL++: An Evidence-Driven Evaluation Protocol for Safety-Constrained Flight Prediction with Large Language Models
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026
summary: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) in safety-critical, physics-governed environments requires more than accuracy-based metrics, because predictions that are numerically close to the ground truth can still violate operational constraints, combine fields in physically inconsistent ways, or fail to produce usable structured outputs. Existing evaluation protocols do not measure these failure modes reliably. We propose FLY-EVAL++, an evidence-driven evaluation protocol that combines deterministic verification of protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety constraints with fixed rubric-guided aggregation into interpretable multi-dimensional scores. We instantiate FLY-EVAL++ for Flight Trajectory and Attitude Prediction (FTAP) by extending the PilotBench setting with history-conditioned and multi-step prediction tasks. Across 66 LLMs, safety compliance is the most discriminative dimension of model behavior: models with comparable predictive performance differ by more than 28 points in safety score, and we observe recurrent failures including safety violations under physically plausible predictions and instability in multi-step rollouts. These results show that evaluation in safety-critical domains should measure constraint satisfaction and structured validity explicitly rather than rely on accuracy-centric reporting alone.

AI.tldr: Proposes FLY-EVAL++, an evidence-driven, multi-dimensional evaluation protocol for LLM safety in physics-governed tasks, instantiated on FTAP with history-conditioned, multi-step predictions; finds safety compliance to be the most discriminative dimension among 66 LLMs, highlighting failures despite accurate predictions and arguing for constraint-based evaluation over accuracy alone.
AI.motivation: In safety-critical domains governed by physical constraints, evaluation should go beyond accuracy to verify protocol adherence, physical feasibility, and safety constraints.
AI.method: Deterministic verification of protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety constraints, combined with rubric-guided aggregation into interpretable multi-dimensional scores; instantiated on Flight Trajectory and Attitude Prediction (FTAP) by extending the PilotBench setting with history-conditioned and multi-step prediction tasks.
AI.result: Safety compliance dimension is the most discriminative; models with similar predictive performance differ by >28 points in safety score; recurrent safety violations under plausible predictions and instability in multi-step rollouts observed; demonstrates the necessity of evaluating constraint satisfaction and structured validity.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation for safety-critical domains should explicitly measure constraint satisfaction and structured validity, not rely on accuracy-centric reporting alone.

title: Local Updates, Global Learning (LUGL): Playing Games with non-incremental Learners
summary: The dominance of Neural Networks (NNs) in RL is partially due to their incremental learning capability, which naturally suits the online, non-stationary nature of self-play training. However, gradient-boosted trees like LightGBM are widely recognised as the state of the art for tabular data in supervised learning, often outperforming NNs in accuracy and efficiency. Game states are inherently tabular---discrete actions, categorical card identities, structured board positions---which makes them an ideal candidate for tree-based methods. We introduce LUGL (Local Updates, Global Learning), a framework that decouples data collection from model fitting, enabling non-incremental learners such as GBTs to operate in RL settings where they would otherwise fail due to distributional shift.
