LUGL alternates between a local updates phase, where the agent plays self-play games and accumulates tabular updates (Q-values, V-values, policies, or regret values) in a finite table, and a global learning phase, where the table is used to train a function approximator that generalises to unseen states before the table is reset. We test our approach in four standard perfect-information games (Tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, Othello, and Hex) and five imperfect-information games (Kuhn's poker, Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel, and Flop5 Hold'em), and show that our results are competitive with or superior to DQN and DeepCFR. Our experiments demonstrate that the community's strong bias towards NNs in game-playing may be unwarranted, since LightGBM-based agents achieve competitive or superior performance across all tested benchmarks.

AI.tldr: LUGL uses Local Updates and Global Learning to enable gradient-boosted trees in RL by decoupling data collection from model fitting; achieves competitive/superior performance to NN-based baselines across nine board-game benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To overcome the online non-stationary distribution in RL self-play and show that tabular/GBT methods can match NN-based approaches in game-playing, challenging NN-dominance.
AI.method: Alternates between local updates collecting tabular Q/V/policy/regret values in a finite table during self-play and a global learning phase training a function approximator (LightGBM) from the table, then resetting the table; evaluated on four perfect-information and five imperfect-information games; compares to DQN and Deep CFR.
AI.result: LightGBM-based agents achieve competitive or superior performance relative to DQN and Deep CFR across all tested games.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that strong NN bias in game-playing is not strictly necessary; tabular/GBT-based RL with a decoupled data-collection pipeline is viable and effective in diverse game settings.

title: Instruction Duplication as an Inference-Time Control Primitive
comment: 7 pages, 2 tables. Code and frozen reproduction artifacts: https://github.com/victorlavrenko/answer-engineering/releases/tag/instruction-duplication-arxiv-v1
summary: Procedural instruction following is a basic requirement for controllable language-model systems, especially when generated trajectories are inspected or repaired downstream. We introduce instruction duplication, a minimal black-box inference-time control that repeats only the procedural instruction, without retraining or decoding changes. Across seven instruction-tuned models, 300 medical multiple-choice questions, eight placement conditions, and 16,800 scheduled generations, moving from one to two copies raises the deterministic All-8 diagnostic--responses passing all eight observable tests--from 90.22% to 93.17% (+2.95 percentage points), eliminating 30.2% of the failures remaining after one copy. Pre-provisional TF-IDF recall rises from 73.44% to 74.81% (+1.38 points; Holm-adjusted p < .001), while final-answer accuracy remains exactly 60.21%. Premature commitment increases from 1.52% to 2.30% (p_Holm = .00536). A blinded challenge audit yields 10/30 directional confirmations, 20/30 perceptual ties, and no reversals; its prespecified 28/30 confirmation criterion is not met. Yet this distinction can matter operationally when a downstream system acts on the generated trajectory. In Answer Engineering (AE), where explicit trajectory state determines local repair, the published reason-first no-editing SSNHL endpoint was 25.1%; system-only AE was later reproduced at 84.2%, and the same trailing duplicate raised it to 97.1%. For conductive diagnostic branch preservation, the corresponding values are 58.9% published without editing, 78.6% with reproduced AE, and 73.8% with AE plus duplication--a within-AE decrease, but still 14.9 points above the no-editing baseline. Instruction duplication is therefore a low-complexity, placement-sensitive control whose practical value can emerge through the downstream system that consumes the exposed trajectory.

AI.tldr: Inference-time instruction duplication increases determinism and downstream control by repeating only the procedural instruction; yields modest improvements in All-8 and recall across models, with mixed effects on other metrics; value depends on downstream trajectory consumers.
AI.motivation: Enhance controllability and reliability of instruction-tuned LMs during trajectory generation without retraining or decoding changes, by a minimal black-box intervention at inference.
AI.method: Apply a second copy of the procedural instruction at inference across seven instruction-tuned models, 300 medical MCQs, eight placement conditions, and 16,800 generations; measure All-8 success, TF-IDF recall, final-answer accuracy, premature commitment, blinded challenge audit, and Answer Engineering endpoints.
AI.result: All-8 pass rate rises 90.22% to 93.17% (+2.95 pp); recall 73.44% to 74.81% (+1.38 pp; Holm-adjusted p < .001); final-answer accuracy remains 60.21%; premature commitment 1.52% to 2.30% (p_Holm = .00536); blinded audit yields 10/30 directional confirmations, 20/30 perceptual ties, no reversals; prespecified 28/30 criterion not met; Answer Engineering (AE) endpoint 25.1% (no-editing published SSNHL); reproduced at 84.2%, and with duplication 97.1%; conductive diagnostic branch: 58.9% published without editing, 78.6% reproduced AE, 73.8% with AE+duplication (within-AE decrease but 14.9 points above no-editing baseline).
AI.conclusion: Instruction duplication is a low-complexity, placement-sensitive control whose practical value emerges when the downstream system consumes the exposed trajectory; beneficial for certain endpoints but not a universal fix, with context-dependent gains and some metrics unchanged or worse.

title: Extracting Forgotten Prompts from Targeted Unlearned Models
summary: Recent unlearning methods (e.g. NPO, DPO, LUNAR) make use of refusal alignment to suppress forgotten data. However, it has been shown that refusal responses might leave traces of unlearning, and recent attacks have been able to successfully recover some of the unlearned knowledge. In this paper, we uncover a new vulnerability. Existing attacks typically assume that the forgotten prompts are already known to the adversary and focus on recovering their answers. However, we show that the forgotten prompts themselves can be extracted by using the retained data and black-box access to the model. Our attack, Targeted Active Search (TAS), first identifies the forgotten entities by constructing canonical templates and entity pool, and selectively querying the model using the most informative template-entity pair under a limited query budget. Once the entities are identified, TAS instantiates prompt templates with those entities to probe the unlearned model and reconstruct the forgotten prompts. Experiments across three unlearning methods with three datasets and three LLMs shows that TAS recovers the forgotten entity with $100\%$ accuracy and reconstructs up to $95\%$ of forgotten prompts, all while using up to $99.7\%$ fewer queries than naive probing.

AI.tldr: A new active attack (TAS) can extract forgotten prompts from unlearning models by leveraging retained data and black-box access, achieving full recovery of forgotten entities and up to 95% prompt reconstruction with substantial query efficiency.
AI.motivation: Refusal-based unlearning methods may leave traces; prior attacks assume forgotten prompts/entities are known. This work shows prompts themselves can be extracted, enabling reconstruction of forgotten knowledge.
AI.method: Targeted Active Search (TAS) builds canonical templates and an entity pool, then selectively queries the model with the most informative template-entity pairs under a limited budget to identify forgotten entities. After identification, it instantiates prompt templates with those entities to probe and reconstruct forgotten prompts.
AI.result: TAS recovers the forgotten entity with 100% accuracy and reconstructs up to 95% of forgotten prompts, using up to 99.7% fewer queries than naive probing across three unlearning methods, three datasets, and three LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Prompt leakage poses a serious risk to unlearning systems; TAS demonstrates an effective attack requiring only retained data and black-box access. Defenses should go beyond refusal strategies to mitigate prompt extraction and prompt-level leakage.

title: ToPO: Token-Conditioned Preference Routing for Attention-Based Latent Diffusion Models
summary: Pairwise preference labels rank complete images, yet Diffusion-DPO applies their effect over many spatial and denoising-time coordinates. For attention-based, noise-prediction latent diffusion, ToPO (Token-Oriented Preference Optimization) constructs a per-minibatch, detached, separable spatial-temporal route from branchwise squared-residual contrast in a frozen reference denoiser. Preferred-branch cross-attention uses content tokens to modulate the spatial factor, and an auxiliary pixel-midpoint ordering term is added without local labels or a learned reward model. In matched three-seed retrainings with a shared update schedule, ToPO has higher endpoint estimates than Diffusion-DPO on all five reported SD-1.5 metrics and on HPSv2, ImageReward, and CLIP for SDXL. It also receives larger raw win shares in an aggregate blind SDXL A/B study. These findings are scoped to the reported equal-update U-Net protocols rather than an equal-compute comparison.

title: IRWOZ 2.0: A Large Language Model-driven Dialogue Dataset for Industrial Robot Conversations
summary: IRWOZ has improved industrial human-robot interaction (HRI) dialogue systems through domain-specific annotations. However, its initial version contains substantial noise in dialogue states and utterances, limiting state-tracking accuracy. We introduce IRWOZ 2.0, which addresses these limitations through large language model (LLM) enhanced generation (Mistral/Claude-3.5) and quality refinements. Our improved dataset expands to 390 dialogues across 4 industrial domains (Assembly, Delivery, Position, Relocation), featuring manual corrections and automated typo removal. Benchmark experiments on dialogue state tracking demonstrate significant improvements, with GPT-2's BLEU-4 score increasing from 0.1651 to 0.5604 compared to original IRWOZ. To support industrial HRI research, we publicly released IRWOZ 2.0 dataset at https://ieee-dataport.org/documents/irwoz-20-large-language-model-driven-dialogue-dataset-industrial-robot-conversations

AI.tldr: IRWOZ 2.0 uses LLM-driven data generation and manual/ automated refinements to reduce noise in industrial HRI dialogues, expanding to 390 dialogues over 4 domains; yields large BLEU-4 gains on GPT-2 and better state-tracking, with public release.
AI.motivation: Address substantial noise in dialogue states and utterances in the original IRWOZ that limited state-tracking accuracy in industrial HRI dialogues.
AI.method: Enhance generation with large language models (Mistral/Claude-3.5) and perform quality refinements (manual corrections, automated typo removal). Expand dataset to 390 dialogues across Assembly, Delivery, Position, Relocation domains. Evaluate using dialogue-state-tracking benchmarks with GPT-2/ BLEU-4.
AI.result: BLEU-4 on GPT-2 rises from 0.1651 (original IRWOZ) to 0.5604 (IRWOZ 2.0), indicating substantial improvement in generation quality and state-tracking signals; dataset publicly released at IEEE Dataport.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven generation and rigorous quality refinement can markedly improve industrial HRI dialogue datasets and state-tracking performance; IRWOZ 2.0 provides a valuable resource for industrial-domain dialogue research.

title: Out-of-Distribution Generalisation with Sequence Models in Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Generalising to unseen tasks remains a fundamental challenge in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). In this work, we present a principled analysis of zero-shot task generalisation in the offline setting and conduct an extensive empirical investigation into the scaling behaviour governing task diversity, dataset size, and network capacity. To facilitate this study, we extend offline sequence modelling architectures to handle multi-task observation and action spaces alongside variable agent counts across tasks. Our primary finding is that scaling task diversity---rather than sheer dataset size is the dominant factor in achieving robust zero-shot transfer. Through large-scale experiments across four challenging environments (Connector, RWARE, SMAX, and LBF), we demonstrate that our multi-task approach achieves a mean improvement of 3.2x on held-out test tasks compared to single-task models and consistently outperforms strong behaviour cloning baselines. These results suggest that the development of generalisable MARL agents should prioritise the diversity of the training distribution with varying numbers of agents, providing a roadmap for scaling offline MARL effectively.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot task generalisation in offline MARL is dominated by task diversity over dataset size; multi-task sequence modelling with varying agent counts yields substantial transfer gains, outperforming single-task models and BC baselines across four environments.
AI.motivation: Understand how offline MARL generalises to unseen tasks; quantify scaling with task diversity, dataset size, and network capacity; enable multi-task handling of observations/actions and different agent counts.
AI.method: Extend offline sequence modelling architectures to multi-task settings with heterogeneous observation/action spaces and variable agent counts; conduct large-scale empirical evaluation across four environments; compare multi-task models to single-task and behaviour cloning baselines.
AI.result: Scaling task diversity yields the strongest improvement in zero-shot transfer; multi-task models outperform single-task and BC baselines, achieving a mean 3.2x improvement on held-out tasks across Connector, RWARE, SMAX, and LBF.
AI.conclusion: Prioritize diversity in the training distribution—varying numbers of agents—to build generalisable offline MARL agents; the work provides a scalable roadmap for extending offline MARL via task-diversity-driven training.

title: Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model for WSI Classification in Histopathology
summary: Histopathological subtyping relies on the recognition of characteristic histological patterns. These patterns may be expressed by individual tissue structures or by the spatial distribution and co-occurrence of multiple structures, and they often span irregularly shaped tissue regions, termed semantic units in this work. However, conventional patch-based representations may fragment such units and fail to explicitly preserve their internal spatial organization, while efficiently modeling relationships among numerous spatially separated units remains challenging. To address these limitations, we propose the Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model (SASG-SSM), a flexible and efficient framework for whole slide image (WSI) classification. Semantic-Aware Subgraphs (SASGs) first approximate irregularly shaped semantic units by adaptively grouping spatially connected patches guided by class-agnostic visual-semantic priors. By representing patches as graph nodes with adjacency edges, SASGs preserve their internal spatial organization rather than treating them as an unordered set. A Subgraph State Space Module (SG-SSM) subsequently combines a graph neural network encoder for intra-subgraph topology encoding with a Mamba-based state space encoder for efficient contextualization across large numbers of subgraphs. This module integrates local structural information within semantic units with global contextual information arising from their distribution and co-occurrence across the WSI, while efficiently modeling a large number of spatially distributed regions. Extensive experiments across four WSI subtyping datasets demonstrate consistent advantages over representative state-of-the-art methods. Further evaluations under small-cohort and few-shot settings demonstrate robustness and data efficiency under limited training data. Code will be released at https://github.com/HLSvois/SASG-SSM.

AI.tldr: Introduces Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model (SASG-SSM) for whole-slide image classification that preserves internal spatial structure of semantic units via semantic-aware subgraphs and combines intra-subgraph GNN encoding with a scalable state-space module to model global context across many subgraphs; achieves state-of-the-art performance and data efficiency.
AI.motivation: Patch-based WSIs often fragment irregular semantic units and fail to preserve their internal spatial organization; modeling relationships among numerous spatially distributed units is computationally challenging. A flexible framework is needed to retain local structure and scale to large WSIs with many regions.
AI.method: Construct Semantic-Aware Subgraphs (SASGs) by adaptively grouping spatially connected patches using class-agnostic visual-semantic priors. Represent patches as graph nodes with edges to preserve local topology. Use a Subgraph State Space Module (SG-SSM) combining a graph neural network (GNN) encoder for intra-subgraph topology with a Mamba-based state-space encoder for efficient contextualization across a large set of subgraphs, integrating local and global information across the WSI.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on four WSI subtyping datasets shows consistent advantages over representative state-of-the-art methods; robust and data-efficient in small-cohort and few-shot settings; code to be released at the given repository.
AI.conclusion: SASG-SSM provides a flexible and efficient WSI classification framework that preserves the spatial organization of semantic units while scaling to large numbers of subgraphs, yielding strong performance and robustness in data-limited scenarios.

title: Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely studied for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where its advantage estimator assigns each rollout a magnitude from within-group reward statistics. In the common case, this magnitude rewards rollouts that reach the correct answer through reasoning. Yet, an overlooked case shares the same surface: a rollout may land on it by guessing, and the formula still assigns a high magnitude, which we identify as the spurious advantage. This arises in three cases: bounded-answer tasks with a small candidate set; open-answer sets hosting bounded sub-cases; and search agents whose budget opens many paths to the same answer. In all three, this misleads the policy toward guess-like behaviors. We propose SIGNBALANCE, whose magnitude is composition-free: it keeps the verifier sign, uses a global scale, and restores zero-mean balance via a stop-gradient per-class rescaling. Across math and search agent benchmarks at different scales, SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math and improves on bounded-answer math and search agents. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: Identifies spurious advantage in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) where guessing yields high magnitude; proposes SIGNBALANCE to make the magnitude composition-free, using a per-class stop-gradient rescaling and a global scale; shows SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math and improves performance on bounded-answer math and search agents; code to be released.
AI.motivation: GRPO's advantage estimator can overestimate the value of rollouts that reach the correct answer by guessing, due to within-group reward statistics. This spurious signal biases policies toward guess-like behavior, especially in bounded or multi-path settings.
AI.method: Introduce SIGNBALANCE: a composition-free magnitude estimator that (1) keeps the verifier sign, (2) applies a global scale, and (3) restores zero-mean balance via per-class stop-gradient rescaling.
AI.result: SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math tasks and outperforms GRPO on bounded-answer math and on search-agent benchmarks across scales.
AI.conclusion: SIGNBALANCE mitigates spurious advantage in GRPO by removing composition from the magnitude and balancing class-wise signals, yielding robust performance and broad applicability; code will be released.

title: Resolution-Aware Experimental Design under Partial Identifiability
summary: Experimental design is commonly framed as choosing the experiment expected to provide the most information. Under partial identifiability however, persistent nuisance uncertainty can make the same observation carry different structural meanings. We introduce Resolution-Aware Experimental Design (RAED), which selects an experiment by the smallest expected nonempty structural candidate set achievable subject to false-exclusion control. We prove an exact cross-nuisance aliasing separation: an experiment can be preferred by structural and full-latent information gain, average classification, and nuisance-marginalized informativeness while having arbitrarily poorer valid structural resolution. RAED nevertheless preserves the expected ordering under a genuine composite Blackwell comparison. To make this criterion operational, we develop a learned score-based implementation with finite-sample nuisance-average and positive-tail calibration, and characterize a rare-tail sample-complexity obstruction. Under constrained sensing, two subsurface-flow benchmarks exhibit genuine RAED--expected-information-gain (EIG) experiment-selection disagreements, with the clearest and largest held-out resolution differences in WCA. In a fluvial benchmark, tail protection changes the selected physical experiment and replaces hard-region false exclusions primarily with explicit ambiguity. In a mechanistic methane-oxidation benchmark, a prospectively specified 5\% false-exclusion tolerance also yields a nontrivial finite-sample population guarantee for tail-sensitive nuisance risk, with 95\% joint confidence across all three structural families.

AI.tldr: Introduces Resolution-Aware Experimental Design (RAED) to select experiments under partial identifiability by minimizing the expected nonempty structural candidate set subject to false-exclusion control; establishes exact cross-nuisance aliasing separation and develops a calibrated score-based implementation; demonstrates disagreement with traditional information-gain criteria under constrained sensing across benchmarks, with finite-sample guarantees and tail-awareness.
AI.motivation: Partial identifiability and persistent nuisance uncertainty create multiple structural interpretations of observations; standard information-theoretic criteria may mis-order experiments when nuisance effects are prominent. RAED targets minimal residual structural ambiguity under controlled false exclusions.
AI.method: Propose RAED: select experiments by minimizing the expected size of the nonempty structural candidate set under a false-exclusion constraint; prove exact cross-nuisance aliasing separation ensuring consistent ordering under composite Blackwell comparisons; develop a learned score-based estimator with finite-sample nuisance-average calibration and positive-tail calibration, and analyze a rare-tail sample-complexity obstruction; apply under constrained sensing to benchmark problems.
AI.result: RAED preserves the expected ordering under genuine composite Blackwell comparisons; in constrained-sensing benchmarks across subsurface flow, fluvial, and methane-oxidation domains, RAED yields different, apparently more resolution-aware selections than EIG, with tail-protection shifting selections and ambiguity replacement; in the methane-oxidation case, a 5% false-exclusion tolerance yields finite-sample population guarantees for tail-sensitive nuisance risk, with 95% joint confidence across three structural families.
AI.conclusion: RAED delivers an operational, tail-aware experimental-design criterion that explicitly accounts for structural resolution and nuisance uncertainty, offering cases where traditional EIG-based selection diverges and providing finite-sample guarantees under bounded false-exclusion tolerance.

title: MetaStructAtlas: A Grounded 3D Vision-Language Dataset and Benchmark for Functional and Structural Reasoning in Whole-Body PET/CT
summary: The joint interpretation of metabolic function and anatomical structure is essential for clinical diagnosis in whole-body PET/CT. Although recent advances in 3D medical vision-language models have demonstrated remarkable progress, current efforts are limited to regional CT imaging, leaving a critical void in comprehensive whole-body PET/CT analysis. In this work, we introduce MetaStructAtlas, a large-scale dataset for grounded whole-body PET/CT interpretation that synthesizes multimodal imaging with integrated anatomical, metabolic, and semantic annotations. MetaStructAtlas provides 490 co-registered 3D PET and CT volumes with 50,470 organ-level segmentation masks and grounded radiology reports. To facilitate interactive reasoning, we further developed MetaStructVQA, a standardized 3D grounded visual question-answering benchmark containing 100,565 QA pairs. This framework explicitly links diagnostic queries to visual evidence across modalities, encompassing anatomical, morphological, and metabolic characteristics. Finally, we evaluate state-of-the-art 3D medical VLMs on MetaStructVQA, establishing a robust foundation for multimodal representation learning and integrated whole-body reasoning in nuclear medicine.

AI.tldr: MetaStructAtlas and MetaStructVQA establish a large-scale, fully grounded, whole-body PET/CT dataset with 490 co-registered volumes, ~50k organ masks, and 100k QA pairs, enabling 3D multimodal reasoning across anatomy, morphology, and metabolism; results include baseline evaluation of 3D medical VLMs on the QA benchmark.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of existing 3D medical models to regional CT by providing a comprehensive whole-body PET/CT resource with integrated anatomical, metabolic, and semantic annotations to support interactive reasoning and multimodal representation learning in nuclear medicine.
AI.method: Construct MetaStructAtlas with co-registered PET/CT volumes, organ-level segmentation masks, and grounded reports; develop MetaStructVQA as a 3D grounded VQA benchmark with QA pairs linked to multimodal visual evidence; evaluate state-of-the-art 3D medical VLMs on MetaStructVQA.
AI.result: Provided dataset and benchmark; demonstrated feasibility of grounding QA across modalities; established baselines on 3D VLMs for whole-body multimodal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: MetaStructAtlas and MetaStructVQA lay a robust foundation for multimodal whole-body interpretation in nuclear medicine and enable future research in integrated diagnosis, reporting, and interactive imaging analysis.

title: DRACO: Fine-Grained Credit Assignment with Dynamic Rubrics for Long-Horizon Agent Training
summary: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards works well when a task has a programmatic checker, but most long-horizon agent domains have none. We work in the outcome-blind setting, where ground-truth success signals are not available. Multi-criteria rubrics are a popular way to supply such a reward; they are scored once per trajectory, but a single scalar is a poor signal across tens of steps. We propose DRACO: Distributing Rubric-based Advantage for Credit Optimization. It generates rubrics dynamically during training to track the policy's evolving capability, scores those rubrics once per completed trajectory, and redistributes that judgment over the steps responsible for annotated rubrics to produce differentiated per-step advantages in GRPO. The redistribution is closed-form and does not introduce any trained attribution module. On AppWorld, DRACO gains 15.9 points over the base model and 5.3 points over GRPO trained with a sparse ground-truth reward, despite not using any verifiers itself. On out-of-domain Tau-Bench, it gains 5.3 points over the base model even without a frontier judge, beating both ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based training settings. The code for DRACO is available at https://github.com/IBM/draco.

AI.tldr: DRACO distributes dynamically generated rubric-based judgments across the time steps that contributed to them, enabling per-step credit assignment in long-horizon RL without verifiers.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon tasks often lack verifiable success signals. A single rubric score per trajectory struggles to provide learning signal across many steps; rubrics alone can be insufficient without proper credit assignment.
AI.method: Dynamically generate rubrics during training; score each completed trajectory once; redistributes that trajectory-level judgment over the steps responsible for annotated rubrics via a closed-form, train-free attribution; integrate with GRPO (policy optimization).
AI.result: In AppWorld, DRACO yields +15.9 points over the base model and +5.3 points over GRPO with sparse ground-truth reward; in Tau-Bench, DRACO yields +5.3 points over the base model and outperforms ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based settings; code available at IBM/draco.
AI.conclusion: DRACO enables effective credit assignment in rubric-based, outcome-blind RL by dynamically adapting rubrics and analytically redistributing rewards, improving performance without requiring verifiers.

title: Federated Causal Discovery via Regression-Directed Cumulants
comment: Accepted at the 12th International Conference on Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGM 2026)
summary:
In this paper we study linear non-Gaussian acyclic models (LiNGAM) when used in federated environments. These causal models allow one to go beyond Markov equivalence. However, in many domains data are scarce, and increasing the sample size by centralising data from different clients is not advisable due to regulations such as the GDPR. The federated environment offers an attractive option to balance privacy and causal discovery accuracy. Unfortunately, the standard centralised estimator in the LiNGAM setting, i.e., DirectLiNGAM, cannot be straightforwardly federated. Higher-order cumulant tensors offer a way around this obstacle: they depend only on the joint distribution of the variables involved and add exactly across independent sample groups, so a single communication round suffices in horizontal, vertical, and hybrid partitions.
  However, FedISHC, i.e., the current federated method along these lines, breaks down under near-symmetric noise. To overcome the above limitation, we introduce the FedRCD family of causal discovery algorithms, and investigate three variants that trade off communication rounds against algebraic noise; two of them are exact federated counterparts of the centralised high-order cumulant (HC) and HC-LiNGAM algorithms, and the single-round variants further effectively support exact unlearning at any granularity, from a single observation to a whole client. Numerical experiments show that at sample sizes typical of real deployments, the entire cumulant-based federated family does not actually rank variables by the population asymmetry that the scores encode at zero. It ranks them by a variance ladder induced by the DAG along its directed paths, the cumulant counterpart of varsortability. Marginal standardisation collapses every cumulant method to near-random ordering, while scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM, not federable under this protocol, is unaffected.

AI.tldr: Federated LiNGAM using high-order cumulants to enable privacy-preserving causal discovery; introduces FedRCD with three variants, addressing FedISHC limitations, but observes ranking by a DAG-induced variance rather than population asymmetry; marginal standardisation harms performance, and scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM remains non-federable under this protocol.
AI.motivation: Enable causal discovery with LiNGAM in privacy-regulated federated settings without centralising data; circumvent centralised DirectLiNGAM limitations using high-order cumulants that compose across independent sample groups.
AI.method: Develop FedRCD family with three variants; two exact federated counterparts of centralised HC and HC-LiNGAM; single-round variants allow exact unlearning; applicable to horizontal, vertical, and hybrid partitions; evaluate under near-symmetric noise scenario (FedISHC weakness).
AI.result: Cumulant-based federated methods fail to rank variables by population asymmetry as intended; ranking aligns with a variance ladder along DAG paths (cumulant varsortability). Marginal standardisation collapses performance to near random; scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM is unaffected but not federable under this protocol.
AI.conclusion: While the FedRCD family enables privacy-preserving federated causal discovery, its variable ranking mechanism via cumulants is flawed in typical sample regimes; standardisation and non-federable scale-invariant variants limit practicality. Further refinement is needed to recover population-asymmetry-based ranking and robust unlearning in federated LiNGAM.

title: Observation-Conditioned Latent Energy Priors for Sparse Implicit Neural Shape Completion
comment: Accepted for publication in the MICCAI 2026 Workshop Proceedings (LNCS) as part of Off-Grid, the 1st Workshop on Continuous Representations and Grid-Free Methods in Medical Imaging. 12 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) can model continuous 3D shapes with a shared coordinate decoder and per-instance latent codes. At test time, autodecoder-style models commonly freeze the decoder and optimize a new latent code from sparse off-grid SDF samples. When these samples underconstrain inference, the latent can drift toward regions that fit the observations but decode implausible unobserved geometry. We propose a post-hoc observation-conditioned latent energy prior for frozen INR decoders. The energy scores standardized latents conditioned on a permutation-invariant encoding of the sparse observation set and is used as a residual expert alongside an L2 latent prior selected on validation data. We evaluate on a controlled cell-nucleus SDF dataset and a public MedShapeNet-derived SDF completion dataset. The proposed L2 objective augmented with conditional energy improves consistently over a validation-selected L2 baseline in the sparsest cell-nucleus regimes and, on MedShapeNet, outperforms both L2 and a six-component GMM latent-density prior across all reported readouts. A shuffled-context ablation is consistently weaker than matched context, supporting an observation-specific contribution. These results suggest that lightweight conditional energies can make pretrained INR decoders more observation-aware without retraining.

AI.tldr: Post-hoc observation-conditioned latent energy priors are added to frozen INR decoders to regularize latent optimization under sparse observations, improving reconstruction quality without retraining.
AI.motivation: Underconstrained latent inference in autodecoder-style INRs leads to drift to geometries that fit observations but are implausible for unobserved regions; a lightweight, non-retraining prior is needed to make decoders more observation-aware.
AI.method: Introduce a post-hoc energy-based prior: latent scores conditioned on a permutation-invariant encoding of the sparse observation set; normalize as a residual expert alongside an L2 latent prior; select the L2 scale via validation; evaluate on a controlled cell-nucleus SDF dataset and MedShapeNet-derived SDF completion dataset; include ablations with shuffled context.
AI.result: The conditional energy-augmented L2 objective consistently improves over a validation-selected L2 baseline in the sparsest regimes; on MedShapeNet, it outperforms both L2 and a six-component GMM latent-density prior across reported readouts; shuffled-context ablations are weaker than matched-context, supporting observation-specific contribution.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight conditional energies can make pretrained INR decoders more observation-aware without retraining.

title: Why Gated DeltaNet Survives 4-Bit Quantization: NVFP4 W4A4 for the Recurrent Half of a Hybrid 27B LLM
summary: Hybrid LLMs pair softmax attention with linear-attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), whose recurrent state summarizes the context in fixed size. Early community 4-bit quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B (48 GDN layers, 16 attention layers) left the GDN block in 8- or 16-bit precision -- especially its decay and write-strength gates -- on the intuition that errors in a recurrence accumulate over long contexts. We test that intuition by building Minima: NVFP4 W4A4 on all 496 linear layers, GDN included. Across perplexity at 4K/32K, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, AIME'25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench, and RULER retrieval to 64K, Minima matches BF16 within seed noise (5-task average -0.52) while being the smallest (17.5 GiB) and fastest-prefill (+14-19%) recipe we compare, and its 32K perplexity gap shrinks with position. A four-part mechanism study explains why: (i) NVFP4's 16-element block scaling localizes the residual stream's extreme outliers, equalizing activation error across layer roles; (ii) the supposedly fragile gate projections are the least sensitive -- softplus/exponential and sigmoid parameterizations compress ~11% GEMM error to ~2% output error; (iii) the delta-rule recurrence holds injected noise at a flat plateau over 32K tokens and forgets a state impulse within hundreds of steps, because each write overwrites the state along the current key direction; (iv) the per-token quantization cost washes out with context instead of compounding. We also repair a global-scale mismatch that arises when per-module-calibrated NVFP4 checkpoints are served by kernels that fuse those modules into one GEMM, and show calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales are performance-free. The result: a practical recipe -- quantize everything, ship KV scales -- and a mechanistic account of why the recurrent half of a hybrid LLM is the easy half to quantize. Checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/minima-ai/mnma_qwen3.8_27b_nvfp4

AI.tldr: Quantizing all 496 linear layers, including the GDN recurrent block, to NVFP4 W4A4 yields a compact, fast Minima model that matches BF16 performance within seed noise across multiple benchmarks, with a mechanistic explanation for why the recurrent half is robust to quantization.
AI.motivation: Test whether the recurrent GDN component in a hybrid LLM is as sensitive to extreme quantization as previously assumed, by pushing 4-bit precision onto the entire linear stack.
AI.method: Quantize all 496 linear layers to NVFP4 W4A4 (including GDN); evaluate perplexity at 4K and 32K, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, AIME'25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench, and RULER retrieval to 64K; compare against BF16; analyze a four-part mechanism; fix kernel-fusion mismatch; assess FP8 KV-cache scaling.
AI.result: Minima matches BF16 within seed noise (5-task average −0.52); smallest model at 17.5 GiB and fastest prefill (+14–19%) among the comparisons; 32K perplexity gap shrinks with position; four-part mechanism explains robustness: (i) 16-element NVFP4 block localizes residual outliers, equalizing layer error; (ii) fragile gate projections are surprisingly robust; (iii) delta-rule recurrence preserves noise at a plateau and forgets impulses quickly due to overwriting along current key direction; (iv) per-token quantization cost does not accumulate with context; remediation for a global-scale mismatch when per-module NVFP4 checkpoints are fused into a single GEMM; calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales are performance-free.
AI.conclusion: A practical recipe emerges: quantize everything and ship KV scales; the recurrent half of a hybrid LLM is the easier half to quantize, with a mechanistic understanding of why.

title: Projected Riemannian Gradient Descent for the Bures-Wasserstein Barycenter: Dimension-Independent Linear Convergence at Unit Step Size
summary: The computation of the Bures-Wasserstein (BW) barycenter of an ensemble of positive definite matrices arises throughout machine learning, optimal transport, and quantum information. Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) at unit step size -- the fixed-point iteration used in practice -- converges rapidly, yet existing analyses present a dichotomy: unit-step guarantees carry worst-case exponential dependence on the dimension, while dimension-independent guarantees require small step sizes that forfeit the empirical speed. We resolve this dichotomy, not by improving the guarantees for unit-step RGD, but by proposing a Projected RGD algorithm that achieves dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step size. The achieved rate, $(1 - κ^{-3/2})$, where $κ$ is the condition number of the ensemble, also polynomially improves on the best small-step guarantee ($κ^{3/2}$ versus $κ^{5/2}$ iteration complexity). The crux is a novel Projection Lemma: clipping the eigenvalues of a positive matrix to an interval $[α, β]$ is the closed-form, non-expansive (1-Lipschitz) BW-metric projection onto the set $\{S : αI \leq S \leq βI\}$ -- a statement which, unlike its known one-sided counterpart, does not follow from convexity. The projection is moreover free: it reuses an eigendecomposition the next iteration must perform in any case, so the projected and unprojected iterations cost the same per step. The same analysis covers the invariant matrix projection problem of Brahmachari et al. (2025), whose fixed-point algorithm we identify as unit-step RGD on a totally geodesic submanifold, thereby extending the dimension-independent guarantee to that setting verbatim.

AI.tldr: Projected Riemannian gradient descent with eigenvalue clipping achieves dimension-independent linear convergence for Bures-Wasserstein barycenters at unit step, with rate 1−κ^{−3/2}, and per-step cost equal to unprojected RG; extends to invariant matrix projection on totally geodesic submanifolds.
AI.motivation: To overcome the unit-step vs dimension-dependence dichotomy in BW barycenter optimization: unit-step RGD has exponential dimension dependence, while small-step guarantees are dimension-independent but slow. A projection-based approach aims to retain unit-step speed with dimension-independent convergence.
AI.method: Introduce a Projection Lemma: clipping eigenvalues of a positive matrix to [α,β] provides the closed-form, non-expansive BW-metric projection onto {S: αI ≤ S ≤ βI}. Use this projection in a Projected RGD algorithm, reusing the eigendecomposition each step so per-iteration cost matches unprojected RGD. Analyze convergence to obtain linear rate (1−κ^{−3/2}) with κ the ensemble condition number. Extend to invariant matrix projection problem by viewing its fixed-point as unit-step RGD on a totally geodesic submanifold.
AI.result: Proves dimension-independent linear convergence at unit-step for BW barycenters with rate 1−κ^{−3/2}; improves iteration complexity compared to small-step κ^{3/2} vs κ^{5/2}; shows the Projection Lemma yields a 1-Lipschitz BW projection, enabling the same per-iteration cost as unprojected RD. Also extends to Brahmachari et al.'s invariant projection problem.
AI.conclusion: The Projection Lemma enables a simple, cost-neutral projection step that preserves the fast unit-step iteration while achieving dimension-independent convergence, resolving the dichotomy and extending to related fixed-point problems on totally geodesic submanifolds.

title: SignSeek: Learning Transferable Representations for Sign Dictionary Retrieval
summary: Sign language dictionaries are essential resources for sign language learners, yet automatically retrieving a sign from a dictionary, given only a query video, remains a challenging problem due to the natural variability between signers. Existing sign representation learning methods are built for closed-set recognition, producing embeddings that do not generalise to the open-set, signer-independent setting that retrieval demands. \textbf{SignSeek} closes this gap by contrastively learning sign representations with saliency-guided articulator masking. A contrastive objective aligns same-gloss signs across signers, while our Articulator Saliency-Guided Masking (ASGM) pinpoints the single most critical articulator per sign. This drives two complementary objectives, a masked contrastive alignment (MAC) loss that sees the sign through a single articulator and a masked prediction (MAP) loss that reconstructs it in latent space from the surrounding spatio-temporal context. Pretrained on 266K samples ($\sim$5,700 glosses) across multiple sign languages, \textbf{SignSeek} sets a new state-of-the-art performance in cross-corpus retrieval on ASL-Citizen, WLASL, and NMFs-CSL without any downstream fine-tuning. Strikingly, it achieves zero-shot generalisation to an entirely unseen British Sign Language (BSL), surpassing methods explicitly trained on BSL, and transfers seamlessly to isolated sign recognition and subtitle alignment, outperforming prior skeleton-based methods.

AI.tldr: SignSeek uses saliency-guided articulator masking for cross-signer sign representation learning, achieving state-of-the-art open-set cross-corpus retrieval and zero-shot cross-linguistic generalization.
AI.motivation: Current sign-language representation methods are tailored to closed-set recognition and signer-dependent embeddings, hindering open-set, signer-independent retrieval across corpora and languages.
AI.method: Contrastive learning aligning same-gloss signs across signers; Articulator Saliency-Guided Masking (ASGM) identifies the single most critical articulator per sign. This yields a masked contrastive alignment (MAC) loss focusing on one articulator and a masked prediction (MAP) loss reconstructing the sign in latent space from surrounding spatio-temporal context. Pretraining on 266k samples (≈5,700 glosses) across multiple sign languages.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art cross-corpus retrieval on ASL-Citizen, WLASL, and NMFs-CSL without downstream fine-tuning; zero-shot generalisation to an unseen British Sign Language (BSL), outperforming methods trained on BSL; transfers to isolated sign recognition and subtitle alignment, outperforming prior skeleton-based methods.
AI.conclusion: SignSeek bridges the gap to open-set, signer-independent cross-corpus retrieval, demonstrating strong zero-shot and cross-linguistic generalization via ASGM and the MAC/MAP objective design.

title: Epistemic Warrant for LLM Recommendations: Characterizing the Basis for Reliance When Ground Truth Is Unavailable
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to support organizational decisions, yet users often lack a principled basis for assessing whether to rely on a specific recommendation. Existing approaches typically evaluate broad model properties, such as reliability, uncertainty, or robustness, or focus on user trust, rather than the underlying basis for relying on an individual recommendation. Adapting theoretical foundations from epistemology, we introduce epistemic warrant, a decision-level construct that characterizes the stability of a model's preference and the scope over which that preference holds. We operationalize this construct through a four-tier reliance certificate for pairwise recommendations, distinguishing among unstable, context-dependent, locally supported, and broadly supported recommendations. We validate the construct using contemporary methodologies: known-groups tests successfully recover expert-prespecified warrant orderings, and stronger warrants systematically align with independent consensus from crowd workers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that epistemic warrant provides information distinct from verbalized confidence and is not readily explained by decision difficulty. Ultimately, this framework offers a theoretically grounded, implementable approach for characterizing the warrant of individual LLM recommendations when objective ground truth is unavailable.

AI.tldr: Introduces epistemic warrant and a four-tier reliance certificate for LLM recommendations, validated against expert and crowd judgments, offering a decision-level, implementable basis for relying on individual outputs.
AI.motivation: Practitioners lack principled tools to judge whether to rely on a single LLM recommendation; existing metrics are broad or trust-focused and ignore the underlying basis for reliance on a specific item.
AI.method: Define epistemic warrant as stability of preference and its scope; operationalize as four-tier certificate: unstable, context-dependent, locally supported, broadly supported; use known-groups tests to recover expert orderings and crowd consensus to validate; distinguish warrant from confidence and decision difficulty.
AI.result: Epistemic warrant orders align with expert and crowd judgments; warrant provides information beyond verbal confidence and is not explained by decision difficulty.
AI.conclusion: Provides a theoretically grounded, implementable framework to characterize warrant of individual LLM recommendations when objective ground truth is unavailable.

title: From Nowcasting to Forecasting: Adapting a Reanalysis-Trained
summary: Accurate cloud-cover forecasts are important for temperature prediction, radiation forecasting, and solar-power operations. Short-range forecasting methods can preserve observed cloud placement during the first forecast hours, but their skill decreases when cloud fields evolve through formation, dissipation and deformation. Longer lead times require accounting for atmospheric evolution, but operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts may not accurately represent the satellite-observed cloud state at initialization. We develop CloudCast v2, a machine-learning model for 12-hour cloud-cover forecasting from observation-based initial conditions. The model is first trained on the Copernicus European Regional Reanalysis (Ridal2024) to learn cloud-evolution dynamics, and is then adapted to satellite-derived cloud fields using conditional flow matching (Lipman2023), a generative method that transforms noise into cloud-cover forecasts conditioned on the observed initial cloud fields and NWP inputs. CloudCast v2 reduces mean absolute error by 10% relative to its predecessor, CloudCast v1 (Partio2025), over the 1-12 h range. It also overtakes CloudCast v1 in fractions skill score, a neighborhood-based measure of spatial agreement, after approximately 3-6 h, depending on the cloudiness category. These results show that observation-initialized machine-learning forecasts can extend beyond the usual 1-3-hour nowcasting range while retaining spatial detail from satellite cloud fields.

AI.tldr: CloudCast v2 advances 12-h cloud-cover forecasting by conditioning a generative model on observed initial cloud fields and NWP data, trained on reanalysis and adapted to satellite clouds; it yields ~10% MAE improvement over CloudCast v1 and earlier spatial-skill gains after 3–6 h.
AI.motivation: Extend accurate cloud-cover forecasts beyond short-range nowcasting while preserving satellite-observed spatial structure, addressing initialization-model mismatch in operational NWP.
AI.method: Train on Copernicus European Regional Reanalysis to learn cloud-evolution dynamics; adapt to satellite-derived clouds using conditional flow matching to transform noise into forecasts conditioned on initial clouds and NWP inputs.
AI.result: Mean absolute error reduced by about 10% relative to CloudCast v1 over 1–12 h; fractions skill score surpasses v1 after ~3–6 h, depending on cloudiness category.
AI.conclusion: Observation-initialized ML forecasts can extend reliable cloud-cover predictions beyond 1–3 h while retaining high spatial fidelity from satellite observations; conditional flow matching enables effective assimilation of initial state and NWP information into 12-h forecasts.

title: Unfold The World: Factorize 4D Properties in Reinforcing Spatial Reasoning
summary: Despite the remarkable prowess of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in general multimodal tasks, they remain fundamentally ``flat'' when reasoning about the physical world. We argue that this spatial bottleneck stems from a profound dimensional mismatch: while VLMs are trained to interpret 2D projections, true spatial reasoning demands the recovery of latent 3D geometry and temporal continuity. To conquer this high-dimensional complexity, we advocate a shift from monolithic learning to a ``divide and conquer'' paradigm. We present FactoSR, a factorized reinforcement learning framework that explicitly interpret the dimensions collapsed by visual projection. At its core, FactoSR decomposes the monolithic problem of world-consistent reasoning into three orthogonal, geometric sub-objectives: planar correspondence ($XY$), depth consistency ($Z$), and temporal reversibility ($T$). By optimizing these verifiable constraints within a unified policy learning mechanism, we effectively transform an ill-posed projection recovery problem into a series of tangible reasoning steps. Extensive evaluations on multi-view and video benchmarks demonstrate that this elegant decomposition yields substantial gains in 3D and 4D reasoning, achieving a 5.9% boost on VSI-Bench and 4.5% on All-Angles-Bench. Our findings suggest that reinforcing explicit, factorized 4D consistency is a critical step toward evolving VLMs into robust, world-aware reasoners.

AI.tldr: FactoSR introduces a factorized RL approach to 3D/4D scene reasoning in Vision-Language Models by decomposing projected information into three orthogonal constraints: XY planar correspondence, Z depth consistency, and T temporal reversibility, turning projection recovery into verifiable steps.
AI.motivation: VLMs excel with 2D projections but lack robust spatial-temporal reasoning due to a dimensional mismatch between training (2D) and the target (3D/4D). A divide-and-conquer strategy—explicitly interpreting collapsed dimensions—can mitigate this ill-posedness and enhance world-aware reasoning.
AI.method: A factorized reinforcement learning framework (FactoSR) that splits the monolithic reasoning task into three geometric sub-objectives: XY planar correspondence, Z depth consistency, and T temporal reversibility. These constraints are optimized within a unified policy learning setup to achieve robust 4D consistency.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on multi-view and video benchmarks show substantial gains in 3D/4D reasoning, reporting a 5.9% improvement on VSI-Bench and a 4.5% improvement on All-Angles-Bench.
AI.conclusion: Explicit factorization of 4D consistency is a promising direction to evolve Vision-Language Models into robust, world-aware reasoners by converting projection recovery into tractable, verifiable steps.

title: Environment Evolution for Terminal Agents
summary: Scaling interactive and verifiable environments is critical for training terminal agents. As frontier models become more capable, environments synthesized from scratch become less challenging and thus provide limited learning signals. Recent co-evolution methods iteratively synthesize environments near the model's learnable frontier based on weaknesses exposed during rollouts. However, their dependence on on-policy rollouts limits generalization and the continuous provision of learning signals as the model becomes stronger. In this paper, we propose environment evolution, which incrementally increases environment difficulty off-policy and schedules the evolved environments generation by generation during training to provide continuous learning signals. We derive three evolution directions that influence environment difficulty from the multi-turn learning objective and then implement evolution along these directions through a loop-engineered multi-agent harness. Quantitative rollout experiments with Hy4 preview, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Sol show that environment evolution consistently produces more difficult environments. We validate its effectiveness on Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B through simple long-horizon RL training, improving their performance by 14.4 and 18.0 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, respectively.

AI.tldr: Proposes environment evolution to gradually increase environment difficulty off-policy across training generations, yielding stronger learning signals and improved terminal RL performance on large models.
AI.motivation: Current co-evolution relies on on-policy rollouts; as frontier models grow, environments generated from scratch become less challenging, reducing learning signals and limiting generalization.
AI.method: Derives three directions of environment difficulty from a multi-turn learning objective and implements these via a loop-engineered multi-agent harness that evolves environments generation-by-generation during training.
AI.result: Empirical rollout results show environment evolution produces consistently harder environments. In simple long-horizon RL training for Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, performance improves by 14.4 and 18.0 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Additional rollout experiments with Hy4 preview, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Sol corroborate increased difficulty of environments.
AI.conclusion: Environment evolution provides continuous learning signals and improves performance for frontier-model-based RL; off-policy, generation-based curriculum scheduling is effective for scaling interactive and verifiable environments.

title: OBER+: Continuity-Aware Reporting and Traceable Continuous Improvement in Outcome-Based Education
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies
summary: Institutions practising outcome-based education compute learning outcome attainment routinely, while reviews of curriculum analytics report an absence of evidence on how that computation informs decisions. This paper presents OBER+, an extension of a deployed institutional attainment platform that computes the step from a measured shortfall to an evaluated corrective action. Five connected stages accumulate attainment across deliveries of a course, signal a shortfall and a persistent shortfall, grade it on cutoffs the regulator already uses, record the decision against a catalogue of practices annotated with their evidence, log the change, and quantify the subsequent movement in the shortfall. A further rule compares successive statements of an outcome, so attainment is never read as a series across a point at which the outcome changed. Applying the rules to the live record of two real courses produced three results. Every outcome of a core course was substantively redefined between consecutive deliveries, with subject matter moving between outcome numbers, so a naive reading would have reported a twenty-five point collapse between quantities that do not refer to the same learning. Recomputing the platform's figures from its documented rule showed six of ten differing by more than rounding explains, in a pattern that identified a defect since reported to the institution. Across fifteen statement pairs from three transitions, five were identical character for character, and among the ten that were not, the outcome carrying a given number was nearest to a differently numbered earlier outcome in six, a result resting on an ordering of similarities and requiring no threshold and no labelling. The contribution is a computational design for outcome-based reporting, stated as rules any attainment platform can implement, with evidence of what they make visible in a live institutional record.

AI.tldr: OBER+ provides a rule-based extension to attainment platforms that links measured shortfalls to corrective actions, ensuring stable interpretation of learning outcomes across deliveries and exposing defects in live data.
AI.motivation: Curriculum analytics lacks transparent, evidence-backed methods for turning attainment measurements into decisions; need principled rules to preserve outcome identity and traceability.
AI.method: Extend an institutional attainment platform with five stages for accumulation, signaling, grading against regulator cutoffs, recording evidence-based practices, logging changes, and measuring shortfall movement; add a rule to compare successive outcome statements to prevent treating outcome changes as a continuous series; test on live records from two real courses.
AI.result: Applied rules produced three main findings: (1) every core-course outcome was substantively redefined between deliveries, with subject matter moving between outcomes; (2) recomputing figures with documented rules revealed six of ten differences due to rounding, indicating a defect; (3) across fifteen statement pairs, five were identical; among non-identical ten, six had the same outcome number nearest a differently numbered earlier outcome, showing a pattern of similarity ordering without relying on thresholds or labeling.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a computational design for outcome-based reporting—implementable as rules in any attainment platform—and provides live-record evidence of what these rules reveal about outcomes and decisions.

title: Fill My Mirror: Geometry-Constrained Mirror Inpainting
summary: Mirrors are common in real-world images, yet producing geometrically consistent reflections with generative models remains challenging. Unlike most objects, mirror appearance depends on scene geometry and viewpoint, making it hard to synthesize using learned appearance priors alone. We address this in the mirror inpainting setting, where the scene is fixed and only the mirror region is generated. Our key insight is that much mirror content is geometrically constrained by the visible scene and need not be hallucinated. We estimate scene geometry and project visible content into the mirror to recover reflection regions determined by geometry. A generative model then completes the mirror region via a two-mask diffusion strategy balancing geometric constraints with the model's learned priors, reducing projection artifacts and improving reflection consistency. The method is training-free and applicable to complex real-world scenes. We evaluate on MirrorBench-V2 (synthetic) and real images. Using standard and geometry-aware metrics, we show that explicitly using scene geometry improves consistency.

AI.tldr: A training-free, geometry-aware mirror inpainting method that enforces reflection geometry via scene-projected content and a two-mask diffusion to complete mirrors with better consistency.
AI.motivation: Mirror reflections are geometry-dependent; naive generative priors often hallucinate inconsistent content. Leveraging visible scene geometry can constrain the reflection region and improve realism.
AI.method: 1) Estimate scene geometry. 2) Project visible content into the mirror to identify reflection regions. 3) Use a two-mask diffusion model to complete the mirror region, balancing geometric constraints with learned priors. 4) Training-free and applicable to complex real-world scenes.
AI.result: On MirrorBench-V2 (synthetic) and real images, geometry-aware completion yields more consistent reflections, as shown by standard and geometry-aware metrics and reduced projection artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly enforcing scene geometry in mirror inpainting improves reflection consistency and generalizes to real-world scenes without requiring training.

title: The Natural Language Interaction Protocol and Standard for AI Agents
summary: AI agents are increasingly being developed and deployed across organizations using heterogeneous agent-development frameworks, AI models, tool interfaces, protocols, and execution environments. To realize their potential social and business impact, these agents must be able to interoperate through a common communication protocol. The Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP), developed by researchers and practitioners across companies and universities and standardized by Ecma International, addresses this need by defining a standards-based application-layer protocol for AI-agent interaction. NLIP provides a lightweight semantic message envelope that can be carried over existing transports such as HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket, and AMQP, while allowing NLIP-aware agents and gateways to adapt between clients, agents, local context stores, ontologies, tools, enterprise services, and heterogeneous underlying protocols. This paper presents the motivation and design rationale of NLIP, its message model and transport bindings, security-by-design considerations, reference implementation, representative applications, adoption signals, and relationship to emerging agent protocols such as MCP and A2A.

AI.tldr: NLIP is a standards-based, transport-agnostic protocol for AI-agent interaction that provides a lightweight semantic envelope to enable interoperability across heterogeneous agent frameworks, with defined message model, transport bindings, security considerations, a reference implementation, and alignment with MCP/A2A.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of AI agents across organizations using diverse frameworks, models, tools, and execution environments necessitates a common protocol to enable interoperable communication and to realize social and business impact.
AI.method: The paper outlines the motivation and design rationale for NLIP, and details its message model and transport bindings; it discusses security-by-design considerations; presents a reference implementation; showcases representative applications and adoption signals; and analyzes NLIP’s relationship to emerging protocols such as MCP and A2A.
AI.result: NLIP introduces a lightweight semantic message envelope and associated transport bindings, along with security-by-design considerations, a reference implementation, representative applications, and adoption signals; it also contextualizes NLIP with respect to MCP and A2A.
AI.conclusion: NLIP provides a standards-based foundation for interoperable AI agents and gateways, enabling clients, agents, local context stores, ontologies, tools, and enterprise services to interoperate across heterogeneous protocols, while aligning with evolving agent ecosystems such as MCP and A2A; ongoing adoption and conformance efforts will determine its broader impact.

title: Landmark-Based Discrimination of Injury-Associated Athlete-Sessions from Minute-Resolution Multimodal Football Monitoring Data
summary:
Athlete monitoring data may be recorded minute by minute throughout a match or training session, while injury information may only indicate whether the entire session was injury-associated.
  This creates a modelling problem: assigning the same session-level label to every minute would imply that injury status is known at each exact time, even though within-session injury onset is unknown.
  Our novelty is a fixed-landmark, one-representation-per-athlete-session formulation that directly addresses this mismatch. Instead of labelling every minute, we construct one representation per athlete-session at each landmark using information observed up to that point. This keeps the target at the session level and avoids unsupported minute-level injury supervision.
  A landmark is a fixed time point within the same session, such as 10, 20, or 30 minutes. At each landmark, we assess whether the whole session is injury-associated or non-injury-associated and examine how discrimination changes as more within-session information becomes available.
  Using 2020 SoccerMon data, we analyse 3,743 athlete-sessions from 48 elite women's football athletes, including 22 injury-associated sessions from five athletes. We evaluate pre-session, cumulative, dynamic, and combined representations with athlete-disjoint validation, athlete-cluster bootstrap uncertainty, common-cohort sensitivity analysis, alternative negative-athlete fold allocations, equal-athlete weighting, and Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost benchmarks.
  Primary CUM+DYN Logistic Regression yields ROC-AUC 0.367-0.607 and PR-AUC 0.0080-0.0150 across landmarks, with wide uncertainty. PRE-containing representations show higher point estimates at several landmarks but remain uncertain.

AI.tldr: Fixed-landmark representation per athlete-session to align minute-level data with session-level injury labels; evaluates how injury-discrimination evolves within a session using 2020 SoccerMon data; results show modest performance with high uncertainty.
AI.motivation: To resolve the mismatch between minute-by-minute monitoring data and session-level injury labels, avoiding erroneous inference of precise injury onset.
AI.method: Construct one representation per athlete-session at predefined landmarks within the session; use information up to each landmark; compare pre-session, cumulative, dynamic, and combined representations; evaluate with logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost; robust validation and sensitivity analyses.
AI.result: Primary CUM+DYN Logistic Regression yields ROC-AUC 0.367-0.607 and PR-AUC 0.0080-0.0150 across landmarks; PRE-containing representations show higher point estimates at some landmarks but uncertainty remains.
AI.conclusion: The landmark-based approach addresses label-information mismatch and provides a framework to study how discrimination evolves as more within-session data becomes available; however, predictive performance is modest with substantial uncertainty, signaling need for improved modeling or data.

title: KnowVis: Knowledge-Centric Visual Summarization for Video Lectures
comment: This work is published on EMNLP 2026 (Findings). Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/yixu-cityu/KnowVis and https://huggingface.co/datasets/yixu-cityu/KnowVis
summary: Video lectures are valuable educational resources, but their dense and lengthy formats often overwhelm novice learners. This difficulty stems from a fundamental pedagogical mismatch: while videos deliver transient information linearly, human learning requires constructing interconnected cognitive networks, a task that induces severe cognitive overload for novice learners lacking prior domain knowledge. Existing video summarization methods fail to resolve this mismatch, as they primarily produce text-heavy, linear condensations that still demand high cognitive effort. To bridge this gap, we propose KnowVis, a framework that transforms linear video lectures into pedagogically grounded visual narratives. KnowVis first extracts a detailed concept map from multimodal video content to identify important and challenging threshold concepts, then constructs structured knowledge units, and finally synthesizes engaging visual summaries. Alongside the framework, we introduce a curated dataset of 125 educational videos across 10 academic disciplines, paired with 1,079 generated visual summaries. Extensive automated evaluations and a human study demonstrate that, compared to state-of-the-art baselines, KnowVis generates more accurate and clear visuals that successfully reduce cognitive load and significantly improve student learning effectiveness and knowledge retention.

AI.tldr: KnowVis converts linear video lectures into pedagogy-grounded visual narratives by constructing concept maps and structured knowledge units from multimodal content, producing visual summaries that reduce cognitive load and improve learning; accompanied by a dataset of 125 videos and 1,079 visuals.
AI.motivation: There is a fundamental mismatch between linear video delivery and the need for interconnected cognitive networks in novices. Existing video summarization yields text-heavy, linear condensations that still impose cognitive effort.
AI.method: Extract concept maps from multimodal video content, identify important and challenging threshold concepts, construct structured knowledge units, and synthesize engaging visual summaries to form pedagogical visual narratives.
AI.result: Automated evaluations and a human study show that KnowVis produces more accurate, clearer visuals that reduce cognitive load and significantly improve learning effectiveness and knowledge retention versus state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: KnowVis bridges the gap between linear video delivery and constructive knowledge formation by generating visual narratives; the accompanying dataset enables further research and benchmarking.

title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation through Human-AI Interaction
summary: AI agents are trained on population-scale data to encode broad capabilities spanning those of many practitioners. Yet the artifacts they produce rarely meet the personal bar professionals need to stake their reputation on. On realistic, open-ended tasks where success criteria are heterogeneous and insufficiently documented, individual expertise lives precisely in the elevation and departure from the average. In practice, iterative human-agent interaction surfaces criteria that users cannot fully specify up front, yet apply repeatedly across tasks. We argue this cross-session interaction data is a rich, underused signal for closing the gap to individual expertise. In this work, we propose test-time adaptation through human-agent interaction (TAHI), which integrates these signals into agent context and weights, and crystallizes each user's training and evaluation criteria via an evolving rubric module. We adapt agents to 30 individuals in two high-utility domains, writing and visual creation, on a total of 600 tasks. Our agents improve solo task success by 4.5-20.9% within only tens of tasks. Meanwhile, our evolving rubric module serves as a scalable annotation tool, creating evaluation rubrics that catch 16.0-22.3% more failures than those from LMs or humans alone. While agents are adapted towards individuals, we show these personalized agents also produce improvements in success of up to 8.8% that generalize across users.

AI.tldr: Test-time adaptation via human–agent interaction tailors AI assistants to individuals using cross-session signals and an evolving rubric, improving task success and evaluation accuracy while generalizing to new users.
AI.motivation: Professional tasks involve open-ended criteria that vary by user; average-capability models miss personal standards. Cross-session interaction data can encode individual preferences and evaluation criteria, enabling personalized adaptivity.
AI.method: Introduce test-time adaptation through human-agent interaction (TAHI) that incorporates user signals into agent context and weighting. Develop an evolving rubric module to crystallize each user's criteria. Evaluate personalization across 30 individuals in two domains (writing and visual creation) over 600 tasks.
AI.result: Agents improved solo task success by 4.5–20.9% within tens of tasks. The evolving rubric caught 16.0–22.3% more failures than LMs or humans alone. Personalization also yielded up to 8.8% performance gains for other users.
AI.conclusion: TAHI with an evolving rubric enables scalable, cross-user personalization that boosts performance and improves evaluation signals, with benefits that generalize beyond the initial users.

title: From Ordered Bernoulli Levels to Critical-Line Geometry: Integer Quantization, Bernoulli Residual Phase, and Prime-Power Spectra
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures. Includes exact algebraic constructions, finite-sample numerical controls, and conditional Weyl diagnostics
summary: We study the ordered Bernoulli-word kernel f(p,n,k)=p^k(1-p)^(n-k) and the geometry generated by its inverse-integer level sets. The binary level 2^(-n) selects p=1/2 as the unique real split-independent anchor. Under complement-preserving complex continuation, the pair becomes z=1/2+iu and 1-z=1/2-iu, producing a conjugation-symmetric vertical geometry before any zeta-function input is introduced. The quadratic coordinate Q(z)=z(1-z)=1/4+u^2 has a sharp minimum at the central point and admits an exact integer quantization. For critical-line zero ordinates gamma_k, the induced levels L_k=1/4+gamma_k^2 are decomposed exactly as L_k=N_k+delta_k, where N_k is the nearest integer and delta_k is a periodic first-Bernoulli residual. Circularization gives Z_k=exp(2 pi i delta_k), isolating gamma_k^2 mod 1 as the residual phase variable. Unique factorization resolves the integer shells into prime-generator coordinates, while a distinct complex exponent s lifts the same construction to the Dirichlet atoms m^(-s), linking the Dirichlet-series and Euler-product assemblies. Exact identities, classical zeta connections, numerical controls, and open conditional Weyl tests are kept explicitly separate. No proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is claimed.

AI.tldr: A geometric/decomposition framework for the ordered Bernoulli-word kernel f(p,n,k) and its inverse-integer level sets, yielding conjugation-symmetric geometry, exact Q(z) quantization, a gamma_k^2 mod 1 residual phase via Z_k, and a prime-generator factorization linked to Dirichlet-series/Euler products, with explicit identities and Weyl-test discussions, but no RH proof.
AI.motivation: To connect a simple probabilistic kernel to zeta-related arithmetic through exact decompositions, enabling a modular bridge between level-set geometry, Bernoulli residuals, and Dirichlet-series structures, while examining prospects for RH via conditional Weyl tests.
AI.method: Complex-analytic continuation of the kernel via z = 1/2 + i u; study Q(z) = z(1-z); decompose L_k = 1/4 + gamma_k^2 as N_k + delta_k with delta_k periodic first-Bernoulli residual; circularize to Z_k; factorize integer shells into prime-generator coordinates; lift to Dirichlet atoms m^{-s}; keep identities, zeta connections, numerical controls, and Weyl tests separate.
AI.result: Exact integer quantization of Q(z); exact decomposition L_k = N_k + delta_k; Z_k isolates gamma_k^2 mod 1; a unique factorization into prime-generator coordinates; a parallel Dirichlet-series connection via m^{-s}; explicit separation of identities from zeta connections; recognition of open conditional Weyl tests; no RH proof claimed.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a structured bridge between a simple kernel's level geometry and zeta-analytic arithmetic, enabling modular decomposition and numerical control while clearly avoiding claims about RH; it invites further rigorous justification of the proposed decompositions and their arithmetic implications.

title: ENEAS: Embedding-guided Neural Ensemble for Adaptive Segmentation
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Code and models: https://github.com/speridlabs/eneas
summary:
We present ENEAS, a unified, text-promptable method for instance tracking and semantic discovery. Text-promptable segmentation models, including the latest foundation models such as SAM 3, still suffer from temporal hallucinations, spatial fragmentation, and semantic misclassification: they fail to report target absence when an object leaves the field of view, segment local textures instead of the complete object during extreme close-ups, and prioritize visual features over ontological reality, so that visually similar artifacts such as statues, paintings, or reflections are segmented as target entities.
  ENEAS works two ways from a single method: precise tracking and high-quality segmentation of a unique instance, and open-concept discovery of every instance a text query names, resolved by a semantic verification layer.
