Replay can reduce this burden by reusing past trajectories, but existing methods typically embed it within larger training pipelines involving exploration, experience restructuring, or mixed-policy optimization. This makes replay's own contribution difficult to isolate. We ask a focused question: how far can principled replay selection alone go? We introduce Headroom-Drift Replay, a group-level replay control primitive for GRPO that separates reuse into two decisions. Headroom ranks stored groups by remaining learning value, while Drift gates them by compatibility with the current policy. The fresh on-policy stream remains unchanged, and the method adds no auxiliary generation or training machinery. Across mathematical reasoning, multimodal reasoning, and Agentic Search benchmarks, this single intervention outperforms naive replay and matches or exceeds broader replay methods on Avg Mean@32. In Agentic Search, where environment interaction dominates cost, it delivers comparable quality at materially lower wall-clock time.

AI.tldr: Headroom-Drift Replay is a lightweight, two-decision group-level replay control primitive for GRPO that isolates replay's contribution: rank stored groups by remaining learning value (Headroom) and gate them by policy compatibility (Drift). It requires no extra training machinery and improves performance across reasoning benchmarks, with lower wall-clock time in Agentic Search.
AI.motivation: To quantify how far principled replay selection alone can improve RL post-training when environment interaction is costly, and to isolate replay's impact from other training components.
AI.method: Two-stage replay control for GRPO: (1) Headroom ranks stored trajectory groups by remaining learning value; (2) Drift gates groups by compatibility with the current policy. The on-policy data stream is unchanged and no auxiliary generation or training machinery is added; replay decisions operate at the group level.
AI.result: Across math reasoning, multimodal reasoning, and Agentic Search benchmarks, Headroom-Drift Replay outperforms naive replay and matches or exceeds broader replay methods on Avg Mean@32. In Agentic Search, where environment interaction dominates cost, it achieves comparable quality at substantially lower wall-clock time.
AI.conclusion: A principled, minimal replay-control primitive can yield meaningful gains without additional training infrastructure, indicating replay selection itself can be a strong lever for efficiency in post-training RL for reasoning models.

title: VestigeKV: The NoPE-MLA KV Cache Carries Its Own Eviction Signal in a Vestigial Branch
summary: The problem. A long-lived KV cache must be compressed before the queries that will read it exist; selection by observed attention (H2O, SnapKV) collapses there (0.00-0.33 needle retrieval on a NoPE MLA model), because a token's importance has not yet been observed. The method. On Kimi Linear, VestigeKV evicts by a query-independent signal the cache already carries: the 64-dimensional decoupled branch, a vestige of RoPE that NoPE training repurposes into a salience channel. Reading 11% of each row, it partitions the cache: the top-m rows stay in the attended tier; every other row moves -- exactly, never deleted -- to a GPU-resident archive reachable per step by a certified trigger. No training, no quantization, no weight or kernel change. Cost. Nothing measurable: retrieval holds at 1.00 under 8x and 0.92 under 32x from 8k to 65k context, zero gap to full-row selection. The attended tier is 0.25 KB of Kimi Linear's 8.1 KB per-token cache at 32x; the archive stays bit-exact and GPU-resident, with host offload as the VRAM-reclaiming variant. The recall tier -- the standard configuration -- holds 128x at 1.00. Kimi K3 is reported to use a NoPE Gated-MLA variant; if its cache layout matches, the method plausibly extends there -- we make no claim beyond the measured model. NoPE exclusivity. The identical operator on a RoPE MLA collapses to 0.08 (plain eviction: 0.42); query-independent salience itself exists only without rotation (top-1 targets span 2.3-6.7% of tokens vs. 10.2-46.8%), and query-universal exact merging is provably impossible under RoPE. All thresholds were frozen before data; 20 archived verdicts and 8 closed routes accompany the paper.

AI.tldr: VestigeKV: a training-free, query-independent eviction mechanism for long-lived KV caches that splits data into an attended tier and a GPU-resident archive, achieving high recall with substantial compression (attended tier ~0.25 KB per token) and 8–32x speedups while preserving bit-exact archival data.
AI.motivation: Reduce memory footprint and latency of long-lived KV caches without relying on query-time attention signals, which are unavailable before queries; aim for zero-training, zero-quantization memory savings with exact archival data.
AI.method: Use a 64-dimensional decoupled RoPE vestige repurposed as a salience channel. Read 11% of each row to partition the cache: top-m rows remain in an attended tier; remaining rows move to a GPU-resident archive reachable per step by a certified trigger. No training, no quantization, no weight or kernel changes. Cache layout: ~8.1 KB per-token; attended tier ~0.25 KB; archive is bit-exact and GPU-resident with optional host offload.
AI.result: Retrieval performance shows 1.00 recall at 8x and 0.92 recall at 32x across contexts from 8k to 65k; the attended tier holds 0.25 KB per token, while the archive can reach 128x recall under standard configuration (1.00). The RoPE-NoPE variants show differing behaviors: pure eviction yields 0.42 or 0.08 depending on configuration, and query-independent salience is not possible with rotation; thresholds were fixed a priori; 20 archived verdicts and 8 routes accompany the paper.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates a practical, training-free method to maintain exact archival data while achieving substantial cache compression and fast recall; effectiveness depends on the RoPE/NoPE configuration, with RoPE undermining exact merging and requiring careful handling of the salience signal. Applicability suggested to Kimi Linear and RoPE MLA-like setups; results are model- and configuration-specific.

title: Concept of a Sensor Test Environment for Dusty Agricultural Conditions
summary: Dust in agriculture presents a significant challenge for autonomous agricultural machinery. Dust can impair the performance of sensors and algorithms. This work, therefore, presents a concept for a proving ground consisting of an indoor and outdoor area. The indoor area comprises a laboratory test bench where dust circulates in a closed system and a test hall where life-size objects can be placed. The outdoor area features dedicated test setups that enable reproducible data to be recorded with and without dust during real-world agriculture work. The proving ground and the setups are visualized in 3D.

AI.tldr: A concept for a dual indoor–outdoor proving ground to study dust effects on sensors/algorithms for autonomous agricultural machinery, including a closed-dust lab bench, a life-size object test hall, and outdoor setups with reproducible dust data collection and 3D visualization.
AI.motivation: Dust reduces perception reliability and algorithm performance in field robots. There is a need for controlled, repeatable, realistic dust exposure environments to evaluate robustness and train mitigation strategies.
AI.method: A conceptual design of an integrated proving ground: (1) indoor lab with dust circulating in a closed system; (2) indoor test hall for validating with life-size objects; (3) outdoor test setups for real-world farming tasks under dust and clean conditions; data collection with reproducible conditions; 3D visualization of the facility.
AI.result: Conceptual proposal with architectural/experimental setup descriptions; no empirical results reported.
AI.conclusion: The proposed proving ground offers a reproducible, multi-environment platform to study and improve autonomous agricultural systems under dust exposure, bridging lab and field testing and enabling robust sensor/algorithm development.

title: OSR: Output Space Redistribution for Adaptive Label Removal in Classification Models
summary: Label removal occurs frequently in classification systems with evolving taxonomies, where categories must be dynamically updated or eliminated. To accommodate such changes, classification models must adapt accordingly. Existing solutions, broadly categorized as retraining-based and feature-space-adjustment-based, share common limitations despite their variations, including reliance on access to original data, substantial computational and storage costs, inconsistent results, poor scalability, and degradation of model utility. To address this, we propose a novel approach that leverages statistical redistribution in the output space to approximate the post-removal confidence vectors of a retrained model. Applicable as a modular output filter, our method bypasses the burden of feature-space adjustments or loss-function convergence, alleviating scalability limitations. Furthermore, by requiring only existing labels and prior output confidences, the method potentially mitigates privacy concerns inherent to data-dependent solutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive performance against full retraining, with improvements in computational efficiency and privacy preservation across several classification tasks.

AI.tldr: A modular output-space redistribution approach for label removal in evolving taxonomies, avoiding retraining and feature-space adjustments; achieves competitive accuracy with better efficiency and privacy.
AI.motivation: Label removal in dynamic taxonomies is common, but existing retraining-based and feature-space-adjustment methods suffer from data access, compute/storage costs, scalability, and privacy concerns.
AI.method: Introduce a statistical redistribution in the model's output space as an output filter to approximate the post-removal confidences of a retrained model, using only existing labels and prior output confidences.
AI.result: Experiments show competitive performance with full retraining while improving computational efficiency and privacy preservation across multiple classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: A scalable, privacy-friendly drop-in module for label removal that eschews feature-space changes and loss-function convergence while maintaining performance.

title: OctWorld: Long-Range World-Consistent Video Generation with Octree-Based 3D Mapping
summary: We present OctWorld, a video diffusion framework with persistent 3D memory for generating explorable, world-consistent, and high-fidelity visual scenes. Given a single image, OctWorld performs stable autoregressive world generation along user-specified camera trajectories. We focus on long-range generation, characterized by extended camera paths and wide viewpoint coverage, where preserving spatial consistency is particularly challenging when previously generated regions are revisited. To address this problem, we introduce OctMap, an extensible and spatially adaptive 3D memory that progressively fuses generated visual observations and their corresponding depth maps into a global representation. OctMap employs TSDF fusion within a dynamic sparse octree whose spatial resolution adapts to image evidence. This design preserves geometric and appearance details across diverse scene scales while maintaining low memory overhead. Experiments demonstrate that OctWorld generates long-range, spatially consistent videos and outperforms prior methods on both existing benchmarks and challenging long-range generation settings. OctMap also provides clear advantages over point-based caches and fixed-resolution TSDF volumes. Project page: https://maxtirerror.github.io/octworldpage/

AI.tldr: OctWorld introduces a diffusion-based video generation framework with persistent 3D memory (OctMap) that fuses generated observations and depth via TSDF fusion in a dynamic sparse octree, enabling long-range, world-consistent, high-fidelity video generation from a single image along user-defined camera trajectories.
AI.motivation: Preserve spatial consistency across revisited regions while extending camera trajectory coverage for long-range generation, all with controlled memory usage.
AI.method: Autoregressive video generation conditioned on a persistent 3D memory (OctMap). OctMap uses TSDF fusion inside a dynamic sparse octree to fuse color observations and depth maps, with resolution adapting to image evidence to maintain geometry and appearance across scales; outperforms point caches and fixed-resolution TSDF volumes.
AI.result: OctWorld produces long-range, spatially consistent videos and outperforms prior methods on standard benchmarks and challenging long-range settings; OctMap yields advantages over alternative memory schemes.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables scalable, world-consistent video generation from a single image via adaptive 3D memory; OctMap's fusion-driven memory offers improved geometry and appearance preservation with efficient memory usage.

title: RobustSeiz: An Open-Source Framework for Benchmarking the Robustness of EEG Seizure Detection Models
comment: 28 pages, 13 numbered figures, 9 tables; full-page graphical abstract and supplementary material included. Submitted to the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (JAMIA)
summary: Despite strong performance on held-out electroencephalography (EEG) data, seizure detectors may fail under real-world acquisition variability, artifacts, and adversarial inputs. We introduce RobustSeiz, an open-source, model-agnostic framework that provides a standardized, reproducible protocol for stress-testing and comparing seizure detectors under controlled, clinically motivated distribution shifts before deployment. We standardize four public scalp-EEG corpora (CHB-MIT, TUSZ, Siena, and SeizeIT1) into BIDS-EEG trees and evaluate subject-independent detectors on held-out splits. Environment, noise, and adversarial transforms are swept over predefined hyperparameter grids. Each run reports sample- and event-level sensitivity, precision, F1, false positives per 24 h, Lead and Lag onset timing, and Monte Carlo dropout predictive agreement. RobustSeiz includes a Dockerized GPU pipeline, experiment registry, and full-evaluation and research-subset modes. We demonstrate the framework with a contemporary seizure detector on TUSZ across the complete implemented shift grid; an AWGN analysis illustrates how perturbation severity changes detection quality, onset timing, and predictive agreement. RobustSeiz provides a shared benchmarking standard for evaluating seizure-detector robustness under realistic clinical stressors, extending pre-deployment assessment beyond clean-data accuracy.

AI.tldr: RobustSeiz provides an open-source framework to stress-test seizure detectors under distribution shifts (environment, noise, adversarial perturbations) using standardized BIDS-EEG datasets, enabling reproducible, model-agnostic robustness benchmarking prior to deployment.
AI.motivation: Real-world EEG seizure detectors face variability, artifacts, and adversarial inputs that degrade performance. A standardized, reproducible benchmark is needed to evaluate robustness beyond clean data.
AI.method: Standardize CHB-MIT, TUSZ, Siena, SeizeIT1 into BIDS-EEG; evaluate subject-independent detectors on held-out splits; sweep environment, noise, and adversarial transforms over predefined grids; report sample- and event-level metrics, onset timing (Lead/Lag), and Monte Carlo dropout agreement; provide a Dockerized GPU pipeline, experiment registry, and research-subset modes.
AI.result: Demonstrated with a contemporary detector on TUSZ across the full shift grid; AWGN analysis shows perturbation severity modulates detection quality, onset timing, and predictive agreement; establishes a shared benchmarking standard for robustness under clinical stressors.
AI.conclusion: RobustSeiz extends pre-deployment assessment to robustness under realistic clinical stressors, beyond clean-data accuracy, by offering a standardized, reproducible benchmarking protocol.

title: Sparse auto-regressive modeling for scene generation from multi-view images
summary: Generating complete 3D scenes from sparse, unconstrained views is a fundamental challenge in 3D vision which requires reasoning beyond observed content while remaining computationally tractable. Existing feed-forward reconstruction methods are inherently limited to content visible in the input images, while 3D generative modeling is hindered by the high computational cost of dense volumetric representations and the scarcity of large-scale 3D supervision. We introduce SPAR3S, a sparse voxel-aligned 3D latent generative model for conditional scene completion without requiring ground-truth 3D data for supervision. Our key insight is to formulate 3D scene generation in a structured, compact, voxel-aligned 3D latent space where only occupied voxels are represented. We learn this sparse latent space directly from multi-view images using photometric supervision via differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. Given a partial set of observed voxels encoded from sparse input views, scene completion reduces to predicting the missing latent tokens and their spatial support within the voxel grid. To this end, we train a masked autoregressive transformer that jointly models voxel occupancy and latent token values, enabling efficient and spatially consistent generation of unseen regions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on synthetic indoor scenes, achieving higher novel-view quality than prior work. We further validate its generalization on RealEstate10k, highlighting its applicability to real-world data.

AI.tldr: SPAR3S is a sparse voxel-aligned 3D latent generative model for conditional scene completion that learns a voxel-occupancy latent space from multi-view images via differentiable 3D Gaussian splatting and completes unseen regions with a masked autoregressive transformer, achieving superior novel-view quality on synthetic indoor scenes and generalizing to RealEstate10k without ground-truth 3D supervision.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of feed-forward reconstruction limited to observed content and dense 3D generative models requiring heavy supervision/dense representations; aim for a computationally tractable, sparse 3D latent space learned from 2D views.
AI.method: Learn sparse voxel-aligned latent space representing only occupied voxels. Use differentiable 3D Gaussian splatting to provide photometric supervision from multi-view images. Given partial observed voxels encoded from input views, train a masked autoregressive transformer to predict missing latent tokens and their spatial support, jointly modeling voxel occupancy and token values for spatially consistent generation.
AI.result: On synthetic indoor scenes, achieves higher novel-view quality than prior work; demonstrates generalization on RealEstate10k.
AI.conclusion: Offers a scalable approach to 3D scene completion requiring no ground-truth 3D data; efficient due to sparse latent representation and autoregressive modeling; potential for broader real-world data.

title: Unlocking Lossless Speedups in LLMs via Discrete Diffusion
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) owe much of their success to next-token prediction (NTP), but their autoregressive (AR) structure requires slow, sequential token generation. To overcome this bottleneck, we introduce diffusion-augmented LLMs, a new class of models that defines an AR model distribution while using diffusion to draw multiple tokens in parallel from that distribution. We decouple the parameters of these models into two sets: AR weights, trained using the standard NTP objective, and lightweight diffusion weights, trained to generate multiple tokens simultaneously. The diffusion weights are learned through a simple Diffusion Distillation phase that adds negligible overhead to existing LLM training pipelines. We also introduce $Ψ$-Spec, a family of samplers that enables lossless acceleration and inference-time scaling at a fixed context length. Unlike speculative decoding, our method requires no separate draft model. Unlike diffusion LLMs (d-LLMs), it accelerates generation without sacrificing the quality of the underlying AR model. The resulting models, called Uno, can be trained from scratch or built by augmenting existing open-weight AR LLMs. Uno achieves higher throughput than leading speculative-decoding methods at every evaluated batch size and delivers up to $3\times$ speedups over the base AR model, including at the largest batch size supported by the device. Notably, our 8B Uno model outperforms the leading open d-LLM, the 26B DiffusionGemma, and the proprietary Mercury 2 across all evaluated benchmarks in agentic tool use, coding, and long-context reasoning. We release code and checkpoints at: https://s-sahoo.github.io/uno/

AI.tldr: Uno proposes diffusion-augmented LLMs that decouple AR and diffusion weights to generate multiple tokens in parallel, achieving up to 3x speedups while maintaining AR quality and outperforming larger diffusion models on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: AR-based LLMs are bottlenecked by sequential next-token prediction. The approach seeks to accelerate generation without sacrificing the autoregressive model's quality by enabling parallel token sampling via diffusion, with lightweight diffusion weights.
AI.method: Split parameters into AR weights trained with standard next-token prediction, and lightweight diffusion weights trained via a Diffusion Distillation phase to draw multiple tokens per step. Introduce Ψ-Spec samplers for lossless acceleration at fixed context length. Uno can be trained from scratch or by augmenting existing open-weight AR LLMs; code and checkpoints released.
AI.result: Uno achieves higher throughput than leading speculative-decoding methods across batch sizes and provides up to 3x speedups over the base AR model. An 8B Uno model outperforms larger diffusion LLMs (26B DiffusionGemma) and a proprietary Mercury 2 across agentic tool use, coding, and long-context reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Uno offers a practical and scalable route to accelerating autoregressive LLM inference by augmenting with diffusion-based parallel token sampling, without requiring a separate draft model or sacrificing AR quality. It is compatible with existing AR LLMs and demonstrates strong performance relative to competitive diffusion-based and speculative decoding approaches.

title: WorldReward: Reward Modeling for Camera-Conditioned World Models
summary: Camera-conditioned world models generate interactive videos in which commanded actions should induce the expected scene changes while appearance, geometry, and temporal dynamics remain coherent. Existing rewards assess these requirements separately: geometry-based rewards estimate trajectory execution but cannot judge the visual quality of the executed motion, whereas image-based rewards measure frame quality without capturing action execution or temporal dynamics. We posit that a vision-language model (VLM) offers a shared reasoning space for relating actions to their visual outcomes. However, judging a complete long video against its full action sequence creates a lengthy, noisy context in which short-lived local action evidence can be missed or diluted. We present WorldReward, a VLM-based pairwise preference reward model that unifies action-consistency and visual-quality evaluation for camera-conditioned world models. WorldReward decomposes paired videos into action-aligned chunks, organizes each chunk into structured visual evidence, and aggregates chunk-level decisions by voting into separate video-level action and visual-quality preferences. To train it, we construct a large-scale reasoning-augmented preference dataset using structured judgments generated by a frontier VLM and refined through tool-based agent auditing and targeted human review. We further introduce WorldReward-Bench, a human-annotated benchmark measuring reward-model agreement with human preferences across action consistency, appearance quality, and motion quality. WorldReward achieves the highest agreement on all three dimensions, exceeding GPT-5.5 by 3.42, 1.45, and 3.56 percentage points, respectively. When used for RL post-training of HY-WorldPlay 1.5, it consistently improves both action execution and visual quality across short- to long-term horizons.

AI.tldr: A VLM-based pairwise preference reward (WorldReward) unifies action-consistency and visual-quality evaluation for camera-conditioned world models by chunking videos into action-aligned segments, training on a reasoning-augmented dataset, and benchmarking with WorldReward-Bench; it improves RL outcomes and aligns well with human preferences.
AI.motivation: Existing rewards separate geometry-based trajectory accuracy and image quality, missing coherent action execution and temporal dynamics in long videos; a shared VLM reasoning space can relate actions to visual outcomes.
AI.method: Decompose paired videos into action-aligned chunks; structure each chunk's visual evidence; aggregate chunk-level decisions via voting into video-level action and visual-quality preferences; train on a large-scale reasoning-augmented preference dataset generated by a frontier VLM and refined with tool-based auditing and human review; introduce WorldReward-Bench; apply to RL post-training (HY-WorldPlay 1.5).
AI.result: WorldReward achieves the highest agreement with human preferences across action consistency, appearance quality, and motion quality; outperforms GPT-5.5 by 3.42, 1.45, and 3.56 percentage points respectively; improves action execution and visual quality across short- to long-term horizons in RL post-training.
AI.conclusion: A unified, VLM-based reward framework (WorldReward) effectively evaluates and guides camera-conditioned world models, enabling better action execution and visual quality, backed by a human-aligned benchmark and demonstrated gains in RL performance.

title: A location-invariant estimator of extremal quantile treatment effects for heavy-tailed distributions
summary: Quantile treatment effects (QTEs) measure the effect of a treatment on the distribution of an outcome, and their estimation at extreme quantile levels is of central interest in applications where the target quantiles lie far beyond the range of the data. For heavy-tailed potential outcomes, existing extremal QTE estimators rely on extrapolation combined with a causal extreme value index (EVI) estimator, but the resulting estimator is not invariant under a common location shift of the potential outcome distributions, even though the population QTE is. We address this issue in two steps. First, we adapt the location-invariant Fraga estimator of the EVI to the causal setting using inverse propensity score weighting. Second, we replace the original extrapolation formula with a difference-based scheme, under which the location parameter cancels when quantile differences are taken. The resulting QTE estimator is therefore location invariant. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed extremal QTE estimators, and provide a consistent variance estimator, leading to asymptotically valid inference. A simulation study confirms the location invariance, the stability with respect to the threshold, and the coverage of the proposed methods.

AI.tldr: Extremal quantile treatment effect (QTE) estimation under heavy tails is made location-invariant by combining a location-invariant EVI estimator (Fraga-type) with inverse propensity score weighting and a difference-based extrapolation; consistency and asymptotic normality are established with a consistent variance estimator, validated by simulations.
AI.motivation: To achieve reliable extremal QTE inference that is invariant to common location shifts of potential outcome distributions, addressing a flaw in existing extrapolation-based estimators.
AI.method: 1) Adapt the Fraga estimator of the extreme value index to a causal setting via inverse propensity score weighting to achieve location invariance. 2) Replace the original extrapolation with a difference-based scheme so that the location parameter cancels when taking quantile differences. 3) Prove consistency and asymptotic normality; provide a consistent variance estimator. 4) Validate via simulations assessing location invariance, threshold sensitivity, and coverage.
AI.result: The proposed extremal QTE estimator is location-invariant. It has established consistency and asymptotic normality, with a consistent variance estimator for valid inference. Simulations support invariance to location shifts, stability with threshold choice, and correct coverage.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields a robust, location-invariant framework for extremal QTE estimation under heavy-tailed outcomes, with sound theoretical guarantees and empirical validation; suitable for applied causal inference in extreme quantile settings.

title: RARF: Region-Aware Rectified Flows for 3D Brain MRI Inpainting
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. Preprint version corresponding to the initial submission prior to peer review, submitted as part of our participation in the BraTS 2026 Challenge. The final accepted version will be openly available in the official MICCAI proceedings on the conference website
summary: Medical image inpainting has the potential to improve automated brain MRI analysis by reconstructing healthy tissue within pathological regions. We introduce RARF, a task-agnostic region-aware rectified flow framework for masked data generation. We instantiate the framework for 3D brain MRI inpainting as our submission to the BraTS Inpainting Challenge 2026. RARF restricts the stochastic interpolation process to the inpainting region, while the observed voxels remain fixed and provide patient-specific anatomical context. A three-dimensional neural network receives the partially voided image, with Gaussian noise filling the missing region, together with the inpainting mask and the corresponding timestep. The model is trained using masked flow-matching and reconstruction-consistency objectives, combined with mask-aware preprocessing and data augmentation. During inference, the learned velocity field transports the initial noise toward a plausible reconstruction of the missing tissue, which is then combined with the unchanged observed anatomy. Experiments under the BraTS evaluation protocol show that the proposed approach produces competitive reconstructions while maintaining anatomical consistency. Source code is available at: https://github.com/TomasGuija/rarf.

AI.tldr: RARF is a task-agnostic region-aware rectified flow for masked data generation applied to 3D brain MRI inpainting, achieving competitive, anatomically consistent reconstructions in BraTS 2026.
AI.motivation: Improve automated brain MRI analysis by reconstructing healthy tissue within pathological regions, addressing global inpainting limitations by localizing stochastic interpolation to the inpainting region and leveraging observed voxels as anatomical context.
AI.method: A 3D neural network processes the partially voided image with Gaussian noise in the missing region, the inpainting mask, and the timestep. The model learns velocity fields via masked flow-matching and reconstruction-consistency losses, with mask-aware preprocessing/augmentation. Inference transports noise toward a plausible tissue reconstruction within the masked region, merging with fixed observed anatomy.
AI.result: Under the BraTS evaluation protocol, RARF yields competitive reconstructions with good anatomical consistency; source code is available at the provided GitHub repo.
AI.conclusion: RARF demonstrates effective region-aware, flow-based masked data generation for 3D brain MRI inpainting, extending masked data generation with task-agnostic, anatomically consistent reconstructions.

title: Sharpening the Ensemble: An SSIM-Aligned Residual Refiner for Brain-MRI Inpainting Post-Processing
comment: Accepted at the MICCAI BraTS Local Synthesis of Brain Tissue Inpainting Challenge (Task 4), MICCAI 2026. 12 pages, 2 figures
summary: Brain-MRI inpainting replaces a masked region of a scan with synthesized, anatomically plausible healthy tissue, so that analysis tools built for healthy brains can be applied to images they would otherwise reject. On the BraTS local-synthesis benchmark, which ranks submissions on the structural similarity index (SSIM), the peak signal-to-noise ratio, and the mean squared error (MSE) jointly, the strongest recent models are accurate, but several report blurry synthesized regions and attribute this to the mean-seeking behavior of the $\ell_1$ and MSE terms in their training losses. We address this in post-processing, forming a deep ensemble of the two co-first-place 2025 models and training a lightweight residual refiner on the ensemble's own outputs under an $\ell_1$ loss augmented with a structural-similarity term whose weight $λ$ we vary. At a moderate $λ$ the refiner improves SSIM over the ensemble, from $0.8767$ to $0.8780$ on a held-out reproduction of the official scorer and from $0.8555$ to $0.8572$ on the official validation leaderboard, with essentially no change in MSE. The gain is small but consistent, improving $62.6\%$ of the held-out cases with a signed-rank $p=2.2\times10^{-7}$, whereas over-weighting the structural term reverses it. Two ablations bound the effect. Adding any third model to the two-model ensemble degrades it, and classical unsharp masking fails to improve SSIM at any strength (best $0.8765$ against $0.8767$), so the gain reflects learned rather than indiscriminate sharpening. The result is a cheap, reproducible post-processing stage that improves an already strong ensemble without any large-scale retraining.

AI.tldr: A lightweight residual refiner applied as a post-processing step to a two-model ensemble yields small but robust SSIM gains in brain-MRI inpainting without retraining, with ablations showing gains are learned rather than sharpening and that an extra model or simple unsharp masking do not help.
AI.motivation: MRI inpainting aims to fill masked brain regions with plausible healthy tissue to enable analyses designed for healthy brains. State-of-the-art local-synthesis models are accurate but often produce blur due to mean-seeking losses (L1/MSE). The work seeks a cheap post-processing method to improve structural similarity (SSIM) without large-scale retraining.
AI.method: Create a deep ensemble of two co-first-place 2025 models. Train a lightweight residual refiner on the ensemble outputs, using an L1 loss augmented with an SSIM term. Vary the SSIM-term weight λ and evaluate on held-out data replicating the official scorer and on the official validation leaderboard. Perform ablations: (i) add a third model to the ensemble, (ii) compare with classical unsharp masking.
AI.result: Moderate λ improves SSIM from 0.8767 to 0.8780 on held-out data and from 0.8555 to 0.8572 on the official validation leaderboard, with essentially no change in MSE. The improvement covers 62.6% of held-out cases (signed-rank p = 2.2e-7). Over-weighting λ reverses the gain. Adding a third model degrades performance; unsharp masking fails to improve SSIM (best 0.8765).
AI.conclusion: A cheap, reproducible post-processing stage yields consistent SSIM gains on top of a strong ensemble without retraining, and gains arise from learned sharpening rather than simple filtering.

title: Conditioning Degenerate Diffusion Models
summary: Current conditioned generative models heavily rely on score functions for guidance during training. When the generative model is a diffusion process with a singular diffusion coefficient and the underlying (conditional) densities either do not exist or are not smooth, we use causal optimal transport to define \emph{approximate} loss functions that identify a minimum-entropy control for guidance under minimal assumptions. Our approach relies on causal optimal transport and its characterization through the predictable representation property of (conditioned) diffusion processes whose associated martingale problem is well posed, à la Üstünel.

AI.tldr: Proposes a causal optimal transport framework to derive approximate guidance losses for diffusion models with singular diffusion coefficients and non-smooth densities, yielding minimum-entropy control under weak assumptions.
AI.motivation: Score-based guidance in conditioned generative models struggles when densities are non-existent or non-smooth due to singular diffusions; a principled, weak-assumption framework is needed.
AI.method: Employ causal optimal transport and the predictable representation property for conditioned diffusions; ground the approach in Üstünel's well-posed martingale problem to obtain approximate loss functions that identify minimum-entropy control.
AI.result: Defines approximate guidance losses via causal OT, characterized by a minimum-entropy control under minimal regularity; extends score-based guidance to singular diffusion settings.
AI.conclusion: Causal OT provides a principled mechanism to obtain guidance for diffusion models under challenging regularity, connecting stochastic control with score-based methods under weak assumptions.

title: IchthyoNoma: Nomenclature and Context Sensitivity of Zero-Shot Biological Vision--Language Models for Bangladeshi Freshwater Fish Recognition
summary: Zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as training-free species recognizers, but reported accuracy can reflect more than visual species knowledge. We audit CLIP, BioCLIP, BioCLIP2, and a multilingual Jina CLIP v2 control on seven freshwater-fish categories from two Bangladeshi sources (10,321 images). BioCLIP2 reaches 72.36% on BFF-15 with English common names and 68.91% on SylFishBD with scientific names, versus 25.15% and 14.40% for generic CLIP. BioCLIP2 Bengali prompts are near chance in balanced accuracy (14.22-14.29%); Jina partially recovers Bengali discrimination to 21.89% and 16.36%, but bare Bengali names return to 14.29% on both sources. Paired SylFishBD interventions show no significant weak-blur effect, modest losses from stronger blur/gray masking, a larger white-mask artifact, and strong species dependence. Zero-shot biological VLM scores therefore jointly reflect biological specialization, multilingual alignment, nomenclature, prompt formulation, and context.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot vision-language models' reported accuracy on freshwater fishes is shaped by biological knowledge, language alignment, nomenclature, and prompt design. BioCLIP2 substantially outperforms generic CLIP across English and scientific naming, while Bengali-language prompts underperform, with mixed gains from multilingual controls. Interventions on SylFishBD show limited blur sensitivity but strong species dependence, indicating performance reflects multiple interacting factors beyond pure visual recognition.
AI.motivation: Assess how zero-shot VLMs encode domain knowledge vs linguistic and prompt-related biases by auditing multiple models on a culturally and linguistically diverse fish dataset.
AI.method: Evaluate CLIP, BioCLIP, BioCLIP2, and a multilingual Jina CLIP v2 control on seven freshwater-fish categories from two Bangladeshi sources (total n=10,321 images). Use English common names and scientific names; Bengali prompts; analyze zero-shot classification accuracy. Conduct SylFishBD-prompts interventions to examine robustness to blur, masking, and context; assess Bengali-name discrimination vs multilingual prompts.
AI.result: BioCLIP2 achieves 72.36% on BFF-15 with English common names and 68.91% on SylFishBD with scientific names, compared to 25.15% and 14.40% for generic CLIP. Bengali prompts are near chance (14.22–14.29%). Jina CLIP v2 control partially recovers Bengali discrimination to 21.89% and 16.36%, but Bengali names remain at 14.29%. Paired SylFishBD interventions show no significant weak-blur effect, modest losses from stronger blur/gray masking, a larger white-mask artifact, and strong species dependence.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot visual-language scores reflect a combination of biological specialization, multilingual alignment, nomenclature, prompt formulation, and context. Effective interpretation requires accounting for domain-specific knowledge and language-consistent prompts; improvements hinge on domain-aligned training and robust multilingual prompt strategies.

title: Hardware-Aware FP4 FlashAttention-4
summary: Blackwell's 4-bit floating-point (FP4) tensor cores do not automatically make attention faster because softmax conversion and on-chip dependencies dominate once its matrix products shrink. We address this with \emph{Direct-P} for noncausal inference and a causal path that passes the forward quantization directly into backward. Direct-P maps scores directly to FP4 probabilities and reaches up to 2.13$\times$ the bfloat16 (BF16) forward throughput on an NVIDIA GB200. The causal path reconstructs probabilities from saved quantized queries and keys and uses 8-bit floating-point (FP8) gradient operands, accelerating a complete single-GPU 8-billion-parameter update by up to 1.14$\times$. Matched distributed training retains FP8 probabilities and values; every tested MXFP4 probability/value training trajectory diverges.

AI.tldr: Direct-P enables FP4-based attention to reach up to 2.13x forward throughput over BF16 on GB200; a causal path uses FP8 gradients to speed up an 8B-parameter single-GPU update by 1.14x; distributed training preserves FP8 probabilities/values, but MXFP4 probability/value trajectories diverge, indicating instability.
AI.motivation: Address softmax and on-chip dependency bottlenecks in attention on 4-bit FP4 tensor cores; enable faster noncausal inference and accelerated backward pass via a quantization-aware causal path.
AI.method: Introduce Direct-P that maps scores directly to FP4 probabilities for noncausal inference; implement a causal path that reconstructs probabilities from saved quantized Q/K and performs backward with 8-bit FP gradients; evaluate on MXFP4 hardware with matched distributed training.
AI.result: Forward throughput up to 2.13x BF16 baseline on GB200; single-GPU 8B-parameter update accelerated by up to 1.14x; observed divergence of all MXFP4 probability/value training trajectories; distributed training retains FP8 probabilities/values.
AI.conclusion: Direct-P and FP8-based causal path show potential for accelerating attention on FP4 hardware, but FP4-based training exhibits severe numerical instability (divergence) requiring stabilization strategies for reliable training.

title: Constant regret in general games via higher-order optimism
summary: We introduce an uncoupled learning algorithm which, when employed by all players of an arbitrary $N$-player normal form game with up to $K$ actions per player, guarantees $O(N^3\log^2 K)$ individual regret, uniformly over the horizon of play. The proposed algorithm - which we call higher-order optimism with discounting (HOOD) is a variant of optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader (OptFTRL) that combines a discounted $(N+1)$-th order predictor with entropic regularization over a suitable "lifting" of the game's strategy space. This combination of ingredients is purposefully designed to dampen large oscillations of the induced sequence of play in a controlled manner, removing in this way a key stumbling block of previous attempts to achieve constant regret in general games. Our approach bears several striking similarities to the concurrent - and completely independent - work of Liu, Farina, and Ozdaglar (arXiv:2608.31166), who very recently derived an $O(N^{21}\log^{4} K)$ regret bound through the use of higher-order optimism and an exponential moving average estimator.

AI.tldr: HOOD is an uncoupled algorithm for N-player normal-form games with up to K actions, achieving per-player regret O(N^3 log^2 K) uniformly over time via higher-order optimism with discounting and entropic regularization on a lifted strategy space; it is related to concurrent work achieving O(N^21 log^4 K) regret.
AI.motivation: Obtain sublinear, per-player regret in general-sum, multi-agent settings with scalable action spaces while avoiding inter-player coupling and large oscillations.
AI.method: Variant of OptFTRL that uses a discounted (N+1)-th order predictor combined with entropic regularization over a lifted game strategy space to damp oscillations.
AI.result: Proves regret bound O(N^3 log^2 K) per player, uniformly over horizon; algorithm is uncoupled; demonstrates reduced oscillations.
AI.conclusion: HOOD advances online learning in general-sum games by achieving sublinear regret with a scalable, uncoupled, high-order optimism approach, and aligns with concurrent independent results showing similar improvements.

title: The Blind Spot in 2D Infants' Pose Estimation:Robust Learning from Noisy Annotations
summary: Noisy annotations pose a significant challenge for supervised deep learning, as neural networks rely on large-scale, high-quality labeled data whose corruption can severely impair model performance. Although robustness to label noise has been extensively studied for classification tasks, it remains relatively underexplored in Pose Estimation (PE). This limitation becomes critical in clinical contexts, including neonatology, where PE of preterm infants is used to support the assessment of spontaneous motility, a key indicator of neurodevelopmental trajectories. In such settings, infants' images labeling is further hindered by visual challenges (e.g., keypoint self-occlusions, caregiver interference), making the annotation process inherently susceptible to errors. To tackle noisy annotations in PE, we introduce REliable keypoint selection via Memory of traINing Dynamics (REMIND), a clustering-based keypoint-selection strategy that exploits keypoint-wise training dynamics to identify noisy labels without assuming any prior knowledge of the noise distribution, thus enabling noise-free model training. When evaluated on the proprietary NeoPose dataset, comprising 46 videos of 46 preterm infants recorded in real clinical settings, REMIND correctly identifies noisy annotations across multiple corruption scenarios, achieving up to 93\% Area Under the Curve (AUC) with three different PE architectures used in the relevant literature. To our knowledge, this is the first study to explicitly address label noise in preterm infants' PE, paving the way for the design of trustworthy learning-based algorithms for infants'monitoring support when data quality cannot be guaranteed.

AI.tldr: REMIND is a clustering-based, memory-of-training-dynamics approach for keypoint selection that identifies and filters noisy annotations in pose estimation for preterm infants, enabling noise-free training. It achieves up to 93% AUC on NeoPose across three PE architectures.
AI.motivation: Label noise in pose estimation, especially in clinical neonatology, is prevalent due to occlusions and caregiver interference. Existing noise-robust methods are largely classification-focused; there is a gap for PE where data quality is critical for infant monitoring.
AI.method: Introduce REMIND: a clustering-based keypoint-selection strategy that leverages keypoint-wise training dynamics (memory) to identify noisy labels without assuming a prior noise distribution. Applies to preterm infant PE; evaluated on proprietary NeoPose dataset (46 videos, 46 infants) across three PE architectures.
AI.result: REMIND effectively identifies noisy annotations across multiple corruption scenarios, achieving up to 93% AUC. Demonstrates broad applicability across several PE architectures and is the first study to address label noise in preterm infant PE.
AI.conclusion: Presents a path toward trustworthy, noise-robust infant monitoring via PE by explicitly handling label noise. The approach holds promise for clinical deployment, though validation on non-proprietary datasets and assessment of generalizability and runtime/resource requirements are warranted.

title: Prospective Coding Improves Learning in Deep Continuous-Time Recurrent Networks
summary: Temporal integration gives continuous-time recurrent networks memory, but in deep stacks it also delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors. We develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated complex-valued temporal filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models (SSMs), and ask whether this failure mode can be addressed by making each layer's bottom-up input prospective. Starting from an energy model, we derive the RQF dynamics and show that each RQF is a band-pass filter whose learnable parameters control its tuning frequency and bandwidth. We then make each layer's bottom-up input prospective using a parameter-free two-tap update that leaves the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged. We extend this correction to general diagonal SSMs and show that it mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated, i.e., spatial-only backpropagation. We evaluate the intervention in RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs (a nonlinear gated RNN) trained using full backpropagation through time (BPTT) and spatial-only backpropagation. Under full BPTT, prospective variants match or outperform their non-prospective controls in every model and configuration. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF reaches 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with 31.9k parameters; a width-64 six-layer RQF reaches 83.56% on the 16,384-step Path-X task. These results identify RQFs as a parameter-efficient recurrent substrate and prospective-input coding as an input-side correction for deep continuous-time recurrent networks.

AI.tldr: Proposes Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), a biologically inspired complex-valued temporal filter family derived from diagonal state-space models, to address depth-induced delays and gradient attenuation in deep continuous-time RNNs by introducing prospective bottom-up inputs. Demonstrates that RQFs act as tunable band-pass filters and that a simple two-tap, zero-parameter prospective input correction can mitigate depth-related gradient attenuation in diagonal SSMs under spatial-only backpropagation. Empirically, prospective variants match or outperform baseline models with full BPTT across RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs, achieving strong performance with parameter-efficient architectures (e.g., 96.09% on Speech Commands with 31.9k params). Concludes that RQFs offer a compact recurrent substrate and prospective-input coding as an input-side correction for deep CT recurrent networks.
AI.motivation: Address the clash between memory in continuous-time recurrent networks and depth-induced delays/gradient attenuation when stacking layers. Seek a parameter-efficient, biologically plausible mechanism to preserve bottom-up signal fidelity while maintaining effective learning in deep temporal architectures.
AI.method: Derive RQF dynamics from an energy model as a special case of diagonal state-space models. Show each RQF is a band-pass filter with tunable frequency and bandwidth. Introduce a parameter-free two-tap update to make (bottom-up) input prospective without altering recurrent transitions or scan. Generalize the correction to diagonal SSMs, analyzing its effect on gradient attenuation under spatial backpropagation. Evaluate on RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs under full BPTT and spatial-only backprop.
AI.result: Prospective variants match or exceed non-prospective controls across all models and configurations under full BPTT. Quantitative demonstrations include a width-32 six-layer RQF achieving 96.09% on Speech Commands (31.9k params) and a width-64 six-layer RQF achieving 83.56% on the Path-X task (16,384 steps). These findings position RQFs as a compact recurrent substrate and validate prospective-input coding as an effective input-side correction.
AI.conclusion: RQFs provide a parameter-efficient, biologically plausible recurrent substrate. Prospective-input coding effectively mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation in deep continuous-time recurrent networks, especially under spatial-only backpropagation, and perform competitively with full backpropagation when assessed on standard temporal tasks.

title: Stable and Scalable Bundle Adjustment of Holistic 3D Structures
comment: To appear at ECCV 2026. Code available as part of the LIMAP toolbox at https://github.com/cvg/limap/
summary: Bundle Adjustment (BA) is a cornerstone of 3D computer vision and has benefited from decades of advances in sparse optimization and numerical methods. It was originally developed for jointly optimizing camera intrinsics, poses and sparse 3D points. While extensions incorporate lines and other primitives, integrating richer geometric structures such as parallelism, coplanarity, or wireframes often introduces significantly increased computational cost and reduced numerical stability. In this paper, we propose a unified framework that extends bundle adjustment to jointly optimize geometric features and higher-order relations. We first introduce a taxonomy that distinguishes scalable geometric features with direct 2D measurements (e.g., points and lines), from groups encoding higher-order relations (e.g., coplanarity, parallelism, etc.), where we show that groups can be modeled as camera-like entities within the bundle adjustment framework. Building on this formulation, we propose that both group constraints and cross-feature relations (i.e., point-line associations) can be expressed through 2D reprojection measurements. By formulating group-induced and cross-feature reprojection errors, we preserve the sparsity structure of classical point-based BA under Schur elimination, while avoiding direct 3D regularization that degrades the conditioning and stability. Experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate runtime performance comparable to classical point-only bundle adjustment, while producing significantly richer 3D structures and improved geometric accuracy.

AI.tldr: Extends bundle adjustment to jointly optimize higher-order geometric relations by modeling groups as camera-like entities and expressing all constraints as 2D reprojection errors, preserving sparsity and achieving richer geometry with similar runtimes to point-only BA.
AI.motivation: Enable rich geometric modeling (coplanarity, parallelism, wireframes) within BA without compromising conditioning or efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce a taxonomy distinguishing scalable features with direct 2D measurements (points, lines) from higher-order groups; model groups as camera-like entities; formulate group-induced and cross-feature reprojection errors; maintain sparsity via 2D reprojections; avoid 3D regularization; leverage Schur elimination.
AI.result: Real and synthetic experiments show runtime on par with classical BA, while yielding richer 3D structures and improved geometric accuracy.
AI.conclusion: A unified BA framework for features and higher-order relations that preserves sparsity/stability and scales to practical problems, enabling more faithful scene representations.

title: DSAQuant: Denoising-Stage-Aligned Quantization-Aware Training for Video Generation
summary: Video diffusion models (VDMs) have achieved impressive progress in text-to-video generation, but their high memory and computational costs hinder practical deployment. Quantization-aware training (QAT) is an effective solution for compressing and accelerating advanced generative models without runtime overhead at inference. However, existing QAT methods suffer from a distinctive challenge in VDMs: while they often preserve prompt semantics, global layout, and coarse motion, the quantized model severely degrades visual details, texture fidelity, and sharpness. In this paper, we trace this degradation to the timestep-agnostic design of conventional quantization pipelines, which overlooks the stage-wise functionality of video denoising. In VDMs, early denoising steps mainly establish global structure and motion, whereas middle and late steps refine local appearance and high-frequency details. Based on this insight, we propose DSAQuant, a Denoising-Stage-Aligned Quantization-aware training framework for VDMs. During training, Denoising-Stage Oriented Supervision preserves teacher distillation in early steps for stable structure planning, while shifting later steps toward target-driven optimization to enhance detail reconstruction. During inference, Denoising-Stage Gated Guidance disables CFG in the final denoising steps to prevent it from amplifying quantization-induced errors into high-frequency artifacts. Extensive experiments on the Wan and CogVideoX families under W4A4 and W3A3 settings show that DSAQuant consistently outperforms the SOTA QAT baseline, improving the VBench average score by up to 6.60 under aggressive W3A3 quantization while preserving strong text-video alignment. These results demonstrate that effective VDM quantization requires not only reducing quantization error, but also aligning quantization training and inference with the stage-wise nature of video diffusion.

AI.tldr: DSAQuant introduces denoising-stage aligned QAT for video diffusion models, aligning training and inference with stage-wise denoising to preserve details in quantized VDMs, while maintaining prompt structure and alignment.
AI.motivation: VDMs are memory-intensive; quantization-based compression is appealing but existing QAT methods degrade texture, detail, and sharpness due to timestep-agnostic quantization that ignores stage-wise denoising dynamics.
AI.method: Denoising-Stage Oriented Supervision: apply teacher distillation in early steps to stabilize global structure planning, then shift later steps toward target-driven optimization for detail reconstruction. Denoising-Stage Gated Guidance: during inference, disable classifier-free guidance (CFG) in final denoising steps to prevent amplification of quantization errors into high-frequency artifacts.
AI.result: Experiments on Wan and CogVideoX under W4A4 and W3A3 show DSAQuant consistently surpasses the state-of-the-art QAT baseline, improving VBench average score by up to 6.60 while preserving strong text-video alignment.
AI.conclusion: Effective VDM quantization requires aligning quantization training and inference with the stage-wise nature of video denoising; stage-aware supervision and gating are essential to maintain visual detail without sacrificing structure or alignment.

title: Robust PAC Learning of Concurrent Stochastic Games
comment: Main text: 10 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables; Appendix: 22 pages, 2 figures, 1 table
summary: We introduce the first Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning framework for general-sum concurrent stochastic games (CSGs) with transition uncertainty, while addressing the challenge of Nash equilibrium (NE) existence. Our algorithm maintains data-driven $L^1$ confidence sets over transition kernels and solves a robust CSG to compute a social-welfare optimal $\varepsilon$-NE, using a robust MDP-based exploration mechanism to drive joint state-action coverage. Crucially, we introduce a Nash margin characterisation that enables principled reasoning about equilibrium existence: the framework either returns an $\varepsilon$-approximate NE whose social-welfare value is $\varepsilon$-close to optimal, or provides a sound certificate that no exact NE exists. Under a minimum reachability condition $p_{\mathrm{reach}}>0$ over relevant state-action pairs, the algorithm terminates after a polynomial number of trajectory samples, with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( {R_{\max}^2 H^4 |S|^2 |A| / (p_{\mathrm{reach}} \varepsilon^2)} \right)$. Empirical results on benchmark CSGs demonstrate near-optimal performance, correct handling of equilibrium (non-)existence, and sample complexity consistent with theory.

AI.tldr: A PAC learning framework for general-sum concurrent stochastic games with transition uncertainty that either finds a near-optimal epsilon-NE or certifies that no exact NE exists; with polynomial sample complexity and empirical validation.
AI.motivation: To address transition uncertainty and the challenge of NE existence in general-sum CSGs, enabling data-driven robust decision-making with theoretical guarantees.
AI.method: Maintain data-driven L1 confidence sets over transition kernels; solve a robust CSG to obtain a social-welfare optimal epsilon-NE; use robust MDP-based exploration to ensure coverage; introduce a Nash margin characterization to decide NE existence; provide termination guarantee under reachability p_reach > 0; derive sample complexity bound; provide empirical evaluation.
AI.result: The algorithm returns either an epsilon-approximate NE with social welfare within epsilon of optimal, or a sound certificate that no exact NE exists; sample complexity bound: ~R_max^2 H^4 |S|^2 |A| /(p_reach epsilon^2); empirical benchmarks show near-optimal performance and correct handling of equilibrium existence.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes PAC guarantees for NE existence in general-sum CSGs under transition uncertainty, with a practical robust optimization-and-learning approach and polynomial sample complexity; validated empirically.

title: Editable Visual Design
summary:
While diffusion base models such as GPT-Image-2 and Nano-Banana exhibit remarkable visual expressiveness, their end-to-end generation inherently yields flattened bitmaps with error-prone text, precluding layer-wise post-editing. Conversely, code-based visual generation via Coding Agents provides precise layout control and decoupled layers, yet remains constrained by a lack of global aesthetic intuition and the difficulty of coding complex visual assets.
  To address this, we propose Editable Visual Design, a new paradigm driven by a Coding Agent. We designate the VLM as the ``creative brain'' for requirement comprehension, task planning, and aesthetic judgment, while utilizing the image generation model as an on-demand ``visual world simulator'' to synthesize standalone visual assets. Operating under an ``imagine first, then act'' closed-loop workflow, the agent generates isolated assets, writes native HTML/CSS, and iteratively refines the design against visual rendering feedback.
  Furthermore, Agent Design Replay faithfully reproduces the creative and reasoning trajectory akin to that of professional human designers. Ultimately, the system delivers editable artifacts with decoupled layers and real text, enabling users to perform intuitive mouse dragging and layout adjustments on a graphical user interface. Validations on posters, infographics, and other scenarios show that this paradigm successfully achieves both refined aesthetics and production-grade editability.

AI.tldr: Editable Visual Design with a Coding Agent enables decoupled, editable, text-rich design assets via an imagined-then-acted loop and Agent Design Replay, combining a VLM for planning and aesthetic judgment with an image-generator as a visual world simulator.
AI.motivation: Overcome end-to-end diffusion limitations (flattened bitmaps, text leakage) and coding-driven but aesthetically naive design; requires modular layers and genuine editability.
AI.method: Use Coding Agent; VLM acts as creative brain; image model as world simulator; imagine-first-then-act loop; writes HTML/CSS; produces isolated assets; Agent Design Replay traces reasoning; GUI supports drag-and-edit; deliver editable assets.
AI.result: Validated on posters, infographics, etc., achieving refined aesthetics and production-grade editability.
AI.conclusion: The paradigm successfully combines planning, aesthetics, and editability, enabling scalable production workflows for visually rich assets.

title: TAP-Path: Task-Adaptive Structural and Token Pruning for Efficient and Trustworthy Pathology Foundation Models
summary: Pathology foundation models improve transferable representation learning for histopathology, but recent gains often rely on encoders with hundreds of millions of parameters and high inference cost. We propose TAP-Path, a task-adaptive compression framework that directly restructures a pretrained Virchow2 encoder rather than distilling it into a separate student. TAP-Path combines validation-driven transformer-block selection, physical removal of redundant blocks, input-adaptive patch-token pruning, multi-depth feature recovery, and a lightweight gated task head. The final model retains 24 of 32 transformer blocks and 70% of patch tokens after pruning, reducing encoder parameters by 24.96% (631.24M to 473.70M) and analytical encoder compute by 35.20% (340.13G to 220.40G FLOPs). Across three task-head optimization seeds, TAP-Path achieved $87.98 \pm 0.067%$ test accuracy, $81.26 \pm 0.49%$ balanced accuracy, and $82.38 \pm 0.48%$ macro-F1 on a 32-class histopathology benchmark, compared with 86.89% for full Virchow2 and 87.67% for UNI2-h. TAP-Path achieved a Brier score of $0.1800 \pm 0.0005$ and failure-detection AUROC of $0.9047 \pm 0.0060$. A validation-only rare-aware objective improved rare-class balanced accuracy in a secondary operating analysis. Frozen external evaluation on 433 CPTAC samples yielded $91.22 \pm 0.83%$ accuracy and $91.10 \pm 0.81%$ balanced accuracy. These results show that task-adaptive structural and token sparsification can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of large pathology foundation models while preserving reliability under internal and external evaluation.

AI.tldr: Task-adaptive compression TAP-Path prunes a Virchow2 encoder by removing transformer blocks and patch tokens, achieving a 24.96% parameter reduction and 35.20% FLOPs reduction while maintaining competitive accuracy and reliability on histopathology tasks.
AI.motivation: Reduce compute and parameter cost of large pathology foundation models without sacrificing performance or reliability, addressing the heavy inference burden of current encoders.
AI.method: Validation-driven transformer-block selection, physical removal of redundant blocks, input-adaptive patch-token pruning, multi-depth feature recovery, and a lightweight gated task head. The model preserves 24 of 32 blocks and 70% of patch tokens. Evaluation includes multiple task-head seeds, internal and external datasets (32-class histopathology benchmark and CPTAC samples), and a rare-aware objective.
AI.result: Parameter count drops from 631.24M to 473.70M (~24.96% reduction); FLOPs drop from 340.13G to 220.40G (~35.20% reduction). Performance on a 32-class benchmark: 87.98 ±0.067% test accuracy, 81.26 ±0.49% balanced accuracy, 82.38 ±0.48% macro-F1 (vs 86.89% full Virchow2 and 87.67% UNI2-h). Brier score 0.1800 ±0.0005; failure-detection AUROC 0.9047 ±0.0060. External CPTAC: 91.22 ±0.83% accuracy, 91.10 ±0.81% balanced accuracy. A validation-only rare-aware objective improved rare-class balanced accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Task-adaptive structural and token sparsification can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of large pathology foundation models while preserving reliability across internal and external evaluations; the approach demonstrates effective pruning at both architectural and input-token levels.

title: CORE: Improving Compositional Reasoning in MLLM Embedding via Reranker Distillation
summary: MLLM-based embedding models remain limited in compositional retrieval, often failing to distinguish scenes containing the same concepts but different attribute-object bindings. Yet the same backbone can resolve such distinctions when used as a cross-attentive reranker, motivating us to distill its compositional judgments into the embedding model. We propose CORE, which synthesizes candidate lists spanning five compositional matching levels and introduces a Rank-KL objective that trains the embedding model to reproduce the reranker's fine-grained ranking. We further introduce a graded evaluation protocol and compare contrastive learning, pairwise CoSENT, and listwise Rank-KL under the same data and tuning budget. Our comparison shows that both CoSENT and Rank-KL use the multi-level supervision more effectively than contrastive learning, with Rank-KL achieving the strongest overall performance. Across three compositional reasoning benchmarks (COLA, SUGARCREPE++, NEGBENCH), CORE-RERANKER-8B achieves an 82.7% total average, outperforming Jina-Reranker by 10.7 points, while CORE-EMBED-8B achieves the best total average (0.666) among all evaluated embedding models. The improvements transfer to the MCMR benchmark without sacrificing retrieval performance on COCO and Flickr30K.

AI.tldr: CORE distills a cross-attentive reranker into MLLM embeddings for compositional retrieval using a Rank-KL objective across five matching levels; achieves state-of-the-art on COLA, SUGARCREPE++, NEGBENCH and strong transfer to MCMR, with embedding models reaching top performance.
AI.motivation: MLLM-based embedding models struggle with compositional retrieval, specifically distinguishing scenes with identical concepts but different attribute-object bindings. A cross-attentive reranker resolves these distinctions, suggesting that its fine-grained judgments can be distilled into the embedding model.
AI.method: CORE synthesizes candidate lists spanning five compositional matching levels and trains embedding models with a Rank-KL objective to reproduce the reranker’s ranking. The work includes a graded evaluation protocol and a comparison among contrastive learning, pairwise CoSENT, and listwise Rank-KL under equal data and tuning budgets.
AI.result: Rank-KL and CoSENT outperform plain contrastive learning; Rank-KL delivers the strongest overall performance. On three compositional reasoning benchmarks (COLA, SUGARCREPE++, NEGBENCH), CORE-RERANKER-8B achieves 82.7% total average, outperforming Jina-Reranker by 10.7 points, while CORE-EMBED-8B attains the best total average (0.666) among embedding models. The improvements transfer to MCMR without sacrificing retrieval performance on COCO and Flickr30K.
AI.conclusion: Distilling a reranker’s fine-grained compositional judgments into an embedding model via the Rank-KL objective yields substantial gains in compositional reasoning, with strong cross-benchmark transfer and maintained retrieval performance on standard benchmarks.

title: Efficient Semantic Understanding from Digital Foveation
comment: Accepted at the 3rd Human-inspired Computer Vision Workshop at ECCV 2026
summary: Dense semantic segmentation allocates computational resources uniformly across the entire image, regardless of scene complexity or task relevance. Inspired by biological vision, we investigate whether semantic understanding can be achieved more efficiently through digital foveated perception. We introduce a lightweight active-vision pipeline that combines saliency-driven fixation selection, high-resolution foveal observations, low-resolution contextual information, semantic accumulation, and adaptive computation. Beyond conventional dense prediction metrics, we use object-level evaluation to measure semantic understanding under sparse observations. On ADE20K-Object, a single foveated observation achieves 95.9% of the baseline Top-1 accuracy and 96.9% of the baseline Top-3 accuracy while requiring only 4.7% of the computational cost. At the scene level, semantic accumulation recovers 90.6% of the baseline object recall while using 58.6% of the computation. These results suggest that substantial semantic understanding can emerge from sparse observations when computation is allocated selectively, highlighting active vision as an efficient alternative to uniform dense processing and motivating evaluation protocols beyond conventional pixel-wise segmentation metrics.

AI.tldr: A lightweight active-vision pipeline with foveated observations achieves near-baseline semantic understanding at a fraction of the compute, challenging dense uniform processing.
AI.motivation: Dense semantic segmentation wastes resources; inspired by biological vision; explore if selective attention and sparse observations can yield similar semantic understanding.
AI.method: Saliency-driven fixation selection, high-resolution foveal observations, low-resolution context, semantic accumulation, adaptive computation; object-level evaluation on ADE20K-Object.
AI.result: Single foveated observation yields 95.9% Top-1 and 96.9% Top-3 of baseline with 4.7% compute; scene-level accumulation recovers 90.6% object recall with 58.6% compute.
AI.conclusion: Active vision with selective computation can achieve substantial semantic understanding; evaluation should extend beyond pixel-wise metrics.

title: The Shape of Time: Video-Token Contrast for Temporal Understanding in VideoLMs
summary: Seeing frames in order does not mean representing time. Modern VideoLMs receive ordered video streams, yet their main supervision acts on generated text rather than video-token representations where event dynamics should first emerge. This mismatch allows models to learn temporal answers from shortcuts such as objects, scenes, and language priors, without requiring internal video representations to capture event progression. To address this, we propose VT-Contrast, a representation-level temporal counterfactual objective for VideoLMs. Its design asks where temporal supervision should act and what temporal differences it should expose. VT-Contrast supervises selected late-layer last-frame video tokens, where temporal information is expected to be integrated before language generation, and contrasts order-preserving views with same-video reordered counterfactuals graded by Kendall tau distance. It requires no architectural changes, is compatible with diverse VideoLM training tasks, and improves overall performance across temporal understanding benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ANDgate99/VT-Contrast.

AI.tldr: Proposes VT-Contrast, a representation-level, temporal counterfactual objective for VideoLMs that aligns temporal supervision with internal video representations by supervising late-frame tokens and contrasting order-preserving views with reordered counterfactuals (via Kendall tau).
AI.motivation: There is a mismatch where VideoLMs trained with text supervision rely on shortcuts (objects, scenes, language priors) rather than learning genuine event dynamics in video-token representations; a representation-level temporal objective is needed to force models to capture temporal progression.
AI.method: Apply a contrastive, counterfactual objective at late-layer video tokens. Generate order-preserving views and same-video reordered counterfactuals; compute Kendall tau distance to grade counterfactuals; optimize without architectural changes, compatible with existing VideoLM training tasks.
AI.result: Improvements observed across temporal understanding benchmarks for VideoLMs, indicating better internal representation of event dynamics.
AI.conclusion: VT-Contrast can provide effective, architecture-agnostic temporal supervision at the representation level, improving temporal understanding without modifying model architectures; code is available.

title: BooM-VVT: Boosting Mask-Free Video Virtual Try-On with Image-Level Pseudo Data
comment: 23 pages, 18 figures, 8 tables. Accepted to ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26)
summary:
Video virtual try-on (VVT) aims to generate realistic videos of a person wearing a target garment. Recent methods leverage a keyframe-driven video generation paradigm to improve in-the-wild performance, yet they still rely on masks to localize try-on regions, making them vulnerable to large motions and severe occlusions. Although mask-free image-based try-on methods have shown promising results by leveraging large-scale pseudo data, extending this paradigm to videos remains difficult, as constructing video-level pseudo data is prohibitively expensive. Furthermore, coarse keyframe sampling and the scarcity of multi-view try-on data limit existing keyframe-driven methods in maintaining garment consistency and handling diverse try-on tasks.
  To address these challenges, we propose BooM-VVT, a mask-free VVT framework built upon the keyframe-driven paradigm. To achieve mask-free VVT, we introduce a multi-stage training strategy that leverages image-level pseudo data for mask-free localization learning, substantially reducing the need for costly video-level pseudo data. To improve garment consistency, we propose Garment-Sensitive Keyframe Sampling, which selects keyframes based on garment-relevant body regions to better capture garment appearance. We further introduce Frame-Shared 3D-RoPE to establish spatiotemporal correspondences between keyframes and target video frames for accurate garment-detail transfer. Finally, we construct OmniView, a large-scale multi-view try-on dataset to support reliable try-on video generation under complex camera viewpoints and diverse try-on tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BooM-VVT achieves superior temporal consistency and garment fidelity over existing methods. Project page: https://boomvvt.github.io/boomvvt.

AI.tldr: BooM-VVT is a mask-free, keyframe-driven video virtual try-on framework that uses image-level pseudo data, garment-aware keyframe sampling, Frame-Shared 3D-RoPE, and a new OmniView dataset to improve temporal consistency and garment fidelity in VVT.
AI.motivation: To overcome mask-based localization vulnerabilities in video VVT, reduce reliance on costly video-level pseudo data, and improve garment consistency under large motions and occlusions with limited multi-view data.
AI.method: 1) Multi-stage training with image-level pseudo data for mask-free localization learning. 2) Garment-Sensitive Keyframe Sampling to select keyframes from garment-relevant regions. 3) Frame-Shared 3D-RoPE to establish spatiotemporal correspondences between keyframes and target frames for accurate garment-detail transfer. 4) OmniView, a large-scale multi-view try-on dataset for diverse viewpoints and tasks.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show BooM-VVT achieves superior temporal consistency and garment fidelity compared to existing mask-free and mask-based methods.
AI.conclusion: BooM-VVT demonstrates effective mask-free video virtual try-on with enhanced garment consistency and temporal stability, supported by a new large multi-view dataset (OmniView). The project page provides implementation and results.

title: Beyond Retrieval: Progressive Latent Memory Evolution for Streaming Video Understanding
summary: Streaming video understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to process continuous visual inputs and respond to user queries under strict causality and bounded memory. Existing approaches typically compress historical observations into an external memory bank and retrieve query-relevant evidence as additional visual context. Though effective, this store-and-retrieve paradigm keeps historical evidence as external visual context, preventing it from being internalized into a compact, evolving latent memory that can continuously guide streaming reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce LatentStream, a progressive latent working memory framework that shifts streaming memory from store-and-retrieve to retrieve-and-internalize. Specifically, LatentStream comprises three coordinated components. First, Query-agnostic Hierarchical Streaming Memory organizes visual history into short-, mid-, and long-term levels under a fixed memory budget through Jenks-guided adaptive consolidation.
